sections.h2: For anyone in fresh loss
paras: If you cannot imagine feeling right again, this book is written for the moment you are in. The author says she stood where you are, "not just thinking about it, but saying out loud, 'It's never going to get better.'" She also tells you, "It's OK to not be OK," and asks you to believe that "IT IS NOT TRUE THAT THE WAY YOU THINK AND FEEL NOW IS THE WAY YOU WILL ALWAYS THINK AND FEEL."

sections.h2: For widows and widowers
paras: Lesson 4 is about losing a spouse, and the author writes it from her own life. She lists the questions that come in the first months: who will cut the grass, how to start the washer, how to pay the bills without his income. She names the firsts you will face, from your anniversary to going to church for the first time without them. And she is honest: "I had to learn that I COULD exist without my husband. I did not want to, but, I HAD to."

sections.h2: For friends and family who want to understand
paras: If someone you love is grieving and you do not know what to say, the book can help you see what they may be going through. It explains that "Grief is the price you pay for loving someone" and why a friend may seem to move more slowly than you expect. One lesson is about "poor comforters," people who mean well and say hurtful things, and asks grieving people to forgive them.

sections.h2: For grief support groups and ministries
paras: The author writes that her lessons come from leading groups and classes. The last page speaks to leaders: "this is just a manual to assist YOU while you are helping others walk their Journey Through Grief." Each lesson stands on its own, with takeaways that a group can read aloud and discuss.

audience.headline: Your world is broken right now. It does not have to stay that way.
audience.body: For anyone who has lost someone they love and wonders whether life can ever feel right again, and for the friends, families and support groups who walk beside them. Annie Brown writes from more than fifteen years of grief counseling and ministry and almost thirty-four years of knowing grief personally, in six short lessons, each ending with key takeaways. A note on subjects: this book speaks openly about death, including an accident, suicide, murder and the loss of a child, and about guilt, anger and despair. It is told with care and without graphic detail. It is a counselor's guide and a personal account, not therapy, medical advice or a substitute for professional help. If you are thinking about harming yourself, please contact local emergency services or a crisis line right away.

quote.text: But be assured, THERE IS LIFE AFTER DEATH, I AM LIVING PROOF.
quote.cite: A Journey Through Grief, Introduction

what_makes.title: What makes this book for people walking through loss
paras: A short, compassionate guide arranged as six lessons, from an author whose own husband was killed when she was in her mid-thirties. It was not the ministry she would have chosen, she says, but "out of my loss, out of the deepest darkest season of my life, my ministry was born."
Five things set it apart:
list: It tells the truth about grief. There is "no right way or wrong way to grieve," no schedule and no timeframe, and the book says it plainly, and it explains secondary losses, such as the nightly phone call, the family connection and the dreams you had.
It makes room for every kind of loss. It speaks to an anticipated death after a long illness, a sudden accident, suicide and murder, and it names the guilt, anger and "what if" questions that follow.
It keeps each lesson short. Every lesson ends with key takeaways you can reread when your mind cannot hold much.
It is rooted in Scripture without being heavy-handed. It draws on Psalm 23 and Deuteronomy 31:8 and says that "Faith does not isolate us from tragedy."
It is honest about helpers. It includes lessons gathered from people who lost someone and practical things to do and not do, and advice for friends who do not know what to say.

paras: In the introduction, the author recalls the weeks after her husband was killed, when she and her sixteen-year-old son moved in with her mother and she could not manage the house. One day she stepped on a glass plate hidden in the overgrown grass, and it broke. "Even after all these years, I remember looking down at the broken plate and saying aloud, 'You might as well break....everything else in my life is broken.'" Out of that sorrow, she says, she learned how to connect with hurting people.

Lesson 2 says "There is no right way or wrong way to grieve," and gives her own example. "I found comfort in sleeping with my husband's blue jeans." She brought five pairs to her mother's house, and her mother could tell what kind of day she had had by how many pairs she tucked around her at night. A physician who knew her situation told her she wasn't losing her mind and that the need would fade, and "you know, he was right." Her point: "it's OK to take comfort in different measures."

Lesson 5 explains that children do not grieve like adults. "Children move in and out of grief." The book gives an everyday picture: "One minute they are playing basketball with their buddies, the next, they are in their room sitting in the dark." It adds that children revisit grief at milestones such as graduation and weddings, and that parents should not grieve behind closed doors: "It's appropriate for your children to see you sad."

author.bio: Annie Brown has been involved in grief counseling and ministry for more than fifteen years and has known grief intimately for almost thirty-four. Before that season she taught Sunday School, sang in the choir and taught Bible studies. Out of her darkest season her ministry was born, and she now leads grief groups and classes for hurting people.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The author's reason is simple. "Out of my sorrow, I learned how to connect with hurting people, how to minister to them, help them, and show them that although they cannot believe it now, in the middle of their darkest season, there IS life after death."

She wrote it as a manual for people in grief and for those who walk beside them, and her closing words say so: "God bless you in this ministry." Throughout, her message is that "Grief recovery is intentional and it takes work," and that "Faith does not isolate us from tragedy. What faith does, is sustain us through our loss."

faq.q: What is A Journey Through Grief about?
faq.a: It is a short guide for anyone who has lost a loved one, from a grief counselor who was widowed in her mid-thirties. Six lessons cover what grief looks and feels like and how to live through it, and each ends with key takeaways.

faq.q: What are the six lessons?
faq.a: They are, in order: Living with grief; How do I live with this life-changing event?; Emotions connected with death; How life will change when your spouse dies; Learning to live as a grieving family; and Am I ever going to get better, or am I stuck in grief? And more things to remember on this journey.

faq.q: What is the grieving process?
faq.a: The author says grief is a process, not an event. "Grief recovery is a process." She says it is something we get through, that there are good days and bad days, and that "Grief recovery is intentional and it takes work."

faq.q: Does it cover sudden loss?
faq.a: Yes. It addresses anticipated deaths after a long illness and sudden tragedies, including accidents, suicide and murder, and the guilt and "what if" questions that follow.

faq.q: Is it a grief support book for individuals or groups?
faq.a: Both. It is written for individuals in fresh loss and for friends and family, and its closing words are addressed to anyone "helping others walk their Journey Through Grief." The lessons suit a support group or class.

faq.q: Does it help with losing a spouse?
faq.a: Lesson 4 is entirely about it: loneliness, "firsts" without a spouse, fear of the future, and a caution about hasty decisions. The author lost her own husband in her mid-thirties.

faq.q: Does it speak to healing after loss?
faq.a: It says "Even though you cannot believe that you will EVER feel right again, you will," and that grief is a process you walk through, not one you live in. It does not promise a timetable: "There is no schedule to stick to, and there is no timeframe."

faq.q: Is it a Christian book, and is it therapy?
faq.a: It is rooted in Scripture, including Psalm 23 and Deuteronomy 31:8, and holds that faith sustains us through tragedy. It is one counselor's guide and personal account, not therapy or medical advice.

faq.q: What about loss to suicide?
faq.a: Lesson 3 speaks about suicide and the "haunting questions" that follow, in a short section. It is one part of a book on many kinds of loss, not a book devoted to suicide loss, and it is not a crisis resource.

sections.h2: For anyone who is suffering physically or spiritually
paras: The author says he likes "to share my story with others who are suffering physically and spiritually." His message is simple: "We are His. So, we don't need to worry about anything in life. The only thing that matters is to trust and obey Him." If you are tired of being told to try harder, a short book in the voice of someone who has little may be easier to hear than a long argument.

sections.h2: For readers who want a testimony from Manipur, India
paras: Few books in English come from this corner of northeast India. The first chapter describes a homeland he compares to "the Garden of Eden that the serpent spoiled," and then he turns to the reader: "So, dear friend, if you are in a similar situation, never give up your faith in God. Manipur may be gone forever, but you don't have to be. Keep trusting in His promises."

sections.h2: For readers who love stories of hope, miracles and trusting God
paras: If you enjoy first-person testimonies, this one is plain, specific and told with dates. The miracle chapter says, "God has shown me several miracles. They testified of His existence to me." It is a book of faith rather than of argument, offered to be read in a sitting or two.

sections.h2: For readers asking how faith and politics fit together
paras: Chapter 12, Social, Political, and Religious Systems, is the author's own view, written plainly. He notes that "Politics are at the center of the story of Jesus," and then argues that a Christian is an ambassador of Christ and should stay out of the politics of this world. He writes that "No political ideology can solve people's problems," because those problems are spiritual. It is one believer's conviction, not a party platform.

audience.headline: A plain, honest testimony from a poor village in Manipur, India, for anyone who needs to hear that God is good.
audience.body: For readers who are suffering physically or spiritually, who want a true story of hope, miracles and trusting God when a situation looks hopeless, and who would like to hear it in the voice of a man who has little and has known God's love. Leivon Canary Kom grew up the fifth of seven children in a tiny, underprivileged village, the son of daily wage laborers, and he wrote this book to "encourage poor people like me wherever my voice can't go to testify of God." A note on subjects: the author speaks of violence and killing in his homeland and has a chapter on suicide, told without graphic detail. He also records his own opinions on social, political and religious systems and his testimony of miracles. It is one man's personal testimony, written plainly, and is not news reporting or medical advice.

quote.text: This book is all about myself being hopeful when my situation is hopeless.
quote.cite: A Shepherd's Story, Dedication

what_makes.title: What makes this book for readers who want an honest testimony
paras: A short life story in twenty-three chapters, from his homeland and his childhood to his Bible ministry, his regrets, his views on selfishness and peace, and closing testimonies from his family. It is told plainly, without trying to sound like an essay. He calls it a book about "being hopeful when my situation is hopeless."
Five things set it apart:
list: It is brief on purpose. The author writes that he made "every possible effort to be brief" and lined up his thoughts "separately, but all connected end to end."
It begins with the Bible he fell in love with. His first book was the King James Version, introduced to him by his grandfather, and he studied it from age thirteen.
It tells the miracles he has seen. One chapter records three, with the month and year of each.
It is honest about regrets. A whole chapter is given to mistakes he wishes he had not made, and the comfort he found in Scripture.
It carries other voices. The closing chapters are testimonies as narrated by his wife, his father and a relative of his wife.

paras: Chapter 5 begins, "The first book that I ever fell in love with was the Holy Bible in King James Version." His grandfather had told him the Bible "is where God speaks to man and gives him all the information that he needs for the welfare of his physical and spiritual life," so the boy grew interested. At thirteen he began studying it, praying every day, and used the Manipuri Bible and English grammar books to understand each verse. He became a bookworm, and writes that, "if I didn't get to read a book during the day, I couldn't sleep at night."

In Chapter 6 he tells of three miracles. In one, on a Sunday morning in June 1997, he climbed a mountain near his village to fast and pray, and studied Psalms and Proverbs for hours. Then the sky darkened and thunder began, and he prayed that it would not rain on him and his Bible. He writes that it rained at a distance and that "my Bible and I didn't even get one drop of rain." Looking around afterward, he says, "a circle with a diameter of 10 meters where I prayed wasn't wet!" He offers it as his testimony.

stories.h2: Six things his mother told him
paras: Chapter 4 remembers a mother who carried traditional sarongs and a basket of homemade fermented fish on foot to towns miles away to sell. He writes that a hundred-mile distance kept him from seeing her one last time. He also writes, "I will never forget the six things that she used to tell us." The first is "Never forget what people did for you," and the last is "If you want God and man to be happy with you, be generous."

author.bio: Leivon Canary Kom grew up in Manipur, India, the fifth of seven children in a nominally Christian family, in a small, underprivileged village, the son of daily wage laborers. The first book he fell in love with was the King James Bible, introduced to him by his grandfather. Since 2000 he has worked in different parts of India, not as a pastor but as a daily bread earner, sharing God's love and plan of salvation through his teaching and Bible ministry. A Shepherd's Story is his first book.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: "I never even imagined in my wildest fantasies that I would write a book," the author writes. "Life just went on, and at long last, I wrote a book on 'GOD'S LOVE.'" He credits the encouragement of a few people and the publisher: "They helped me to publish the book successfully in almost no time."

His purpose is stated plainly in the dedication. He wrote to "share my story and encourage poor people like me wherever my voice can't go to testify of God," and he hopes the book will "testify of GOD'S LOVE, giving you health, happiness, truth, and peace." He adds that it is "not the work of one person but a combination of several persons from India and America."

faq.q: What is A Shepherd's Story about?
faq.a: It is Leivon Canary Kom's plain, honest testimony of God's love, from a poor village in Manipur, India, through miracles, ministry and loss. He wrote it to "encourage poor people like me wherever my voice can't go to testify of God."

faq.q: Is it set in Manipur, northeast India?
faq.a: Yes. The author grew up in a small village in Manipur, in northeast India, and the first chapter describes his homeland and its Shirui Lily. Later chapters follow his education and his work in different parts of India since 2000.

faq.q: What does it say about the miracles of God?
faq.a: Chapter 6 records three miracles the author says God has shown him, with the month and year of each. In one, he prayed on a mountain in June 1997 and writes that it rained at a distance but not on him and his Bible. He tells them as personal testimony.

faq.q: What does it say about the kingdom of God?
faq.a: Chapter 12 says the heart of Jesus' message was the coming of "the kingdom of God" and that "The kingdom of God is for the earth." It is a short testimony, not a full study of the subject.

faq.q: What does it say about Jesus and politics?
faq.a: The author writes that a Christian is an ambassador of Christ and should not get involved in the politics of this world, as long as local laws do not conflict with the laws of God. These are one man's views, not a statement for any church or group.

faq.q: Does it speak about spiritual warfare?
faq.a: Some of it. There is a chapter on Satan, and others on selfishness, scams and the peace and security that come from trusting God. It is a testimony, not a spiritual warfare manual.

faq.q: Is the author a pastor?
faq.a: No. He writes that since 2000 he has worked in different parts of India "not as a pastor but as a daily bread earner," sharing God's love and plan of salvation through teaching and Bible ministry.

faq.q: Does it include other voices?
faq.a: Yes. The last three chapters are testimonies as narrated by the author's wife, his father and his wife's grandfather.

sections.h2: For believers who want to give but feel maxed out
paras: The author knows the feeling. "Unfortunately, most of us have no margin in our life for generosity. We are maxed out financially. We are already overbooked." If you have ever felt pressured to give, the book offers a better way and promises to help you "exchange any sense of pressure and regret for genuine confidence and satisfaction."

sections.h2: For readers who want a story of faith, courage and miracles
paras: If you enjoy first-person accounts, the author tells his in plain terms: a church job lost, a trip to India that changed his life, a family down to four dollars in a pocket, and what he saw God do next. He writes that "Hoard it and lose it. Give it, and it returns." He is careful to say that none of this is about "bossing God around" or "faith being some force that guarantees prosperity."

sections.h2: For churches and small groups
paras: If your group is studying giving as an attribute of God, the book gives you chapters with Scripture, application sections and a clear structure. The author suggests keeping a journal "to record significant things God says as you read," and hopes the book will become "a worshipful encounter with God." Each section ends with a practical application you can talk through together.

sections.h2: For givers who already tithe
paras: If you have given a tenth for years and wonder what comes next, Chapter 12, Get or Give?, is written for you. The author lists what changed after he flipped "the switch from getting to giving": from feeding his family to feeding thousands of families a month, from losing a house to foreclosure to building houses for other families, and from a 10 percent tithe to giving away more in one year than his whole salary the year before. He adds, "I am not trying to brag here, either. I am boasting about Almighty God."

audience.headline: You do not have to be rich to be generous. You have to be willing to open your hands.
audience.body: For believers who want to give but feel maxed out, overbooked or afraid, and for churches and small groups studying generosity as an attribute of God. Kevin White tells how a prayer for food that others might eat, while his family lived on less than $500 a month, grew into a ministry that fed five hundred families a month, and shows three steps to set God, yourself and others free. A note on subjects: the author describes a season of exhaustion in which he "wanted to die," a family without food, and a time of fear. They are told briefly and without graphic detail, as the background to how he learned to give. The book is not about pressure, guilt or getting rich, and it is not financial advice.

quote.text: Audacious generosity is a willingness to take surprisingly bold risks by being kind and plentiful.
quote.cite: Audacious Generosity, Introduction

what_makes.title: What makes this book for people who want to give with courage
paras: A faith-and-giving guide in fifteen chapters, built on three steps and a story that begins with an empty cupboard. The author is a pastor and ministry founder who writes from more than twenty years of living openhandedly.
Five things set it apart:
list: It starts with a true story. In the year 2000, with no food in the cabinets, the author prayed, "Father, give us food that others might eat," and within days a grocery store deli manager pointed him to three carts of expired but edible food.

It defines the word, then fences it. Audacious generosity is "a willingness to take surprisingly bold risks by being kind and plentiful," and the author says three things it is not about: beating you up for not giving, pressuring you to give what you can produce, or giving with entitlement for personal gain.
It gives you three steps. Set God free, set yourself free and set others free, each with three points of encouragement and an application chapter.
It makes room for fear. Two full chapters are given to courage, and a chapter is given to fear versus freedom, because, he writes, "Courage results in freedom."
It points past your own wallet. The book keeps returning to the Great Commission and to the people of India, where the author has led mission trips more than fifty times.

stories.h2: Father, give us food that others might eat
paras: Chapter 1 tells of the year the author's support dropped to less than $500 a month and the cupboards were bare. He prayed and looked for work, and God gave him new words to pray: "Father, give us food that others might eat." One morning he stopped a store employee, learned she was the deli manager and asked what she did with expired products. The next day she "pointed to three grocery carts full of rotisserie chicken, pizza, pasta, and everything the deli and bakery sold." It happened the next day, and the next. "One year later, we were feeding five hundred needy families per month with the help of twenty-five volunteer families."

Chapter 3 begins with a question, "Have you ever realized a gift you didn't know you'd been given?" The author's answer is courage. He writes that "Courage is a choice and an act of obedience," that "Courage results from yielding to the Holy Spirit," and he points to 2 Timothy 1:7, where God has given "a spirit of fear and timidity, but of power, love, and self-discipline." He adds that his own need for courage has grown over four decades as a Christ-follower, not shrunk, because it "keeps me dependent on God."

Chapter 7 opens bluntly: "Fear is a B-word, a bully." The author describes living in fear for years: "I lived in fear for twenty years after I accepted Jesus for salvation. It wasn't until I was thirty years old that I began to understand what the Bible says about our identity in Christ." The chapter ends with the shift: "Once we are alive in Christ, we are secure, significant, and accepted in Christ," and the boxing match between fear and freedom comes to an end.

author.bio: Kevin White gave his life to Christ at ten years old. Twenty years later, after being fired from a church as an insecure workaholic for God, a trip to India changed his life and he committed to pursue the presence of God. In 2000, while his family lived on less than $500 a month, a simple prayer for food for others began With Love from Jesus Ministries in Raleigh, North Carolina. He went on his first mission trip to India more than twenty years ago, and he is the Founder and Executive Director of Global Hope India, a mission organization providing access to the gospel to Indian Nationals. He has traveled to India over fifty times, hosting a thousand people on mission trips.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The author dedicates the book "To the estimated three billion precious men, women, boys, and girls worldwide who still have limited access to know about Jesus," and to believers "living intentionally every day to fulfill the Great Commission." He writes that "Audacious generosity is a movement where Believers around the world unite to fulfill the Great Commission."

He wrote it, he says, because he wants to change what most believers feel when they hear the word giving. "Together, we are going to change audacious generosity from being the exception to being the norm for ALL followers of Christ." His goal for the reader is plain: "to enjoy a living relationship with God that's fueled by courage, characterized by freedom, and overflowing with audacious generosity."

faq.q: What is Audacious Generosity about?
faq.a: Kevin White tells how a prayer for food that others might eat, while his family lived on less than $500 a month, grew into a ministry feeding five hundred families, and shows three steps to set God, yourself and others free.

faq.q: What are the three steps?
faq.a: They are, in order: Set God Free, by living recklessly for God and asking Him for more; Set Yourself Free, by moving from fear to freedom; and Set Others Free, by turning from getting to giving. Each section ends with an application chapter.

faq.q: Is it a faith over fear book?
faq.a: Yes, in substance. Two chapters are about courage, one is titled Fear Versus Freedom, and the author builds on 2 Timothy 1:7, which says God has not given us "a spirit of fear and timidity, but of power, love, and self-discipline." The exact phrase faith over fear is not used.

faq.q: Is it about pressure to give?
faq.a: No. The author says audacious generosity is not about beating you up for not giving, pressuring you to give what you can produce, or giving for personal gain. He says it is not about faith being "some force that guarantees prosperity."

faq.q: Is it about biblical generosity and stewardship?
faq.a: It is about biblical generosity as an attribute of God, with Scripture throughout. Stewardship of money is a smaller subject. The author tells how his own giving grew beyond a 10 percent tithe, but the book is not a financial guide.

faq.q: What does the book say about freedom in Christ and the presence of God?
faq.a: The second step, Set Yourself Free, is about identity in Christ, "secure, significant, and accepted," and the author says that on a flight home from India he committed to "passionately pursue the presence of God."

faq.q: What is the link to India and the Great Commission?
faq.a: The author has traveled to India over fifty times and writes that for over twenty years "God has had me staring at the 1.3 billion Indian Nationals who desperately need to know about Jesus." The book keeps the Great Commission in view.

faq.q: Does it speak of the joy of giving?
faq.a: The author wants readers to "exchange any sense of pressure and regret for genuine confidence and satisfaction," and says "The surprising thing is the more I give, the more I receive."

hero.audience_line: For believers who want to give but feel maxed out, overbooked or afraid, and for churches and small groups studying generosity as an attribute of God.
hero.tagline: A prayer for food that others might eat, prayed while a family lived on less than $500 a month, grew into a ministry feeding five hundred families a month. Kevin White shows the three steps behind it.

audience.headline: A blind and deaf dog, a bully on the bus and a tornado in the yard: six ordinary days that become God moments for one family.
audience.body: For parents and grandparents who want an easy way to start a God conversation at bedtime. Mary and John face a grumpy neighbor, a bully on the bus, a tornado warning, a prayer that goes unanswered, a race with a bike as the prize, and a day for helping neighbors. Each story ends with a family talk and a Bible verse. As the foreword asks, "Have you ever had things happen in your life or the lives of your children where you missed an opportunity for a God moment?" A note on subjects: one story includes a tornado warning, and another shows a man who collapses during a race and receives CPR. Both are told gently, and the family prays and talks about them afterward.

quote.text: “You can do anything when the Creator of the world is your Father.”
quote.cite: The Blessing Trail 3, I Am A Child of God

what_makes.title: What makes this book for families who want Bible lessons children actually remember
paras: Many children's Bible books explain a story. This one starts with a situation a child could meet this week.
Five things set it apart:
list: The stories are about ordinary days. A blind and deaf dog, a school bus, a storm in the yard, a toy in a store and a neighbor with a hurt foot give children something they recognize.
Mama and Daddy talk it through. Each story has a short family conversation that connects the day to a verse, so a parent can copy the way of talking.
Scripture is quoted in the moment. Romans 12:10, John 1:12-13, James 4:2-3, Philippians 2:3-4, John 15:12 and 1 Peter 5:7 are among the verses the family opens.
Prayer is part of the plot. The family prays for a frightened child in a basement, for a bully, for a neighbor and for a stranger, and the stories show what happened afterward.
The questions are honest. Mary asks why her prayer for a doll was not answered. Daddy answers that God wants us to pray about what is important to Him, and that God "always knows best."

sections.h2: For parents who want a bedtime devotional
paras: Each story is short enough for one evening. The family conversations give you words to use, and the verses are short enough to repeat.

sections.h2: For grandparents and Sunday school teachers
paras: The stories work read aloud, one at a time. A teacher can pause after Mary or John asks a question and let the class answer before Daddy does.

sections.h2: For children who ask hard questions
paras: Why did my prayer not get answered? Why is that man grumpy? Can a person stay happy when life is hard? The stories let Mary and John ask out loud and let the parents answer with the Bible.

sections.h2: For homeschool families
paras: The six stories cover choices, identity, courage, prayer, putting others first and serving neighbors, each tied to a verse.

paras: A boy on the school bus mocks a younger boy until he cries. John tells the younger boy that he is a child of God and can ask for help. The family prays for both boys. A few days later, an older girl thanks John because her brother's fear of the dark has vanished.

Mary, John and Daddy run in a race with a bicycle as the prize. When an older man falls beside the path, Daddy stops to help and the children stay with him until the ambulance comes. The finish line is empty when they get there. A reporter had been waiting, and the next morning's paper calls them "The Good Samaritan Family."

Six people huddle under the basement steps when a tornado warning comes. Mama prays aloud: "God, You are in control of the weather because You created it." Afterward, Mary asks whether they could have stopped the tornado by telling it to stop, and Daddy talks with the children about Jesus calming a storm and the faith of a mustard seed.

author.bio: Wendy Reardon writes The Blessing Trail books, read-aloud stories about two children, Mary and John, and their Mama and Daddy; this is the third. The book prints no biography of her. Its foreword, which she wrote with Susan Lynch, says the stories help parents revisit the teaching moments busy families miss, and that "Wendy is not holding back on the truth of our mission here on earth as Christ followers."

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The foreword begins with a question every parent knows:
“Have you ever had things happen in your life or the lives of your children where you missed an opportunity for a God moment?”

It says the stories "guide children into a Biblical way of responding to things they can, and do, experience in their young lives," from how to give of your time to how to respond in a disaster or be compassionate in an emergency. Its invitation is simple: join your children in reading it together.

faq.q: What is The Blessing Trail 3?
faq.a: It is a 98-page full-color book of six read-aloud stories about two children, Mary and John, each ending with a family talk and a Bible verse. They are, in order: Choices; I Am A Child of God; The Big Storm; Ask God; The Race; and Help Your Neighbor Day.

faq.q: What ages is it for?
faq.a: It is written for children ages 4 to 8, to be read aloud with a parent.

faq.q: Is it a book of bedtime Bible stories?
faq.a: It works well at bedtime. Each story is short enough for one evening, and in I Am A Child of God, Daddy reads a verse at bedtime because hearing God's words just before sleep calms you. Most stories end with an evening devotion.

faq.q: Can we use it as a family devotional?
faq.a: Yes. Each story ends with a family talk, usually at supper or evening devotions, a verse such as Romans 12:10, John 1:12-13, James 4:2-3, Philippians 2:3-4, John 15:12 or 1 Peter 5:7, and a short talk a parent can copy.

faq.q: Does it teach faith like a mustard seed?
faq.a: Yes. After the tornado warning in The Big Storm, Daddy tells the children about Jesus calming the storm and says that with faith as small as a mustard seed we can move a mountain, though never on our own without God's help.

faq.q: Does it retell the Good Samaritan story?
faq.a: Yes. In The Race, the family stops to help a man who collapses, while every other runner passes by. That evening Daddy tells the story of the Good Samaritan and reads Philippians 2:3-4, and the next day the local paper calls them The Good Samaritan Family.

faq.q: Is the blind and deaf dog real?
faq.a: Yes, in the story Mama says Piglet is a real dog, a little pink dog who is blind and deaf and was adopted by a veterinarian. She uses him to teach the children about trust and about choosing to depend on God.

faq.q: Does it teach kindness and putting others first?
faq.a: Yes. In Help Your Neighbor Day, the family cleans a neighbor's yard after his foot surgery, buys his groceries and fixes a broken porch step for a mother down the road, and will not take payment. Daddy reads Jesus' command in John 15:12 to love each other as He has loved us.

faq.q: Does it help parents talk with children about faith?
faq.a: That is its aim. The foreword says teaching moments with our children can be missed easily with our busy lives, and in every story Mama and Daddy show one way to turn a question into a conversation about God, including Mary's honest question about why her prayer for a doll was not answered.

faq.q: Do I need to read the first two books first?
faq.a: No. Each story stands alone. The same family appears in The Blessing Trail 2, with a different set of stories.

sections.h2: For Christian professionals
paras: If you lead a team, solve problems and make decisions all week and rarely connect any of it to your faith, this guide is for you. It promises to help you "lead with integrity, wisdom, and spiritual authority without being preachy, awkward, or irrelevant." The weekly challenges are small and concrete: ask a colleague about their story, tell your own, ask someone you trust for input on a decision, invite someone to coffee.

sections.h2: For church and workplace small groups
paras: The guide is built for a group that meets once a week for about 60 minutes. Each meeting opens with one question, "Where did you see God at work this week?", moves into a guided discussion on the week's theme and closes with a prayer and a challenge for the week ahead. It works in a church setting, a workplace lunchroom, a virtual group or a living room, and the leader does not need to be a pastor or teacher.

sections.h2: For pastors and ministry leaders
paras: A section is written just for you. It says this study is a tool for discipling "staff, volunteers, donors, or business leaders in your congregation," and it gives a way to start: "Hand-select 6–12 people who show leadership, curiosity, and relational strength," walk through the ten weeks together, then use the group to train the next facilitators.

sections.h2: For marketplace leaders who want to start a group
paras: "You don't need permission to start a group." The guide gives three steps for an owner, an executive or a team leader: pray and prepare, choose a time and place (a lunch hour, an early morning, a virtual meeting, "whatever works"), and follow the weekly rhythm. It works in a church, a workplace lunchroom, a virtual group or a living room.

audience.headline: Church taught them how to worship. Work taught them how to perform. This study teaches how to bring the two together.
audience.body: For Christian professionals who are tired of keeping their faith in a Sunday box, and for pastors and ministry leaders who want a practical way to disciple people beyond Sunday. Mark Thompson, a business coach and Chief Revenue Officer, gives you a ten-week small-group study with a weekly Scripture theme, discussion questions, an at-work challenge, a midweek message and a closing prayer. A note on subjects: Week Nine talks about stress, burnout and temptation at work, and the author shares from his own life and invites you to share from yours. It is a faith study guide, not professional counseling.

quote.text: Church taught them how to worship. Work taught them how to perform. But no one taught them how to integrate the two.
quote.cite: Mark Thompson, Introduction

what_makes.title: What makes this book for people who want faith and work to meet
paras: A short, practical guide of ten weekly sessions, an eight-step communication framework and a plan for launching your own group. It began when the author noticed that his own faith stopped at the office door.
Five things set it apart:
list: It starts from honest experience. The preface describes a faith that stayed "compartmentalized" for years, "a box I checked on Sunday mornings, not a lens through which I lived," until small groups helped the author and his wife weave God into daily life.

It gives each session a clear shape. A meeting is about sixty minutes: a check-in, a guided discussion, then a wrap-up with the at-work challenge and a closing prayer, with a short message sent midweek to keep the study alive.

It teaches relationship skills, not just ideas. The Four Spaces of Belonging (public, social, personal, intimate) and the eight-step Communication Framework give you tactical ways to move from surface-level connection toward trust.
It does not require a seminary degree. The group leader's job, the guide says, is to facilitate, not to teach, and you do not need to be "a pastor, teacher, or expert to lead this study."
It is built to multiply. The guide ends with how to launch a group in a church or an office, and invites finishing groups to start new ones.

stories.h2: Week One: Building authentic relationships at work
paras: The theme is "Trust is the foundation of spiritual leadership." The guide says that "Most people don't struggle with knowing what's right, they struggle with knowing who's safe," and it opens with icebreaker questions about your name, your work, what drew you to the group and how you would describe your relationship with God right now. Then it teaches the Four Spaces: public, social, personal and intimate. The first two steps of the Communication Framework, being curious about someone else's story and telling your own, become that week's practice.

stories.h2: Week Three: Integrity and ethics in business
paras: The theme is that integrity "isn't just about avoiding wrongdoing, it's about aligning our decisions with God's character." The Scripture focus includes Proverbs 11:3 and Psalm 15:1-2. The midweek message asks, "Where are you tempted to compromise this week? Who could you invite into that moment?" The challenge is step three of the framework, seek counsel, and the closing prayer asks for "courage to ask for help" and "humility to receive it."

stories.h2: Week Nine: Handling stress, burnout and temptations at work
paras: This session begins from a plain statement: "Stress, burnout, and temptation are part of every workplace. But they don't have to define our story." The Scripture focus runs from Matthew 11:28-30 ("Come to me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest") to Isaiah 40:31. The teaching moment says, "We're not called to power through, but we are called to abide," and invites the leader to share a personal story of burnout, temptation or pressure.

author.bio: Mark Thompson is a business coach and Chief Revenue Officer. He grew up in a small town, where his faith was shaped by his mother's devotion to God and Jesus Christ, yet for years that faith stayed compartmentalized. After he and his wife moved to North Carolina and joined a church, small groups helped them weave God into their daily rhythms. He has worked with immigrant customers and offshore clients across dozens of countries, whose integration of faith into professional life inspired this study.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The author calls the problem a firewall. "Everything shifted," he writes, when he and his wife joined a church where small groups showed them a faith that "permeated every aspect of our lives." One frontier remained, the workplace. Working with clients who brought their faith to their jobs was "a revelation." It "exposed the firewall I'd unknowingly accepted," the place where his faith stopped at the office door.

Conversations with other Christians echoed the same frustration, so he wrote a study to close the gap. "It's not about perfection, it's about progress," he says, and the goal is to "transform your workplace into a mission field, where you live boldly as a witness to God's love and truth."

faq.q: What is Bringing Jesus to Work?
faq.a: A practical ten-week study by Mark Thompson for Christian professionals, with a weekly Scripture theme, discussion questions, an at-work challenge, a midweek message and a closing prayer. It works in a church, a workplace or a living room.

faq.q: What topics do the ten weeks cover?
faq.a: Authentic relationships, wise decisions, integrity and ethics, hard work and diligence, communication and listening, resilience, financial responsibility and generosity, mentorship and discipleship, handling stress and burnout, and legacy and impact.

faq.q: Is it good for workplace relationships and communication?
faq.a: Yes. Relationships are the thread through all ten weeks. Week One teaches the Four Spaces of Belonging, and the eight-step Communication Framework gives practical steps such as being curious about someone's story and inviting someone to coffee.

faq.q: Does it cover business ethics?
faq.a: One weekly session, Week Three, is about integrity and ethics in business, with Scripture, discussion questions and a challenge to seek counsel. It is a faith study with one session on ethics, not a business ethics textbook.

faq.q: Does it help with workplace stress and burnout?
faq.a: Week Nine is devoted to stress, burnout and temptation, with Scripture on rest, peace and perseverance and a call to bring burdens to God. It is a faith study, not counseling or medical advice.

faq.q: Is there a communication framework?
faq.a: Yes. The appendix lays out the eight steps, from being curious about someone else's story to asking about someone's faith history, and the weekly sessions introduce them one at a time.

faq.q: Does it include prayers for the workplace?
faq.a: Every weekly session ends with a written closing prayer, for example one for integrity and wise counsel and one for carrying a legacy of grace, truth and spiritual impact.

faq.q: Does it cover mentoring and leaving a legacy?
faq.a: Week Eight is about mentorship and discipleship, and Week Ten is about living and leaving a spiritual legacy, with 2 Timothy 4:7 and Psalm 78:4 among its Scriptures.

hero.tagline: A practical ten-week study for Christian professionals that closes the gap between Sunday faith and Monday work.

sections.h2: For parents and grandparents who read aloud
paras: If you love bedtime stories with a point worth talking about, this one gives you plenty to stop for. The scenes are short, the dialogue is lively, and the brothers are easy to voice. Ima's line about sharing comes back twice, once from Asher and once at the very end, so a child can hear it, see it happen and say it back.

sections.h2: For Sunday school teachers and children's ministry leaders
paras: A feeding-of-the-five-thousand lesson needs a way in for the youngest children, and this gives you one. The Note to Parents, Teachers, and Ministry Leaders lists values to explore, namely generosity, obedience, curiosity and faith, and it suggests reading John 6:1-14 together afterward to talk about how Jesus multiplied the loaves and fish and what that shows about faith and compassion.

sections.h2: For kids who ask big questions
paras: Asher is the boy who asks why the sky turns orange before sunrise, and he is also the boy who asks what would happen if they gave away their lunch. The other brothers doubt him, grumble about being hungry and wonder how anything could be enough. The book lets those feelings be real, and then it lets the miracle happen.

sections.h2: For families with children who are all different
paras: The four brothers are four kinds of children: the curious one, the adventurous one, the careful one and the peacemaker. The closing note turns that into a way to affirm your own child, with four short lines to say out loud: “Curiosity is a gift.” “Adventurous hearts can lead others.” “Cautious thinkers help keep everyone grounded.” “Peacemakers reflect the heart of Jesus.” It also suggests asking which brother your child relates to most, and why.

audience.headline: A small lunch. A crowd too big to count. A miracle four brothers saw up close.
audience.body: For parents, grandparents and teachers who want a warm way to tell a child the story of the loaves and fishes. Four brothers stop on their way to school, find a hillside full of hungry people, and Asher asks a question that changes the day: what if we gave them our lunch?

quote.text: But David, remember how Ima always says that when we share what we have, even if it's just a little, God can use it to bless many?
quote.cite: The Brothers and Their Lunch Basket, Asher to his brother David on the hillside

what_makes.title: What makes this book for children who are learning that a small gift can matter
paras: A picture-book retelling of Jesus feeding the five thousand, seen through the eyes of children. It begins at a kitchen table with pancakes and ends back at that same home, with a mother who has one more thing to say about sharing.
Five things set it apart:
list: It is told through four brothers. Asher is full of questions, Elijah rushes in tying his shoes, Samuel is the careful one who checks the weather, and David hums quietly and pulls out chairs for everyone. Children often find themselves in one of them.

It keeps the Bible event clear. The author's note says the miracle is drawn from the Bible while the characters and some events are fictional, and it reminds readers that “the Bible tells the true account.” The note to parents points to John 6:1-14 so the two can be read side by side.
It puts a child at the center of the miracle. The basket holds five loaves of bread and two fish, and it is Asher, not a grown-up, who walks over and offers it.
It is made for reading aloud. There are 40 pages, 8 x 10 inches, in color, with short scenes of two or three lines that are easy to pause on and talk about.

It gives you the questions to ask. A closing note for parents, teachers and ministry leaders suggests ways to read with expression and to talk afterward, including “What would you have done if you were Asher?”

blocks.text: Every copy opens with a copyright page and a Note from the Author, and then the story begins on page 6. The note reads:

paras: This story, The Brothers and Their Lunch Basket, is a creative retelling of the miracle of Jesus feeding the 5,000. While the miracle is drawn from the Bible, the characters and some events are fictional, designed to help young readers engage with the story in a fun and imaginative way.
We encourage readers to remember that the Bible tells the true account, and this story adds creative elements to help children understand and enjoy the message more deeply.

blocks.text: The story opens like this:

paras: The morning sun peeked through the window as the smell of pancakes filled the kitchen. Ima was already up, cooking breakfast like she always did.
Asher was the first to bounce in, eyes wide with curiosity. “Ima, why does the sky turn orange before the sun comes up?” he asked.

Elijah burst in right behind him, still tying his shoes, ready for whatever adventure the day might bring. Samuel followed slowly, his brow furrowed as he checked the weather through the window—always the careful one. And last came David, quietly humming a tune, gently pulling out chairs for his brothers. He liked when everyone got along.

blocks.text: The book closes with a Note to Parents, Teachers, and Ministry Leaders and a short “How to Use This Book” list.

We encourage readers to remember that the Bible tells the true account, and this story adds creative elements to help children understand and enjoy the message more deeply.
The morning sun peeked through the window as the smell of pancakes filled the kitchen. Ima was already up, cooking breakfast like she always did.
Asher was the first to bounce in, eyes wide with curiosity. “Ima, why does the sky turn orange before the sun comes up?” he asked.

Elijah burst in right behind him, still tying his shoes, ready for whatever adventure the day might bring. Samuel followed slowly, his brow furrowed as he checked the weather through the window—always the careful one. And last came David, quietly humming a tune, gently pulling out chairs for his brothers. He liked when everyone got along.

paras: On the way to school, the brothers hear a commotion, and Elijah decides they should look. “Oh, who cares if we're late!” he says, running toward the crowd. They find a huge gathering of men, women and children talking, laughing and playing, “and even babies were there!” David notices a smaller group of men standing aside with worried faces. The brothers creep up behind a tree to listen, and hear a man ask Philip where they are to buy bread so these people can eat. Philip's answer is honest: there are too many people, and they do not have enough money.

stories.h2: What if we gave them our lunch?
paras: Asher looks at the basket and thinks of all those hungry faces. “I know it's not much—just five loaves of bread and two fish—but I can't stop thinking about all those hungry faces. Maybe it could help.” David pushes back: “Then we will be hungry and without any food for our lunch.” Asher reminds him what Ima always says, and David gives in: “You're right Asher, they do need our help. We'll be okay.” Asher walks up to the man with brown eyes and says, “It's not much, but... you can have our lunch.”

After the crowd has been fed, the brothers realize they are late, and school is hard. Asher stares at his lunch cubby, wondering if it still holds a miracle. David doodles loaves and fish all over his worksheet. Elijah fiddles with his pencil during read-aloud time. Samuel raises his hand to answer a math question and forgets what he was going to say. When they get home, Ima asks only, “Did you boys remember to be kind today?” and David blurts out, “We shared our lunch,” and then, “And somehow... it fed everyone!”

Her book comes with a note for the adults who read it with children.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The closing note says the book “was written to help children imagine themselves as part of one of Jesus' most famous miracles—the feeding of the five thousand.” It describes the four brothers as having “unique personalities” so that children can explore “important values like generosity, obedience, curiosity, and faith.”

The note offers the story as “a springboard for deeper conversations about how God can use even small offerings in big ways when we choose to share and trust Him.” Its final hope is that children will believe “that God can use them—just as they are—to make a difference in the world.”

faq.q: What is The Brothers and Their Lunch Basket about?
faq.a: It is a retelling of Jesus feeding a crowd with five loaves and two fish, told through four brothers, one of whom, Asher, offers the family's lunch basket.

faq.q: Is this the loaves and fishes story?
faq.a: Yes. The basket holds five loaves of bread and two fish, Asher gives it to Philip, and Jesus feeds the crowd. The brothers and their mother are story characters; the miracle is the Bible event.

faq.q: What does the book teach children about sharing?
faq.a: Asher remembers what his mother says: when we share what we have, even if it is just a little, God can use it to bless many. The book is about sharing and trusting God with something small.

faq.q: What ages is it for?
faq.a: It is made for early readers and read-aloud, ages 4 to 8. It is 40 pages, 8 x 10 inches, in color.

faq.q: Can it be used in Sunday school or children's ministry?
faq.a: Yes. It suits Sunday school lessons and children's ministry, and it is also suited to read-aloud time with parents and grandparents.

faq.q: Is it one of the Bible stories for kids that works at bedtime?
faq.a: It is a Bible story for kids, a retelling of the feeding of the five thousand from John 6:1-14. The book does not mention bedtime, but its scenes are short, its dialogue is lively and its closing note recommends reading aloud with expression, so it suits a quiet read before sleep as well as a classroom.

faq.q: Are the brothers in the Bible?
faq.a: No. The author's note says the characters and some events are fictional and that the Bible tells the true account. The feeding of the five thousand is found in John 6:1-14, and the book's closing note suggests reading it together.

faq.q: Does it include questions to talk about afterward?
faq.a: Yes. The closing note suggests pausing to ask three questions. They are, in order: “What would you have done if you were Asher?”; “Have you ever shared something and watched God bless it?”; and “Which brother do you relate to most and why?” It also lists ways to affirm a child's God-given traits.

faq.q: Is it a read-aloud picture book?
faq.a: Yes. It has short scenes, lively dialogue and full-color pages, and the closing note recommends reading aloud with expression to help young listeners engage with the story.

If you or someone you know is thinking about suicide, please contact your local emergency services or a crisis line right away, and talk to a physician or licensed counselor about what you are carrying.

what_makes.title: What makes this book for people who want to pray for others
paras: Can I Pray for You? begins with a question the author asks strangers in campgrounds, grocery stores and airports, and it grows from there. Part 1, Inward Progression, builds the private foundation of prayer: living with open hands, knowing God as Father, hearing His voice, praying Scripture and fasting. Part 2, Outward Expression, turns that foundation outward.
Five things set it apart:
list: It begins with a real encounter. The first chapter is one morning at a nearly empty RV resort in Texas, told simply and with care.
It starts in private. The author says "If you want to pray powerfully for strangers in public, start by praying intimately in private."
It is practical. Chapters include models for prayer, praying Scripture, fasting, lament and a personal prayer plan, and thirteen chapters close with a short challenge called Your Turn.
It is honest about fear. A full chapter, Looking Like Weirdos, argues that feeling awkward is a sign you are on the right track.
It does not make you the savior. The author's rule is that "outcomes are His responsibility. Obedience is ours."

sections.h2: For believers who freeze at praying out loud
paras: The author knows the feeling and says so plainly: "Praying in public takes courage, no question." His answer is not a technique. It is a way of living that gives you room to say yes: hold life with open hands, and expect interruptions as invitations. He calls it going off script, and it begins long before you meet anyone who needs prayer.

sections.h2: For parents and families
paras: A chapter on prayer in the family opens with a joke that rings true: "If praying in public feels like jumping out of a plane, then praying with your family sometimes feels like jumping without a parachute." He walks through how to begin with your spouse, how to pray with children, and why a praying family does not need to be perfect.

sections.h2: For professionals and workplaces
paras: Most of us spend more waking hours at work than anywhere else. The workplace chapter makes the case for bringing prayer there, quietly and without a title: "Peace is magnetic, peace is noticeable, peace is evangelism without trying."

sections.h2: For people who want to hear from God
paras: The chapter Hearing from God is for anyone who finds prayer one-sided. The author says hearing from God is not mystical but relational, and he gives practical rhythms: coffee and Scripture in the morning, a walk, a drive, a quiet pause.

stories.h2: One morning at a nearly empty RV resort
paras: Wherever his family parks their RV, the author sets a sandwich-board sign beside the campsite: Can We Pray For You? With it is a phone number and the words Call or Text. At a resort in Texas, assigned a site at the back, he laughs to himself that no one will see it. On Monday morning, reading outside, which he rarely does, he notices the resort's general manager come out of the woods, stop, and walk toward him to ask about the sign. The man tells him he had planned to end his life the night before. The author does not preach. He tells him, "Tell me everything," and then adds:
"But I want you to know something first—I'm broken too."

He puts a hand on the man's shoulder and prays, and they both cry. He offers his number and an invitation: "Let's get together and start reading the Bible from the beginning. I'll give you as much time as you need." While the author is away for work, the man tells his closest friends everything. "They surrounded him with love." The author draws one lesson: "That's how God works. That's how He multiplies."

stories.h2: Keeping the phone off the hook
paras: Hearing from God, says the author, is simpler than most people imagine. He compares it to an old landline phone left off the hook, so the line stays open and the conversation never has to end. "You don't hang up the phone with Heaven. You keep the line open." The point is not constant talking but constant connection: "This is why hearing God isn't mystical; it's relational." Then comes the line that gives the chapter its weight: "You can't recognize a voice you never spend time with."

A chapter for hard seasons says what many readers need to hear. "Lament is not complaining, lament is not faithlessness. Lament is worship with tears in your eyes." The author reminds readers that "The Lord is close to the brokenhearted and saves those who are crushed in spirit (Psalm 34:18)." He then turns to the one who prays for others: when someone is suffering, real compassion begins with humility, not a quick spiritual answer.

author.bio: Ryan Schraffenberger graduated from college in 2010 and spent his early twenties in the Florida Keys, bartending, DJing weddings and fishing. At twenty-four he was elected City Commissioner of Key Colony Beach, Florida, and served one term. In 2014 he started Promotions Guy with screen-printing equipment bought on a credit card, and the business now supports ministries around the world. He and his family live as full-time RVers, and wherever they park he sets out a prayer sign.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The author says the book is a starting point: "This book was written to equip you to pray boldly, live courageously, and carry Christ into the world with compassion and confidence. But this book isn't the end. It's the launchpad." He closes by telling readers what to do next: "Wear the shirt. Be the bridge. Tell your story. Pray with strangers. Walk in boldness."

faq.q: What is Can I Pray for You? about?
faq.a: It is Ryan Schraffenberger's account of setting out a Can We Pray For You? sign wherever his family parks their RV, and a practical guide to building a prayer life that flows naturally into everyday boldness.

faq.q: Is it a book about praying for others?
faq.a: Yes. Part 2, Outward Expression, covers boldness in faith, telling your testimony and the Gospel in plain words, supporting people after the moment has passed, and becoming the local chaplain of the places you already go. Part 1 builds the private prayer life that makes that possible.

faq.q: Does it teach praying Scripture?
faq.a: Yes. A full chapter, Praying Scripture, explains why to do it and gives simple methods, such as turning a verse into a personal prayer, praying slowly through a passage, and praying Scripture over someone else. The author writes that "when you pray Scripture, you are praying God's thoughts back to God."

faq.q: Is there a chapter on prayer and fasting?
faq.a: Yes. Prayer and Fasting is in Part 1. It looks at fasting in the Bible and in modern life and says, "Prayer connects you to God; fasting clears space so you can hear Him."

faq.q: Does it help with building a relationship with God?
faq.a: That is the foundation of the book. In Relationship with Your Father the author writes that "you must understand something foundational: God is your Father, and He desires a relationship with you." He adds that "Your Father wants your presence more than your perfection."

faq.q: Does it teach how to hear God's voice?
faq.a: It has a full chapter, Hearing from God. The author says God most often speaks in a whisper, that He may use a nudge, a Scripture or a moment of peace, and that "The more you quiet your life, the louder His whisper becomes." The book offers habits, not guarantees.

faq.q: Does it teach how to share the gospel and your testimony?
faq.a: Yes. The chapter Sharing Your Testimony & the Gospel says you don't need to go to seminary or memorize anything, only be willing to tell your story. It names four parts of a great testimony. They are, in order: Your Life Before Jesus Helped You; What Happened When Jesus Stepped In; Your Life After Jesus Changed You; and What God Can Do for Them.

faq.q: Is it only for people who already pray in public?
faq.a: No. It is written for people who find it hard. A chapter called Looking Like Weirdos says that the feeling of awkwardness is common, and that "The awkwardness is temporary, but the fruit is eternal." The author also admits, "Praying in public takes courage, no question."

sections.h2: For readers who love warm, funny and moving true stories
paras: If you like Christian memoir that makes you smile first and tear up second, this one is for you. There is a pastor who needs convincing, a congregation that gasps, a friend who offers to help with the sign language, and a man in a nursing home who never forgets his clown. Cindy writes with the same gentleness she showed in the room, and she does not pretend that every day was easy.

sections.h2: For readers who feel called to bring joy to others
paras: You do not need greasepaint to be touched by this book. Cindy writes, “you don't have to dress up as a clown to touch someone's life in a positive way, just be YOU.” If you are thinking about clown ministry, hospital visits or simply being a kinder presence at church, you will find ideas, courage and a good sense of what the work really asks of you. It is a memoir, not a how-to manual, but the tool box at the back is generous.

sections.h2: For anyone who has visited or worked in hospitals, nursing homes or schools
paras: Many of the chapters take place in rooms where people are hurting, lonely or afraid: a children's ward, a nursing home on Christmas Eve, a school auditorium full of teenagers. If you are a volunteer, a chaplain, a nurse, a teacher or a family member sitting by a bed, you will recognize the quiet work of showing up and listening.

sections.h2: For church clowns, mimes and children's ministry teams
paras: If you already wear a red nose, or you lead children's church, this book is a colleague's story. Cindy tells how she learned makeup, balloon animals, sleight-of-hand magic and mime, how she chose her outfits over the years, and how she staged a Christmas play in sign language with children before a church service. Sparkle's Tool Box at the back gives her three favorite tricks step by step, with the message she used each one to carry.

what_makes.title: What makes this book for readers who want a message of love they can pass on
paras: Clowning From The Heart is a memoir in twenty-seven short chapters, so you can read one at a bedside, on a break or over a cup of coffee. Cindy tells it plainly, with humor and tears, and with a gentle push to go and do something kind.
Five things set it apart:
list: It begins in the Mojave Desert in 1965. A seven-year-old Cindy and her sisters line up in clown makeup for their town's first-ever clown contest, and her little sister wins a trip to Catalina Island.

It grows out of a hospital job. Years later, working in a hospital billing office, Cindy and a friend put on makeup and red noses to visit patients. She realizes that clowning can be more than a hobby: it can be a ministry.

It is full of the work itself. You will meet the stickers that read “I Hugged A Clown Today,” the makeup, the balloon animals, the sleight-of-hand magic and the mime routines, and you will walk through parades, a rehab center, a graduation and a 12-step retreat.
It is honest about the cost. A car accident in 2016 left Cindy unable to hold small children or kneel to meet their eyes, and the book follows her through the grief of stepping away from Sparkle.
It leaves you tools. “Sparkle's Tool Box” shares three of her favorite magic tricks with the messages that go with them, and a reference page explains the six main types of clowns.

stories.h2: The boy in the body cast
paras: In her late twenties, Cindy works in a hospital billing office in Walla Walla, Washington, and visits patients in her free time dressed as a clown. One day she is asked to come see a frightened toddler who is in a full body cast and will let no one near him. When he sees the clown, his little body relaxes and he smiles for the first time. She leaves him a Polaroid of the two of them. Later that day he does not recognize her without the makeup, until she holds up the picture and tells him she is the clown. For six weeks she visits on her breaks, and on the day he goes home he tells her, “I love you too.”

Driving to go Christmas shopping with a friend, Cindy hears a song on the radio and cannot shake it. She tracks down the recording, adds sign language she learned partly because her mother was hard of hearing, and asks her pastor if she can stage it with children before the service. He agrees, nervously. She appears as Sparkle in the middle of a congregation that is mostly elderly. When the song ends and she kneels by the cradle, the room bursts into applause and calls of “Amen.”

Asked to perform for an entire school in Adams, Oregon, a town of 389 people, Cindy dreads the high school assembly most. The older students turn out to be the best audience. She invites two strong volunteers to push a fifteen-inch needle through a balloon. Theirs pop; hers does not, because she was prepared. The trick carries a message about preparing for life, and she follows it with “The Torn Heart,” a paper heart she tears apart and then shows made whole again, to talk about what love can mend.

author.bio: Cindy Love grew up in California City, a small retirement town in the Mojave Desert. In her late twenties, while working in the billing department of a hospital in Walla Walla, Washington, she first put on clown makeup to visit patients. In 1989 she began clowning in earnest, and for thirty-five years she served as Sparkle, a gospel clown, at hospitals, nursing homes, schools, churches, parks and community events. Around 2010 she founded a nonprofit called Smiles For Life so that this kind of caring could continue through other people.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: Cindy says Sparkle has “touched the lives of thousands of people over the past few decades,” and she writes, “I hope her story can touch you as well.” The book is also an act of letting go. In the last chapter she writes a letter to Sparkle and tells her that this book “is your legacy now.”

She says the most important thing she can do for anyone is to listen: “Everyone has stories to tell, whether the stories are exciting and good, or scary and bad.” Sparkle was the way she was able to sit and listen, and to tell each person how loved and valued they are. This book is her way of passing that on.

faq.q: What is Clowning From The Heart about?
faq.a: It is Cindy Love's true story of becoming Sparkle, a gospel clown, and of thirty-five years of clown ministry in hospitals, nursing homes, schools, churches and parades, told in twenty-seven short chapters.

faq.q: Is it a book about a message of love?
faq.a: One conviction runs through it: everyone needs to be heard and to know how loved and valued they are. Sparkle listens to the lonely, the sick, the frightened and the grieving and points them to the love of the Lord.

faq.q: Does it teach clown makeup and balloon animals?
faq.a: It tells how Cindy learned makeup, balloon animals and sleight-of-hand magic, and it closes with Sparkle's Tool Box and a reference page on the types of clowns. It is a memoir, not a how-to manual.

faq.q: Does it include magic tricks for kids?
faq.a: Yes. Sparkle's Tool Box gives three tricks she performed for thirty-five years, with the props and the message for each. They are, in order: The Needle and the Balloon; The Polka-Dotted Scarves; and Torn Heart. She writes that Torn Heart is her favorite and works for kids and adults.

faq.q: Does the book take place in hospitals?
faq.a: Many chapters do. The first came when she and a friend put on clown makeup to visit patients at the hospital where she worked; the book also covers nursing homes, a rehab center, schools, churches and parades.

faq.q: Does it say anything about Happy Birthday Jesus?
faq.a: Yes. Chapter 11 tells how she found the song, built a mime-and-sign-language Christmas play with children from her church, and performed it with her pastor's trust.

faq.q: Does it carry a message that people are beautiful and valued?
faq.a: Yes. The Foreword says Cindy wants people to feel “how beautiful and special they are inside and out,” and she gives a hug and a sticker to prove it, in hospital rooms, on parade routes and to strangers on the street.

faq.q: What are the types of clowns?
faq.a: A reference page near the end says there are six main types of clowns. They are, in order: the rodeo clown; the tramp or hobo clown; the auguste clown; the mime clown; the classic white-faced clown; and the grotesque white-faced clown.

faq.q: Who is it for?
faq.a: Christian readers who enjoy warm, funny and moving true stories, readers who feel called to bring joy to others, including through clown ministry, and anyone who has visited or worked in hospitals, nursing homes or schools and wants encouragement.

sections.h2: For parents who want to start the conversation
paras: If you have been looking for a way to talk about God with a three-year-old, this book starts with a question and keeps the sentences short. "He made you with special care and attention" is a line a child can repeat back to you. Stop at any spread and ask the question again, and let your child answer.

sections.h2: For grandparents and gift-givers
paras: A picture book with a message you want the child to keep. The Scripture is printed in full, and the last spreads give a child a place to write a prayer to God. It suits a birthday, Easter, Christmas, a baptism or a dedication.

sections.h2: For teachers, Sunday school and children's ministry
paras: The book moves in clear steps, from who God is to why Jesus came to how a child can pray, so it fits a short lesson. Each spread carries one idea and often a verse a class can read together.

sections.h2: For families who want to pray together
paras: The last spreads turn the book into a starting point. The author prints the prayer she is praying over every reader, asking that children "set time apart daily to talk to You and grow an intimate relationship with You." Then a page begins "Now, you can pray... Dear God," with blank lines for a child to write or say their own prayer, and closes "In the name of Jesus, Amen." Read it, then pray it together.

audience.headline: Do you know God? A picture book that asks a young child the biggest questions, one page at a time.
audience.body: For children ages 3 to 8 and the grown-ups who read with them: parents, grandparents, Sunday school teachers and anyone giving a first book about faith. Katherine Robinson asks "Do you know?" again and again. Do you know God? Do you know Jesus Christ? Do you know that God knows you by name? Do you know you can pray directly to God? Each answer is a few short sentences in large print over a full-color painting, often with a verse. The book is short, warm and simple. It names sin plainly, as making bad choices that displease God, and moves straight to forgiveness.

quote.text: He made you on purpose and with purpose.
quote.cite: Do You Know?, page 12

what_makes.title: What makes this book for children who are just starting to learn about faith
paras: A 30-page picture book in full color, with short sentences a young child can follow and a key verse on many of the spreads.
Five things set it apart:
list: It asks a question. "Do you know?" returns as a refrain, so a child is invited to answer, not just to listen.
It answers simply. God is the creator, He is all holy, all sovereign, all mighty, all loving and all faithful, He is our Heavenly Father, and He is merciful, graceful and forgiving.
It tells why Jesus came, in words a child can follow. Everyone needs help making Godly choices, and that is why God sent His Son, who left His Holy Spirit.
It tells each child they were made on purpose, the heart of the middle spreads.
It ends with a prayer and a place to pray, with lines for the child to write their own.

paras: The first words of the story sit over the earth in space: God "is the creator of the heavens, the earth, everything and everyone in it." The next spread says a child cannot see or touch God but can feel Him, and introduces five words to learn: all holy, all sovereign, all mighty, all loving, all faithful.

Halfway through, the book turns from who God is to who the child is. Over a moon above a dark sea it asks, "Do you know that God knows you by name?" The answer: "He made you just as you are, with the ability to complete His will over your life." Jeremiah 1:5 follows: "Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, before you were born I set you apart."

Near the end, the book asks, "Do you know you can pray directly to God?" It prints a prayer the author prays over the reader, then turns to the child: "Now, you can pray... Dear God," followed by blank lines and the closing, "In the name of Jesus, Amen."

author.bio: Katherine Robinson writes for young children and the adults who read with them. She dedicates Do You Know? "to the great I Am" and closes it with a prayer of her own over every child who hears it. She also wrote ¿Sabes Qué?, a Spanish picture book for children.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The book answers a question in the author's own words. Her dedication reads, "Dedicated to the great I Am. It's only possible because you so willed it. Thank you for trusting me." The prayer on the last spreads says what she hopes for every child: "I pray the message in this book reaches the hearts and ears of all who hear it."
She also hopes children will keep listening: "The closer you get to God, the more you can hear Him and feel Him navigate your life."

faq.q: What is Do You Know? about?
faq.a: It is a read-aloud picture book that tells young children who God is and how much He loves them. It asks one question again and again, "Do you know?", and answers it with short sentences and a Bible verse on many pages.

faq.q: How does it explain who God is to a child?
faq.a: In a few plain lines. God is the creator of the heavens and the earth. He is all holy, all sovereign, all mighty, all loving and all faithful. And "He is our Heavenly Father. He loves you and wants a relationship with you."

faq.q: Does it say Jesus loves and saves me?
faq.a: It explains that humankind struggles with sin and "that's why He sent His son Jesus Christ, to save us," and that Jesus left His Holy Spirit. The prayer thanks God "for loving us so much that You sent Your son to save us." The exact words "Jesus loves you" are not printed in the book.

faq.q: Does it teach a child to pray?
faq.a: Yes. A spread asks, "Do you know you can pray directly to God?" and another gives the child lines to write their own prayer to God, beginning "Dear God" and ending "In the name of Jesus, Amen."

faq.q: Does it tell a child that God loves them and made them?
faq.a: Yes. It says God made the child "with special care and attention," that "He made you on purpose and with purpose," and that He knows the child by name, with Jeremiah 1:5.

faq.q: Does it say God has a plan for my child?
faq.a: Yes. A page asks, "Do you know that God has a plan for your life?" The book says God lets a child choose their own path but "hopes that you will choose the path He already designed for you," and quotes Romans 8:28.

faq.q: Which Bible verses are in it?
faq.a: They are, in order: Genesis 1:1; Revelation 1:8; John 14:6; Jeremiah 1:5; Ephesians 2:10; and Romans 8:28. The copyright page names the New Living Translation and the New International Version.

faq.q: What ages is it for, and when would I read it?
faq.a: Ages 3 to 8. It works for bedtime, family devotion time, Sunday school, children's ministry and homeschool faith lessons, and as a gift for a birthday, Easter, Christmas, a baptism or a dedication.
