audience.headline: Una niña de un pueblo pequeño de Grecia sueña con ser chef, algunos se ríen de ella, y ella decide seguir creyendo.
audience.body: Para niños de 5 a 8 años, para las familias hispanohablantes que leen juntas en voz alta y para los abuelos que quieren contar de dónde vienen. Tyler Stavlas cuenta la historia real de su abuela griega, YiaYia Voula: una cocinera que llega a Estados Unidos sin hablar el idioma, que oye que no en cada puerta, que cría sola a sus tres hijos y que confía en Dios hasta ver su tzatziki en los supermercados. Una nota sobre los temas: es un cuento ilustrado, breve y con final esperanzador. En él la protagonista pasa por la pobreza, por noches sin un lugar donde dormir, por tres trabajos a la vez y por una enfermedad grave que la deja en coma. El texto lo cuenta con sencillez, y su familia ora a su lado. Si un niño a su cargo ha vivido una pérdida o una enfermedad en casa, conviene leerlo juntos y dejarlo hacer preguntas.

quote.text: “Voy a seguir creyendo. ¡No voy a renunciar a mis sueños!”
quote.cite: El Gran Sueño de la YiaYia Voula, Voula después de que se rieran de ella

what_makes.title: Qué hace especial este libro para niños que sueñan en grande
paras: Es la historia de una persona real, contada por su nieto. Desde la primera página, un niño sabe que Voula existió y que su sueño de ser chef se cumplió. Lo que cuenta el libro es todo lo que pasó entre una cosa y la otra.
Cinco cosas lo distinguen:
list: Es una historia real. El subtítulo lo dice: una historia real de no rendirse nunca. La primera página explica cómo se pronuncia YiaYia Voula (YA-ya VÚ-la) y que el nombre significa abuela Voula.

Muestra el rechazo sin esconderlo. Cuando Voula pide trabajo en Estados Unidos, el libro dice que lo intentó una y otra vez, y que en cada trabajo le decían que no, hasta que un hotel la contrata como chef.

Pone la fe en los momentos más difíciles. Voula ora al mudarse y la familia sigue orando mientras ella está enferma. El libro no presenta la fe como un adorno al final, sino como lo que sostiene a la familia.
Está escrito para leerse en voz alta. Las frases son cortas, y casi cada página cierra con una acción: ella respira hondo, estudia, prueba, sonríe, sigue.

Termina con dos preguntas para el niño: "¿Cuál es tu sueño?" y "¿Qué lograrás si nunca te rindes?". Después de ellas, el libro cuenta qué fue de la marca de la familia, YiaYia Voula's Foods, que según el libro nació en 2024 y hoy está en más de 300 tiendas.

sections.h2: Para familias hispanohablantes que buscan cuentos infantiles con valores
paras: Si busca un libro en español que hable de esfuerzo, de familia y de fe sin dejar de ser un cuento, este lo hace. Es corto, tiene una heroína con nombre y apellido de familia, y cada página avanza un paso en su vida.

sections.h2: Para abuelos y nietos
paras: El libro nace en una cocina, entre un nieto y su abuela. Si usted es abuelo o abuela, puede leerlo y luego contarle a su nieto cómo fueron sus propios comienzos. La pregunta del final sirve para eso: ¿cuál es tu sueño?

sections.h2: Para maestros y bibliotecas
paras: Es una lectura breve para el aula, con una historia clara, un personaje que se levanta después de cada no y una pregunta para conversar. Según la nota del autor, se dona un ejemplar de este libro a cada biblioteca pública de su condado.

sections.h2: Para niños que tienen un sueño y miedo de que se rían
paras: La primera dificultad de Voula no es el idioma ni el dinero. Es que otros se ríen de ella siendo niña. El libro muestra qué hace: llora, se aleja, respira hondo y decide seguir. Es una escena corta que un niño reconoce de inmediato.

blocks.text: El libro empieza con una invitación a quien lo abre:

paras: puedes confiar en Dios, seguir soñando y no rendirte nunca

blocks.text: Esa frase aparece al principio, después de explicar el nombre YiaYia Voula, y vuelve al final. La historia arranca con esta línea:

paras: En un pequeño pueblo de Grecia vivía una niña llamada Voula que tenía un sueño muy grande.

blocks.text: En la siguiente página, la niña dice en voz alta lo que quiere ser:

paras: ¡Algún día seré chef y todas mis recetas se compartirán en todo el mundo!

items: Una niña de un pueblo de Grecia que sueña con cocinar

Los años de estudio, trabajo y recetas nuevas
La mudanza a Estados Unidos, sin el idioma ni el alfabeto

Los tres trabajos, la fe y los corazones generosos
La enfermedad, el coma y la familia que ora
La recuperación y el plan para llevar su salsa a los supermercados
El dueño de una tienda que prueba el tzatziki
La pregunta final para el lector

details.Título: El Gran Sueño de la YiaYia Voula
details.Subtítulo: Una historia real de no rendirse nunca

paras: Poco después del comienzo, algunos oyen a Voula decir que será chef y se ríen: ¿cómo va a ser una gran chef una niña pobre de un pueblo pequeño? A Voula le corren las lágrimas por la cara. Entonces se aleja, respira hondo y toma una decisión. Es la decisión que sostiene el resto del libro y la que el niño recordará.

stories.h2: Tres trabajos y un techo prestado
paras: Ya en Estados Unidos, Voula se queda sola a cargo de sus tres hijos. Acepta tres trabajos: en una pescadería muy fría, de mesera y de chef. El libro dice que su fe en Dios le daba fuerzas. Y dice algo más: "Algunas noches, Voula y sus hijos no tenían dónde dormir." Pero corazones generosos les abrieron sus puertas, y poco a poco la esperanza volvió a encontrarlos.

stories.h2: De la cama del hospital al supermercado
paras: Cuando Voula enferma gravemente, la familia no se aparta de su lado. Ahí viene la pregunta que el libro deja flotando: "¿Se recuperaría Voula? ¿Llegaría a ver su sueño hecho realidad?" Ella abre los ojos, los médicos quedan asombrados y la familia da gracias a Dios. Después empiezan a llevar su tzatziki a las tiendas. Unas dicen que no hay espacio. En una, el dueño lo prueba y exclama que esa salsa tiene que estar en todas sus tiendas.

author.bio: Tyler Stavlas creció en la cocina con su YiaYia, su abuela griega, ayudándola a preparar su famoso tzatziki y escuchando las historias de las dificultades que enfrentó y de cómo nunca se rindió. Hoy es director de producto de YiaYia Voula's Foods. Fundó Hunger for Change, una organización sin fines de lucro que, según el libro, ha donado 750 libras de tzatziki sin vender a bancos de alimentos locales. Da charlas sobre perseverancia, emprendimiento y liderazgo de servicio.

why.title: Por qué existe este libro
paras: La página sobre el autor lo dice con sus propias palabras: él "escribió este libro para compartir su mensaje con los niños de todas partes: sueña en grande y no te rindas nunca".

El libro cierra con el mismo mensaje, dicho de otra forma. "El mayor regalo de YiaYia Voula no fueron solo sus recetas: fue mostrarle al mundo que, aunque la vida sea difícil, puedes confiar en Dios, seguir intentándolo y nunca renunciar a tus sueños."

faq.q: ¿De qué trata El Gran Sueño de la YiaYia Voula?
faq.a: Es un cuento infantil ilustrado, basado en una historia real, sobre una niña de un pequeño pueblo de Grecia que sueña con ser chef. Voula se muda a Estados Unidos, enfrenta puertas cerradas, cría sola a sus tres hijos y sigue creyendo hasta que su salsa tzatziki llega a los supermercados.

faq.q: ¿Es uno de esos cuentos infantiles que son reales o inventados?
faq.a: Es real. Según el libro, cuenta la historia de la abuela griega del autor. La expresión cuento infantil es nuestra descripción: el texto de las páginas no la usa, y lo que se lee es una historia contada en tercera persona, en frases cortas.

faq.q: ¿Sirve como cuento infantil para dormir?
faq.a: Sí, para leer en voz alta en familia. Es corto y termina bien, con una pregunta tranquila para el niño. Pero tiene una escena de enfermedad grave y coma, así que algunos padres lo preferirán de día o junto a una conversación. La palabra dormir aparece una sola vez en el texto, y no es para describir el libro.

faq.q: ¿Es un libro infantil en español o una traducción?
faq.a: Es la edición en español de YiaYia Voula's Big Dream: A True Story of Never Giving Up. La traducción es de Spirit Media Publishing, según la página de datos del libro.

faq.q: ¿Es una historia de inmigrantes?
faq.a: Cuenta cómo la familia de Voula deja Grecia para mudarse a Estados Unidos con la esperanza de un hogar nuevo. La palabra inmigrante no aparece, pero el libro dice que no hablaba el idioma, que no podía leer el nuevo alfabeto y que cada día traía un nuevo desafío.

faq.q: ¿Enseña a superar obstáculos?
faq.a: Sí, mediante la historia y no con una lista de consejos. Voula supera el rechazo, la falta de dinero, el cansancio de tres trabajos y una enfermedad grave. La frase superar obstáculos no aparece en el libro, y su lección más clara es la que está en la última página.

faq.q: ¿Para qué edades es este libro?
faq.a: Para niños de 5 a 8 años, según los datos del libro. Un niño menor puede disfrutarlo en voz alta, y un lector de ocho años puede leerlo solo.

faq.q: ¿Habla de Dios?
faq.a: Sí. Voula ora al mudarse a Estados Unidos, su fe le da fuerzas durante los tres trabajos, y su familia ora y confía en Dios mientras ella está enferma. Es una historia cristiana contada sin sermones.

sections.h2: For Christians who wrestle with worry
paras: If you want a short, Scripture-rooted reading to steady your thinking before the day starts, the book is built for that. The author says "I choose faith over fear!" and "I choose the positive over the negative!" and then shows what each choice looks like in an ordinary week.

sections.h2: For couples and families
paras: A full section is about home. It includes Lessons from Grandparents, What Makes a Strong Family, Your Children's Roots and Wings and three readings on marriage. In Fear is Our Enemy he writes that "Families with positive interaction breed more secure children who can cope with their fears," and he invites families to talk it over: "Let your family be the place where there are no fears."

sections.h2: For anyone carrying bitterness, regret or grief
paras: The book has readings on letting go of the past, eliminating bitterness, forgiveness and grief. In Forgiven to Forgive the author draws on the story Jesus told about a father and two sons and on years of counseling to say that forgiving others is "one of the most difficult things any of us can be asked to do." A short reading for Christmas begins with a young woman at a funeral who asked him a question about her broken heart.

sections.h2: For pastors, counselors and small groups
paras: The readings are short enough for a morning devotion or a group discussion, and each is built around one clear idea that a leader can set beside a passage of Scripture. The author also writes as a fellow pastor, with stories from the pulpit and the counseling room.

audience.headline: Choose faith over fear, one short reading at a time.
audience.body: For Christians who wrestle with worry, couples and families who want stronger relationships, anyone carrying bitterness, regret or grief, and pastors, counselors and small groups who want brief readings rooted in Scripture. Dr. James E. Kilgore draws on more than sixty-five years as a marriage and family therapist and pastor to offer fifty-nine short readings, each a power idea for turning difficulties into discoveries. A note on subjects: this is a book of faith-based readings from one counselor's experience, not medical advice and not a substitute for care. It speaks about anxiety, grief, bitterness and, in one reading, a counseling story about childhood abuse, told briefly and without graphic detail. If anxiety or low mood is affecting your daily life, please contact a physician or licensed mental health professional, and if you are in crisis or thinking about harming yourself, contact your local emergency services or a crisis line right away.

quote.text: Fear knocked at the door. Faith answered. No one was there.
quote.cite: Escaping Anxiety, Delete Anxious Thinking (a plaque given to the author by a couple he counseled)

what_makes.title: What makes this book for people who want to choose faith over fear
paras: A collection of brief readings from a pastor and family therapist, arranged in five sections and written to be read in a few minutes. The author is candid that anxiety is common: "Everyone who lives has some anxious moments." His answer is not a technique but a change of mind, and he takes Paul's call to be "transformed by the renewing of your mind" as the guide for the whole book.
Five things set it apart:
list: It comes from the counseling office. The author has listened to people struggle with anxiety for more than sixty-five years, and the readings carry stories from that work.
Each reading is short. Fifty-nine readings across five sections, from escaping anxiety and positive wholeness to seasonal lessons, family and marriage, and turning the mundane into the magnificent.

It names more than one cure and says where grace fits. The introduction notes that medicine is necessary for some, that groups can help belonging and that psychology offers guiding ideas, then says "Only the transformational power of grace can bring real change."
It takes Scripture seriously. Verses run through the readings, quoted mainly from the Holman Christian Standard Bible, with the Living Bible, The Message and the King James Version where marked.
It reaches past the individual. A full section on family and marriage, and readings on forgiveness, grief and listening, speak to the relationships where worry often lives.

details.Title: Escaping Anxiety
details.Subtitle: Power Ideas for Positive Living
details.Author: Dr. James E. Kilgore
details.Binding: Paperback (perfect bound, matte laminate), black and white interior

paras: In the first reading, Delete Anxious Thinking, the author recalls that "Over forty years ago, a couple I had worked with in marriage counseling brought me a small gift." It was a framed plaque, and he has never forgotten its words. Fear, he says, "locks us in place and keeps the key to freedom," while "Faith is the key that unlocks the prison cell." He sets that beside David and Goliath: every one of us faces giants, and a small stone in a practiced sling is faith used with the skills we already have.

A short Christmas reading begins with a little boy who was just learning to read and saw the word backwards. He was trying to read Isaiah's words, God with us. The author thinks of the dogs he has known, including a friend's old dog that, nearly blind and deaf, crawled into bed at night and patted his owner on the leg. It was no longer a sign that he needed to go out. He "simply wanted to know that his master was still there." A country physician sitting at the bedside of a dying man tells him that "My dog doesn't know what else is in this room, but he knows I'm in here." The author's point for anxious hours is that "It doesn't really matter what's behind the door when we know Who is behind it."

stories.h2: How do you fill a hole in your heart?
paras: Coping with Grief at Christmas begins at a funeral, where a young woman looks up through tears and asks, "How do you fill a hole in your heart?" The author answers with permission and honesty. Start with good grief, he says, and do not deny yourself the right to feel anything. Feelings "are neither right nor wrong," tears "assure us that we are neither pain less nor dead," and out of opening ourselves to pain we often discover strength to help others.

author.bio: James E. Kilgore, Ph.D., has served as a marriage and family therapist and a pastor for more than sixty-five years. Across six decades in the counseling office he has listened to couples and individuals wrestle with anxiety, bitterness, grief and the search for identity, and has watched forgiveness open the way to happiness. He dedicates this book to his wife of sixty-five years, whose faith and love, he writes, have helped him escape anxiety.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The author says the book is "the result of discovering the ideas that transform our difficulties into discoveries." He wrote it because culture, medicine, groups and psychology each offer a partial cure, and he believes a deeper change is needed: "We can be transformed only by a powerful change within us."
His hope for the reader is stated in his last lines to them: "May these power ideas create a foundation for positive living for you!"

faq.q: What is Escaping Anxiety about?
faq.a: It is a book of short, practical readings from a marriage and family therapist and pastor. Each is a power idea for turning anxious thinking into a calmer, more hopeful life through faith and grace. The author calls them ideas that "transform our difficulties into discoveries."

faq.q: Is it a book of words of encouragement?
faq.a: It is a book of short faith-filled readings meant to encourage. One reading is titled Be an Encourager, and others speak to forgiveness, grief and hope. It is not a collection of quotations, and it is written as readings, not as daily affirmations.

faq.q: What does faith over fear mean in this book?
faq.a: The first reading says "I choose faith over fear!" and uses a plaque on the author's wall to make the point: when faith answers the door, fear is gone. It is also one of the book's recurring themes, from the reading on David and Goliath to Fear is Our Enemy.

faq.q: What does renewing your mind mean here?
faq.a: The author says he has been "captured by Paul's admonition" to be "transformed by the renewing of your mind," and that a transformed mind leads to a more satisfying day-by-day experience of life. The book's power ideas are meant to feed that renewal.

faq.q: Does it have Scripture about fear?
faq.a: Yes. Scripture runs through every reading. In Fear is Our Enemy, the author notes that so many angelic announcements in the Gospels begin "Do not be afraid" and writes that "God does NOT want you to live in fear."

faq.q: Does it say anything about the power of prayer?
faq.a: In a reading on prayer he describes a crusade he worked on in 1957 and calls the result "a marvelous example of the power of prayer." He also says prayer "includes speaking and listening," and that too often "all we do is talk."

faq.q: Does it help with forgiving others or yourself?
faq.a: It has a full reading on forgiveness, Forgiven to Forgive, built on the story of a father and two sons. It speaks mainly of forgiving others and of receiving forgiveness, not of a program for forgiving yourself.

faq.q: Is it medical advice or therapy?
faq.a: No. It is a collection of readings from one counselor's experience and from Scripture. If anxiety is affecting your health or daily life, please talk with a physician or licensed professional, and contact a crisis line if you are in danger.

hero.tagline: A network engineer who says he is not a pastor or a theologian explains, in twenty short chapters, why following God is simple, and why we make it so hard.

audience.headline: The book opens with one sentence, "Following God is Easy," and then asks the question every honest reader is thinking: why does it feel so hard?
audience.body: For readers who feel stuck between church rules, nagging questions and a quiet prayer life. Vern Kaska III is not a pastor, a theologian or a seminary graduate, and he says so on the first page of chapter one. He writes as a man who reads the Bible daily, prays regularly and still struggles, with one idea he returns to in every chapter: "Following God is Easy." A note on subjects: Chapter Five describes the crucifixion from the point of view of the Trinity, and the author calls it meditation, not theology. The book takes firm positions on the Bible, evil and salvation, which readers from different traditions may weigh differently.

quote.text: “Your relationship with God is between you and Him alone. No one else gets a vote.”
quote.cite: Following God Is Easy, Chapter Two: Why Am I Reading this Book?

what_makes.title: What makes this book for readers who want faith to feel simpler
paras: Many books on faith add more to do. This one keeps pulling the reader back to a single step.
Five things set it apart:
list: It starts from one sentence and keeps returning to it. The opening says that all you have to do is give every area of your life to God and trust Him, then admits "Wouldn’t it be nice if it were that easy?" The twenty chapters are the author's attempt to explain why it is simple and still feels hard.
The author is honest about his limits. He says he is not qualified to write it, tells how he came to write it, and in two chapters admits that he struggled to write at all.

It takes the hard questions head on. Chapters cover contradiction, free will, suffering, why there are so many religions, religion versus relationship, and how to pray for healing when not everyone you pray for is healed.

It gives practical starting points for prayer. One short chapter says that if you have lost contact with God, "all you have to do is start praying," and shows how, from the Lord's Prayer to simply asking the Holy Spirit to pray for you.
It ends every chapter with a question for you. Twenty Reflection pages carry a question and blank lines to write your answer.

sections.h2: For readers who pray but hear nothing back
paras: A full chapter is written for you. The author describes weeks of praying with nothing coming, what he noticed while he waited, and what he did next. If prayer feels like talking to the ceiling, start there.

sections.h2: For new believers and people returning to faith
paras: The book assumes no Bible training. It explains salvation, what a relationship with God can look like day to day, and how to begin praying when you have no words.

sections.h2: For people who have been hurt by church
paras: The early chapters speak directly to readers who hesitate because of how other believers behaved. The author says the behavior of other people has nothing to do with whether God is real or whether He loves you.

sections.h2: For small groups and one-on-one mentors
paras: Each Reflection question is short enough to bring to a table. Twenty questions, one after every chapter, with space to write, make the book easy to read together a chapter at a time.

stories.h2: Why a man with no credentials wrote this
paras: The author tells how a disappointing movie led him to try writing, how he struggled with spelling and typing, and how two years of writing on work trips produced a first book that sold about forty-six copies. He says that book taught him he could finish one, and that this book is the one he believes God asked for.

stories.h2: What to do when you lose contact with God
paras: Chapter Six is short on purpose. It says to start praying anywhere, any time, and points to the Lord's Prayer as a place to begin. If you run out of words, it points to Romans 8:26 and the idea that the Spirit prays on your behalf.

In Chapter Twelve the author admits that for two weeks he prayed for ideas for this book and nothing came. He kept praying, asked how long he would have to wait, and waited. As he sat, his mind drifted to chores, to relationships and to people he needed to pray for. Then he saw what was happening:
“The Holy Spirit hadn't gone silent. I had stopped listening.”
He adds that if he had stopped asking the question, he would never have found the answer.

author.bio: Vern Kaska is a Colorado-based Christian author and a voice and network engineer who has designed global networks in more than fifteen countries. He is not formally trained in theology. He writes from daily prayer, Scripture study and a personal relationship with Jesus Christ, and his passion is Christian living, spiritual growth and helping readers build a stronger relationship with God. In the first chapter he tells how he began writing on work flights and in hotels, and how a first book that sold about forty-six copies taught him he could finish one.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The author says he began writing because he believes God asked him to:
“I’m not a pastor, theologian, or seminary graduate. I’m someone who reads the Bible daily, prays regularly, and still struggles—just like you probably do.”
He asks readers to stay open-minded, to set aside points they disagree with, and to focus on what helps them grow in a relationship with God. The book ends with his prayer for every reader:
“God, please let today be the beginning of a greater relationship between you and the readers of this book.”

faq.q: Does Following God Is Easy teach how to pray?
faq.a: Yes, in plain steps. Chapter Six says that if you have lost contact with God, all you have to do is start praying, anywhere and at any time. It points to the Lord's Prayer as a place to begin, says you can simply talk to God as you would to anyone, and, when words run out, to ask the Holy Spirit to pray for you (Romans 8:26).

faq.q: Will it help me get closer to God?
faq.a: That is its whole aim. The author says spending time with God matters more than figuring out all the mysteries of the universe, and the Reflection after Chapter Six asks how much time you spend with the Lord each day and how much you would like to.

faq.q: What does it say about trusting God?
faq.a: The opening says that all you have to do is give every area of your life to God and trust Him, then admits it is not that easy. The rest of the book explains why. In the healing chapter he writes that once you put your worries and cares in God's hands and accept the outcome, the stress of life begins to fade.

faq.q: What does it say about unanswered prayer?
faq.a: Chapter Twelve, I Pray but Hear Nothing, is about exactly that. After two weeks of hearing nothing, the author realized that his mind was so full of his own concerns that he had stopped listening. He suggests that if you are not getting an answer, you may not be taking the time to listen for it.

faq.q: Does it cover praying for healing?
faq.a: Yes. Chapter Fifteen admits that not everyone the author prays for is healed, and says both one-time and persistent prayer can be right. It gives three things the Bible says to consider. They are, in order: do not carry hate toward others; believe that what you ask for is possible; and be willing to accept the healing.

faq.q: Does it explain why God allows suffering?
faq.a: No, and it says so. Chapter Five says the author cannot answer that question. Instead it offers a meditation on what the day of the crucifixion might have meant for the Father, the Son and the Spirit, to show that God knows suffering.

faq.q: Does it help with hearing God's voice?
faq.a: Some of it. Chapter Twelve is about learning to listen in prayer, and Chapter Fourteen looks at opening the Bible at random for an answer. The author encourages seeking the answer through prayer first and taking any verse back to God to make sure it came from Him.

faq.q: Is it a good book for a new believer?
faq.a: Yes. It assumes no Bible training, and the author says plainly that he is not a pastor or a theologian. It explains salvation and religion versus relationship in everyday words, and each chapter ends with one Reflection question to write about.

content_note.title: Content note
paras: Chapter Five describes the crucifixion from the point of view of the Father, the Son and the Spirit. The author calls it "meditation, not theology." The book also takes firm positions on the Bible, evil and salvation, which readers from different traditions may weigh differently. The author invites you to keep reading and bring your questions to God.

sections.h2: For believers who want a daily quiet time
paras: If you want to start the day in prayer but do not know what to say, this book gives you words and then asks you to find your own. The author invites you to "take a breath," to "take the days as they come," and to "walk them with God." One day's passage, prayer and questions is enough to begin.

sections.h2: For anyone in a hard season
paras: The prayers do not pretend life is tidy. Day 17 is titled Life Is Not a Bed of Roses, Day 27 is about resisting fear, Day 29 asks to be pulled through, Day 30 is a prayer for recovery and Day 40 is about enduring pain. If you are tired, anxious or grieving, you can open the day that matches where you are and pray it as your own.

sections.h2: For small groups and prayer partners
paras: The introduction calls the forty days a "sacred rhythm" and a "deliberate space to pause, reflect, and realign." Each day ends with questions that a group can talk through, from how fear has played a role in your spiritual life to which lessons we can learn from Israel's failures. A group can take a day at a time, or pick days by theme.

sections.h2: For anyone ready for a season of renewal
paras: The introduction walks through the forties of Scripture, from Moses on Mount Sinai to Jesus in the wilderness, and calls each one a threshold between what was and what would be. These forty days are not tied to Lent or any other season, so you can begin on any morning of the year. The author's hope is that you come out of them with a deeper sense of faith and a greater awareness of your need for God.

audience.headline: Forty days to pray, reflect and draw closer to God, one day at a time.
audience.body: For believers who want a daily quiet time, a personal season of renewal, or a prayer-and-journal devotional to share with a small group. Pastor Andre d'Arden opens every day with a passage from the New King James Version, follows it with a heartfelt prayer and a short reflection, and leaves room for you to answer and write your own prayer. A note on subjects: some of the prayers speak plainly about grief, broken hearts, illness, fear and pain, and one asks for relief from cancer. They are prayers, not treatment advice, and the book makes no medical claims.

quote.text: This journey is not just about getting through forty days—it's about what God does in you during them.
quote.cite: Pastor Andre d'Arden, Introduction

what_makes.title: What makes this book for people who want to pray with more confidence
paras: A guided devotional journal in forty short days. It grew straight out of a pastor's own prayer life, after a friend who loved hearing his prayers told him, "I would love to have a collection of them. Put them in a book."
Five things set it apart:
list: Every day has the same simple rhythm. A Scripture passage from the New King James Version, a prayer written out for you to pray along with, a brief reflection, then questions with lined space for your own answers.

It explains why forty. The introduction traces the number through Scripture: Moses on Mount Sinai, Israel in the wilderness, Elijah's trip to Horeb, the spies in the land and Jesus fasting in the wilderness, each one a threshold between what was and what would be.

It is honest about real life. The introduction says the devotional "reflects the unpredictability of life itself," so the days move from healing and wholeness to fear, frustration, recovery, feeling insignificant and enduring pain.
It teaches by example. If you have ever wondered how to pray, forty finished prayers show how a believer can thank, ask, confess and trust, and each day invites you to write one of your own.

It is not tied to a season. The days are "not bound to a particular liturgical season like Lent," though they echo Lent's call to reflection, repentance and renewal, so you can start on any morning of the year.

paras: The prayer begins, "Lord God, in a universe that seems so immense, it is easy to feel insignificant." It answers by reminding the reader of being "precious in Your sight" and "created in Your image: to shine in the world, to reflect Your love and character." The passage beside it is Psalm 8:3-4, which asks what man is that God is mindful of him. The questions are simple and personal: how important are God's children to Him, and what would you say to Him about the depth of His love for you?

stories.h2: Day 27: Resistance to the Effect of Fear
paras: This day sits beside 2 Timothy 1:7, "For God has not given us a spirit of fear, but of power and of love and of a sound mind." The prayer asks to live "not in fear, but in faith," and is careful about what it is not asking: "We are not asking You to allow us to walk on serpents or coals of fire without harm, not even that. We are simply asking to live our lives in peace, without fear." The reflection that follows asks how fear has played a role in your spiritual life and what tools you need to overcome it.

The last day pairs James 1:2-4 with a prayer for hard times: "Heavenly Father, when times are difficult and heartbreaking, I need to remember that You are the One who strengthens me." It closes on hope, "The darkness of night makes the dawn of morning brighter," and a reflection that admits it is not easy to consider trials a joyful experience. The questions ask whether there is a trial you need to thank God for and whether the Scriptures have given you a way to endure.

author.bio: Pastor Andre d'Arden writes as a pastor whose own prayers are the heart of this book. A friend who loved hearing him pray asked him to put his prayers in a book, and he did, with contributions from his wife that he says helped bring it to completion. He grounds every day in Scripture, opening each one with a passage from the New King James Version, and he prays that the book will be a blessing to many others.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: It started with encouragement. The author writes that "One of the most inspiring gifts we can receive is an unexpected word of encouragement." A friend told him how much she enjoyed hearing his prayers, and then added something he could not forget: "I would love to have a collection of them. Put them in a book." He says that "planted the seed for this project."

He wrote it with a clear hope for readers. "I pray this book will be a blessing to many others," he writes, "just as their words were a blessing to me." In the introduction he describes what he wants these days to do: help you "gain a greater awareness of your need for God" and "embrace a life marked by humility, self-discipline, and trust."

faq.q: What is Forty Days of Prayer and Reflection?
faq.a: A guided devotional journal by Pastor Andre d'Arden: forty days, each with New King James Version Scripture, a prayer, a short reflection and questions with lined space to write.

faq.q: How do I use it?
faq.a: Take one day at a time. Read the passage, pray the written prayer, read the reflection, then answer the questions and write your own prayer in the lined space. The introduction asks you not to rush.

faq.q: Is it a book of Bible verses for encouragement?
faq.a: Every day is paired with a Scripture passage, and the book is meant to encourage, but it is a prayer journal rather than a list of verses. Each passage comes with a prayer, a reflection and questions.

faq.q: Can it help me learn how to pray?
faq.a: It models forty prayers, in a pastor's own words, for different needs, and every day asks you to write a prayer of your own. It is a good companion if you want to learn how to pray by praying alongside someone.

faq.q: Does it pray for healing?
faq.a: Healing and wholeness of mind, body and soul is the theme of Day 1, and Day 30 is a prayer for recovery. These are prayers of petition and trust. The book is not medical advice and makes no medical claims.

faq.q: Does it speak to fear?
faq.a: Yes. Day 1 includes Isaiah 41, "Fear not, for I am with you," and Day 27 is devoted to resisting the effect of fear, beside the verse that God has not given us a spirit of fear.

faq.q: Is it about finding strength in God?
faq.a: Strength runs through the book. Day 33 pairs Isaiah 40:31 with a prayer to "rest in Your loving arms," and Day 40 asks God to be the One who strengthens in times of pain.

faq.q: Is it tied to Lent, and can a group use it?
faq.a: It is not tied to Lent or any liturgical season, though it echoes Lent's call to reflection and renewal. It suits a personal season of renewal, a daily quiet time or a small group.

audience.headline: Two thousand years of church history, told through the people who lived it.
audience.body: For adult Sunday school classes, small groups and any believer who has found history dull. Julie Boone walks from Pentecost to the iPhone century in twenty-four chapters, with martyrs, monks, scholars, reformers and missionaries, and every chapter ends with Bible study and questions you can talk through together.

quote.text: History can be eye-opening, as when we realize that only 1 in 10 people living in Rome in Jesus' lifetime knew how to read, and that books (including the Bible itself) have been widely available to nurture faith for less than six hundred years.
quote.cite: From Jesus 'til Now, the introduction

what_makes.title: What makes this book for readers who want church history they can actually enjoy
paras: A church history that reads like stories, and a study guide that sends you back to Scripture. It begins in the world of the Bible, which the introduction says is "geographically a good bit larger than the typical Holy Land tourist imagines," and it keeps going until now.
Five things set it apart:
list: It is told through people. Each chapter details a period of church history "and the people who were notable in it," from Origen and Augustine to John Newton, William Wilberforce and John Woolman.

It is honest about failure. The introduction calls church history "a story of great faith lived out in challenges, of great fears overcome by faith, and sometimes – when we're honest -- of great failures by those who thought they were trying to do God's will."
It ends every chapter with something to do. Questions for thought and discussion, a Bible passage to study, questions for your response, and internet keywords to search if you want to go further.

It is built for a group. The questions compare the historic issues in the chapter with issues "that may be experienced in the contemporary church," which makes it easy to use in a class or small group.
It is a mother's life work. Julie Boone spent much of her life developing the text, and her son, Mark Boone, saw it into print after she passed into glory.

sections.h2: For adult Sunday school classes and small groups
paras: Each chapter gives a class what it needs in one sitting: a stretch of history to read, discussion questions to talk through, a Bible passage and a personal response. The questions ask things like what you would say to a person of another faith about the value of the meetings at your church, and what your church does with the money it collects.

sections.h2: For believers who have found history dull
paras: If school made church history feel like names and dates, this is a different kind of book. You will meet Origen, whose mother hid his clothes to keep him from rushing out to be martyred, and Augustine, who first went to church to study a preacher's speaking style. Alexander the Great bows to a high priest in the prologue. The details are the point.

sections.h2: For readers who want real stories of martyrs, monks, scholars, crusaders and missionaries
paras: The chapters range from the early church and its persecutions to the Nicene Creed, from monasteries to the Crusades, from the plague and the mystics to the Reformation and the missionaries who went to the far corners of the world. A long chapter on "Amazing Grace" follows John Newton, William Wilberforce and John Woolman, and the closing chapters bring the story into the iPhone century.

sections.h2: For readers who want to know how the creeds and the Reformation came about
paras: Chapter Three explains the decisions made at the Nicene Convention and how the Nicene Creed was written, and why the Apostles' Creed became even more popular. Chapter Fourteen, The Fabulous Sixteenth, follows Martin Luther from his early years and shows how Bibles in the language of the people could at last be bought legally. The book is plain that the reformers wanted change long before it came.

paras: In the 21st century world, many of us live as if the only history that matters is the one we've seen personally. That can narrow our frame of reference dangerously when it's time to consider how best to live as people of faith in our own time.

stories.h2: The king who bowed to a priest
paras: When Alexander the Great reached Jerusalem, the high priest was frantic with fear that he would destroy the city. That night he saw in a dream the gates open, the people in white and the priests in their robes, and he asked everyone to recreate the scene. Alexander stopped his army, rode up alone, dismounted and bowed. Asked by an officer why he, before whom people showed adoration, would honor a priest, he replied that he honored, not the priest, but the God the priest worshiped. Jerusalem was not attacked.

Origen was born in Egypt around A.D. 185 and tutored by his father, and he learned to quote long passages from the Bible when he was only a boy. He asked so many questions that his father reproved him for being too inquisitive, yet "secretly thanked God for such a child." When Origen was seventeen, his father was arrested and killed because of his faith. The youth tried to join his father in death, but his mother kept him home by hiding his clothes. He went on to head a Christian school in Alexandria and to compile the Hexapla, a massive book of Bible translations set in parallel columns.

Augustine preferred the theater to church, and his mother, Monica, prayed and wept almost continuously for him. She asked a priest to talk with him, and he answered, "Leave me and go in peace. It cannot be that the son of those tears should be lost." In Milan, Augustine began attending Ambrose's church only to study his eloquence, then found he could not ignore the meaning. The book prints Augustine's own account of weeping beneath a fig tree: "How long shall I go on saying 'tomorrow, tomorrow'? Why not now?" Then a child's voice nearby chanted, "Take it and read, take it and read."

author.bio: Julie Boone spent much of her life developing From Jesus 'til Now, a storyteller's timeline of the Christian church written to help believers learn its history and draw lessons for church life today. why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The book exists so that readers can "both learn about the history of God's church and discover lessons from church history for church life today." In his introduction, Mark Boone writes that "helping you to find, reflect on, and make good use of those lessons is a primary goal of this book."

The conclusion is humble about it. "People usually think the time in which they live has unique challenges never before overcome," it begins, and it adds that monasteries, the Reformation and revivals "solved some problems and created others." Its closing hope is: "By God's grace, may each of us live closer to God's purposes for our own times."

faq.q: What is From Jesus 'til Now about?
faq.a: A guided walk through two thousand years of the Christian church, from Pentecost to the iPhone century, told through real people in twenty-four chapters.

faq.q: Is it a Bible study guide?
faq.a: It is church history with study tools. Every chapter ends with questions for thought and discussion, a Bible passage to study, questions for your response and internet keywords to search for further study.

faq.q: Does it work for a small group Bible study?
faq.a: Yes. How to Use This Book says the questions compare the issues in each chapter with issues that may be experienced in the contemporary church, which makes each chapter easy to use for one meeting of a class or small group.

faq.q: Does it cover the book of Acts and the early Christians?
faq.a: Yes. Chapter One, The Genesis of the Church, starts with Luke's account in Acts, from Jesus' last visit with his disciples to Pentecost, and Chapters Two and Three follow the early Christians through rumors, persecution and, at last, power.

faq.q: Does it tell the story of Saint Augustine?
faq.a: Yes. Chapter Five tells how Augustine preferred the theater to church, how his mother prayed for him, and how he went to hear Ambrose preach in Milan and was converted.

faq.q: What does it say about the Nicene Creed?
faq.a: Chapter Three explains the decisions made at the Nicene Convention and how the Nicene Creed was written. It adds that the unity it set forth did not last long, and that the Apostles' Creed became even more popular.

faq.q: Does it cover the Protestant Reformation?
faq.a: Yes. Chapter Fourteen, The Fabulous Sixteenth, tells of the reformers before the Reformation and of Martin Luther, from his early years on. Later chapters follow the changes that came after it.

faq.q: Does it cover the Crusades?
faq.a: Yes. Chapter Eleven is The Crusades. It tells why people joined them and does not soften what happened: "Tragic is far too small a word for the crusades. They created hate and destruction."

faq.q: How is each chapter organized?
faq.a: Each chapter tells the history of a period and its notable people, then offers questions for thought and discussion, a Bible study passage, questions for your response and internet keywords to search for further study.

sections.h2: For busy people who say "I don't have time to cook"
paras: The author has an answer for you, and it is arithmetic. "The process of preparing and eating a meal takes the same amount of time whether you cook it yourself, wait in a drive through, or go out to eat." Her advice is to choose one dish to master and fill in the rest with store-bought sides, and she shows you how little a good weeknight dinner needs.

sections.h2: For beginners and self-described kitchen failures
paras: If your dinner has never looked like the photo, this book is on your side. The author defines "failure" in a way that lets you off the hook, then points you to simple recipes you can make from the start. The glossary, the equipment tips and the notes on prepping fruits, vegetables and meats are written for people just beginning to expand their cooking skills.

sections.h2: For home cooks who want easy recipes for weeknights and company
paras: Weekend guests who arrive on Friday after work, kids who bring friends home for dinner, or a table planned for four that ends up serving eight: the author has fed all of them. You will find casseroles, soups, Southern mains and a large chapter of appetizers and dips, plus tips for keeping food fresh, using leftovers on purpose and throwing away less.

sections.h2: For anyone who cooks to show love
paras: The book closes its opening chapters with Feed People with Love. The author grew up on a farm watching her grandmother cook three big meals a day, and she writes that feeding family is a point of pride and a love language. She reminds you that Jesus cooked fish on a fire to feed His followers, and she asks you to say a prayer for success and trust God to help you succeed. Whether you cook for yourself, a family or a houseful of guests, the book treats each meal as a way to care for someone.

what_makes.title: What makes this book for busy people and beginner cooks
paras: A 319-page, full-color cookbook of everyday recipes that "are simple and have only a few steps," with ingredients that are "inexpensive and easy to buy." It is as much a cooking teacher as a recipe book.
Five things set it apart:
list: It starts where beginners start. Two short chapters answer "But I've Always Been a Kitchen Failure!" and "But I Don't Have Time to Cook!" before a single recipe appears, and a glossary of cooking terms waits at the back.

It covers the whole week. Main dishes, casseroles, Southern favorites, pasta, egg dishes, soups and stews, sides, breads, candies, cookies, cakes, pies and cobblers, and a long chapter of appetizers and dips.

It gives you ways to bend each recipe. Many recipes carry time-saving tips, cooking-for-one tips and variations, and a section teaches you to create your own recipe variations by testing an idea on a single portion.
It plans for company. There is a section on how to stretch dinner for unexpected guests and how to enhance a boxed cake mix, drawn from years of feeding a full house.
It is rooted in faith and love. The author reminds you that Jesus cooked fish on a fire to feed His followers, and that "God cares to feed all the people He loves."

details.Author: Toni R. Young-Huber
details.Binding: Paperback (perfect bound) and hardback, color interior

paras: The cookbook began when the author, then a traveling nurse in North Carolina, taught a coworker how to cook. He wanted to break the fast-food habit, so he told her what he wanted to make and they made it together. He did all the work and she helped him succeed. When he mastered a baked-salmon main course, she told him, "Go buy some frozen peas and Uncle Ben's ninety-second rice, and that's your dinner!" It is the book's whole philosophy in one line: master one dish, then buy the rest.

stories.h2: A dish that does not look like the picture
paras: The chapter for self-described kitchen failures begins by asking whether your dish failed if it does not look like the one in a cooking magazine. Her answer is no. She tells readers that "Perfection is elusive and appearances are just that—appearances," and she makes her point with a tomato: "Not every tomato is worthy of a picture on the cover of a magazine, but every tomato adds flavor to tomato sauce." The lesson is to give yourself grace, learn a few terms and techniques, and grow as you go.

stories.h2: Chicken and dumplings, and cooking for one
paras: Chicken and Dumplings is the first recipe in the book, a simple stew for cold fall days that the author likes to make from scratch. When she taught a friend to make it, the hardest part was recognizing when the noodle dough was the right texture. Once you have felt it, the author says, "you'll never forget how to make this dough perfectly." A time-saving tip shows how to cook one chicken and use it three ways, in the dumplings, a chicken salad and a simple soup, and a cooking-for-one tip says that if you make a full pot, "your coworkers will love you."

author.bio: Toni R. Young-Huber grew up on a farm watching her grandmother cook three big meals a day. In her culture, she writes, feeding family is a point of pride and a love language, so cooking for and with other people comes naturally to her. She has worked as a traveling nurse in North Carolina, where she spent many Sunday afternoons teaching a coworker to cook American foods. She lived for a time in the foothills above Denver, where weekend and weeknight guests were common and she learned to stretch a meal. For her, cooking can be therapeutic, and she encourages every cook to give themselves grace when they make mistakes.

faq.q: What is Get Out of the Fast (Food) Lane! about?
faq.a: It is a warm, practical cookbook of simple, inexpensive recipes with only a few steps, written to help busy people and beginners cook at home instead of using the drive-through.

faq.q: Does it have family dinner ideas?
faq.a: Yes. It offers main dishes such as Chicken and Dumplings, Baked Salmon, Meatloaf and Chicken Piccata, casseroles like Five-Ingredient Chicken Pot Pie, Southern favorites, pasta and more, and a section on stretching dinner for unexpected guests.

faq.q: Does it have beef stew and chicken recipes?
faq.a: Yes. The Soups and Stews section includes Guinness Beef Stew and Beef Stroganoff, and the book has many chicken dishes, among them Chicken and Dumplings, Chicken Piccata, Baked Chicken with Gravy, Southern Fried Chicken, Chicken Noodle Soup and Chicken Tortilla Soup. It is a general home-cooking book, not a single-category one.

faq.q: Are there soup recipes, such as French onion or tomato?
faq.a: Yes. Soups and Stews has fourteen recipes, including French Onion Soup, Creamy Tomato Soup, New England Clam Chowder, Roasted Broccoli Soup and Chicken and Wild Rice Soup.

faq.q: Does it include casserole and quiche recipes?
faq.a: Yes. There is a Main Dish Casseroles section with Five-Ingredient Chicken Pot Pie, Ground Beef and Ravioli Casserole, Pizza Casserole and Ham and Beans, and an Egg Main Dishes section with No-Crust Quiche and a Breakfast Vegetable Tart.

faq.q: Is it a beginner cookbook?
faq.a: Yes. It is written for beginner and home cooks, many recipes carry time-saving tips and cooking-for-one tips, and a glossary of cooking terms is included.

faq.q: Is it a Christian cookbook?
faq.a: Yes. It is rooted in the conviction that cooking is a love language and that God cares to feed all the people He loves.

faq.q: Can I make the recipes my own?
faq.a: Yes. A section called "Creating Your Own Recipe Variations" encourages you to scoop a single portion into a bowl and test an idea there, so you do not risk the whole dish, and many recipes list suggested variations.

sections.h2: For every believer who has prayed the sinner's prayer
paras: The author says it plainly: "Every person who prays the sinner's prayer needs this book." If you thought you had done everything you needed to do to be a Christian and still feel a gap, this book is written to meet you there.

sections.h2: For pastors and ministry leaders
paras: The introduction says that "Congregations need pastors who help them get to the point." The author wrote as a pastor who served three churches and who was dismissed from a church he helped start, and who then spent years learning what the point looks like in ministry.

sections.h2: For couples, parents and students
paras: "Before anyone gets married, they should be required to read this book." The author also writes that "Parents should lead their children through the principles in this book" and says that when his own children were small, he and his wife taught them how to get to the point.

sections.h2: For anyone struggling with addiction or settling for less
paras: "Anyone struggling with any addiction needs to read this book," the author writes. The book is not a recovery program, and it makes no medical claims. It is an invitation to live in a presence that, he says, fills a person with the Giver and not only the gifts.

audience.headline: You can be a Christian, even a pastor, and still totally miss the point.
audience.body: For every believer who has prayed the sinner's prayer, pastors and ministry leaders who want their congregations to get to the point, couples preparing for marriage, parents, students and anyone who senses they have been settling for less. Kevin White makes one case from Scripture across ten chapters: the whole point of life is to live moment by moment in the presence of God, and in His presence you will find every guidance and provision you will ever need, today. A note on subjects: the author tells of his own season of burnout and fear of failure and of being dismissed from a church. It is one pastor's testimony and a teaching book, not counseling or medical advice, and it is told without graphic detail. If a hard season is weighing on you, please talk with a trusted pastor, counselor or physician, and if you are in crisis, contact your local emergency services or a crisis line.

quote.text: Every guidance and provision you will ever need can be found right now, today, in the presence of God.
quote.cite: Get to the Point, Chapter 10

what_makes.title: What makes this book for people who want the point of life
paras: A short book with a single idea, argued from Scripture and from the author's own story. He prayed the sinner's prayer at ten, answered a call into ministry as a teenager, served three churches and helped plant a new church, and then discovered, he says, that "I had reached the top of the ladder only to realize it was leaning up against the wrong wall."
Five things set it apart:
list: It says the point plainly. "God's whole point is giving you His presence." Not religion, not ministry, not even salvation by itself, but living with God moment by moment.

It names what the point is not. A chapter titled Salvation Is Not the Point argues that salvation serves the point, and the author writes that "God could have given you a gift, but He filled you with the Giver instead."
It follows the point through your why, your what and your how. Three chapters show how the point shapes your reasons, your work and your methods.
It uses real-life stories and a climbing metaphor. The author weaves in the challenge of climbing Mount Everest, and the idea of a ladder leaning against the wrong wall.
It is built to be taught. It speaks to children, pastors, couples, students and people struggling with addiction, and it opens with a foreword by the founder of South Mountain Christian Camp.

details.Title: Get to the Point
details.Subtitle: Every Guidance or Provision You Will Ever Need Can Be Found Today in God's Presence
details.Author: Kevin White
details.Binding: Paperback (perfect bound, matte laminate), black and white interior

paras: In the introduction, the author tells his own story in short steps, each one ending in the same line. He prayed the sinner's prayer at ten and was baptized. He became a husband, a minister, a father and a pastor of three churches. In the third year of a new church he helped plant, he was dismissed, devastated and crushed. "I was a husband, father, fired Christian pastor, and I was totally missing the point." "Two months later, God flew me over 8,000 miles away to India." A short ten-day mission trip became a life-changing experience, and in India, he writes, "I saw the point. It was clear as day!"

stories.h2: Climbing Everest and the wrong ladder
paras: The book uses the world's highest mountain as a picture. It describes the danger of the climb: "At 29,035 feet, Everest's summit has approximately one-third the air pressure that exists at sea level." It also tells how George Mallory answered the question of why people climb it: "Because it's there!" Then it turns to a ladder. "We climb ladders called careers, marriage, family, parenting only to find ourselves at the bottom of ladders called divorce, empty nesting, and retirement." Its answer: "Once you climb to the top of the ladder of God's presence, you won't need to climb any other ladder for the rest of your life."

In the chapter on how the point determines your what, the author describes learning to rest. For years he went into God's presence looking for an assignment, afraid that if he were not always busy he would be lazy. What he sensed instead was a call to simply be there. "God was teaching me that we are human 'Beings,' not human 'Doings.' It was a real struggle for me." He writes that it took him years "to stop fighting God for His gifts instead of receiving Him as the gift."

author.bio: Kevin White is a pastor who gave his life to Jesus at age ten and answered God's call into Christian ministry during his senior year of high school. After college he served at three churches before helping to start a new church in Cary, North Carolina. When that church dismissed him in its third year, a ten-day mission trip to India became the turning point of his life, as the pastors and churches there taught him to passionately pursue the presence of God. He is the founder and executive director of Global Hope India and has called Cary home for thirty years.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The author's reason is in his dedication: "That's the whole point!" He dedicates the book "to every pastor, teacher, worship leader, and believer around the world who faithfully pursues God's presence first, and then helps others live, moment by moment, in the presence of God."

He wrote it because, he says, he wishes it had been handed to him years ago: "Let me apologize in advance that it has taken someone this long to help you understand God's whole point and how to get to it."

faq.q: What is Get to the Point about?
faq.a: It makes one case from Scripture: the whole point of life is to live moment by moment in the presence of God, and in His presence you will find every guidance and provision you will ever need, today.

faq.q: What are the ten chapters?
faq.a: They are, in order: The Point; The Point of the Point; How to Get to the Point; Salvation Is Not the Point; The Power of the Point; The Point Explains Everything; The Point Determines Your Why; The Point Determines Your What; The Point Determines Your How; and Get to the Point. A conclusion, I Want Eden Back!, follows.

faq.q: What does the book say is the purpose of life?
faq.a: Living moment by moment in the presence of God. The author writes that "Engaging God's presence in you is the whole point of life," and that the point determines your why, your what and your how.

faq.q: Is Get to the Point a book for pastors and church leaders?
faq.a: Yes, among others. Kevin White wrote it as a pastor who was dismissed from a church he helped plant, and it is written for pastors who want to help their congregations get to the point, as well as for believers, parents, couples and students.

faq.q: Is it about intimacy with God?
faq.a: In its own words, it is about connection and presence. Chapter 1 says Adam and Eve "shared an intimate connection with God," and the conclusion says the author wants "Eden back today." It does not teach a technique for intimacy, it argues for a daily life in His presence.

faq.q: Does it teach a prayer life or listening to God?
faq.a: Yes, within the larger argument. He writes that "Prayer is an ongoing conversation we have with God while living moment by moment in His presence," and suggests talking to God a third of the time and listening the other two thirds.

faq.q: Why does the book say salvation is not the point?
faq.a: One chapter argues that salvation serves the point of living in God's presence. The author writes that God "could have given you a gift, but He filled you with the Giver instead."

faq.q: What happened in India?
faq.a: Two months after the church dismissed him, a ten-day mission trip to India, more than 8,000 miles away, was where Kevin White says he first saw the point, taught by the pastors and churches there to pursue God's presence.

faq.q: Is it a recovery program or counseling?
faq.a: No. It is a teaching book from one pastor's life and from Scripture. If you are struggling with addiction or your mental health, please also seek help from a trained professional, and contact a crisis line if you are in danger.

audience.body: For believers who want to see God's promises to give in one place, readers who struggle to believe God wants to give good gifts to them, and pastors and small groups praying over big needs who want a Scripture-based list. Kevin White and his team spent months collecting every verse in which God promises to give something, and GIFTS publishes that list in the New Living Translation, organized into land, life, family, increase, empowerment and everything. A note on subjects: the book speaks about money, financing and needs, and about prayer for healing, land and provision. It is a Scripture list with the author's teaching, not financial, legal or medical advice, and it does not promise any particular outcome. The author is clear that it is not about controlling God.

what_makes.title: What makes this book for people who want to see God's promises to give
paras: A book that reads like a discovery tour. The author came home from two weeks in India and Nepal, where he and local leaders prayed over hundreds of millions of dollars of human need, and he says God told him: "Now, I want you to go write down everything in my Word that I promise to GIVE."
Five things set it apart:
list: It is the list itself. The author writes, "This book publishes the list of everything God promises to GIVE us in the Bible. Here is your opportunity to see and hear for yourself the very Word of God."
It is organized so you can find a promise. Six categories hold the verses: land, life, family, increase, empowerment and everything.
It reports three discoveries from the study. There are more verses about God giving land than anything else, the word YOU runs all through God's gifts, and the word ASK appears alongside them.
It is honest about what it is not. "This book doesn't revolve around the notions of entitlement or attempting to control God," and a genuine gift is "undeserved, without any strings attached."
It ends with dependence. The last two chapters, Ask and Depend, turn the list into prayer and a way of living.

sections.h2: For believers who want God's promises in one place
paras: If you have read the Bible and still missed how often God promises to give, this book gathers the verses. The author counts the word gift about 80 times in the New Living Translation, and the word give about 1,073 times. The promises are grouped into land, life, family, increase, empowerment and everything, so you can read one kind at a time.

sections.h2: For readers who struggle to believe God wants to give to them
paras: The book speaks to that doubt directly. "God didn't make any mistake, nor is He a God of confusion. God doesn't say 'you' but mean 'them' or 'others.'" He asks you to read the word YOU in each promise as written.

sections.h2: For pastors and small groups praying over big needs
paras: The author's own prayers in India and Nepal included land, buildings, salaries for pastors, food for the poor, homes for orphans, Bible colleges and water projects. The verses are grouped by category, so a group can read through one set at a time, and the book asks you to read slowly: "Don't skip or rush through the scriptures."

sections.h2: For anyone learning to pray with expectancy
paras: The chapter on asking is careful. "Jesus is not saying that believers always get what they ask for," the author writes, and wrong motives hinder answers to prayer. Then it turns to comfort: "Remember that He hears you." The last chapter, Depend, asks you to live each day relying on what God gives rather than on your own effort.

stories.h2: Hundreds of millions of dollars of need
paras: The introduction tells how the author had just finished writing his fifth book and, with his company not yet a year old and living month to month, felt called to leave it in God's hands and go to India and Nepal. "We had no choice but to depend on the GIFTS of God daily for our very survival." In the hills of Northeast India and Nepal, leaders kept asking him to pray over needs too big for any person to fund: land, buildings, healing, food for widows, homes for orphans. "Any human soul would be totally crushed and devastated if it weren't for the revelation: The Father's going to GIVE it!" It was also there that God told him, "You're thinking too small."

In the chapter on the word YOU, the author asks why God's promises so often say it. "All throughout the Bible, you will see God using the word YOU along with the word GIFTS. God says: I will GIVE to YOU." He counts how often the word appears in the English Standard Version and the New King James Version, and he writes: "YOU means you. Don't accept some words but reject others." The chapter pairs it with a promise from Jeremiah 29:12: "when you pray, I will listen."

In the conclusion, the author writes that "every day is Christmas." Jesus "isn't a tiny baby in a manger but has been imparted into every believer through the Holy Spirit," and "Emmanuel means God with us, but some days, we live like God came and then left." For him the greatest gift is God Himself, and he asks readers to live each day with the expectancy of a child at Christmas: "discovering God's GIFTS in every direction you turn."

author.bio: Kevin White leads Spirit Media, a publishing company he has trusted God to sustain since its cash-strapped first year. Since his first trip to India in 1998 he has entered India fifty-five times in twenty-five years, and his first trip to Nepal came while teaching the message of his fifth book, Only God Works. His first book is Audacious Generosity. On mission he speaks in the hills of Northeast India and Nepal, praying with leaders over human need. GIFTS grew from God's instruction to him to write down everything His Word promises to give.

publisher.about: Spirit Media Publishing is a Christian publishing and marketing company with a vision to reveal our Father's heart to all nations. It offers full-service book creation and publishing in paperback, hardback, digital and audiobook formats, along with children's titles, compact Express Books, website design and SEO, and podcast and video production. We are honored to publish Kevin White's book of God's promises to give.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The author's reason comes from what he saw on the trip. "I'm convinced God took me over 8,000 miles away to India and Nepal to rub my nose in all He desires to GIVE."

He offers the book as an invitation to "think differently, pray differently, live differently and GIVE differently." And he wants readers to know where the gift ends: "The GIFT is experiencing God. It's knowing His Word, heart, will, and way."

faq.q: What is GIFTS about?
faq.a: A book by Kevin White that publishes every Bible verse where God promises to give, organized into land, life, family, increase, empowerment and everything, with chapters on You, Ask and Depend.

faq.q: Is it about God's blessings?
faq.a: It is about God's promises to give, which the Bible often calls blessings. The exact words "God's blessings" are not the book's frame, and it is not a collection of blessings or benedictions. It is a list of promised gifts with the author's teaching on each.

faq.q: Does the book show God's goodness?
faq.a: It shows God as a good Giver. The author builds on Jesus' words, "So if you sinful people know how to GIVE good GIFTS to your children, how much more will your heavenly Father GIVE good GIFTS to those who ask him." The book does not argue about goodness in the abstract. It lets the verses speak.

faq.q: What does it say about grace?
faq.a: It says a gift is not earned: "A genuine GIFT is undeserved, without any strings attached, and without any manipulation of return." It is not a study of grace as a topic, but the idea runs through the chapters.

faq.q: Does it teach that God will give us whatever we ask?
faq.a: No. It says "This book doesn't revolve around the notions of entitlement or attempting to control God," and that sometimes "the true GIFT lies in trusting God enough to ask, regardless of whether we receive."

faq.q: Does it show God as Father?
faq.a: Yes. The refrain of the book is "The Father's going to GIVE it!" The author builds on Jesus' words about how much more "your heavenly Father" will give good gifts to those who ask him.

faq.q: Does it cover God's provision?
faq.a: Yes. The Increase chapter gathers the verses where God promises provision, from rain to harvest, and the Everything chapter includes Jesus' promise in Luke 12:31: "he will GIVE you everything you need." The author adds that the book does not focus only on material gifts.

faq.q: Does it cover the promise of land to Abraham?
faq.a: Land is the category with the most verses, the author says, and the chapter quotes the land promises to Abraham and his descendants and says the promise rests on faith. It is not a study of the covenant, it is a list of what God promised to give.

sections.h2: For readers who want to see God at work in a life that began with nothing
paras: The author says plainly that he had nothing special to offer: "I truly felt there was nothing special about it." His story is told so that you can see what God did with empty hands. One of its last lines puts it this way: "Empty hands don't matter so long as you have God's dream in your heart."

sections.h2: For supporters of missions and children's ministry in India
paras: If you give, pray for or visit ministries in India, this book is the story behind one of them. It shows how LIGHT Home began with one boy, how provision arrived week by week, and how the home grew into schools, feeding programs and a hospital project. Its last chapters invite readers to take part.

sections.h2: For readers who want to understand what education changes
paras: The conclusion argues that education is "one of the most powerful tools for driving positive change in society" and says that "only a few Dalit children are given the opportunity to be educated." The author writes from experience: he was the first in his family to go to school.

sections.h2: For anyone who feels unqualified
paras: The author opens by admitting he failed English in school, and he wrote this book in English anyway. He studied under a street light, worked part time as a photographer to pay for college, and could not afford to study further. When he started LIGHT Home he had one boy, no regular support and, as the subtitle says, empty hands. If you think your story is too small for God to use, start with Chapter 1: "I truly felt there was nothing special about it."

audience.headline: Born with nothing in an Indian village, he followed God's dream for orphaned children.
audience.body: For readers who want to see God at work in a life that began with nothing, supporters of missions and children's ministry in India who want the story behind LIGHT, and anyone who wants to understand what education changes for Dalit children. Elisha Chowtapalli tells it in his own words, across thirteen chapters, from a one-room mud home to a children's home, schools, a feeding program and a hospital for mothers. A note on subjects: this is a memoir of poverty and of caste discrimination in India, written by someone who lived it. It speaks of hunger, deaths in families, children who beg or work instead of going to school, and, briefly, of violence and abuse that children face. It is one man's account and testimony, not a history of the caste system, and it is told without graphic detail.

quote.text: Though I am part of this story, it's not really about me. Mainly, it is about the One who created me, who called me, who guided me, who gave me the vision, who entrusted me with work, and who is using me for His glory in India.
quote.cite: God's Dream, Preface

what_makes.title: What makes this book for people who want to see God work through an empty-handed life
paras: A memoir in thirteen chapters and a conclusion, by the founder and president of LIGHT Society. He was born into a Dalit Christian family in a remote village in Andhra Pradesh, South India, and he insists the book is about God, not himself.
Five things set it apart:
list: It starts with real poverty and does not soften it. His father was a quarry laborer paid about one U.S. dollar a day, the family lived in one room with a palm-leaf roof, and there was no electricity in the home until he was nineteen.

It explains what it means to be a Dalit from the inside. A full chapter, Untouchables of India, includes a section on the caste system, and the author says his friends urged him to write about his people so the rest of the world could understand.

It follows one calling to concrete results. From a prayer and a first child in 2006, the work grew into LIGHT Home, an English medium school, a tailoring training program, a feeding program for the elderly, a Bible school, church building and rural healthcare.
It is honest about betrayal and forgiveness. One short section tells of a painful email that questioned his integrity while he was traveling, and of how God helped him forgive.
It ends with the children. The conclusion speaks of children's dreams, of what education can change, and of a sponsorship plan for readers who want to help.

paras: In the section Our Humble Home, the author describes the one-room house his family lived in. "The roof was made of palm leaves and the walls made of mud, with no proper floor." When the rains came, the family moved everything to the one corner that still had a roof. There was no electricity. "I use to study under a street light pole at night where I could get some light to study." He remembers the group study with other children as fun at the time, and anger at his poverty came later. "We got electricity when I was nineteen years old."

stories.h2: One boy, three children, no stove
paras: LIGHT Home began on August 1, 2006, with one boy, and in a week there were three children and no regular support. He kept praying, and in the days that followed gifts arrived from friends in Australia. The early months were hard. "My mother used to cook food with firewood. It used to produce a lot of smoke but she never complained and didn't give up." For a time there was no running water. "My father took the responsibility of bringing water to us from the village tap and well." He carried it on his head, and the author writes that he did it "with great joy as it was part of God's dream."

stories.h2: A woman who had not eaten
paras: On January 1, 2008, the author was praying for the new year when a passage from Matthew 25 came to his mind. Then a woman who "hadn't eaten for the last few days" came to his office and begged for food, and she came again each day. He realized that this was how God was sharing His dream: to look after widows and old people who were dying for lack of food. Land was bought, a building went up, and in February 2009 the feeding of fifty widows and old people began. "Though we had a place to give food we didn't have the finances to feed them on a regular basis." He started anyway, "just looking to Jesus for guidance."

author.bio: Elisha Chowtapalli was born into an impoverished Dalit Christian family in a remote village in Andhra Pradesh, South India, and was the first in his family to go to school. He followed God's call to serve the orphaned, poor and needy children of India. He is the founder and president of LIGHT Society, pastors a church and is building a hospital where at-risk mothers can safely deliver their babies.
