why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The author's reason is stated at the start. "It is my sincere prayer and hope that God will speak to you through this book to be able to see the need and to take action together to show His love to the orphan, poor, and needy children of India."

He ends with the same invitation. "I do not know what God's dream is for your life, but I do know that He will speak to you and guide you in the right path." Sharing God's plan with LIGHT Society, he says, is already a blessing, and he asks readers to open their hearts to God: "May God speak to you!"

faq.q: What is God's Dream about?
faq.a: Elisha Chowtapalli's own account of a life that began in a poor Dalit village in South India and how, he says, God used it to build a children's home, schools, churches and a hospital.

faq.q: Does the book explain the caste system in India?
faq.a: It gives the author's view of it in a chapter on who the Dalits are, and says Dalits "are still in a hopeless situation with no hope for the future." It is a memoir, not a history of caste, and it tells one man's life among the people India once called untouchable.

faq.q: Where is it set? Is it about South India and Andhra Pradesh?
faq.a: Yes. The author was "born and brought up in an impoverished, Dalit Christian family in a remote village" in the state of Andhra Pradesh, South India, and has spent his life there.

faq.q: What is LIGHT?
faq.a: LIGHT Home cares for orphaned and needy children, alongside an English medium school, tailoring training, feeding the hungry, Light Bible School, church building and rural healthcare growing toward a hospital for at-risk mothers.

faq.q: Does it tell the story of feeding the hungry and of food for the poor?
faq.a: Yes. The section Feeding the Hungry tells how one passage in Matthew 25 and a hungry woman at his office became a feeding program for fifty widows and old people.

faq.q: Is it about the power of prayer?
faq.a: Prayer runs through it. When he wanted land for a garden beside the home and had no money, he writes, "My hands were empty, but I did know one thing – the power of prayer!" Gifts and land arrive again and again after he prays.

faq.q: What does it say about poverty in India?
faq.a: It speaks from the inside: a quarry wage of about a dollar a day, a family without electricity, children who beg or work instead of going to school. It is the author's testimony, not a statistical study.

faq.q: Can readers help?
faq.a: Yes. The book closes with a sponsorship plan and says "just the act of sharing God's plan with LIGHT Society will already be a huge blessing."

sections.h2: For mothers who have known this kind of loss
paras: If you are searching for language, this book may lend you some. The author describes the silent morning after, the milk that came in with no baby to feed, and the way she woke each day and thought of the same Friday. She writes that she did not soften it: "So I don't soften it." She also writes that she no longer needs to make people comfortable in her grief.

sections.h2: For fathers and the people who love them
paras: The author writes about her husband with respect. Their grief is the same loss from different places. She names it in a line that returns through the chapter: "Same loss. Different heart journey." The book does not instruct a father. It shows two people choosing, again and again, to stay beside each other.

sections.h2: For friends, family and caregivers who want to know what helps
paras: A chapter called I Can't Imagine turns a familiar sentence around, and a chapter called How Are You Doing? asks what that question costs. She writes that people who choose to sit in the valley with her are doing "holy work without knowing it." A reader who wants to sit with someone grieving will find what that can look like.

sections.h2: For anyone wrestling with why a child
paras: The book gives space to anger, numbness and the question itself. It does not say that a child's death makes sense. It says that Scripture rarely explains and often shows. The author asks her questions of God in the open and also writes: "There were moments I felt undeniably held."

audience.headline: A mother tells the story of her son, who lived twelve days, and finds a place for her grief to breathe.
audience.body: For mothers who have known the loss of a baby and are searching for language for the pain, for the fathers who stand beside them, and for anyone who has lost a child or loves someone who has. Meredith P. Nolasco writes in twenty-six short chapters, with dated entries addressed to her son, about a birth at twenty-seven weeks, the NICU, the night he died and the long months after. It offers companionship rather than answers. A note on subjects: this is a memoir of the death of a baby. It describes an emergency birth, intensive care, the moments of the baby's death, cremation, and the physical and emotional weight of grief, told honestly and without graphic detail. It is a mother's telling, not medical, counseling or mental health advice. If grief or trauma is overwhelming you, please contact a physician or licensed professional, and if you are in crisis or thinking about harming yourself, contact your local emergency services or a crisis line right away.

quote.text: I write for the mothers who have known this kind of loss, who are searching for language for a pain that feels unspeakable.
quote.cite: Hallelujah Even Here, the Introduction

what_makes.title: What makes this book for people carrying the loss of a baby
paras: This is the story of a baby boy born at twenty-seven weeks, weighing two pounds, six ounces. His nursery was finished and his name was chosen. Then an ordinary Sunday came apart in minutes. The author does not hand the reader a method. She tells what happened, what she asked God, and what she learned about holding sorrow and love in the same hands.
Five things set it apart:
list: It is a telling, not a guide. The Introduction says so in plain words: "This is not a guide on how to grieve."
It stays close to one family and one baby. The chapters follow the emergency, the NICU days, the one hour of holding him on Day 12, the night he died, and the months after.

It speaks to fathers and to the people around a grieving family. A chapter on what people say, a chapter on a marriage under strain and a chapter on mothering a toddler while mourning an infant sit beside the hospital chapters.
It brings the hardest question to God and does not tidy the answer. One chapter is titled Why a Child?, another Wrestling, another A Stubborn Hope.
Hope is present but not loud. The author writes that hope here "exists right alongside the pain" and is "sometimes steady, sometimes barely there, but real."

details.Title: Hallelujah Even Here
details.Subtitle: A Place for Your Grief to Breathe
details.Author: Meredith P. Nolasco
details.Binding: Paperback (perfect bound, matte laminate), black and white interior on creme paper

paras: Chapter 2 begins with a normal Sunday: church in the morning, waffles after, a soccer ball in the backyard. Then pain, then the floor, then sirens. At twenty-seven weeks, her water broke, and she writes that "What had been a normal Sunday unraveled in minutes." A nurse held the baby in until the surgical team could take her in for an emergency C-section. She whispered prayers, asking God to go where she could not. Then, she writes, "He was here. Tiny. Fighting. Alive."

Chapter 4 begins with a gift. The lead physician asked whether she would like to hold him, and for the first time she did, with him resting on her chest. "I felt my whole body exhale," she writes. She went home planning to spend the whole next day with him. She had no way to know, she writes, that "it would be the only time I would ever hold him full of life." That evening came three calls from the hospital. Chapter 4 ends in the NICU, in her arms, with the monitors fading and her son gone.

In Chapter 7, the author looks at a photograph and thinks that she should have kept a small piece of his hair. Days later, sitting in his room with his hospital blanket in her lap, she peels back a fold and finds "two small pieces of his hair, intertwined, caught in the fabric." She does not claim to understand why a child died. She does write that "God knew I would need that moment," and that He "left a couple for his mom." It is one of the book's smallest and most tender chapters.

author.bio: Meredith P. Nolasco is a wife, a mother and a coach who, with her husband, walks with people toward better health, helping them plan, prepare and build steady rhythms. Her faith in Jesus is personal, something she chose beyond the foundation she was raised in. In January 2026 her second son was born at twenty-seven weeks and lived for twelve days in the NICU. During those days she began writing to him, and those words grew into this book.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The author asks the question herself in the first paragraph and answers it plainly: "Because I have to." She writes of "A sacred urgency that settles in my chest and does not lift until I let the words out."
She says who the book is for and what it will not do. "This book is simply a telling," she writes, "Of our baby who lived." And her last sentence to the reader is the title: "Hallelujah even here."

faq.q: What is Hallelujah Even Here about?
faq.a: It is Meredith P. Nolasco's honest telling of her son, born at twenty-seven weeks, who lived twelve days in the NICU, and of grief, faith and the hardest question: why a child? It is told in twenty-six short chapters with dated entries written to her son.

faq.q: Is it a book about pregnancy and infant loss?
faq.a: Yes, in the sense that it follows one family through the birth and death of a baby who lived twelve days. The phrase pregnancy and infant loss does not appear in the interior, and the book does not claim to cover the subject broadly. The author also mentions an earlier miscarriage in one line. It is one mother's story, not a reference book.

faq.q: Is it about a premature baby?
faq.a: Yes. The baby was born at twenty-seven weeks after a sudden emergency, spent twelve days in the NICU and died there. The word premature does not appear in the book. It speaks of twenty-seven weeks, the NICU, monitors and a two pound, six ounce baby.

faq.q: Is it a guide on how to grieve?
faq.a: No. The Introduction says it is "not a roadmap, or a list of steps." It offers companionship and does not tie itself up neatly: "It's not a story that ties itself up neatly in the end."

faq.q: What does the book say about surrender to God?
faq.a: She describes surrender as "a posture. A choice," not giving up but "loosening my grip." Looking back, she would tell her earlier self to loosen her grip and to cling more to God's sovereignty than to statistics. She also writes that surrender "doesn't feel like peace" at first.

faq.q: Does it speak to healing after loss?
faq.a: It does not promise a cure or a timeline. It describes a slow, uneven mercy: shock that shelters, sorrow that arrives later, joy and grief that "stand side by side," and a purpose that grows quieter. The author writes that the hope she found "doesn't erase sorrow or rush healing."

faq.q: Is it for grieving parents, including fathers?
faq.a: Yes. The Introduction names mothers and fathers, and a chapter is given to what grief looks like inside a marriage. It is also written for anyone who has lost a child or loves someone who has.

faq.q: Does the book talk about her baby in heaven?
faq.a: Yes, simply and without speculation. She writes that while her son knew the voice and touch of his mommy, he also knows that of his Heavenly Father. Her closing lines are "Our baby lived. He is with Jesus. And I am still his mommy."

hero.audience_line: For mothers who have known the loss of a baby, for the fathers who stand beside them, and for anyone who has lost a child or loves someone who has.
hero.tagline: A mother's telling of a baby born at twenty-seven weeks who lived twelve days, written as companionship rather than answers.

hero.audience_line: For anyone searching for a place to belong: readers who never felt at home, people who have lost a home or a country, readers of Christian memoirs, and believers drawn to visions and dreams.
hero.tagline: What if home is not a place you can lose, but a place within you? A Ukrainian author walks through the rooms of a heavenly house, with Scripture and questions for your own search.

audience.headline: She moved six times in one year as a child, fled on the first day of the full-scale war in Ukraine, and wrote a book about the home no one can take from you.
audience.body: For readers who have been searching for a place to belong. Aleksa Aishpur grew up in Ukraine in the lawless years after the Soviet Union fell apart, moved from house to house as a child, and did not know what it was to call a place home until she was thirty. Home pairs the visions she believes came from God with Scripture and with questions for you to answer, and it asks whether home might be something you carry inside. A note on subjects: this is a memoir about war, grief and loss, and the author describes visions she believes came from God. It also mentions addiction, patterns of abuse and fear. It is written for adult readers.

quote.text: “HOME is my inner balance, rest, peace, joy, and happiness.”
quote.cite: Home, Introduction

what_makes.title: What makes this book for readers who feel they have no place of their own
paras: Most books about belonging tell you how to find a house or a community. This one starts from the other direction. It is short, quiet and visual, and it invites you to write the ending yourself.
Five things set it apart:
list: It is told as a house with rooms. The author is led through a castle of light, and each room, from Gifts and Foundation to War, Past, Storm, Seasons, Mirror, Inheritance and Changes, shows her something about herself and God.

It comes out of real loss. She writes about growing up without a father, about delivering bread to people near the fighting in eastern Ukraine, and about fleeing on the first day of the full-scale war in 2022.
It ties nearly every vision to the Bible. Most chapters have a Bible Scriptures section, so the reader can test what she saw against the Word.
It asks you to answer. Every room ends with four to six questions, and one chapter, Yours, asks you to close your eyes and find your own room.
It is honest about what she did not understand. She says she nearly left out the last room, because it took years before it made sense to her.

sections.h2: For readers who have moved a lot and wonder where they belong
paras: The author moved six times in a year as a child. She says that for a long time she looked into other people's windows and fell into unhealthy relationships, searching for home. If that sounds like you, her story will feel familiar.

sections.h2: For people who have lost a home, a country or someone they love
paras: She writes about ruins, shelling and people fighting over a loaf of bread, and about the grief that follows. She asks hard questions of God and does not hurry the answer. She is clear that she is one of millions who lost a physical home in 2022.

sections.h2: For readers who think in pictures and prayer
paras: The book is made of visions, colors and rooms, and it asks you to imagine along with her. It may suit someone who prays with their eyes closed, or who keeps a journal, or who simply wants a slow book with room to think.

sections.h2: For small groups, counselors and coaches
paras: Each chapter closes with questions that can be answered alone or together. The author is herself a coach who helps people find joy in their work and life, and she invites readers to send their stories to her website.

paras: On the second floor, the author finds a hall covered in rubies, with red sofas, chandeliers and a carpet that runs the length of the hall. She falls asleep on a velvet sofa, and when she wakes she sees from the window that she is inside a castle, high on a mountain above the clouds. She reads the red as the power of the blood of Jesus, and she searches the Bible and finds rubies in Isaiah 54 and in the city of Revelation.

In the second room, the author finds a small black-and-white room with a thick book of every war in history. She writes about delivering bread near the front line in 2014, and about two men fighting over a loaf. She writes that she hates war, that hatred rose in her heart in that room, and that she felt God with her, understanding all of it.
The last room is absolute darkness. She screamed into it to measure the space, and learned that it was a small room with a floor, walls and a ceiling:
"What I don't see doesn't mean danger."
It took her years to understand this room. She decides, in the end, that when we are close to God His light can blind us for a while, and that only later do we see how close He was.

author.bio: Aleksa Aishpur is from Kyiv, Ukraine. She holds a bachelor's degree from the National University of Kyiv-Mohyla Academy, co-founded a crowdfunding platform in Ukraine, and co-founded a church. As a teenager she volunteered with young people in prison, children with cancer and people with disabilities, and in 2022 she worked on humanitarian efforts across the United States, Ukraine and Romania. She works as a coach in personal development, business and career, and says that she wants to help people find joy in their work and in their lives. She began writing Home in 2017.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The author says she began writing Home in 2017, after war began in eastern Ukraine, and that the pain around her raised the question of where our home is when a house can be destroyed. She tells the reader so on the first page:
“It is a living book that has no ending. I authored it in this way so that those who read my book can create their own endings.”
She believes home is inner rest, peace and joy, a place to be your real self without masks, and she hopes each reader will find their own rooms.

faq.q: What is Home?
faq.a: It is a 108-page spiritual memoir by Aleksa Aishpur. It describes visions of a heavenly house, room by room, with Scripture and reflection questions after each one, and it asks where home really is when you have lost the one you had.

faq.q: Is it a story about the war in Ukraine?
faq.a: It is shaped by the war, and the author writes about delivering bread in the Donbas region in 2014 and about fleeing on the first day of the full-scale war in 2022. But it is not a news account. It is a faith memoir about belonging, loss and finding rest.

faq.q: Are the visions from God presented as fact?
faq.a: The author writes that she believes they are from God, and she shares them as her own experience. She also ties most of them to Bible passages, so readers can weigh them for themselves.

faq.q: Is it a book about heaven?
faq.a: Some of it. The visions take place in a heavenly house, a castle of light high above the clouds, and the author quotes Revelation 21 on the Holy City. She writes that we can live on Earth as in heaven by finding the heavenly home within us. It is not a near-death account.

faq.q: Does it speak to grief and loss?
faq.a: Yes, from her own life. Her father died when she was a year old, she lost a physical home in 2022, and she writes about the ruins and grief she saw in eastern Ukraine. It is a memoir, not a grief guide, and it does not hurry the answers.

faq.q: What does each chapter contain?
faq.a: A vision or story, usually a Bible Scriptures section, and four to six questions for you to answer. The chapter called Yours asks you to close your eyes, find your own room and write or draw it on paper, on a device or in the book itself.

faq.q: Which edition should I choose?
faq.a: The text and the 108 pages are the same in all four. The Colored editions are printed in color and cost more; the Black and White editions are printed in black and white and cost less. Choose a hardback for a gift or a shelf, and a paperback for carrying and writing in.

faq.q: Is it one of the Christian books only for believers?
faq.a: It is written from a Christian point of view and quotes the Bible throughout. A reader who is curious about faith but has lost their sense of home may still find it a quiet companion.

content_note.title: Content note
paras: This is a memoir about war, grief and loss, and the author describes visions she believes came from God. It also mentions addiction, patterns of abuse and fear. It is for adult readers.

sections.h2: For high-functioning drinkers who keep promising to stop
paras: If you know what it is to manage a day around the next drink, this book speaks your language. The author describes waking at night with anxiety that only a drink would quiet, knowing exactly what he was doing and doing it anyway, and tries more than once to quit on his own. He writes that "The thinking was sound. The follow-through was not." There is no lecture, only a man who has been there saying what it cost.

sections.h2: For people who love someone who looks fine from the outside
paras: Nobody voiced a concern for years. When he told his staff and his closest friends he was going to treatment, none of them were surprised, and that made it lonelier, not easier. If you have said nothing, or said something that was not heard, this book shows what it took for one person to listen. The turning point was a sister who was furious and then, the next morning, someone he could tell she had been right.

sections.h2: For anyone with old wounds and no name for them
paras: Many readers will see themselves in the chapter on the diagnosis. For twenty years he had fought what he calls an invisible enemy, and a name arrived late. He asks the physician whether this is the disorder soldiers get. The chapter does not tell you what you have. It shows that a name can change how a person understands the years behind them.

sections.h2: For readers in or seeking recovery, and for Christian readers
paras: Faith runs through every chapter and is never presented as a shortcut. He started with day four, a Bible he could not yet read, and sermons he could listen to from his bed. He writes that the grace of God was no pink cloud. He also writes that he told his sister he needed help and could not solve the problem alone.

audience.headline: A successful businessman hid behind a full calendar and a 7:30 AM screwdriver. This is what held when willpower could not.
audience.body: For high-functioning drinkers who keep promising themselves they will stop, for people who love someone whose life looks fine from the outside while it quietly falls apart, and for anyone who feels broken, forgotten or burdened by the past and wonders if healing is possible. John P. Boyle writes eight short chapters and an epilogue, and each chapter speaks straight to the reader. It is the true story of addiction, a late diagnosis, treatment and lasting recovery, grounded in faith. A note on subjects: this memoir is about alcohol addiction and recovery. It describes heavy drinking and withdrawal, anxiety, a diagnosis of Complex PTSD, relapse among other patients in treatment, and, in one chapter, a school visit where students describe family violence and one shows signs of self-harm. It is told without graphic detail. It is one man's story and not medical or mental health advice. If you are struggling with alcohol, trauma or thoughts of harming yourself, please contact a physician or licensed treatment professional, and in a crisis contact your local emergency services or a crisis line right away.

quote.text: The question has never been how much anchor you carry. It has always been what your anchor is set into.
quote.cite: Hope That Anchors the Soul, Chapter 7: The 154-Ton Anchor

what_makes.title: What makes this book for people who are carrying a hidden struggle
paras: It does not start with a rock bottom that anyone could see. It starts with a man who looks fine to everyone, sitting on a cafe patio in Las Vegas with shaking hands, ordering vodka at breakfast.
Five things set it apart:
list: It begins at 7:30 in the morning. It is the spring of 2014, the author is thirty-seven, his businesses are profitable, and he asks a server for a double screwdriver with his English muffin.
It takes no shortcuts about blame. He writes, "Every drink I ever took was my own decision," and he says that knowing what he was doing and doing it anyway is "not evidence of freedom."

It names the thing under the drinking. In treatment a physician tells him, "We've diagnosed you with Complex Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder," and the author calls it the diagnosis he had been searching for.
It is honest about odds. The book cites a figure that 90 percent of the few who seek treatment are drinking again within four years, and then looks hard at what might hold.

It is built on a verse and an image. The verse is Hebrews 6:19, "We have this hope as an anchor for the soul, firm and secure." The image is a ship's anchor system that is a tiny fraction of the ship's weight and holds because of what it is set into.

details.Subtitle: A True Story of Addiction, Alcoholism, and Lasting Recovery
details.Author: John P. Boyle
details.Binding: Paperback (perfect bound, gloss laminate), black and white interior

paras: Chapter 1 opens at a small table on the patio of a cafe, under a replica Eiffel Tower. The morning is blue and the fountain across the street is running, and none of it reaches him. He has barely slept. His hands are shaking and his side hurts. He settles on coffee and an English muffin, and then adds one more item. "Can I get a double screwdriver?" The time is seven-thirty and he is thirty-seven years old.

Chapter 2 begins after a Las Vegas trip that ended with a failed attempt to quit cold turkey on the flight home. He spends a sleepless night weighing what treatment would cost him: his career, his reputation, and the privacy he had kept for years. Then one thought will not leave. He did not want his son to grow up without a father. In the morning he walks into his sister's office and tells her she had been right. He agreed to go. She helped him find a facility in Florida, and he left days before his son's birthday, feeling guilty and certain.

In Chapter 4 he lands in Florida sweating and shaking, and a driver offers to stop at a liquor store. He says no. During his intake exam a physician asks if he wants to add anything to his chart. "Write this down: I'm going to beat this." A second physician snarls a warning, "Be wary of pink clouds," and then tells him the symptoms are rooted in one disorder. The book gives the line that follows: "Addiction won't be the only hurdle you'll need to overcome." The diagnosis follows in the next lines.

author.bio: John P. Boyle is the author of Appalachian Kid and Invisible Wounds. A businessman whose companies were profitable and whose career was on an upward trajectory, he spent years as what he calls a highly functioning, ultra-successful alcoholic, hiding anxiety and old wounds behind a full calendar. In the spring of 2014, at the lowest point of his life, he left for a treatment facility in Florida, moved by one conviction: his son would not grow up without a father. He wrote this book to help others find the hope he found in God.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The author says it in the Introduction: "I wrote this book to help others. I believe God will use it for good."

He says who he is writing for: "If you've ever felt broken, forgotten, unloved, or burdened by things that happened to you, this book is for you." And he says what he hopes a reader will find: "By sharing this story, my story, I hope to help others find what I have found: that God loves them, that God was at work in their lives from their childhood, that He's been there all along, and that He'll be there if you call upon him."

faq.q: What is Hope That Anchors the Soul about?
faq.a: It is John P. Boyle's true story of addiction, alcoholism and lasting recovery. A successful businessman who was a highly functioning alcoholic tells what that life cost him, how he chose treatment so his son would not grow up without a father, and the hope that held when willpower could not.

faq.q: Is it a book for a high-functioning alcoholic?
faq.a: Yes. The author's own words are "highly functioning, ultra-successful alcoholic," and the book is written for people like him, who look fine and are not. It is also for those who love them. It is not a treatment guide, and it says that help from professionals mattered.

faq.q: Does it deal with Complex PTSD?
faq.a: Yes. Chapter 4 covers the diagnosis he received in treatment, Complex Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder, which he describes as the single disorder beneath years of symptoms. It is his account of receiving the diagnosis, not a clinical explanation.

faq.q: What is the pink cloud in early recovery?
faq.a: The book explains that a pink cloud is a term for the false euphoria of early sobriety, and that other patients warned him his would crash. Chapter 6 argues that it is not the feeling that holds, but what the feeling is attached to. "If they wanted to call the grace of God a pink cloud, it was fine by me."

faq.q: Is it a book about trying to quit drinking?
faq.a: It is about what he tried and what finally held. He had tried to quit before and could not do it on his own, then chose treatment. The book does not give a program to follow. It tells a story, names what he learned, and encourages the reader to get help.

faq.q: Is it a recovering alcoholic's memoir?
faq.a: Yes. It is the author's own account, from the drinking years through treatment in Florida, early sobriety and the years after. The phrase recovering alcoholic is not his; he tells the story in his own words and says plainly, "Every drink I ever took was my own decision."

faq.q: What is the 154-ton anchor?
faq.a: It is the author's image from Chapter 7. A modern aircraft carrier's two anchors and their chains weigh 154 tons on a ship of 100,000 tons, a very small part of the whole. He writes that the question is not how much anchor you carry but "what your anchor is set into," and links it to the verse that gives the book its title.

faq.q: Is it a Christian book?
faq.a: Yes. It is short, candid and grounded in faith. Scripture runs through the story, along with the author's conviction that God was present even when he could not recognize Him, and a closing word on forgiveness.

audience.headline: You are not in the shadows. You are the reason the mission gets done.
audience.body: For quiet contributors, team players and behind-the-scenes problem-solvers who do vital work without holding the top title. Jim Matuga shows that following is an active, intentional skill, one that asks for humility, courage, loyalty and initiative, and that Scripture treats as preparation for greatness.

quote.text: Followership is a skill, a mindset, and a powerful force.
quote.cite: Humble Influence, Why I Wrote This Book

what_makes.title: What makes this book for people who do great work without the top title
paras: A faith-grounded guide to followership in fourteen chapters, a closing epilogue and a practical roadmap. It began at a leadership conference in 2007 and was shaped by a 36-year business career and hundreds of conversations with leaders.
Five things set it apart:
list: It speaks to the person leadership books skip. The author asks why we celebrate leaders so often "yet rarely acknowledge the followers who make their success possible," and then writes for those followers.

It treats humility as a working skill. Humility to serve without seeking the spotlight comes first among the traits he names, beside courage to speak up respectfully, loyalty to the mission, and initiative.

It is rooted in Scripture. Joshua serving under Moses for forty years, Ruth following Naomi, John the Baptist stepping aside, and Peter following Jesus all appear, and the final chapter closes on Jesus Christ as the greatest follower.

It is full of people you will recognize. Short stories follow a new trainee, a software engineer, a team leader who shares credit, and a friend who spent fifteen years learning beside a demanding chief executive.
It ends with a tool you can use. An epilogue on following from within and a Humble Influence Roadmap give you a way to put each chapter to work on Monday morning.

sections.h2: For team players and quiet contributors
paras: If you are the one who makes the plan work while someone else gets named in the meeting, this book says your role is not second place. The author calls it "the quiet strength of followers" and shows how listening, contributing ideas and staying teachable build trust with a leader and with a team. It gives you words for what you already do well.

sections.h2: For anyone who serves at work, at home, in a church or on a team
paras: Followership is not limited to an org chart. The stories include a trainee, an engineer and a team leader, and the Bible examples are about families, nations and a small band of disciples. If you serve on a church committee, volunteer in your community or keep a household moving, the chapters on connecting, empowerment and credit apply to you too.

sections.h2: For anyone who wants to lead well by first learning to follow
paras: Maybe you hope to lead one day. The book argues that these years are not a waiting room. Joshua spent forty years beside Moses, and the author's own mentor told him that "Great leaders don't just appear." Reading this first means you will step into leadership already knowing what it costs and what your team needs from you.

sections.h2: For anyone who wants to measure their own followership
paras: The book ends with tools, not just ideas. The Humble Influence Roadmap starts with a servant mindset and understanding the mission, then names the traits to cultivate. Exercises to Find Your Why follow, with a self-check on followership skills: communication, collaboration, initiative, judgment and authenticity. You can work through them alone or with a mentor.

blocks.text: Every copy opens with an acknowledgements page, a short "Why I wrote this book" and "What this book is about," and then Chapter 1 begins. Chapter 1 opens like this:

paras: Before you can lead, you must learn to follow.

One of my mentors, Mr. Doug, said these words to me during my early days as a budding entrepreneur. At the time, I dismissed the idea, believing leadership was about charisma, vision, and authority—not about following someone else's direction.
Then one day, he handed me a Bible and opened it to the book of Joshua.

Joshua is celebrated as one of the greatest leaders in history. He led the Israelites into the Promised Land, brought down the walls of Jericho, and secured a legacy of courage and faith. But Joshua's leadership journey didn't begin with a command. It began with obedience, patience, and years of followership. For 40 years, Joshua served under Moses, a towering figure who spoke with God and led the Israelites out of Egypt.

intro: Every copy opens with an acknowledgements page, a short "Why I wrote this book" and "What this book is about," and then Chapter 1 begins. Chapter 1 opens like this:
excerpt: Before you can lead, you must learn to follow.

One of my mentors, Mr. Doug, said these words to me during my early days as a budding entrepreneur. At the time, I dismissed the idea, believing leadership was about charisma, vision, and authority—not about following someone else's direction.
Then one day, he handed me a Bible and opened it to the book of Joshua.

Joshua is celebrated as one of the greatest leaders in history. He led the Israelites into the Promised Land, brought down the walls of Jericho, and secured a legacy of courage and faith. But Joshua's leadership journey didn't begin with a command. It began with obedience, patience, and years of followership. For 40 years, Joshua served under Moses, a towering figure who spoke with God and led the Israelites out of Egypt.

whats_inside: Fourteen chapters on why following is not intuitive, how to connect rather than merely communicate, how close to get to a leader, how to gain real empowerment, when to hold back judgment, and why it does not matter who gets the credit
Humble Influence Stories that show each idea at work in everyday jobs
Bible examples from Joshua and Moses, Ruth and Naomi, John the Baptist and Jesus
An epilogue, "Following from Within," and a Humble Influence Roadmap
Exercises to Find Your Why and a self-check on five followership skills: communication, collaboration, initiative, judgment and authenticity
Paperback and hardback, 174 pages

details.Author: Jim Matuga
details.Binding: Paperback (perfect bound) and hardback (case laminate), black and white interior on cream paper

paras: In the opening chapter, a mentor named Mr. Doug hands the young author a Bible open to Joshua. Joshua led battles, carried out Moses' instructions and watched, up close, what leadership cost, including the day twelve spies went out and only two came back with faith. When Moses died, God chose Joshua. The author draws one conclusion: the mantle was not handed over by chance, it was earned through years of faithful service. A friend of the author shows the same pattern in a modern office. She spent fifteen years under a demanding chief executive, studied how he decided, supported his vision, and was the natural choice to succeed him.

Lisa has an MBA and big plans, and a trainee program that has her shadowing department heads and compiling reports. She thinks, "I didn't endure years of case studies and late-night group projects just to follow others around." Then a senior executive, Mr. Reed, tells her where he started and says, "Leadership isn't just about making decisions—it's about making informed decisions." Lisa begins asking questions in marketing and operations, and three years later she is asked to manage a struggling department, which she turns around within a year. Looking back, she decides her time as a follower "wasn't a detour—it was a masterclass in leadership."

stories.h2: Who cares who gets the credit?
paras: Chapter 11 opens in a marketing agency. A team leader named Lisa, in the middle of a client pitch, pauses to say that the concept would not exist without a colleague's creativity on the visuals. The room responds with admiration, and her team sees what kind of leader she is. The chapter pairs that scene with John the Baptist, who drew a large following and still said of Jesus, "He must increase, but I must decrease." The author's point is that great followers care more about the success of the mission than about their own recognition.

author.bio: Jim Matuga has spent a 36-year business career talking with thousands of business leaders. Since 2017 he has interviewed hundreds of business owners and leaders on his weekly podcast, "Positively West Virginia," and he asks each one about leadership. He writes that he has worked with extraordinary leaders and mentors, among them Milan Puskar, founder of Mylan Laboratories, Doug Leech, founder of Centra Bank, and John Maxwell. The idea for this book was planted on April 17, 2007, when he heard author James Kouzes speak at a leadership conference at West Virginia University. It took eighteen years of experience, conversation and study before he found the courage to put it on the page.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The author traces the book to a coffee shop in New York City, where a young professional told him, "Everyone talks about leadership, but what about people like me?" That conversation was the spark. He writes that "Over the years, I've met countless individuals who feel overshadowed by the leadership narrative."

He also saw a gap: "Surprisingly, resources for followers are scarce." His answer is a book that is not about stepping out of the shadows but about understanding the role you already play. In his words, "This book is a celebration of followership." It is meant for "the quiet contributors, the team players, and the behind-the-scenes problem-solvers who know that their work matters just as much—if not more—than the person at the top."

faq.q: What is Humble Influence about?
faq.a: It is a faith-grounded guide to followership for people who do vital work without holding the top title. Jim Matuga argues that following is an active, intentional skill, not blind obedience.

faq.q: Is it a book about biblical humility?
faq.a: Humility is central. The author names humility to serve without seeking the spotlight as the first trait of great followership, and the book closes with Jesus Christ as the greatest follower, whose submission to the Father's will became the path to ultimate leadership.

faq.q: Is it about servant leadership?
faq.a: It is about following rather than leading. Chapter 14 does look at Jesus as a servant who "did not come to be served," but the subject of the book is the strength of true followership.

faq.q: What does it say about Joshua and Moses?
faq.a: Joshua served under Moses for forty years before leading the Israelites into the Promised Land. The author uses that story to show that following prepares a person to lead, because Joshua learned discipline, empathy and humility along the way.

faq.q: Does it cover Ruth and Naomi?
faq.a: Yes. In chapter 5 Ruth chooses to follow Naomi back to Bethlehem. The author quotes her words, "Where you go, I will go, and where you stay, I will stay," and points to her gleaning in the fields as proof that she followed with initiative, not passively.

faq.q: Is it about leading without authority or leading from the middle?
faq.a: In spirit, yes. The book is for people who want to lead "from the middle," to serve quietly and to influence with humility without a formal leadership role.

faq.q: Is it a Christian leadership book?
faq.a: It is a Christian book about the other half of leadership. It draws on Scripture, including Joshua, Ruth, John the Baptist, Peter and Jesus, alongside history and real-world examples.

faq.q: What traits does the book say a servant-hearted follower needs?
faq.a: The Humble Influence Roadmap starts with a servant mindset and then names the key traits to cultivate. They are, in order: humility; curiosity; courage; loyalty; proactivity; and learning through observation.

sections.h2: For believers who want more than religion
paras: If you have attended church for years and still sense a gap between what you know and Who you know, this book speaks to you. The author says that "genuine relationship with Him often remains elusive" for people raised in religious traditions, and he writes the whole study to move you from knowing about God toward knowing Him. His own testimony in Chapter 8 ends with this conviction: "That's why the relationship matters more than religious knowledge."

sections.h2: For personal Bible study, small groups and Bible classes
paras: Each chapter is short enough to read in one sitting and ends with questions you can answer alone or with others. One asks what other familiar Bible facts might benefit from closer examination of the original text. A group can take a chapter a week, compare the passages, and use the notes pages to record where members agree and where they would like to keep digging.

sections.h2: For readers who still wonder whether there is more
paras: Some readers have sat through sermons on Adam and Eve, Job and Revelation for decades and never been asked to read the verses themselves. This book is for you. It assumes you can read Scripture carefully, and it invites you to weigh what the author finds. He is open that these are his questions and his reading of the text, and he asks you to test them for yourself.

sections.h2: For anyone who has noticed that churches teach salvation differently
paras: The author moved through several denominations and found that the Bible stories stayed the same while the teaching on salvation did not. Some churches stressed baptism and others dismissed it. Some required speaking in tongues and others called it unnecessary. If you have seen the same thing and wondered what Scripture itself says, Chapter 7 gives his reading of what it means to be born again. He says plainly that the chapter is not written to condemn any religion or denomination.

paras: A short Bible study in nine chapters. Each chapter takes one familiar passage or question, lays out what the text says, and closes with reflection questions and lined pages for your own notes.
Five things set it apart:
list: It asks questions instead of handing down answers. The author says he wants you to examine Scripture with fresh eyes and to see what you find when you "look closely at familiar passages."

It goes back to the text. In Chapter 1 he points to Genesis 5:2; in Chapter 4 he lays out "six pieces of textual evidence" for children in the Garden of Eden; in Chapter 5 he compares the Hebrew words used in Job 1.

It covers the questions people whisper in Bible class: what Adam and Eve were really called, what the image of God means, who first got the blame for the fall, whether Job's children died, and whether the seals of Revelation have already been opened.
It speaks plainly about salvation. Chapter 7 begins, "How can my name be written in the Book of Life?" and the author says the chapter is "an invitation to examine the Scriptures afresh."
It is made for personal study. Every chapter ends with reflection questions and a notes page, so it works as a small workbook for a quiet week or a group meeting.

details.Title: In Church for 40 Years and Not Knowing God: Escaping Tradition to Truly Know God
details.Author: Philip Guenaga
details.Binding: Paperback (perfect bound), black and white interior on cream paper

paras: Chapter 1 begins with an assumption most readers share, that the first man and woman were named Adam and Eve. The author points to Genesis 5:2: "Male and female created he them; and blessed them, and called their name Adam, on the day when they were created." In his reading, God named them both Adam, the name Eve was given later by the man, and the change reflects a human perspective that developed over time. The chapter closes with reflection questions about how our understanding of gender roles might change if both were first given the same name.

Chapter 5 takes up one of the hardest passages in Scripture. The author looks at the Hebrew word used by each messenger who brings Job bad news, notes that translators rendered it as servants in three reports and as young men in the fourth, and asks why. He also notices that Job's wife seems distraught only once Job himself is afflicted. He offers a possibility, and he is clear about his purpose: "This perspective doesn't diminish the trials Job endured." The chapter closes with questions about how translation shapes the way we read.

In Chapter 8 the author tells how God changed his life. He grew up in a home where love was absent, one of seven children, and at seventeen he gave his life to God. He writes that "He spoke to me, saying He would be my friend," and that from that moment his life changed. He went on to marry, to serve ten years in the Army and to walk with God through the years. He admits that "some wounds from my childhood linger" and that God continues to heal him. The chapter ends with three questions for the reader about transformation, God's voice and personal struggles that might become testimonies.

author.bio: Philip Guenaga grew up in a deeply religious household and moved through several denominations, where he noticed that the teaching on salvation differed sharply from church to church. As a young man he had an experience with God that carried him through difficult times. He served in the Army for ten years and was stationed at Fort Leonard Wood, Missouri. He came to Rolla in 1986 and attended the church pastored by Larry Thornhill, who wrote the foreword and says he has known him for 34 years. Pastor Thornhill calls the book "first, an act of love, and second, a true understanding of God's word." The author wrote this study at the encouragement of friends.

He wrote it as "an invitation to examine the Scriptures afresh." In his words, "Rather than accepting traditional interpretations without question, I encourage you to examine Scripture with fresh eyes."

Dr. Precious Taylor, the friend who wrote the acknowledgement and edited the book, recalls that he gave her several excuses about why he could not write, and she is proud that he finished it. The foreword says the book "is dedicated to those that are searching for a genuine relationship with the giver of life, Jesus Christ."

faq.q: What is In Church for 40 Years and Not Knowing God about?
faq.a: It is a short Bible study in which Philip Guenaga asks readers to set aside inherited assumptions and examine familiar passages with fresh eyes, moving from knowing about God to a genuine relationship with Him through Jesus Christ.

faq.q: What does the book say about the plan of salvation?
faq.a: Salvation is the issue that opens the book, and Chapter 7, "The Plan of Salvation," asks what it means to be born again. The author says the chapter is not written to condemn any religion or denomination, and that Jesus told Nicodemus the path into the kingdom is to be born again. He writes that the path is "repentance, baptism in Jesus' name, and receiving the Spirit." It is his reading of Scripture, not a denominational statement.

faq.q: Does it discuss baptism and speaking in tongues?
faq.a: Yes. The Introduction notes that some churches emphasize baptism while others dismiss it, and that some require speaking in tongues while others consider it unnecessary. Chapter 7 gives the author's view of both, in the context of being born of water and of the Spirit.

faq.q: Does it talk about the Garden of Eden?
faq.a: Yes. Chapter 4 asks whether Adam and Eve had children in the Garden of Eden and lists six pieces of textual evidence. Chapter 3 looks at the sequence of events in the garden, and the bonus chapter returns to Eden in a question about creation.

faq.q: What does it say about the story of Job?
faq.a: Chapter 5 compares the Hebrew words used in Job 1 and asks whether Job's children died at all. The author offers it as a possibility to consider and says Job's suffering "was still immense."

faq.q: What does it mean to be born again, according to the book?
faq.a: Chapter 7 starts from Jesus' words to Nicodemus that the way into the kingdom is to be born again, of water and of the Spirit. The author reads that as repentance, baptism in Jesus' name and receiving the Spirit. He offers it as his reading of Scripture and invites you to study it for yourself.

faq.q: Does it cover the return of Jesus and the seals of Revelation?
faq.a: Yes. Chapter 6 compares Jesus' words in Matthew 24 with the first five seals of Revelation 6 and asks whether several seals may already have been opened. It does not set dates.

faq.q: What is the image of God, according to the book?
faq.a: Chapter 2 asks what "His image" means when both man and woman were created in it. The author suggests that the union of marriage reflects God's complete image, and he presents it as insight gained through prayer and reflection.

faq.q: Does it take a young earth creation view of dinosaurs?
faq.a: Some of it. The bonus chapter notes that the Bible presents humanity's history as roughly six to seven thousand years, then offers a personal theory: that an earlier creation, including the dinosaurs, may have come between Genesis 1:1 and 1:2. The author calls it "a personal theory meant to stir reflection" and says you do not have to believe it.

faq.q: Is it good for a Bible study workbook or small group?
faq.a: Yes. Each chapter closes with reflection questions and lined pages for notes, which suits personal study, small groups and Bible classes.

audience.headline: Eight months to live. Sixteen years later, a biopsy that came back benign.
audience.body: For anyone facing a serious diagnosis, and for the family walking beside them. Daniel Zebarth tells, in his own words, what happened after a pancreatic cancer diagnosis in July 2009: a neuroendocrine tumor, a hard surgery at Mayo, Stage IV spread to his liver, years of chemotherapy, and what he believes God did through it all. His wife tells the same story from her side in Part IV. A note on subjects: the book describes surgery, hospital complications and chemotherapy side effects plainly, and it touches on the early deaths of his parents, a divorce and the loss of an infant son. It is a personal testimony, not medical advice.

quote.text: I do not believe healing follows a formula or that faith guarantees a specific outcome. God's work in our lives is personal, sovereign, and often mysterious.
quote.cite: In the Hands of Our Heavenly Father, the Faith & Testimony Statement at the front of the book

what_makes.title: What makes this book for readers who need honest hope in a hard season
paras: A true account that does not hide the fear. It began as a testimony written for his family, and friends who walked with them encouraged him to share it with others facing illness.
Five things set it apart:
list: It is told by two people. Dan writes Part III, his cancer journey, in eleven chapters. In Part IV, his wife tells it in her own words, drawing on the emails she sent to family during the weeks he was in the hospital.

It is plain about the numbers. The foreword notes the statistics Dan shares, "over 66,000 Americans diagnosed annually and a mortality rate hovering near 78 percent," and calls the book "a beacon of hope" rather than "a tale of despair."

It says what it is not. A medical disclaimer at the front states that the book "is not intended as medical advice" and that treatment decisions "should never be made based solely on personal stories or spiritual testimony."

It gives you the practical pages too. The back of the book includes a guide to navigating a cancer journey with faith and courage, a collection of patterns of God's interventions, family letters and supporting medical documentation.
It took a decade to write. Dan began in 2011, paused in 2012, and in 2021 felt, he writes, "clearly led by the Holy Spirit to finish it."

sections.h2: For anyone facing a serious illness
paras: If you have just heard hard news, you may want to read one person's account before you decide what you think. Dan writes about the first diagnosis, the day it changed to a neuroendocrine tumor, the surgery, the long recovery and the years of chemotherapy. It is a personal account, not a medical guide, and it does not give treatment advice.

sections.h2: For anyone told they need Whipple surgery
paras: Dan walks through the weeks before his operation: the second opinions, the choice between an open and a laparoscopic Whipple, and the surgeon who told him he would be his sixty-third laparoscopic Whipple patient. He writes that a Whipple procedure is a major operation, "typically lasting anywhere from six to ten hours," and he is honest about the hard recovery that followed. It is one patient's story, not a medical guide.

sections.h2: For the spouses, families and friends who walk beside someone who is ill
paras: Part IV may be the part you need. His wife writes about being away from home for a month, about the hospital vigil and the email updates, and about the fourteen blessings and answered prayers she and Dan listed, from a diagnosis that changed, to the fragrance of roses in the pre-op waiting room. If you are the one keeping watch, there is company here.

sections.h2: For readers of Christian testimony and memoir
paras: This is a first-person account of faith, prayer and trusting God through suffering, written by a man with a business, a marriage and children he adored, who says he has been "blessed throughout my life with visits from Jesus." He writes about what he saw and heard and what he believes, and he says plainly that God's work is "personal, sovereign, and often mysterious."

blocks.text: Every copy opens with a note called Before You Begin, a foreword by George Pardos, acknowledgements, and Dan's opening remarks. Before You Begin reads:

paras: This book began as a personal testimony written for my family, a record of God's faithfulness during my journey through cancer. Friends who walked alongside us encouraged me to share it more broadly, in the hope that others facing illness might find comfort, perspective, and faith along their own journey.

blocks.text: Chapter 1, "Preparing for the Big News," opens like this:

paras: By 2009, I was 57 years old. I had built a successful life: a thriving business, a marriage, and children I adored. I had survived my parents' early deaths, a painful divorce, and the loss of our infant son. I thought I had faced the worst life could throw at me.
I was wrong.
I was about to be ambushed by one of the deadliest forms of cancer. Thankfully, the career changes I made the year before my diagnosis helped me survive what came next.

details.Title: In the Hands of Our Heavenly Father
details.Subtitle: A True Story of Faith, Prayer, and Miraculous Healing from Stage IV Cancer
details.Author: Daniel Zebarth
details.Binding: Paperback (perfect bound), cream paper, black and white interior

stories.h2: A sermon, and a life verse
paras: On August 30, 2009, just weeks after the diagnosis, Dan watched a sermon at the family cabin. The message was on Isaiah 41:10, and he writes that the sermon changed his life. The verse became his Life Verse:
"So do not fear, for I am with you; do not be dismayed, for I am your God. I will strengthen you and help you; I will uphold you with my righteous right hand."
It came two weeks before surgery, which he calls "exactly when I would need it most," and he still prays it before major tests.

stories.h2: One in the morning, day eleven
paras: Ten days after surgery, Dan was not improving. On Saturday, September 26, 2009, he could not sleep for pain. He writes that he turned his head and saw Jesus by his left shoulder, with a woman beside Him he later understood to be Mother Mary. He was in St. Mary's Hospital. According to Dan, Jesus said, "Today you will have a very rough day, but you will get better." That afternoon he vomited blood and lost consciousness, and his wife ran into the corridor calling for help. He writes that the visit "dramatically changed the level of my faith and trust in Him."

stories.h2: The message at the supper table
paras: Years of chemotherapy had passed when Dan, at a July 2021 appointment, asked his doctor, "How would I know if I still have cancer?" A liver biopsy followed on July 29. Two days later his family was together at a restaurant when his phone chirped with the pathology report. The lesion was benign. "I have been healed; I am cancer free!" he told the table. He also records that his children were skeptical at first, and that they shared a wonderful meal and believed, at the very least, that their dad would be around much longer.

author.bio: Daniel Zebarth grew up in Augusta, Wisconsin, where his father ran a gas station, tended the town's two cemeteries and served eight years as mayor. In July 2009 he was diagnosed with pancreatic cancer, which later spread to his liver as Stage IV. After years of chemotherapy, a biopsy came back benign, and he writes that he has been cancer-free for sixteen years. He began this book in 2011 and finished it in 2021.

paras: Dan did not set out to write a book. "At the time, I had no desire to write a book and doubted that I had the ability to do so," he says of 2011, when it began. In 2021, he writes, "I felt clearly led by the Holy Spirit to finish it. This is truly His book, a testimony of miraculous healing from Stage IV pancreatic cancer."

His reason for sharing it is simple: "I am simply a vessel God has used to share that He is alive, faithful, and still working miracles today." Nothing in these pages is offered as a formula. It is one man's true story, with the records at the back, told so that others facing illness might find comfort, perspective and faith along their own journey.

faq.q: What is In the Hands of Our Heavenly Father about?
faq.a: It is Daniel Zebarth's true account of a pancreatic cancer diagnosis in July 2009 that became a pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor, spread to his liver as Stage IV, and, after years of chemotherapy, ended with a liver biopsy in July 2021 that came back benign.

faq.q: What kind of pancreatic tumor did the author have?
faq.a: The first diagnosis was adenocarcinoma of the pancreas, and days later it changed to a pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor (pNET). The book explains the difference as he learned it, and he writes that he was given eight months to live.

faq.q: Does the book describe Whipple surgery and recovery?
faq.a: Yes. Chapters 4 to 6 cover choosing a surgeon at Mayo, his laparoscopic Whipple in September 2009, and a hard hospital recovery with serious complications. It is a personal account, not a medical guide, and it does not give treatment advice.

faq.q: Does it cover cancer that spread to the liver?
faq.a: Yes. In June 2011 scans showed lesions on his liver, and the diagnosis became metastatic pancreatic neuroendocrine carcinoma. Chapters 7 to 10 follow the chemotherapy, an episode of liver failure in February 2021 and the biopsy that came back benign.

faq.q: Does the author write about hearing from God?
faq.a: Yes. He describes a visit from Jesus on day eleven after surgery, the Holy Spirit's promise when the cancer spread, and the moment he believes God told him to ask his doctor whether the cancer was still there. These are told as his own experience.

faq.q: Does the book say God is faithful?
faq.a: That is its theme. The book opens by calling itself "a record of God's faithfulness during my journey through cancer," and Appendix B collects the patterns of God's interventions he saw along the way.

faq.q: Does the book promise that God will heal me?
faq.a: No. The author writes plainly about the statistics and the fear, and his Faith & Testimony Statement says he does not believe healing follows a formula or that faith guarantees a specific outcome. He offers his story as a testimony that God is alive and faithful.

faq.q: Is it a spiritual memoir?
faq.a: Yes. It is a first-person account of faith, prayer and trusting God through suffering, with his life story in Part II, and in Part IV his wife tells the same months from her side. A medical disclaimer at the front says it is not medical advice, and Appendix E holds the supporting medical documentation.

sections.h2: For anyone who has asked why they react so strongly
paras: If a slammed door makes your heart leap, if you tense up before a hard conversation, or if you feel unworthy no matter what you achieve, this book offers language and company. John writes, “My reactions weren't overreactions; they were survival skills that had outlived their usefulness.” It reads like a conversation with someone who has been where you are.

sections.h2: For survivors of childhood trauma, including men who were taught to push through alone
paras: John grew up in a small town in the mountains of West Virginia, with a home that looked normal from the outside. He became an achiever, a funny one, the helpful kid, building what he calls a mask. He writes honestly about hiding symptoms behind success and about drinking and isolation. If you have been told to “man up,” the sentence that follows in the book is worth hearing: “Being a male survivor doesn't make you weak. Speaking about it makes you courageous.”

sections.h2: For readers who want a faith-friendly account of trauma and recovery
paras: God appears here as a gentle Father who meets a worn-out man on his knees, not as a punishing figure. John writes of Psalm 34:18, “The Lord is close to the brokenhearted and saves those who are crushed in spirit,” and of lifelines, the teachers, friends and mentors who stayed. This is a personal and faith-friendly book. It is not medical advice or a treatment guide, and it encourages you to find a trauma-informed professional.

sections.h2: For families, friends, pastors and helpers
paras: If you love someone who carries these wounds, the book shows what helped. Chapter 7, Finding Your Lifelines, honors the people who stayed: a dorm parent at boarding school, teachers, friends and mentors. John writes that lifelines keep you afloat long enough to breathe again. The resources at the back list warning signs in children, organizations that can help and questions to bring to a provider, so a parent, pastor or friend can take a first step too.

audience.headline: You are not crazy. You are injured, and healing is possible.
audience.body: For anyone who has asked why they react so strongly, why they feel unsafe even when they are safe, or why they cannot just get over the past. John P. Boyle lived nearly four decades with Complex PTSD he could not name. Invisible Wounds is the book he needed back then, a four-part walk through what trauma does to the body and brain, and a road toward hope.

quote.text: John, you're not crazy, you're injured.
quote.cite: Invisible Wounds, Chapter 1, You're Not Crazy, You're Injured

what_makes.title: What makes this book for readers who want to understand complex PTSD
paras: Invisible Wounds does not diagnose you, and it does not drown you in jargon. John says his goal is “to explain what is happening in a way that feels like you're finally being spoken to, not spoken about.”
Five things set it apart:
A note before you begin: this book describes childhood abuse and its effects. John says he wants “to share my story in a way that doesn't retraumatize you but helps you recognize your own strength.”
list: It names the enemy. Part One, “Naming the Invisible Enemy,” opens with the author's own story: sleepless nights, startle responses and the quiet certainty that something was wrong with him, until a trauma-informed therapist gave it a name.

It explains the body. Part Two, “The Body Keeps the Score,” shows how trauma lives in muscles, stomachs and sleep, and how a child's brain can be wired for “fight, flight, freeze, or fawn” long after the danger has passed.

It answers the question every survivor asks. Part Three, “The Tangled Puppet Strings,” takes on “Why can't I just get over it?” and a chapter called “Misdiagnosis Roulette,” about the string of labels John collected before the right one.
It speaks directly to male survivors. A page called “The Untold Story of Male Trauma Survivors” begins, “Men are taught to push through.”
It treats faith as rescue, not doctrine. Scripture and prayer appear as comfort and companionship, and Part Four, “The Road to Healing,” ends with lifelines and hope.

details.Title: Invisible Wounds
details.Subtitle: Understanding and Healing from Complex PTSD
details.Author: John P. Boyle, author of Appalachian Kid
details.Binding: Paperback (perfect bound), cream paper, black and white interior

paras: John spends nearly four decades believing his pain means he is defective. He calls the sleepless nights, the startle responses and the headaches stress, anxiety and bad nerves. Then a trauma-informed therapist explains that Complex PTSD comes from chronic, inescapable stress, usually in childhood, “what happens when the people meant to protect you are the ones who cause you pain.” For the first time, the chaos makes sense. He stops asking what is wrong with him and begins asking what happened to him.

At thirty-six, running a fast-growing business and traveling constantly, John wakes with his heart pounding and his chest tight. He ends up in the emergency room convinced he is dying. The physician comes back smiling. “Good news,” he says. “Your heart is perfect. It's probably just stress.” John writes that the physician was right, but not in the way he thought: “It was unresolved trauma that had been simmering for decades.” The chapter becomes an invitation to listen to the body instead of silencing it.

Years later, volunteering at his hometown high school as a successful businessman, John sits in a small-group discussion when a mistreated teenage boy looks at him and says, “God doesn't love everyone. He plays favorites.” John sees himself in that boy: the same hollow ache and quiet despair. He realizes that his success has not healed him, only distracted him. He writes, “That was the day I stopped running from my past.”

author.bio: John P. Boyle grew up in a small town in the mountains of West Virginia. He went on to boarding school and Harvard and built a career as a business leader while living for nearly four decades with Complex PTSD he could not name. Diagnosed by a trauma-informed therapist, he now writes about childhood trauma, male survivors and the role of faith in recovery. He is a husband and father and the author of Appalachian Kid.

We are honored to publish John P. Boyle's story.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: John says he wrote the book because he does not want you to wander as long as he did. “I don't want you to blame yourself for things that were never your fault. I don't want you to feel alone in symptoms that millions of people experience but rarely talk about.”

He also gives a plain reason for writing about something so painful: “Because pain loses power when it's spoken out loud. Because healing grows when it's shared.” He believes “God carried me through things I didn't understand so that I could turn back and help others,” and that “none of us are meant to heal in isolation.” The book ends with a letter to the boy he once was, and an invitation to write your own.

faq.q: What is Invisible Wounds about?
faq.a: It is John P. Boyle's account of living nearly four decades with Complex PTSD he could not name, and a four-part guide to understanding it and walking the road to healing. The subtitle is Understanding and Healing from Complex PTSD.

faq.q: What does the book mean by complex PTSD?
faq.a: In the author's words it is “a disorder of reactions,” and it “is not about what is wrong with you; it is about what happened to you.” He explains that it develops from chronic, inescapable stress, usually in childhood, rather than from one event.

faq.q: What does the book say about hypervigilance and fight, flight, freeze?
faq.a: Part Two shows how trauma lives in the body and rewires a child's brain for fight, flight, freeze or fawn. Hypervigilance, startle responses and panic are among the experiences the author describes in his own life.

faq.q: Is it about childhood trauma and men's mental health?
faq.a: Yes to both. It follows the effects of a chaotic childhood into adulthood, and it speaks directly to male survivors, who are taught to push through alone.

faq.q: Does it explain emotional flashbacks and toxic shame?
faq.a: It does, in Chapter 3. John describes “gray days” that turned out to be emotional flashbacks, and he separates guilt from shame: “Guilt says, 'I did something wrong.' Shame says, 'I am something wrong.'”

faq.q: Are there exercises for calming the nervous system?
faq.a: Yes. Survivor Insight exercises help you name pain and replace self-blame with accuracy, and a 5-4-3-2-1 grounding reset helps when the body goes into panic or freeze mode. The resources section adds a five-step plan for day one.

faq.q: Is Scripture part of the healing?
faq.a: Scripture and prayer run through the book. Psalm 34:18 carried John through many dark nights, and the resources section lists verses for healing and hope. Faith appears as rescue, not doctrine.

faq.q: Does it show how to heal from trauma?
faq.a: It shows where to start. Part Four, The Road to Healing, is about lifelines and hope, and the resources give a five-step Day One Healing Action Plan. They are, in order: Name One Truth; Create One Safe Space; Tell One Safe Person; Make One Appointment; and Choose One Daily Regulation Practice. The book is not a treatment guide and points readers to a trauma-informed professional.

faq.q: Is it a clinical book, and who is it for?
faq.a: No. The author explains what is happening without diagnosing and without overwhelming; it is a personal and faith-friendly account, not medical advice or a treatment guide. It is for anyone who has asked why they react so strongly, for survivors of childhood trauma, and for readers who want a faith-friendly account of recovery.

hero.tagline: John P. Boyle names his invisible enemy, complex post-traumatic stress disorder, and walks the road to healing through lifelines and hope.

sections.h2: For anyone who wants to read the Bible with fresh expectation
paras: The author believed for decades, as many do, that the Bible was old words about other people. When a friend showed her how God speaks to her in Scripture, it changed everything. Here she shows what that looks like in real moments, with real verses. If you have ever opened your Bible and wondered what it has to do with Tuesday, her stories will give you something to look for.

sections.h2: For believers who want to pray about real decisions
paras: Where to live, whether to sell a home, whether to move a family, how to take an unexpected job: these are the decisions at the center of the book. The author prays about each and tells what she says God said in return. Whatever you think of her interpretations, you will see a woman who asks, listens and checks what she hears against the Bible, which is the habit the book encourages.

sections.h2: For readers who enjoy a warm, honest and humorous Christian memoir
paras: If you like a memoir that is both sincere and funny, you are in the right place. The twins who are nothing alike, the husband who is an engineer and rarely wrong, the baby girl she prayed for, and the day she was lost at Disney World make the pages move quickly. The thirty-four chapters are short enough to read one at a time.

sections.h2: For parents who pray for their children
paras: Many of the stories are a mother's prayers. She prays ten years for a baby girl and holds on to a verse through every ultrasound. She asks, twenty-one years later, what her older son saw on the day his brother was spared in a frightening accident. A late chapter in Times and Seasons is about one of her daughters. If you are praying for a child of your own, you will find a mother who kept asking and kept watching for the answer.

audience.headline: God still speaks. Thirty-four true stories of how one woman learned to hear Him.
audience.body: For readers who want to hear God's voice in everyday life, to read the Bible with fresh expectation, and to pray about real decisions. Michele Wilson walks through a lifetime of answered prayer, from marriage at nineteen and raising four children to a night vision, a ten-year prayer, a back porch and a Walmart aisle, and anchors every story in Scripture. A note on subjects: two chapters are the author's personal testimony about a diagnosis of obsessive compulsive disorder and a season of depression, and one chapter touches on a child's close call. They are told without graphic detail. This is a faith memoir, not medical advice, and it makes no treatment claims.

quote.text: I am thrilled that you desire to truly hear the voice of God.
quote.cite: Michele Wilson, Introduction

what_makes.title: What makes this book for readers who want to hear God speak
paras: A Christian memoir in thirty-four short chapters, grouped into parts on foundations of faith, visions and dreams, trials and triumphs, walking in faith, prayer, provision, humility, everyday miracles, gratitude, and times and seasons. Each chapter is a true story and each is anchored in a Bible passage.
Five things set it apart:
list: It is built on a simple discovery. After nearly thirty years in church, the author learned in 1995 that God speaks through the Bible, and she writes so that you do not have to wait that long.
Every story points back to Scripture. Passages are quoted in full so you can see how God used His Word at the very moment it was needed.
It is honest about hard seasons. The author writes about fear, depression, moving from town to town, and years of waiting, along with the moments she says God answered.
It is warm and funny. A day lost at Disney World, an unexpected job as a general contractor, and a conversation in a Walmart aisle sit beside the weighty chapters.

It tells you how to respond. The closing chapter explains that salvation is a gift received by grace through faith, and invites you to pray, to read the Bible daily and to join a Bible-centered church.

details.Author: Michele Wilson

stories.h2: A vision in the night, and a home by February 28
paras: In a rental home the family disliked, the author prayed for help by February 28, the end of the lease. Months later she cried out to God to reveal Himself. Two days after, around 3:00 a.m., she saw a blinding white light in the upper corner of her bedroom, and she writes that she heard, "The whole ordeal you have been through for the last four months will be over very soon." Chapter Five tells what came next. A friend from church called about her house for sale. On the morning of February 28 the author read John 4:50, "You may go, your son will live," and the next word she saw was "pool," and the family bought that home the same day.

For ten years the author had prayed for a baby girl, and she writes that "I had been praying for a baby girl for ten years." On June 19 she asked God to show her in her Bible the word "her" or "she," and it opened to Psalm 87:5. Her husband, an engineer, thought they would have all boys. She kept the promise in her heart through ultrasounds, mailed Christmas cards announcing a girl, and met her daughter three days after the due date. The chapter also tells, honestly, how hard the first months at home were.

stories.h2: An encounter with God in Walmart
paras: On the twenty-first anniversary of a frightening accident in which her son was spared, the author called her older son and asked, for the first time, what he had seen that day. Later, shopping at Walmart, she writes that God said, "For twenty-one years now you have been asking me how you can pay me back for saving your son's life. Let's get something straight; you can't pay me back, so don't ever ask me again." The message she took from it was that she should share the story, and tell others that Jesus died to save their lives eternally.

author.bio: Michele Wilson was raised in West Columbia, South Carolina, by Christian parents who took their four children to church almost every time the doors were open. She has a twin sister and a brother who became a pastor. She accepted Jesus at about age twelve and married at nineteen, and she and her husband raised four children. In 1995 a friend showed her how God speaks through the Bible, a discovery she says changed her life forever. She writes so that readers will learn to hear His voice and come to know Jesus as Savior.
