why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The author says God directed her to write it: "The very reason I am writing this book is because God directed me to do so in Jeremiah 30:2." She hopes readers will do two things: "learn how to hear His voice," and, if they do not yet belong to Him, "come to know Him as your Savior."

She also wants you to see why the Bible matters. "Salvation is a gift from God, not something we can earn by church attendance, good works, or family heritage." And she ends with a promise she says she has seen kept: "As I have testified throughout this book, God keeps His promises."

faq.q: What is Jesus Whispers about?
faq.a: It is Michele Wilson's collection of thirty-four short true stories in which she says God answered prayer, gave direction and drew near through Scripture, a vision in the night, dreams and quiet nudges she learned to recognize as His voice.

faq.q: Does the book use the Bible?
faq.a: Yes. Each story is anchored in Scripture, with passages quoted so readers can see how God used His Word at the moment it was needed.

faq.q: Is Jesus Whispers a memoir?
faq.a: It reads as a Christian memoir told in short chapters, from marriage at nineteen and raising four children to a back-porch encounter and a Walmart aisle. It is classed as a Christian biography and a book on spiritual growth.

faq.q: Does it have stories of answered prayer?
faq.a: Yes. The best known is the ten-year prayer for a baby girl, and there are others, including the home she prayed for by a certain date and a man saved on his deathbed.

faq.q: How does the author say she hears God's voice?
faq.a: Through the Bible first, she writes, and also through a vision in the night, dreams and quiet nudges. She says the goal is to read Scripture and pray each day, and that "Once you experience God speaking to you, you will hunger for more."

faq.q: Does it talk about salvation?
faq.a: Yes. She explains that salvation is a gift received by grace through faith, quoting Ephesians 2:8-9, and the closing chapter gives a short prayer for readers who want to receive it.

faq.q: Does it deal with mental health?
faq.a: Two chapters touch on her own experiences, a diagnosis of obsessive compulsive disorder and a season of deep depression, told as personal testimony. The book is not medical advice and makes no treatment claims.

faq.q: Does it talk about visions and dreams?
faq.a: Yes. Part Two is called Visions and Dreams and includes a vision in the night, "The Greatest Revelation," and a dream from God. They are the author's own accounts, set beside the Bible passages she links to them.

hero.audience_line: For anyone who wants to read the Bible with fresh expectation, believers who want to pray about real decisions and recognize the Lord's voice in everyday life, and readers who enjoy a warm, honest and humorous Christian memoir.
hero.tagline: Michele Wilson shares thirty-four true stories in which God answered prayer, gave direction and drew near through His Word, a vision in the night, dreams and quiet nudges.

sections.h2: For leaders and managers
paras: The book asks leaders to look at what they are modeling. In one story the author is asked to help with a performance matter in a large nursing group and finds two differences between top and bottom performers: expectations were conveyed differently, and the people who asked clarifying questions were rated higher. His conclusion is blunt: "You can't correct what you won't confront."

sections.h2: For learning and talent development professionals
paras: The author says the book looks at each principle for its "implications for organizational and talent development professionals seeking to foster effective, heightened performance." It treats the classroom and the workplace as one learning space, recommends feedback rubrics for written work and projects, and ends with supplemental insights on basic techniques for managing change.

sections.h2: For people early in a career or planning the next step
paras: The author holds career discussions with students and leaders and says he often relates the flight to career planning: preparing for the expected and the unexpected, adapting when delays come, acknowledging a holding pattern and celebrating a safe landing. A section on what the book calls the gap, the distance between expectation and reality, gives a practical way to ask for feedback and use it.

sections.h2: For Christians who want faith at work
paras: Scripture and prayer are part of the method. Short lines from Proverbs sit inside the chapters, and the back of the book gives a prayer for the leader, one for the performer and one for the instructor. The Foreword names the purpose behind it: "to glorify my divine Creator by using my talents in service to others."

audience.headline: A delayed, storm-tossed flight that still landed safely, and seven principles for rising in leadership, learning and work.
audience.body: For leaders and managers who want to rise in effectiveness, clarity and influence, for learning and talent development professionals, and for Christians in the workplace who want Scripture-based wisdom for career and leadership. Ron Tredway draws on more than forty years in management and leadership roles to treat altitude not as a title but as a level of effectiveness. Seven principles each get a chapter, a short set of questions to ponder, and a line of wisdom from Solomon and other sages. A note on what this is: a professional-development book written from a Christian worldview, with Scripture, practical prayers and a stated purpose of glorifying the Creator through service. It draws on the author's own workplace and classroom experience and on published leadership research. It is not human resources, legal or employment advice, and the people in its stories are described without names.

quote.text: Think of altitude not as a title or position, but as a level of effectiveness, clarity, and influence.
quote.cite: Lead at a Higher Altitude, the Foreword

what_makes.title: What makes this book for leaders who want to rise
paras: The book starts in a seat on a plane. A flight to Dallas left an hour late, met rough weather, changed altitude and course, waited in a holding pattern near the airport and still landed safely at the planned destination. The author uses that flight as a picture of a career and of leading others: someone owns the flight, adjusts as conditions change and brings people to the destination.
Five things set it apart:
list: One image runs through the whole book. Preparation, ascent, turbulence, course corrections, cruising altitude and landing are used to describe how performance works.
It treats learning and work as one thing. The seventh principle says it directly: learning is performance.
Each principle has a real scene behind it, from a training room, a nursing department, a team of technical writers, an aviation company and an MBA classroom.

It is built for use. Boxed questions to ponder appear throughout, and the later sections carry an Integrated Practice summary, practical prayers, terms and definitions and the Words of Wisdom in one place.
It speaks to more than managers. The Foreword says leaders at every stage, formal or informal, in the workplace, classroom, ministry or community, can use it.

details.Title: Lead at a Higher Altitude
details.Subtitle: 7 Principles for Rising in Leadership, Learning, and Work
details.Author: Ron Tredway
details.Binding: Paperback (perfect bound, matte laminate), black and white interior

paras: The book's opening scene is a one-hour delay, a rough ride at 30,000 feet, a change of altitude, a slight change of course and a holding pattern near the destination. "Yes, our flight was delayed from the original plan. Yet we arrived safely at the intended destination." The author asks what success looks like when the path is altered but the destination stays intact.

Principle 3 tells of a manager who inherited a team of technical writers. A senior member had been passed between departments with a reputation as a mediocre performer, yet believed himself a top performer. Reviewing the facts, the author found that he had a lot of knowledge and commitment but was working from assumptions, not reality. After an honest conversation he committed to clarify expectations. A year later he was seen by peer managers as one of the strongest performers in the organization. The author's reading is that "he took time to listen to the reality check and do something meaningful with it."

In Principle 7 the author remembers a flight into John Wayne Airport. Power is reduced on descent, and the quiet can feel eerie. This time the captain sang, which changed the mood. Asked why, the captain said: "I do it in the flight simulator, why not do it when it really matters." The author takes it as a reminder of how what we do in the learning space carries over to the workplace.

author.bio: Ron Tredway is a North Carolina native with more than 40 years of management and leadership experience in university, banking, aviation, telecom and military organizations. At the University of Tennessee, until he retired in 2020, he was responsible for statewide leadership development programs, succession planning and other organizational development work. He holds a BSBA from NC Wesleyan, an MBA from Campbell and a doctorate from NC State, has taught undergraduate and MBA courses at several universities, and serves with the faculty at Campbell University. His passion is helping individuals and organizations improve their performance, coupled with a strong desire to serve God as an ambassador for Christ in the marketplace.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The author says the desire behind writing it "is simple, yet weighty: to help others gain a clearer understanding and a more practical application of the joy of learning and peak performance as they pursue their purpose, calling, and passion as leaders."

His hope for the reader is "not only gain insight but also conviction, conviction to learn intentionally, perform faithfully, and lead humbly." And the sentence he would have you carry from the Foreword is: "Altitude is not achieved by accident."

faq.q: What is Lead at a Higher Altitude about?
faq.a: It is a guide to seven principles for rising in leadership, learning and work, using a delayed, storm-tossed flight that still landed safely as the picture of a career. Altitude means effectiveness, clarity and influence.

faq.q: What are the seven principles?
faq.a: There are seven, one to a chapter. They are, in order: Attitude Affects Behavior; Clarity of Direction Shapes Destiny; Reality Check Dispels Wrong Assumptions; Feedback Application on Gap Promotes Achievement; Competency Awareness Sparks Readiness; Leadership Is About Change and Learning; and Learning Is Performance.

faq.q: Is it a book about career development?
faq.a: It is about a career in the sense that the author uses it throughout, from career planning conversations with students and leaders to how learning shapes opportunity. The exact phrase career development does not appear in the interior, and the book is not a job-search guide. It is a leadership and performance book that treats a career as a flight to be prepared for and flown.

faq.q: Does it cover managing change and leading change?
faq.a: Yes. Principle 6, Leadership Is About Change and Learning, covers orchestrating change, sharing the horizon, thinking about change and leading change and learning. It says the key tasks include "reducing resistance, communicating vision, building coalitions, and embedding change into the culture." A supplemental section lists basic techniques for managing change.

faq.q: Does it cover 360 degree feedback?
faq.a: Principle 4 describes a 360-degree feedback process used in a leadership development program for succession planning, and what mattered most was how the feedback was perceived and how it was turned into action. It is a principle about using feedback to close a gap, not a manual for running a feedback survey.

faq.q: Is it for talent development and organizational development professionals?
faq.a: Yes, among others. The Introduction says each principle is looked at for "organizational and talent development professionals." The author's background includes leadership and organizational development roles. The phrase employee development does not appear, and the book speaks of learners, performers and leaders.

faq.q: Does it say anything about workplace performance and how to be a better leader?
faq.a: Both are the subject. Performance is "the deliverance of effort and output toward the expectations and goals for success." It gives leaders seven practices and a model rather than a checklist, and asks them to model learning: "leaders model learning behaviors."

faq.q: Does it talk about being a servant leader?
faq.a: Some of it. The phrase servant leader is not the book's own label, but the Integrated Practice says performers can benefit from leaders with "a humble, servant heart who coach them to seek clarity over confusion and renewed initiative over stagnation." The book's hope is that readers learn intentionally, perform faithfully and lead humbly.

faq.q: Is it a Christian book?
faq.a: Yes. It includes Words of Wisdom from Solomon and other sages and practical prayers, and the author's stated purpose is to glorify his Creator through service. It is also written to be useful to leaders of any background.

audience.headline: After the breakup, the divorce and the shame, Jesus is still waiting at the well.
audience.body: For readers healing from divorce and broken relationships, and for anyone who has asked how a loss changed their sense of worth. Carol Renee Gitthens, a pastor's daughter, tells the truth about her own failures and about the grace that met her on the other side. Each chapter closes with Scripture for healing, questions to journal and a prayer. A note on subjects: this devotional speaks openly about divorce, shame, grief and a season of depression, and about the author's own mistakes. Nothing is described in graphic detail. It is a personal testimony and a book of Scripture and prayer, not counseling or medical advice.

quote.text: Virtue was a sanctuary; the well was my heart.
quote.cite: Lessons from the Well, Chapter One: A Place Once Known as Virtue

what_makes.title: What makes this book for readers healing from divorce and broken relationships
paras: A devotional in nine chapters, built from one woman's story and from Scripture. It opens with an allegory of a place called Virtue, moves through shame and failure, sits for a long chapter with the woman at the well, and ends with steps toward moving forward.
Five things set it apart:
list: It does not excuse and it does not condemn. The foreword says the book does not praise or justify one of the most divisive subjects in the church, and that "it points to the healing power of Jesus, despite our choices in life."
It is told by someone who has been there. The author writes that after "Thirty years, three marriages, and five kids," she had failed herself, her father and God, and she says so plainly.

It stays close to Scripture. Chapters draw on Genesis, John 4, the Psalms, Isaiah, Romans, Paul's letters and more, quoted from the New King James and New American Standard Bibles, with the references listed at the start of each chapter.
It is built for journaling and groups. Every chapter ends with Reflections: questions to discuss or journal, then a prayer.
It centers on the woman at the well. At the heart of the book, a close reading of John 4 shows Jesus choosing to meet one outcast woman, and the author shows how that same love reaches readers today.

sections.h2: For readers healing from divorce and broken relationships
paras: If you are tired of explaining yourself, this book does not ask you to. It asks you to sit down at the well. The author tells her own failures without excuses and then shows, chapter by chapter, where she found grace. You can read one chapter at a time, write your answers on the questions at the end, and pray the prayer when you are ready.

sections.h2: For anyone who has asked what a loss did to their worth
paras: The author writes about a belief that took hold after her first heartbreak: that she was "unworthy of anything better than what I had lost." If that sentence sounds like something you have thought, you will find company here, and you will find the story of a woman in John 4 who was treated the same way and was met by Jesus anyway.

sections.h2: For personal study and small groups
paras: Each chapter lists its Scripture passages up front and closes with questions that suit a quiet morning or a circle of women or men. The discussion questions are honest, for example asking how a breakup or divorce affected your outlook on love and on your sense of self-worth. Groups that want to talk about shame, forgiveness and judgment will find plenty to open up.

sections.h2: For anyone who cannot forgive themselves
paras: The author is honest that knowing God has forgiven you is not the same as forgiving yourself. She describes an afternoon at home on her knees, praying, "Help me …please, God, help me to forgive myself!" The answer that came was Paul's thorn in the flesh and God's word to him, "My grace is sufficient for you." She closes the section with a line many readers will want to keep:
"I must trust in His forgiveness even when I am unable to forgive myself. And He is enough!"

blocks.text: Every copy opens with a dedication to the author's father, a foreword by Stephanie Hensley, the contents, and then Chapter One, A Place Once Known as Virtue, subtitled An Allegory of First Love and Loss of Innocence. It begins like this:

paras: Virtue was mine. It was a landscape adorned with the beauty of innocence, unspoiled, and blooming with endless possibilities. Nothing was dead or brittle. Every plant flourished in youthful anticipation, and every fruit and flower thrived with hope. The meadow was clothed with wild flowers of many vibrant colors, descending gracefully to the clear, babbling stream. Near the stream was a well encircled with large stones, and the water from it was as clean and pure as a young girl's heart. Virtue was a sanctuary; the well was my heart.

blocks.text: A few lines later the story turns:

paras: But with all the love I had shown him, he slowly grew distant. More often, I walked to the well alone. At times, I would find him at the bluff, his eyes fixed on the horizon. His heart seemed a thousand miles from me.

details.Title: Lessons from the Well
details.Subtitle: A Devotional for the Divorced and Relationship Impaired
details.Author: Carol Renee Gitthens
details.Binding: Paperback (perfect bound), black and white interior on cream paper

stories.h2: A well walled in with stones
paras: The allegory begins in a sanctuary of meadows and a clear stream, with a well as pure as a young girl's heart. A young man draws close and then slowly pulls away, and a storm follows. Years later, after much loss, the author describes herself as guarding her heart so fiercely that "I encapsulated the well with thick, impenetrable walls, built up with stones of fear and distrust." At the gate she staked a sign with a new name, "Vulnerable, population: one." The chapter ends with questions that ask readers where they see themselves in the picture.

stories.h2: Jesus sat by the well, and He waited for her
paras: In Chapter Five the author looks hard at John 4. The Samaritan woman came to draw water alone at noon, when the other women were gone. The author writes, "She was an outcast among outcasts." Then comes the line the chapter turns on: "But Jesus, being weary from His journey, sat by the well, and He waited for her." The author admits she once shut people out, did not answer the door or the phone, and that in her aloneness Jesus came to her well too, through His Word and through prayer.

stories.h2: The radio, the roadside and the fear
paras: In Chapter Four the author remembers being seventeen and driving a big maroon car her friends nicknamed The Tank. A wave of fear hit her while she listened to pop music, so she switched off the radio, pulled over and prayed to be forgiven. Looking back she writes, "As a true believer, I should never have been so afraid." The chapter uses that memory to ask, with Genesis in view, who told us we were naked, and what fear was handed to us long before we made our own mistakes. In Chapter Seven her father's question comes back: "Are you a victim or a victor?"

author.bio: Carol Renee Gitthens is a pastor's daughter who grew up in a Christian home. She is the mother of five children and has been through three marriages and the divorces that followed, and she writes about guilt, shame and the grace of God without hiding any of it. The book is dedicated to her father, a bishop and pastor. At his bedside in April 2023 she made him two promises, to carry the torch of his ministry and to finish this book. Stephanie Hensley, author of When the Lilacs Bloom, wrote the foreword.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The author's dedication explains it. "First, I promised my dad that I would carry the torch of his ministry." "Second, I promised him I would finish my book." She found a Father's Day letter to him folded in his Bible, written after their first reconciliation, which thanked him for pointing her to God.

Of the mistakes she mentions there, she writes, "It was through my divorces and, as a result, the ups and downs of our father-daughter relationship, that we both came to a fuller understanding of the grace of God." The book is her way of passing on what that grace taught her. Its purpose, in the foreword's words, is to point readers to "the healing power of Jesus."

faq.q: What is Lessons from the Well about?
faq.a: It is a devotional for the divorced and relationship impaired by Carol Renee Gitthens, a pastor's daughter and mother of five who has been through three marriages and divorces. It combines her story, Scripture and prayer.

faq.q: Does the book include Bible verses for healing?
faq.a: Yes. Each chapter lists its Scripture at the start, and chapters quote passages such as "He heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds" (Psalm 147:3). The Scripture is from the New King James and New American Standard Bibles.

faq.q: What is the woman at the well chapter about?
faq.a: Chapter Five, "Lessons from the Well," is the longest in the book. It looks at John 4, where Jesus waits for a woman the town had pushed to the edges, and it shows what He offered her: Living Water, and a love with no boundaries.

faq.q: Does it justify divorce?
faq.a: No. The foreword says it is not a book that praises or justifies one of the most divisive topics in the church. It points to the healing power of Jesus, despite our choices.

faq.q: Is it a devotional I can use as a journal?
faq.a: Yes. Every chapter closes with Reflections: questions to discuss or journal, lined space to write, Scripture and a prayer.

faq.q: Does it speak to the fear of being abandoned or to feeling worthless after a breakup?
faq.a: The author writes honestly about both. She describes believing she was unworthy after her first heartbreak, and she shows how the woman at the well, and later her own Bible and prayer, answered that belief.

faq.q: Does it help you forgive yourself?
faq.a: Yes. In Chapter Five the author writes that God's forgiveness does not always mean you will just as easily forgive yourself, and she tells how she prayed for exactly that. Her answer came through Paul's words in 2 Corinthians 12, "My grace is sufficient for you."

faq.q: Does it speak to being judged by other Christians?
faq.a: Yes. Chapter Eight, "To Judge, or not to Judge, that is the Question," is subtitled "A Plea to Christ Followers." In it she asks, "Why did I feel like I had to make excuses for myself?"

faq.q: Can I use it in a small group or a women's Bible study?
faq.a: Yes. It suits personal study or small group discussion, with questions at the end of each chapter. It is written for women and men who are healing from broken relationships.

hero.audience_line: For readers ages 8 to 12 who like funny stories about cousins, and for the grandparents and parents who want a warm Christian story of simpler times to share with them.
hero.tagline: Thirteen-year-old RJ and his nine cousins meet every day under the oak tree in Johnny D's field, and trouble is never far behind, in a warm, funny Christian story of simpler times.

audience.headline: Ten cousins, one oak tree and a lot of very bad ideas.
audience.body: For families who want a warm, funny, Christian story of growing up in simpler times, for grandparents and parents who remember a field, a party line and Grandma's biscuits, and for young readers who like stories about cousins who always get into trouble and always stick together. Thirteen-year-old RJ tells seven short chapters about the summer days, Sunday mornings and scrapes that made his family what it is. A note on subjects: this is a gentle story with mischief and a few bumps. A fire brings the fire department, a boy breaks his arm falling off a van, the cousins are spanked and grounded as boys were in that day, and one evening the television news mentions a war, which upsets the family for a moment before a board game turns the evening around. There is no graphic detail.

quote.text: We are cousins, and we are the best of friends.
quote.cite: Life on The Ridge, Chapter 1

what_makes.title: What makes this book for families who miss the good old days
paras: A short story in seven chapters, told by a boy who is proud of his family and honest about his mistakes. The first page sets the tone: "We each had a phone, but it was connected to a cord in our homes." There are no games to play and no texting, only a field, a baseball and ten cousins who "are the best of friends."
Five things set it apart:
list: It is told by a kid. RJ is the oldest of three brothers, and his chapters read like a storyteller at Grandma's table.
It is funny without being unkind. Every mishap is followed by a consequence and by a laugh, and the narrator says of the fire, "To this day, we still laugh about that day."

It remembers real details of a simpler time: a party line, a station wagon, cathead biscuits, a wooden bat, a three-wheeler and a cake walk at the fire station dance. Hard words are explained in parentheses right in the text, so a young reader never gets lost.
Faith is part of the week, not an add-on. Sunday school, a fiery preacher, the blessing before meals and the Golden Rule all show up in ordinary scenes.
It ends with a short, sincere word to the reader about the Bible and prayer.

sections.h2: For grandparents and parents
paras: If you remember a cord on the kitchen phone and a grandmother who gave every cousin a scoop of vanilla ice cream, this is a story to read aloud and talk about. It is also a gentle way to tell children what an ordinary week once looked like.

sections.h2: For families who like funny stories of cousins
paras: The book is built on scenes that are easy to retell: the day the cousins turned a muddy kitchen floor into a sock-sliding rink, or the night a camping trip was nearly ruined by a "bear" that turned out to be one cousin snoring.

sections.h2: For Sunday school classes and church families
paras: Sunday school is part of the story from the first chapter, where the narrator remembers that "There we memorized Bible verses, and I still remember many of them to this day." A Golden Rule scene in chapter 5 gives a leader an easy way into a short talk about kindness.

sections.h2: For young readers ages 8 to 12
paras: The chapters are short, and the pages are in full color. When an old word comes up, the book explains it right there in parentheses, like tetherball, "a ball on a string attached to a pole." A reader who has never used a phone with a cord can still follow every joke.

blocks.text: Chapter 1 opens like this:

paras: Growing up on the ridge was fun, and it was a safe place. We, the cousins, met every day underneath the oak tree in Johnny D's field. There we scuffled, arm wrestled, threw around a baseball, and told jokes, all while enjoying peanut butter sandwiches my mom packed for us.

blocks.text: The book closes like this:

paras: If you are at a place in your life where you don't know what to do, turn to the Bible. Turn to God. Talk to Him. He is always listening. He always loves.

blocks.text: The seven chapters follow the cousins through Grandma's house and Sunday school, a fire and a baseball field, a three-wheeler and a muddy floor, a flower bed, a pool, a dance and an evening in front of the news.

stories.h2: The fire under the oak tree
paras: It is a week before Thanksgiving, and the cousins decide to build a fire. "It burned so high that we started sweating." A neighbor sees the smoke and calls for help, and the cousins run, leaving their jackets hanging on the oak tree. The firefighters know whose they are. The narrator adds, in parentheses, that "Firefighters come quickly when there's a fire, even a small one."

A new water well sends up black mud, and the boys play in it for hours. When they trudge inside for lunch, Dad walks in. They clean with the water hose, then one cousin brings it indoors, and soon they are all in their socks. "We all took turns sliding across the wet, muddy floor." The ending is a spanking and a week of being grounded, which was "the longest week of my life," saved only by an hour a day on the party line.

Chapter 6 ends at the pastor's dinner table, where the narrator, a picky eater, hides his brussels sprouts and peas in his pockets until the pastor's wife offers him more. "You must love green peas! Let me give you some more." One look at his mother settles it: "My pockets were stuffed with green peas that night."

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: There is no separate preface, so the reason is on the last page, where the narrator writes: "I am so thankful for my Sunday school teachers, my pastors, and my parents, who taught me the Bible." The page goes on: "I have seen Bible verses proven true many times in my own life. They have never failed me." Its hope for the reader is the closing invitation to turn to God, who "is always listening."

faq.q: What is Life on The Ridge about?
faq.a: A warm, funny Christian story about RJ and his nine cousins growing up together on a ridge, getting into trouble and always ending up back together. It is told in seven short chapters.

faq.q: Is it a book about the good old days?
faq.a: Yes. The narrator says it in his first chapter: "Those were the good old days." The stories show what he means, from a phone on a cord to biscuits at Grandma's, and the book never complains about today.

faq.q: Is it a story of simpler times?
faq.a: It is. The cousins play ball in a field, share one party line and spend Saturday nights at Grandma's, and one scene mentions the summer of 1975 and a war on the television news. The book does not say it is a memoir or a novel.

faq.q: Who are the brothers and cousins?
faq.a: RJ is the oldest of three brothers, with a sister who is not to be crossed. His uncles are his dad's three brothers, and together there are ten cousins. Grandma raised the four brothers alone after Pa died.

faq.q: Where is the old oak tree?
faq.a: In Johnny D's field. It is where the cousins meet every day, where they hang their jackets on a cold morning and where, one day in chapter 3, two cousins come riding up on a three-wheeler.

faq.q: Is it about growing in faith?
faq.a: Yes, in a gentle way. The cousins attend Sunday school, the family prays before meals, and RJ's mother reminds him of the Golden Rule: "So in everything, do to others what you would have them do to you."

faq.q: Does it have Bible verses for kids?
faq.a: A few. The cousins memorize Bible verses in Sunday school, and the narrator says "I still remember many of them to this day." It is a story, not a verse book, and it ends with a short word about turning to the Bible.

hero.audience_line: For believers who want an honest, hands-on look at love, repentance and surrender, alone, with a study partner or in a small group.
hero.tagline: A study and workbook on agape, the love God commands, with a self-analysis of the fifteen marks of love in 1 Corinthians 13:4-8.

audience.headline: Sixty years after she walked the church aisle, the author realized she had never surrendered. This is the study she wrote on the way.
audience.body: For believers who want to look honestly at their own hearts. The author is over seventy and has followed Jesus for sixty years. She writes that "Later in life, I realized that I was not saved," and that following Jesus as Lord is a life of surrender, not a single moment. This book walks you through what the Bible says about love, checks your own heart against 1 Corinthians 13:4-8, and invites you to bring what you find to God. A note on subjects: the book takes a direct view of sin, repentance and dying to the flesh, and names attitudes such as pride and irritation as sin. Readers in a vulnerable season may prefer to work through the self-analysis with a pastor, counselor or trusted friend.

quote.text: “Love is not a suggestion or a recommendation—it is a commandment.”
quote.cite: LOVE God's Way, Chapter One: What Is Love?

what_makes.title: What makes this book for readers who want a deeper walk, not a quick read
paras: Most devotionals give you a thought for the day. This one asks you to do the work.
Five things set it apart:
list: It is built on one commandment. From the first chapter, "What Is Love?," the study stays on the command to love God and one another, and asks what agape, the highest form of love, looks like in real life.

It includes a self-analysis you complete yourself. Part 3 takes each of fifteen love traits drawn from 1 Corinthians 13:4-8 and sets a column of loving traits beside a column of their opposites. You check what applies to you, write examples, and pray over each one.

It guides you through repentance. Chapter Six defines repentance as more than recognizing sin, and the self-analysis tells you to pray and confess before God, ask His forgiveness and ask the Spirit to help you surrender that area.
It admits the author's own blind spots. In "Intentional or Unintentional," she tells what she felt when she walked into a church and felt invisible, and what God asked her next.
It ends in grace. The conclusion says that "conviction is not condemnation."

sections.h2: For believers who want to study the greatest commandment

paras: The author visits several churches and is welcomed warmly at the door. Inside, the best seats are marked with belongings, and she is mostly ignored. She is hurt, and then she hears God ask how often she has done the same to others. She says the conviction was gripping, and that it changed how she understood loving a neighbor.

stories.h2: An aunt who made everyone feel important
paras: She remembers a large family and an aunt who turned simple moments into adventures. When the children misbehaved, the aunt would hold a group talk instead of shaming one child, asking them whether everyone must have the same ideas and what they could learn from someone else's.
The closing pages say that the walk is daily, not a single decision. Some days will be easier than others, and when you fall short, God's grace is sufficient. The author's last lines sum up the book:
“Agape love is not simply something we study—it is something we are called to live.”

author.bio: Wanda Bailey Clark writes in her preface that she is over seventy and that sixty years have passed since she walked down the church aisle, professed Jesus as her Savior and Lord, and was baptized. Later in life she realized she had not truly surrendered, and she prepared this study as she followed God. She also tells of growing up in a large family that gathered often, and of an aunt who made everyone feel important. The book prints no separate About the Author page.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The preface tells where the book began:
“Later in life, I realized that I was not saved. I came to understand that following Jesus as Lord involves more than a moment—it is a life of surrender.”

She gives four purposes for the study: to fully examine God's first commandment to love, to evaluate the attitudes and behaviors that defy it, to walk through a personal evaluation of acknowledging sin, repenting and dying to flesh-centered behaviors, and to understand the spiritual fruits that follow.

faq.q: What is LOVE God's Way?
faq.a: It is a 132-page Christian study and workbook on agape love, the love God commands. It has four parts and eleven chapters, and its center is a self-analysis of the fifteen marks of love in 1 Corinthians 13:4-8.

faq.q: Is it a study of 1 Corinthians 13?
faq.a: Yes. Part 3 takes each of the fifteen components of agape love in 1 Corinthians 13:4-8 in turn. They are, in order: patient; kind; does not envy; does not boast; is not proud; does not dishonor others; is not self-seeking; keeps no record of wrongs; thinks no evil; does not rejoice in iniquity but rejoices in the truth; bears all things; believes and trusts; always hopes; endures and perseveres; and never gives up.

faq.q: What does it say about the greatest commandment?
faq.a: The chapter Agape Love Is Law quotes Jesus naming the first and greatest commandment, to love the Lord your God, and the second, to love your neighbor as yourself. The author says love is not a suggestion but a commandment, and that ignoring a commandment is sin.

faq.q: Does it explain how to repent?
faq.a: Yes. The chapter Repentance says that confessing sin is acknowledging it, while genuine repentance goes further: it hurts, it is a turning, and it means you will not continue in the same direction. An exercise sets superficial repentance beside genuine repentance and asks for your own memories of forgiveness.

faq.q: Is it a study of the fruit of the Spirit?
faq.a: Some of it. Part 4 quotes Galatians 5, where the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace and the rest, and the preface names the spiritual fruits that follow surrender as one of the book's purposes. The main study, though, is the love described in 1 Corinthians 13.

faq.q: What does it teach about sanctification?
faq.a: Part 3 is titled The Sanctification Process of Agape Love. The conclusion says that each time you submit your thoughts, words, reactions and desires to God, His nature takes deeper root in you, and that this is the process of sanctification.

faq.q: Is it a self-examination workbook?
faq.a: Yes. The self-analysis asks you to check each trait you identify with, write examples and pray over each one. If you see no change at the end, the author asks whether you need to start the study over or seek counsel.

faq.q: What does it mean by dying to self?
faq.a: The book's own phrase is dying to the flesh: your opinions, ideas and feelings, submitted to Jesus as Lord. The author says it is a process, and that the more you die to your flesh, the deeper your relationship with God will grow.

faq.q: Is it a devotional for women?
faq.a: It is written by a woman, but not only for women. It speaks to any believer who wants to grow in love, and it works on your own, with a partner or in a small group.

content_note.title: Content note
paras: The book takes a direct view of sin, repentance and "dying to flesh," and says that attitudes such as pride, irritation and passive-aggression are sin. It is written for believers who want that kind of honesty. Readers who are in a vulnerable season may prefer to work through the self-analysis with a pastor, counselor or trusted friend.

audience.headline: A Christian Bible study workbook for believers who have been forgiven and still feel stuck, from a licensed counselor who joins God's Word with what research says about the mind and the body.
audience.body: For anyone who has come to God, received His forgiveness and still asks why they feel depressed, why they return to the things that hurt them, or whether the blood of Christ is enough for what they have done. Kami Tahyi, MS, LPCC, writes from the counseling office and the church pew. Mended is six short sessions of plain teaching, Scripture to write out and honest questions to answer, so you do the work of healing and not only the reading.

quote.text: “The good news is that God created our brains to heal.”
quote.cite: Mended, Session Two: Wounds

what_makes.title: What makes this book for people who want healing they can work through
paras: Many books on emotional healing are read once and shelved. This one is designed to be written in, talked over in a small group and returned to.
Five things set it apart:
list: It is a working book. Most sessions ask you to write out a verse, list your own thoughts or describe a time you felt something.

It joins faith and research. The author cites Paul Ekman's six basic emotions, the Centers for Disease Control research on adverse childhood experiences, and teachers such as David Seamands, Larry Crabb and Bessel van der Kolk, and she keeps each tied to Scripture.
It names the church's part. Session Two says the church can supply protective factors for people who were wounded, including caring adults, a sense of purpose and social connection.
It treats feelings as information. She says that feelings are not wrong, that we should avoid telling anyone not to feel a certain way, and that our thoughts shape what we feel.
It is built for groups. The back of the book has leader ideas, a set of group rules, and a questionnaire and a morning routine to use alongside the sessions.

sections.h2: For believers who feel forgiven and still feel stuck
paras: The Introduction gives the problem a voice: guilt and shame from the lack of healing, doubts about whether Jesus is enough to cure what plagues us. The sessions go after those doubts with Scripture and with plain explanations of how thoughts, feelings and the brain work.

sections.h2: For small groups and recovery ministries
paras: The book is written to be used in a group. The Leader Ideas say to start on time, share group rules on the first night, pray, read the assigned passage and share answers, and the Group Rules ask for trust, attentive listening, confidence and no cross-talk.

sections.h2: For people healing from childhood wounds
paras: Session Two walks through adverse childhood experiences and the idea of toxic stress, then moves to how God designed the brain to heal, and the church's part in that. It lists principles for healing damaged emotions, including accepting responsibility, asking whether you want to be healed, and forgiving others and yourself.

sections.h2: For counselors, pastors and church leaders
paras: Pastors and lay counselors who want a faith-based way to talk about emotions with a congregation will find a short, structured plan. The book says that, if issues are more significant than what a Bible study can handle, a leader should refer the person to a pastor or a counselor.

paras: In Session Three, the author tells of a huge glass dome built in the desert in the early 1980s, with purified air and water, to see whether people, plants and animals could thrive. Everything did well except the trees, which fell over as they grew. Scientists realized the one thing they had forgotten was wind. The wind, she writes, makes roots grow deeper, and she asks the reader to share about a time when a struggle helped them grow stronger roots.
In Session Two, the author says many people she has worked with know that God has forgiven them and still cannot forgive themselves. She calls that a theology we create and asks one direct question:
"Is the blood of Christ enough for your sins?"

In Session Five the author draws on a film about happiness that she says she has watched with clients 75 times or more. Its first principle is that happiness is not based on circumstances. She notes that the researchers do not share her faith but have some good things to say, and she pairs the principle with Paul's lines on contentment from Philippians 4.

author.bio: Kami Tahyi, MS, LPCC, is a licensed counselor. After painful life experiences, she found a church home at a church plant's first service on Easter Sunday 2009. In the years since, she has attended college, become a licensed counselor and worked as a counselor at a women's residential treatment facility. She writes that the more she studies, the more she knows God's Word has all the answers, and that her education, license and position let her bring together God's natural healing and what research has uncovered.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The author writes that healing begins when we admit our need for help, and that we are often kept from the wholeness the Lord provides by our own experiences, strong beliefs and unhealthy coping mechanisms. The book is her answer to that gap, a place where Scripture and counseling meet. A line from Session Six says what she wants you to hold onto:
"We are God-created beings that are not defined by our desires and thoughts."

faq.q: What is Mended?
faq.a: It is a 48-page Christian workbook by Kami Tahyi, MS, LPCC, in six sessions. Each one pairs teaching with Scripture to write out and questions to answer.

faq.q: Is Mended a Bible study workbook?
faq.a: Yes. The book calls itself The Mended Bible Study, and it is built to be written in. Most sessions ask you to write out a verse, list your own thoughts or describe a time you felt something, and the Leader Ideas and Group Rules at the back are for small groups.

faq.q: What does it teach about emotional healing from the Bible?
faq.a: It pairs Scripture with counseling. Session Two takes David Seamands's principles from Healing Damaged Emotions: share the memory with another, accept your responsibility, ask "Do I want to be healed?" as Jesus asked in John 5:6, forgive everyone involved, forgive yourself, and ask God what the real problem is. Each session asks you to write out verses, such as Philippians 4:6-7.

faq.q: Is it a forgiveness workbook?
faq.a: Forgiveness is one part of it, not the whole. Session Two says we must forgive everyone involved and we must forgive ourselves, and it asks: "Is the blood of Christ enough for your sins?" The other sessions cover feelings, choices, unity and intimacy.

faq.q: Does it help with healing from trauma?
faq.a: Some of it. Session Two says that understanding trauma is essential, and it explains the research on adverse childhood experiences and how God created our brains to heal. It is a faith-based group study, not a trauma treatment program, and it tells leaders to refer anyone whose issues are more significant than a Bible study can handle to a pastor or counselor.

faq.q: Is it a replacement for counseling?
faq.a: No. It is a Christian workbook and Bible study. It says that if issues are more significant than a Bible study can handle, a leader should refer the participant to a pastor or counselor. Anyone in crisis should reach out to medical or crisis help as well.

faq.q: Can I use it on my own?
faq.a: Yes. The writing prompts can be answered alone, and the Leader Ideas show how to use the sessions in a small group.

faq.q: Does it come with videos?
faq.a: The Leader Ideas say a session is designed to begin with a DVD video. The printed book does not include one, so check what your group will use before you begin.

faq.q: How many sessions are there?
faq.a: Six. They are, in order: Feelings; Wounds; Trees; Choices; Unity; and Intimacy.

faq.q: What Bible translation does it use?
faq.a: The book quotes Scripture throughout and does not print a translation notice, so check the verse you write out against the Bible you use.

content_note.title: Content note
paras: This workbook discusses trauma, childhood abuse and neglect, depression, anxiety, lust and shame. The ACE questionnaire in the Resources asks direct questions about abuse, including sexual abuse, in childhood. Answer it only when you feel safe, and bring it to a counselor or pastor if you need support. It is a Christian workbook, not a treatment program.

sections.h2: For parents who want a gentle rhyming read-aloud
paras: The verse moves in short rhymed couplets and returns to the same refrain, which makes it easy to read slowly at bedtime and easy for a child to say along. The lines about holding a sleeping baby make a natural place to pause and talk.

sections.h2: For families who have waited and prayed for a child
paras: The story begins with a question to God about whether to have a baby of her own, and it admits the long wait: “Several years passed by; I doubted that you would even come.” A couple of pages later the news arrives, and the mother treasures the stranger's words in her heart: “I hid these words inside my heart that later I would need.”

sections.h2: For parents of babies who spent time in the hospital
paras: The hospital pages are short. The baby is taken to Children's Hospital on the twenty-first day of his life, the parents stand beside his bed, and the surgeries leave him sleeping. The family does not face it alone: “We were never left alone; we felt an army gathered round our fighting baby boy.” Home comes after a long stay, and a rainbow shines over the ramp as they leave.

audience.headline: A mother tells her son: every flutter, every nap, every night, I was there.
audience.body: For parents who want a gentle rhyming read-aloud about a mother's love for her son, families who have waited and prayed for a child, and parents of babies who spent time in a children's hospital. Dana House tells the true story of the promised baby she carried, the old saying about spoiling a baby with too much holding, and the frightening night his tiny heart needed help, in verse built around one refrain a child can hold on to. A note on subjects: the story includes a newborn found to have an enlarged heart, a long hospital stay and surgeries, told in simple rhyme with no graphic detail and no medical advice. It ends in the hope of home, a rainbow and a mother's steady love. Parents may want to read it first before sharing it with a child who has had hospital time of their own.

quote.text: One day our roles will change, and I'll be sleeping a little more. I know you'll sit beside me, just as I did with you many years before.
quote.cite: I Missed You While You Were Sleeping, the last page

what_makes.title: What makes this book for parents who want a read-aloud about love and trust
paras: It is a picture book told by a mother directly to her son, and its subject is being wanted. A stranger's promise, years of waiting, a surprise, a hard season and a rainbow are all carried by one repeated line.
Five things set it apart:
list: It is true to life. The mother speaks to her son about events from the author's own family.

It is built on a refrain. Again and again the verse comes home to “I missed you while you were sleeping,” and each time it means something different, from a flutter in the womb to a long hospital sleep.
It begins with prayer. Before church one morning the mother prays about big decisions, and a stranger tells her that her baby is on the way.
It speaks about holding a baby. The mother heard the old saying that you will spoil a baby if you hold him too much, and her own mama had taught her otherwise.
It meets a hard season honestly. The hospital pages are brief and gentle, and the family keeps choosing to “find the little joys and not let the worries win.”

paras: One morning before church, I prayed, God, what should we do? We have big decisions to make and need clear direction from You.

blocks.text: Over the next page a stranger speaks:

paras: You can just imagine my feelings of surprise when a lady that I didn't know looked me in the eyes.

blocks.text: And the first refrain arrives when the baby is still unborn:

paras: When you were curled up still, I'd wait to feel you leaping.

blocks.text: The book closes on a verse from Isaiah:

paras: As a mother comforts her child, so I will comfort you.

details.Title: I Missed You While You Were Sleeping
details.Author: Dana House
details.Binding: Paperback (perfect bound) and hardback (case laminate)

paras: On the page before the promise, a praying mother asks what her family should do. A lady she does not know looks her in the eyes and boldly declares, “Your baby is on the way!” She says the child will be a gift from God, and the mother keeps those words close. Years later they carry her through the hardest pages of the book.

When the baby is weeks old, the mother keeps holding him even while he sleeps. She has heard the old saying, “You'll spoil a child if you hold a baby too much,” but her mama taught her otherwise. She knows that “you just needed my touch,” and that someday she will long to hold him and watch him dream, so she holds him now, sowing love into the harvest.

After six months the family goes home. It feels strange to leave, because the hospital had begun to feel like home. As they leave the ramp, “a beautiful rainbow was shining brightly in the sky,” and it reminds them they are never left alone. The mother sees God's reminder through the clouds and says again, “I missed you while you were sleeping.”

author.bio: Dana House wrote this rhyming picture book from her own family's story. In the dedication she thanks her husband, who told her early on that storms would come around them but never between them, the friends and family who surrounded them like an army, and her parents, who taught her that a home should be loving, peaceful and a safe haven. She calls her son her gift from God.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The author dedicates the book to her husband, friends and family, who “surrounded us like an army,” and to her parents, who taught her that a home should be loving, peaceful, and a safe haven. She writes the book to her son in the words she says were spoken to her that Sunday morning: “You are my gift from God, birthed from me, for me.” The last page leaves the reader with the promise of Isaiah: “As a mother comforts her child, so I will comfort you.”

faq.q: What is I Missed You While You Were Sleeping about?
faq.a: It is a rhyming picture book in which a mother tells her son about waiting for him, holding him close and the frightening night his tiny heart needed help, with a refrain every child can treasure: I missed you while you were sleeping.

faq.q: Is it a story about a mom and her son?
faq.a: Yes. The mother speaks to her son on every page, from a stranger's promise before he was born to the day he turns nine. The book calls him her gift from God, her healing boy and her promised one. The words “mom and son” do not appear, since the mother speaks as mama.

faq.q: Is it a book about a mother's love for her son?
faq.a: Yes, from first page to last. The mother tells her son that her feelings “have never changed” since the start, that she held him even while he slept, and that she stood beside his hospital bed. On the last page the roles turn around, and she pictures the grown son sitting beside her.

faq.q: Is it a true story?
faq.a: Yes. It is a true-to-life story told by a mother directly to her son, drawn from the author's own family.

faq.q: Does it talk about answered prayer?
faq.a: It opens with a mother's prayer and a stranger's message that her baby is on the way, and later she says that knowing he was her gift from God gave her strength to overcome her fears. The exact phrase answered prayer does not appear, but the story is built around it.

faq.q: Is the baby called a gift from God?
faq.a: Yes. The phrase comes back several times, in the stranger's message, in the refrain and in the dedication. The mother also says “you'd be a beacon of light in the dark,” and calls her son a victorious one and a heart warrior child.

faq.q: Is it a medical book about a heart condition?
faq.a: No. One scene is a hospital stay when the baby's heart was found to be enlarged. The book gives no medical information and names no diagnosis beyond that.

faq.q: What age is it for?
faq.a: Ages 4 to 8, as a read-aloud with a parent. It is told in short rhyming lines that suit bedtime or a quiet afternoon.

sections.h2: For pastors and church planters
paras: If you are tired, discouraged or just beginning, the author is blunt and kind: "I'm not a self-made martyr, just a fellow pastor who wants to see you and your church reach its highest potential." He also says that "Pulpit ministry counts for approximately 12 percent of their weekly schedule," and that too many of the remaining hours go to damage control.

sections.h2: For elders, staff and lay leaders
paras: Most of his observations relate to churches of fewer than two hundred in attendance, though he says "any leader can benefit from the information presented." Each chapter is short enough to read before a board or leadership meeting.

sections.h2: For believers who want a passion for the local church
paras: The author writes that "Christ-honoring local churches are God's gift to every community," and he asks the Holy Spirit to "rekindle a desire in the hearts of true Christians everywhere and renew their passion for God's house, the local church."

sections.h2: For former pastors
paras: If you left the pulpit and carry rejection or a sense of failure, the introduction speaks to you directly: "You are not a failure! A failure is defined as someone who, after getting knocked down, refused to get back up."

audience.headline: Forty things behind the back-door exits, from a pastor who has been there.
audience.body: For pastors, church planters, staff and elders, lay leaders in churches of every size, believers who want to rekindle a passion for the local church, and former pastors who carry rejection or a sense of failure. Roger Loomis draws on forty-three years of pastoral ministry to name forty issues that arise in contemporary evangelical churches and pairs each with biblical principles. A note on subjects: the book speaks plainly about church conflict, criticism, burnout, pastors who leave the ministry and people who leave a church angry, and it names hurts the author carried. It is one pastor's view from the pulpit, not counseling or a substitute for it. If a hard season is weighing on you, please talk with a trusted pastor, counselor or physician, and if you are in crisis, contact your local emergency services or a crisis line.

quote.text: Nothing on earth matches the wonders of the local church! What can pastors do to stem the tide of Christians who see regular attendance as optional?
quote.cite: Monday Morning Preacher, opening page

what_makes.title: What makes this book for pastors and church leaders
paras: A book of short chapters on church leadership, each pairing a problem that surfaces in many congregations with biblical principles for answering it. The author calls himself a Christian pragmatist: "one who recognizes symptoms, then searches out root causes."
Five things set it apart:
list: It starts from the numbers and does not stop there. The introduction cites research that most American churches now have fewer than one hundred in weekend attendance and asks the hard question of why so many pastors are stepping down.
It looks inside the church first. The enemy and the culture are real, he writes, yet "the answers to much church decline, and solutions, can be found within churches themselves."

It is short on theory and long on cases. Chapters carry titles such as Pastors Are People Too, Virtual Church, Pastor or Hireling?, No-Drama Zone, Church Hoppers, Peacemakers, Not Peacekeepers, The Ten Suggestions, Bring Back Honor, The Heart of Worship and Money, Money, Money.
It is honest about the author's own missteps. He admits that in his third pastorate he used the pulpit to vent his anger, and he says so in order to warn others.
It speaks to people who have left the pulpit. A closing word tells former pastors, now in the secular marketplace, that they are not alone and not second-class Christians.

paras: In the first chapter of Part 1 the author recalls the people who loved his family unconditionally. "Most understood that we lived in a glass house but remained unwilling to throw rocks." He also turns the lens on himself. He tells pastors that other pastors usually do not want to hear their war stories, and admits he has rehearsed his own too often, "and for that, I'm embarrassed and sorry." His advice comes from an old saying: "Write your hurts in dust and your benefits in marble."

The Heart of Worship chapter begins with a song and a conviction that "worship is all about Jesus." He describes praise as "ascribing honor and worth to our King," and says that while praise extols the goodness of the Lord, "worship brings heaven to earth!" He asks worship leaders for humility above skill: "To me, the greatest attribute any worship leader can possess is humility." Skilled musicians can bring excellence to the platform, he says, but without yielded hearts a church will have "a performance but not a life-altering venue."

In Church Hoppers he gives a pastor's reason for staying planted, quoting Psalm 92:13 and asking, "What does it mean to be planted?" His answer is "to be faithful to one church." He tells of a man in his twenties who attended a different church almost every Sunday and eventually gave up on church altogether, and he writes that no one church has all the right answers: "while the Bible remains inerrant and infallible, we are not!"

author.bio: Roger Loomis has served in pastoral ministry for more than four decades, leading six churches in three states. He came to faith in 1970 and took Bible classes at Evangel University, though he credits much of his training to what he calls God's School of Hard Knocks. In 2012 he resigned from pastoral ministry to become a hospice chaplain, and in 2017 he and his wife planted a church in a village in rural northeastern Ohio. A self-described Christian pragmatist, he has a heart to help pastors succeed in their noble calling.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The author gives his reason in a single line. "My sincere desire is that pastors everywhere learn from my mistakes and successes in order to sidestep any potential church setbacks."

He is candid about the exits he lived through. "My intention is to openly confront the reasons people left every church I served." And he sends the book out with a blessing for the people who lead local churches: "May you experience the favor of the Lord!"

faq.q: What is Monday Morning Preacher about?
faq.a: Roger Loomis's look at why people leave the local church and what pastors can do about it. Drawing on forty-three years of pastoral ministry, he identifies forty issues that arise in contemporary evangelical churches and pairs each with biblical principles.

faq.q: Is it a book about church leadership?
faq.a: Yes. It is written for pastors, church planters, staff, elders and lay leaders, and it covers conflict, critics, unreasonable leaders, offenses and money from the point of view of a fellow pastor.

faq.q: Does it have a chapter on the heart of worship?
faq.a: Yes. The Heart of Worship is one chapter. It is about the posture of worship leaders and of the church, not a manual for song selection, and it sits among chapters on conflict, honor and money.

faq.q: Is it about biblical preaching?
faq.a: Not as a how-to. The author calls for "balanced biblical preaching that draws from the entire canon of Scripture" in one chapter, and the introduction urges pastors to preach "the unsearchable riches of Christ" from the pulpit and deal with the other matters in private. It is a book about church life, not a preaching course.

faq.q: What does the book say about prophetic worship?
faq.a: In The Ten Suggestions, one suggestion says so-called prophetic worship songs are meant for private praise and not public worship, and he writes that the object of worship "is Jesus." It is his view as a pastor, offered as a point for leaders to weigh.

faq.q: Does it help with church growth?
faq.a: It addresses declining attendance directly, and says that "a lot of church problems develop from within." It is a book of observations and biblical principles, not a growth system or a set of metrics.

faq.q: Why is it called Monday Morning Preacher?
faq.a: Like Monday morning quarterbacks who review the game, pastors are invited to revisit their Sunday service on Monday, to celebrate their wins and to identify the in-house issues that need wise and righteous attention.

faq.q: Is there anything for former pastors?
faq.a: Yes. A closing word to people now in the secular marketplace who fight rejection, anger or a sense of failure tells them they are not alone, not second-class Christians, and that there is purposeful life and kingdom productivity beyond formal ministry.

audience.headline: A boy whose father left stands up on dads' day at school and tells his class about the Father who never will.
audience.body: For children ages 4 to 8, especially children whose own father is absent or who feel different from the kids around them, and for the parents, grandparents and teachers who read to them. Kelly Pexton tells the story of Caleb, who dreads the Friday when every dad comes to class, prays for courage, and finds the words to describe the One who goes to school with him every day. A note on subjects: the story begins with a boy who has not seen his father since he was little. He is nervous and some classmates giggle. It is told simply and ends warmly. It is a picture book about faith and courage, not a guide for parents or counseling advice. If a child in your care is grieving or struggling, please talk with a pastor, a school counselor or a licensed professional.

quote.text: He is always there. He will never, ever leave you.
quote.cite: My Perfect Daddy, Caleb's last words to his class

what_makes.title: What makes this book for children who feel different from the kids around them
paras: Every child in Mrs. Mackin's class is supposed to stand at the front with their dad. For Caleb it is the scariest day of the year.
Five things set it apart:
list: It starts with dread, not a lesson. On a Friday morning in October Caleb's hands will not stop shaking, and all week he has thought about staying home and pretending to be sick, then decided that would be a lie.
It is honest about an absent father. Caleb tells his class that his dad stopped living with the family and that he has not seen him since.
It lets a child pray in plain words. Caleb whispers "Please don't let them laugh at me" every night, and at the front of the room he whispers "Give me courage."

It answers classmates' real questions. How can God be everyone's Father? How do you know He is always with you? How can you believe in someone you cannot see? Caleb answers like a child, with short true sentences.
It ends with comfort. A warm feeling comes back like "a gentle hug from the inside," and Caleb sits down knowing "the loving arms of his Perfect Daddy" are wrapped tight around him.

sections.h2: For children whose father is absent
paras: This book does not hide the hole. Caleb says so out loud, and then he says what helped. His mom took him to church, and at Sunday School he learned about God. The story does not promise that the father returns. It gives a child a way to say that he has a Father who stays.

sections.h2: For parents, grandparents and caregivers
paras: If a child in your care misses a father, this is a story you can read together without a long explanation. The pages leave room for a child to talk. Caleb's answers to his classmates are the kind a young child can repeat at bedtime: "You have two dads. You have your dad here on earth. And you have God, your Father in heaven."

sections.h2: For Sunday School teachers and classroom readers
paras: The questions are the ones a Sunday School class asks. David says he already has a dad, and Sam wants to know how Caleb can believe in something he cannot see. Teachers can stop after each answer and ask the group what they would say.

sections.h2: For children who are scared to speak in front of the class
paras: Many children know Caleb's Friday: shaking hands, a tummy full of jumping frogs and a clock that ticks too loud. The book does not tell him to stop being afraid. It shows him pray, stand up anyway and take the long walk to the front. "The walk to the front of the room felt very, very long." A child who dreads show and tell or a class talk will recognize every step.

details.Author: Kelly Pexton

stories.h2: The teacher who offers a way out
paras: On Monday Mrs. Mackin told the class that on Friday everyone would bring their dad to school and tell the class all about him. All the kids cheered, but not Caleb. The book says "Caleb did not have a dad." Mrs. Mackin bends down close and says softly, "Caleb, you don't have to do this." Caleb nods, but he has an idea. All week he thinks about staying home, decides that would be a lie, and prays every night with his eyes squeezed shut.

When Mrs. Mackin looks right at Caleb, his heart jumps into his throat. He nods yes and stands up. "The walk to the front of the room felt very, very long." He looks up at the ceiling and whispers, and "right away, something warm spread through his chest." His shoulders relax. He says, "I want to tell you about my Father," and his voice is small but steady.

stories.h2: Two questions from the back of the room
paras: David asks how God can be everyone's Father when he has a dad sitting right there, and Caleb answers that he has two dads. Sam asks how Caleb knows God is always with him, and Caleb smiles for the first time all day. He puts his hand on his chest and says, "I talk to Him all day long. Even without words." And when Sam asks how anyone can believe in something they cannot see, Caleb says, "That's called faith."

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: What the story itself says is plain. Caleb ends the day with a warm feeling: "he could feel the loving arms of his Perfect Daddy wrapped tight around him." And what he wants his classmates to know is this: "He is always there. He will never, ever leave you."

faq.q: What is My Perfect Daddy about?
faq.a: It is a picture book about Caleb, whose father left the family, and the Friday when every child in his class introduces their dad. He prays for courage, stands up, and tells his classmates about God as his Father, who goes to school with him and never leaves.

faq.q: Is it a book about God as Father?
faq.a: Yes. That is the whole story. The phrase God as Father is not printed in the book. The book says it in a child's words: "God made the whole wide world. He made people so He could have children to love. We are all His children. He is a Father to all of us."

faq.q: Is it a show and tell story?
faq.a: It has the same shape: a child stands at the front and tells the class about someone special. The words show and tell do not appear in it, and Caleb has no dad beside him, so he brings the One he cannot see.

faq.q: Does it speak about a heavenly Father?
faq.a: Yes. Caleb tells David that he has God, his Father in heaven. The word heavenly is not used, and the idea comes in plain language: a dad on earth and God in heaven.

faq.q: Is it for a child with an absent father?
faq.a: Caleb's father stopped living with the family, and he has not seen him since. The book shows a boy missing his dad and finding comfort in prayer. It does not offer counseling or promise any change in a real father.

faq.q: Does it teach a prayer for courage?
faq.a: It shows one. Caleb whispers "Give me courage" and then feels warm in his chest. He also prays at night that the others will not laugh at him. The book shows a child praying in his own words.

faq.q: Does it say God is always with me?
faq.a: Yes. Caleb says that when he is scared he asks God for help and "the scared feeling goes away," and that "He always listens." He tells Sam, "He is always there."

sections.h2: For readers of faith-based suspense and family drama
paras: If you like a story where the stakes are personal, this one starts at a breakfast table and stays close to the people at it. Phil, his mother, his friend George and George's wife Marge laugh together over bacon and eggs in the first chapter, and the book makes sure you know them before it begins to turn. There is a crime in this story and the book does not look away from it.

sections.h2: For readers who enjoy a clear spiritual message
paras: The faith in this book is not a coat of paint. Phil listens to a Christian radio station, reads the Bible every day and prays for his brother's repentance. On the morning he buys the ticket, the passages he reads puzzle him, and the novel tells us why: he “didn't realize that by buying the lottery ticket he had compromised what he believed.” Scripture, judgement and mercy run through the plot.

sections.h2: For Christian fiction readers who like a warm hero and a villain with a history
paras: Marge's resentment is not random. The book gives her an old wound, and then shows what she makes of it. George, who is easily led, is caught between his friend and his wife. If you enjoy characters who are neither all good nor all bad, and a story that is willing to ask whether anyone is beyond forgiveness, you will find them here.

audience.headline: One lottery ticket. One hundred seventy-nine million dollars. One choice that cost more than he knew.
audience.body: For readers of faith-based suspense and family drama. Phil Gunn is a born-again mill worker in the small town of Kamish, Idaho, who reads his Bible every day and gives what little he has to his family. Then he buys a lottery ticket he knows he should not buy, and wins. His best friend's wife has never liked him, and she has already begun to scheme. A note on subjects: this is a crime story as well as a faith story. It includes a murder and the investigation that follows, drug and alcohol addiction, homelessness and a criminal underworld, and it ends in a courtroom. It is written for adults.

quote.text: If he didn't win, it wouldn't matter. If he did, everyone would think it was a good idea. He had told himself that if he won, he would share the wealth. So the thought became a plan, and the plan became reality.
quote.cite: Of Judgement and Of Mercy, Chapter 1, The Ticket and the Trap

what_makes.title: What makes this book for readers who want a Christian novel with a real hero and a real villain
paras: A Christian novel about what happens when a good man compromises what he believes. It runs from a trailer by the river and a breakfast café to a long night drive toward the lottery office in Boise, and it keeps asking what one small choice can set in motion.
Five things set it apart:
list: It starts with a hero who is easy to like. Phil is six foot two, strong as a bull, sings only in the shower where nobody can hear, and orders the same breakfast at the café where the waitress knows it by heart.

It takes the temptation seriously. Phil knows his pastor preaches against gambling. The book lets him argue with himself (“Besides, what could one ticket hurt? Who would know anyway?”) and shows the dread that settles in afterward.
It gives the villain a history. Marge has never liked Phil, and the book tells you why, so her scheming is not cartoonish.
It is a family story. Phil sends money to his sister Jeannie, who is away at medical school, meets his mother for breakfast and prays for a brother lost to the streets of Oakland.
It names its theme in the title. Of Judgement and Of Mercy is about temptation, greed and envy, and the hope that God's mercy reaches further than our mistakes.

details.Title: Of Judgement and Of Mercy
details.Author: Roy Roberts
details.Binding: Paperback (perfect bound), cream paper, black and white interior

paras: Phil feels a yearning to buy a lottery ticket and tells himself it would be wrong. He buys one anyway, with a few snacks so he will not look conspicuous. “All the time, he felt guilty but overrode it with what if?” That night he reads three Bible passages, including the story of Samson and Delilah, and cannot find the meaning he usually finds. After his shift he scribbles the numbers on a scrap of paper, races home, checks his ticket twice and whispers, “I won,” and then, “I can't believe it.”

stories.h2: A midnight feast and a quiet plan
paras: Phil calls his friends in the middle of the night and the three set off to celebrate. Over the long drive Marge starts to put a plan together. “Well, let's not tell anyone else about the money until after you get it,” she says, and she offers to drive Phil to Boise, where he must go to the lottery headquarters to collect. “All she needed was to convince George that it was the only thing to do—and she would.”

Chapter 3 begins with Phil asleep and George and Marge awake. Marge tells George a story about what happened at the restaurant, and when he starts to storm out, she asks: “What would hurt him more—your beating him up, or him losing his money?” At first, the narrator tells us, her plan did not include getting rid of Phil. “But the more she thought about it—and the more she told George about it—the more certain she became that it would be necessary.”

author.bio: Roy Roberts is the author of Of Judgement and Of Mercy, a Christian novel of temptation, greed and envy and the consequences of a single choice. In his dedication he thanks four people whose faith and encouragement, he writes, helped bring the story to life.
