why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The book is a story, and it lets the story speak. It is built on two verses that Pastor Whittington's congregation heard on a hot August morning and that George remembers late in the book: “For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord,” and “For the love of money is the root of all evil.”

Those verses are the book's questions. What does one compromise cost? What do envy and greed do to a friendship? And, in the final chapters, what does mercy look like when it is offered to someone who has not earned it? The novel holds out the hope that God's mercy reaches further than our mistakes.

faq.q: What is Of Judgement and Of Mercy about?
faq.a: It is a Christian novel about Phil Gunn, a born-again mill worker who buys a lottery ticket against his convictions, wins one hundred seventy-nine million dollars, and learns what one compromise can cost.

faq.q: Is it Christian fiction?
faq.a: Yes. It is a Christian novel for readers who enjoy faith-based suspense, family drama and stories with a clear spiritual message.

faq.q: What happens with the winning lottery ticket, and is Phil a jackpot winner?
faq.a: Yes. Phil checks the numbers after his shift and has won one hundred seventy-nine million dollars, to be paid over time, or sixty-eight million in cash. He calls his best friend in the middle of the night, and his friend's wife, who has never liked Phil, begins to scheme.

faq.q: Is there family drama in the story?
faq.a: Yes. Phil supports his mother and sister and mourns a brother lost to the streets of Oakland, and the story moves between small-town diners, family obligations and long night drives toward Boise.

faq.q: Does the book deal with forgiveness?
faq.a: Yes. It explores temptation, greed and envy and asks whether mercy can still find us after judgement; it holds out the hope that God's mercy reaches further than our mistakes.

faq.q: What does the wages of sin mean in the story?
faq.a: It is the verse behind the plot. Chapter 36 is titled The Wages of Sin, and late in the book George remembers his pastor reading Romans 6:23: “For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.” The novel sets that verse beside 1 Timothy 6:10 on the love of money, and lets the characters' choices show what both mean.

faq.q: Where is it set?
faq.a: In and around the small town of Kamish, Idaho, with scenes at a local café, a mill, a trailer park by the river and the roads toward the lottery office in Boise.

faq.q: Is it a suspense novel?
faq.a: Yes, in part. It begins as a story of temptation and turns into a story of crime and consequence. The book has a Christian outlook throughout.

faq.a: Readers of faith-based suspense and family drama, readers who enjoy stories with a clear spiritual message, and Christian fiction readers who like a warm, human hero and a villain with a history.

audience.body: For parents of babies, toddlers and teenagers, grandparents and caregivers, praying mothers and Christian families who want to raise faithful children, and any adult who wants to build better habits. Stephanie Mathews teaches ten habits through Scripture, her own life as a mother and true stories, each chapter opening with an original poem. A note on subjects: the book speaks about prayer in hard times, including a premature birth and a stay in the neonatal intensive care unit, a childhood without enough to eat, and the harm bullying and insults can do, including the thought of suicide. It is a parenting and habit-building book from a mother's experience, not medical, mental health or child-development advice. If you or a child you love is struggling, please contact a physician or licensed professional, and if anyone is in crisis or thinking of self-harm, contact your local emergency services or a crisis line right away.

what_makes.title: What makes this book for parents who want to raise outstanding children
paras: A habits book told as stories rather than rules. The author is a mother, wife and small business owner who believes she is a Potter's Child, clay shaped by God's hands, and who prayed for years for a baby before her twins finally arrived, early.
Five things set it apart:
list: It teaches ten habits, one per chapter. The power of prayer; make your bed (get the job done!); clean up and wash up; please, thank you, I'm sorry and excuse me; money matters; work hard and play harder; building relationships; time management; read and learn; and dream big.
It is told through true stories. The stories come from the author's own life, from friends and from people she has met, rather than a checklist.
It puts prayer first. The first chapter is the longest, and it begins with the habit of relying on God in prayer, which the author calls "the habit that fuels a lifetime."
It is for the adult, too. "You can be ten or sixty-five; this book will serve you in some way to understand how good habits can make a difference."
It carries a poem in every chapter. Each chapter opens with an original poem by Susan Ann Samuel, and the book is illustrated by Kalpana Paranjothy.

sections.h2: For parents of babies, toddlers and teenagers
paras: If you want a place to start, begin with one habit. The author says that "Instead of giving children what we never had, it's better to model and teach life lessons to help them in their daily lives," and that "For our children to have the opportunity to imitate good habits, we have to develop good habits for them to emulate."

sections.h2: For grandparents and caregivers
paras: The author thanks her own grandmother and mother for their habits of cleanliness, and one chapter is written from that gratitude. "I am thankful that they instilled this value in me because as a result, cleaning up after myself comes naturally." The book is also an invitation to the village that raises a child: "children are surrounded by their families, peers, and a village of people modeling potential behaviors for them."

sections.h2: For praying mothers and Christian families
paras: "We won't always be able to hover around and protect our children the way we want to, but we can cover them with our prayers." The first chapter collects stories of answered prayer, and the author does not hide that prayer sits alongside action: "praying must also be accompanied by action."

sections.h2: For any adult who wants better habits
paras: "You don't have to be a Christian to read this book. It is a tool that can add value to anyone's life." The author writes that many of the habits are ones she is still building herself.

paras: In the first chapter, the author tells of a childhood prayer. "Most children often pray for things they can touch: toys, bicycles, games and shoes. When I was a child, I prayed for food." Money was very tight, and her mother had nothing to feed the children but green lentils at every meal. She remembers praying, "Lord, can we have something to eat? Not green lentils, please!" She told a senior student at a school Christian group that she was hungry, and the next day the student and her father arrived with fruit and vegetables from their garden, enough for two weeks, and then with more provisions. "I remember that day as if it happened yesterday because it was an answered prayer." Years later she found the student and thanked her, and the woman did not even remember it.

Chapter 2 asks whether it even matters that you made your bed this morning. The author's answer is that "making the bed in the morning sets the tone that begins the day in order." She is not talking about comfort. "This habit is rather about making the bed; the task itself." The chapter quotes Admiral William McRaven: "If you want to change the world, start off by making your bed." And it adds that "If you can't do the little things right, you will never do the big things right."

In the last chapter the author remembers being a child raised by a single mother and working to help pay the bills. "I was constantly daydreaming because that was the only thing I could afford to do." She dreamed of flying on a plane, of performing on stage, of owning a business and of being an author. "Would it amaze you if I said that all my dreams came true?" Some plans didn't work out the way she imagined, she says, but when they became reality "they turned out better than what I dreamed for myself."

author.bio: Stephanie Mathews is a mother, wife and small business owner who believes she is a Potter's Child, clay shaped by God's hands. After years of prayer for a baby, she and her husband welcomed premature twins. Her early years included dance classes at The Temple of Fine Arts in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, and the Jesus Calls messages she began hearing at age nine. She took part in the StartUp Launch Program at UTD and has an event space in Rockwall, Texas. Potter's Child is her first book.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The author's reason is in her introduction. "Potter's Child is written to help you and the children you love build character. The contents are poured out from my heart, life experiences, generous contributors and with the help of God."

She also tells why she believes it is needed. "Our children and our well-lived days are the most important products we can give the world." And her last word to every reader, child or adult, is the book's title: "We are the Potter's Child, the clay."

faq.q: What is Potter's Child about?
faq.a: A parenting book by Stephanie Mathews that offers ten habits parents can instill in their children, drawn from Scripture, her own life as a mother and true stories from friends and people she has met.

faq.q: Is it a Christian parenting book?
faq.a: Yes. It is written from faith, with prayer as the first habit, and it says that when we allow God to be our guiding Parent, "He will mold and shape us to be the best versions of ourselves." It also says you do not have to be a Christian to read it.

faq.q: Does the book cover the habit of making your bed?
faq.a: Yes. Chapter 2, Make Your Bed (Get the Job Done!), is one of the ten habits, alongside cleaning up, manners, money, work and play, relationships, time management, reading and dreaming big.

faq.q: Is it about prayer for my family?
faq.a: Prayer is central, and the first chapter gathers stories of answered prayer. It says "The best gifts you can give your child are those of faith and the habit of prayer." It is not a collection of prayers to read aloud. It is a teaching book with testimonies.

faq.q: Is it about the power of prayer?
faq.a: Yes. The first chapter is titled The Power of Prayer, and the author invites you to "kneel, close your eyes and reach out to God, the creator who made you for a purpose."

faq.q: Is it a book for a praying mom?
faq.a: It is told by a mother who prayed for years for a baby and whose twins were born early. The introduction calls them her "miracle babies." It speaks to mothers and fathers alike, and to grandparents, caregivers and any adult.

faq.q: Is it only for parents of young children?
faq.a: No. It is for parents of babies, toddlers and teenagers, for grandparents and caregivers, and for any adult who wants better habits, since the same practices grow out of what we experience.

faq.q: Why is it called Potter's Child?
faq.a: The author believes we are clay in the Potter's hands, and so are our children. She invites parents to let God shape their homes, teach by example and remind their children every day whose child they are.

audience.headline: Thirty-one young worshipers say what gets in the way of meeting God, and what helped them find Him anyway.
audience.body: For pastors, worship leaders, parents and anyone who plans or sits through a service. Pure and Simple: Advice on Worship from Young People gathers the handwritten stories of children and teenagers, ages 6 to 16, each paired with a short reflection and one question to bring back to your own church. As the introduction puts it, "This may look like a children's book, but it is not." A note on subjects: the stories are the children's own words, and a few mention hard things at home, the loss of a friend's parent, or a health condition. The children are named in the book; this page gives only their ages.

quote.text: “We become like children by listening to them and taking them seriously.”
quote.cite: Pure and Simple, Introduction

what_makes.title: What makes this book for people who want worship that welcomes every age
paras: Most books about worship are written by adults for adults. This one lets the children speak first, in their own handwriting, spelling and drawings.
Five things set it apart:
list: The stories are in the young people's own words and drawings. Each one is a handwritten, illustrated storyboard that follows three points: a possibility, a hurdle and a discovery.

The hurdles are real and familiar. Boredom, distraction, a noisy home, sore feet, a voice that feels too small and kids who give funny looks all show up, and so do the ways the young storytellers found to press on.
Every story has a reflection and a question. A short note draws out what the story teaches, and each ends with a question for the people who design worship to take back to their own congregation.

It covers a wide range of ages. The storytellers are 6 to 16 years old, and their stories reach from a six-year-old who felt happy singing with the music to a sixteen-year-old who chose to bow down when the songs pushed feelings.
It makes no demands on you. The introduction says the stories are not strategies for radical practices but keys that can open doors, when we are willing to look at our habits with fresh eyes.

sections.h2: For worship pastors and worship planning teams
paras: Each reflection ends with a question you can take straight to a planning meeting. The introduction says the questions are designed to "launch a conversation about how a church service" might look if you used your own initiative and courage to try new ways to worship.

sections.h2: For children's ministry leaders, parents and grandparents
paras: The stories show what children actually notice in a service. If you have wondered why a child fidgets, dances, goes quiet or asks about a word in a song, there is likely a story here that sounds like them.

sections.h2: For small groups and church staff
paras: Each story and reflection is short enough to read one at a time. The reflections can open a discussion about distraction, belonging, music, prayer or the Bible, and the introduction says the stories do not dismantle time-tested patterns of worship but inspire additional practices that seek to revitalize it.

sections.h2: For anyone who has felt bored, distracted or out of place in church
paras: The hurdles in these stories are boredom, distraction, worship style, other worshipers, confusion, physical discomfort and the weight of other people's expectations. The introduction says plainly that we all face similar hurdles, not just children. What the young storytellers show is how they pressed on to find their own way to worship.

stories.h2: A lantern going up to God
paras: A ten-year-old thinks of prayers as lanterns rising to God. She says that YouTube and other media are addicting and keep her from worshiping, and that she feels God's comforting presence when she prays. The reflection compares her lanterns to incense in ancient worship, and notes that returning to prayer breaks through whatever stands in the way.

A sixteen-year-old goes into worship hoping to praise God for His glory and faithfulness. The songs seem to push him toward his feelings, so he ignores them and chooses to bow down in reverence. The reflection says worship includes the whole person, and that choosing to worship can set us free from our worries.
A twelve-year-old hoped to sing to the Lord but did not like the sound of their own voice. The third frame of the story says what changed:
“I sang my heart out to the Lord now I am not afraid to sing to Him”
The reflection says that God receives worship from any voice that speaks or sings His praise, and that there is more to worship than singing songs.

author.bio: Ron King is the author of Pure and Simple. The book prints no biography of him. Its introduction tells how the stories were gathered: through "Listen to the Kids!", a storytelling program of the nonprofit Sidebar Stories that asked children ages 6 to 16, without teaching or guiding them, what they know about worshiping God. The copyright page notes that the program was made possible by a Vital Worship, Vital Preaching grant from the Calvin Institute of Christian Worship, with funds from Lilly Endowment.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The stories grew out of "Listen to the Kids!", a storytelling project that asked children ages 6 to 16, without teaching, directing or guiding them, to tell what they know about worshiping God. The introduction sums up what came back:
“It turns out that kids know a lot.”
It says the goal is not to create worship experiences for children, but to lead us all into a deeper and more meaningful relationship with God through worship. The back page puts it this way:
“Common dreams and hurdles children face lead them to out-of-the-box discoveries that challenge us all.”

faq.q: What is Pure and Simple?
faq.a: It is a 74-page book of 31 stories about worship by children and teenagers ages 6 to 16, each with a reflection and a question for people who plan worship.

faq.q: Is it a children's book or a children's ministry resource?
faq.a: Neither, exactly. It looks like a children's book, but the introduction says it is not: it is written by children for the benefit of those who design and lead corporate worship. Children's ministry leaders will find it useful because it shows what children notice in a service, and children can read it alongside you.

faq.q: Who wrote the stories?
faq.a: Young people ages 6 to 16 wrote and drew them as part of the "Listen to the Kids!" storytelling project. They are printed in the children's own handwriting, spelling and drawings. Ron King is the author of the book.

faq.q: What does it say about the heart of worship?
faq.a: That God looks at the heart. One reflection says God does not look for the most talented or best dressed, but for a sincere heart. Another says worship includes the whole person, and that choosing to worship, even when feelings pull the other way, keeps Jesus in the center.

faq.q: Does it cover praise and worship music?
faq.a: Yes, in several stories. A six-year-old felt happy singing with the music, a twelve-year-old who disliked their own voice learned to sing out, and a thirteen-year-old noticed the worship team working to please God, not the crowd. The reflections also say there is much more to worship than singing songs.

faq.q: Does it cover worship and prayer?
faq.a: Yes. A ten-year-old pictures her prayers as lanterns rising to God, and another pictures Jesus during silent prayer at church. The reflection says that time set aside for corporate and personal prayer in worship sends a message of light and hope.

faq.q: Can youth pastors and worship teams use it?
faq.a: Yes. Each reflection ends with a question, and the introduction says the questions are written to launch a conversation about how a service, or worship outside of church, might look. A team can take one story to each planning meeting.

faq.q: Is it a book on spiritual formation?
faq.a: Some of it. It is not a formation program or a curriculum. The introduction says it is designed to lead us all into a deeper and more meaningful relationship with God through worship, and that the stories do not dismantle time-tested patterns of worship but inspire additional practices.

faq.q: Is it full color?
faq.a: Yes. The paperback is printed in full color in a wide 11 x 8.5 inch format, so the children's artwork appears as they drew it.

paras: The stories are children's own words, and a few mention hard things at home, the loss of a friend's parent, or a health condition. It is for adults who lead or plan worship, though it is easy for a child to read alongside you.

audience.headline: A ghost boy, an angel named Mary and ten thousand lost children to bring home.
audience.body: For readers ages 8 to 12 who love adventure, angels and monsters with a hopeful ending, and for parents who want a clean middle-grade story about courage, purpose and helping others. Robie has been a ghost since a blizzard in 1836. When he meets two children who have just escaped a monster's cave, he finally learns what has been happening to children like him, and what he can do about it. A note on subjects: this is an adventure about children who have died and are being kept from Heaven. Robie falls in a blizzard, another boy drowned in a storm, and the captive children are hurt by monsters who feed on pain. The hurt is described briefly, and the story turns on hope, healing and rescue. Parents of younger or more sensitive readers may want to read the first chapters first.

quote.text: You're the first person to talk back to me in one hundred seventy years.
quote.cite: Robie the Ghost, Chapter 1: Robie the Ghost

what_makes.title: What makes this book for readers who love a story of good versus evil
paras: A thirteen-chapter adventure that sets a shape-changing villain and his band of small monsters against a handful of children and an angel with a plan. The plan is a song, "Jesus Loves Me", and a desert where the Bad Man cannot use his power.
Five things set it apart:
list: It begins with an unusual hero. Robie is not a scary ghost. He is a lonely ten-year-old boy, and when a stranger finally speaks to him he says, "You're the first person to talk back to me in one hundred seventy years."
The villain is clever and foolish at once. Bebop can "change his shape to be anyone or anything he wants," and yet he forgets to lock the cage doors.
Heaven is involved from the first chapters. An angel named Mary and her supervising angel, Mac, talk about the missing children, and Jesus Himself comes to meet the four friends.
The children are the rescuers. They learn to jump from place to place by thinking about it very hard, and then teach others to do the same.
It says what it is for. The foreword to parents begins with its theme, purpose, and ends with the joy of helping others.

sections.h2: For readers who love adventure with angels
paras: If your reader wants monsters, secret maps, jumps across the planet and angels who hide in plain sight, this has all of them, and the heroes are children. A warrior angel named Meshech stands unseen at the border of the desert, and the monsters cannot see or hear him unless he allows it.

sections.h2: For parents who want a clean story about courage
paras: Each rescue is followed by healing, and Robie's friends take care of one another. The monsters are frightening but foolish, and the children are never left without help. The foreword calls it a story about "the joys of helping others."

sections.h2: For families who want to talk about purpose
paras: Jimmy asks Mary whether Jesus really needs them. She answers: "Yes, Jimmy. That is how the universe is set up. We each have tasks to fulfill. God waits to see if we will accept those tasks and do them." It is a good place to stop reading and ask what task a young reader might be given.

sections.h2: For readers who like a team and a plan
paras: By chapter 8 the rescue has become an organization. Teams are trained to make the jumps, border guards watch the desert, and Robie briefs the team leaders before a big raid in Liberia: "Tell them ChaCha is coming for them." When a leader asks how he knows Heaven is behind them, he answers, "Because they glow, and they don't hurt you but help you." Readers who like to see how a plan is made, tested and fixed will find a lot to enjoy.

paras: This is a story about purpose. It is important for each person to find their place in life and use their talents to better the human experience. I hope your child enjoys the adventures of Robie, Jimmy, Kono, Sarah, and Mary and their discoveries of the joys of helping others.

stories.h2: The light that was not evil
paras: In chapter 1, a very bright light full of color and music comes down from the sky, and Robie turns to follow it. A red-haired girl screams, "No-o-o! That is an evil light. It will hurt you." The light is gone before he can reach it, and he spends a hundred and seventy-five years alone. Only later does he understand who the girl really was.

In Heaven, Mary tells Mac that "there are ten thousand missing children." Mac tells her about Bebop and then lays out the plan: "Teach it to the kids. When the time is right and all of the children have been gathered, sing it loud and clear." On Earth, Jimmy supplies the missing piece: "We jump into the caves while the monsters are sleeping or gone, free the kids, teach them how to jump out," and the four friends choose the Mojave Desert as the place to take them.

When Jimmy shouts that Mary sounds just like the rest of them, the sky grows bright and a man with a kind face stands before the children. "I am Jesus, the One you seek, even though you knew Me not." Robie bursts into tears as all the pain and loneliness he has carried finally leave him, and Jimmy hugs Him. Jesus tells Sarah, "Keep the faith before them, and all will come home."

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The author's reason is in the foreword to parents: "This is a story about purpose." She writes that "It is important for each person to find their place in life and use their talents to better the human experience." Her hope is that a child reading it will discover "the joys of helping others." The story shows that idea in action. Each of the four friends has a different gift, from teaching to healing to fighting, and each is needed.

faq.q: What is Robie the Ghost about?
faq.a: A boy who has been a ghost since a blizzard in 1836 joins two escaped children and an angel named Mary to rescue lost children from a shape-changer called Bebop and his monsters, and to call Jesus to bring them home.

faq.q: Is it a story of good versus evil?
faq.a: Yes. Bebop and his small monsters keep new souls in cages and "feed off pain and negative emotions," while Heaven sends an angel, a plan and warrior angels to bring the children home. The words "good versus evil" are not used in the book. The contest is the whole plot.

faq.q: Is it scary for kids?
faq.a: It has monsters and underground caves, and the captive children have been hurt. The story is hopeful, the hurt is described briefly and healing follows each rescue. Parents of younger readers may want to read it first.

faq.q: What is the song in the story?
faq.a: Mary's plan includes "Jesus Loves Me," which the children sing together when all of them are gathered. The book names the song early, and the familiar words of the first verse and chorus appear in the final chapters when the children sing. It is a story that uses the song, not a songbook.

faq.q: Does it have angels?
faq.a: Yes. Mary is an angel sent to Earth, her supervising angel is Mac, and other angels, including warrior angels, appear throughout. Mac teases Mary when she is alarmed: "Don't get your wings all bunched up."

faq.q: Is it a story about finding your purpose?
faq.a: The foreword says so in its first line, and each child finds a job that fits: Jimmy teaches the jumps, Sarah heals, and Kono, who has waited five hundred years, joins the rescue. It is not a self-help book. It is an adventure that shows what purpose looks like.

faq.q: Is it a guardian angel story?
faq.a: Partly. Mary explains to Sarah that everyone has a guardian angel, and Sarah's own helper begins to speak up in the cabin. It is one thread of the story, not the whole of it.

sections.h2: Para papás, mamás y abuelos que quieren hablarles de Dios en español
paras: Si usted quiere que su hijo escuche el nombre de Dios en su idioma de casa, este libro le da las palabras. Son frases cortas, de las que se pueden leer de un tirón y repetir después. Cada página abre la conversación y deja que el niño pregunte.

sections.h2: Para maestros de escuela dominical y lectura en voz alta
paras: Las preguntas se prestan para detenerse. Después de cada una, el maestro puede mirar a los niños y preguntarles si ya lo sabían. El libro responde, pero también deja espacio para que el niño conteste con sus propias palabras, y al final lo invita a escribir su oración.

sections.h2: Para niños que empiezan a hablar con su Padre celestial
paras: El último tema del libro es la oración. Dice que se puede rezarle directamente a Dios, y la autora muestra cómo con una oración corta dirigida al Padre Celestial. Luego, en una página con espacio en blanco, le toca al niño.

sections.h2: Para familias bilingües
paras: La misma autora escribió Do You Know?, un libro ilustrado en inglés que hace las mismas preguntas a los niños. En casa donde se hablan los dos idiomas, se pueden leer uno al lado del otro. Esta edición en español usa la Reina-Valera Antigua y termina con una oración que empieza "Querido Papá Dios," para que el niño la complete con sus propias palabras.

audience.headline: Una conversación sencilla con los más pequeños: ¿Sabes quién es Dios? ¿Sabes que te conoce por nombre?
audience.body: Para papás, mamás y abuelos hispanohablantes que quieren presentar a Dios a sus hijos de 4 a 8 años, para maestros de escuela dominical y para las familias que leen juntas en voz alta. Katherine Robinson le habla a cada niño con preguntas cortas y versículos de la Biblia Reina-Valera Antigua: quién es Dios, quién es Cristo Jesús, quién es el Espíritu Santo, que Dios conoce a cada niño por nombre, que tiene un plan para su vida y que puede hablar con Él directamente. Una nota sobre los temas: es un libro ilustrado, tierno y breve. Habla del pecado y del perdón en palabras sencillas, sin imágenes duras. Es una introducción a la fe cristiana para niños, no un manual para padres ni un consejo profesional.

quote.text: Te hizo a propósito y con propósito.
quote.cite: ¿Sabes Qué?, la página ¿Sabes que Dios te conoce por nombre?

what_makes.title: Qué hace especial este libro para niños que empiezan a conocer a Dios
paras: Es un libro de treinta páginas construido sobre una sola pregunta que se repite, la que todo niño hace con los ojos muy abiertos: "¿Sabes...?". Cada página responde con una verdad sencilla y un pasaje de la Biblia.
Cinco cosas lo distinguen:
list: Empieza donde empieza la Biblia. La primera pregunta es "¿Sabes quién es Dios?", y la primera respuesta es el versículo de Génesis 1:1, que dice que Dios creó los cielos y la tierra.
Describe a Dios con cinco palabras que un niño puede repetir: "Santo, Soberano, Amoroso, Fiel y Todopoderoso."
Explica a Jesús como un acto de amor. El libro dice que Dios mandó a su único Hijo a salvarnos y que Jesús regresó al cielo para preparar un hogar para todos los que lo reciben.
Cada verdad trae su versículo. Hay pasajes de Génesis, Apocalipsis, Juan, Jeremías, Efesios y Romanos, todos de la Reina-Valera Antigua.
Termina con una invitación a orar. Primero la autora comparte la oración que hizo por quienes lean el libro, y después deja una página para que el niño escriba la suya.

paras: Dedicado a El Gran Yo Soy. Solo fue posible porque Usted lo quiso. Gracias por confiar en mí.

paras: ¿Sabes quién es Dios?

blocks.text: Y la respuesta empieza así:

paras: Él es el creador de los cielos, la tierra, y todo lo que habita ahí.

blocks.text: Más adelante, el libro habla de la Trinidad con palabras para niños:

paras: Juntos, Dios, Jesús y El Espíritu Santo, son tres en uno.

paras: La primera página abre con la pregunta del título, y la respuesta llega enseguida: Dios creó los cielos y la tierra y todo lo que habita ahí. El libro dice que no lo puedes ver y no lo puedes tocar, pero que "Él se deja sentir a través del trabajo que hace en tu vida." Luego aparecen las cinco palabras que lo describen y el versículo de Apocalipsis 1:8, "Yo soy el Alfa y la Omega".

stories.h2: ¿Sabes que Dios te conoce por nombre?
paras: En la mitad del libro la pregunta se hace personal. El texto contesta que Dios creó a cada niño "con mucho cariño y atención especial", que lo hizo "a propósito y con propósito" y que le dio talentos para usarlos con la gente que lo rodea. El versículo que acompaña la página es Jeremías 1:5.

stories.h2: ¿Sabes que puedes rezarle directamente a Dios?
paras: El libro termina con una invitación. La autora escribe: "Mire aquí cómo recé por ti." Después viene su oración, dirigida al Padre Celestial, por los niños que escuchen el mensaje. En la página siguiente se lee "Ahora te toca a ti. Puedes empezar algo así..." con una línea que empieza "Querido Papá Dios," y el resto en blanco, para que el niño termine con sus palabras.

author.bio: Katherine Robinson escribe para niños pequeños y para los adultos que leen con ellos. Dedica este libro "a El Gran Yo Soy" y lo cierra con una oración propia por cada niño que lo escuche. También es autora de Do You Know?, un libro ilustrado en inglés.

publisher.name: Spirit Media Publishing
publisher.about: Spirit Media Publishing es una empresa cristiana de publicación y mercadeo con la visión de revelar el corazón de nuestro Padre a todas las naciones. Ofrece la creación y publicación completa de libros en tapa blanda, tapa dura, formato digital y audiolibro, además de libros infantiles, Express Books compactos, diseño de sitios web y SEO, y producción de pódcast y video. Nos alegra publicar un libro que presenta a Dios a los niños en español.

why.title: Por qué existe este libro
paras: Lo que el libro mismo dice está a la vista. En la dedicatoria, la autora escribe: "Gracias por confiar en mí." Y en su oración por los lectores pide: "Te pido que el mensaje en este libro llegue a los oídos y corazones de todos los que lo escuchen."

faq.q: ¿De qué trata el libro ¿Sabes Qué??
faq.a: Es un libro en español para niños de 4 a 8 años que, con preguntas sencillas y versículos de la Reina-Valera Antigua, presenta a Dios, a Cristo Jesús y al Espíritu Santo, y anima a cada niño a escribir su propia oración.

faq.q: ¿Dice el libro que Dios es amor?
faq.a: No con esas palabras exactas: la frase Dios es amor no aparece. Pero el libro describe a Dios como Amoroso, lo llama un Padre celestial "que te ama y quiere relación contigo" y explica que enviar a Su único Hijo fue un acto de amor. Es el mismo mensaje en palabras más sencillas.

faq.q: ¿Quién es Dios, según el libro?
faq.a: Es la primera pregunta del libro. La respuesta es que Dios es el creador de los cielos, la tierra y todo lo que habita ahí. No se puede ver ni tocar, pero se deja sentir por el trabajo que hace en la vida de cada niño.

faq.q: ¿Qué significa Alfa y Omega en el libro?
faq.a: El libro cita Apocalipsis 1:8, donde Dios dice: "Yo soy el Alfa y la Omega", "el que es y que era y que ha de venir, el Todopoderoso". Lo pone junto a cinco palabras que describen a Dios. Son, en orden: Santo; Soberano; Amoroso; Fiel; y Todopoderoso.

faq.q: ¿Dice el libro que Dios es fiel?
faq.a: Sí. Fiel es una de las cinco palabras con las que el libro describe a Dios, y el libro le dice al niño que Dios lo conoce por nombre y tiene un plan para su vida.

faq.q: ¿Qué dice el libro sobre Jesús?
faq.a: Responde a la pregunta "¿Sabes quién es Cristo Jesús?" con una idea central: su perdón fue un acto de amor. Dios mandó a su único Hijo a salvarnos, y Jesús regresó al cielo para preparar un hogar para todos los que lo reciben. El versículo es Juan 14:6.

faq.q: ¿Habla del Padre, el Hijo y el Espíritu Santo?
faq.a: Sí, de una forma sencilla. El libro dice que Jesús dejó su Espíritu Santo y que "Juntos, Dios, Jesús y El Espíritu Santo, son tres en uno." Explica también que por medio del Espíritu Santo tenemos acceso a Jesús y, a través de Él, acceso a Dios.

faq.q: ¿Enseña a hablar con Dios?
faq.a: Sí. La última pregunta del libro es "¿Sabes que puedes rezarle directamente a Dios?" La autora comparte su propia oración y deja una página con la frase inicial "Querido Papá Dios," para que cada niño termine la suya.

faq.q: ¿Para qué edad es y qué Biblia usa?
faq.a: Para niños de 4 a 8 años, como lectura en voz alta en español. Usa la Reina-Valera Antigua, con un pasaje junto a cada verdad. Se puede leer en una sentada.

audience.headline: You do not have to be special. You have to say yes.
audience.body: For believers who feel their lives are too small to matter, anyone who has said no to God out of fear, men and women balancing work, family and faith, and small groups and mission teams who want real stories of obedience. Michael J. Gaetke tells the true story of an ordinary businessman who learned to say yes, from a jungle village in Papua New Guinea and a prison Bible study to a gas station on the way home and the ministry that became Africa Servant Leader. A note on subjects: the book tells of a shy childhood, of ministry among people in prison, and of the author's adventures in remote places, and it includes a prayer for readers who wish to begin a relationship with God. It is one man's testimony, not counseling or advice of any other kind. The stories are told without graphic detail.

quote.text: I'm no one special, but I serve a special God!
quote.cite: Michael J. Gaetke, Chapter 1

what_makes.title: What makes this book for people who want an ordinary life of extraordinary adventure
paras: A warm, humble Christian memoir in twenty-two short chapters and a conclusion, arranged in five parts. It covers foundations of faith, building a life of service, global impact, everyday ministry, and reflections on a life with no regrets.
Five things set it apart:
list: It starts with an honest confession. "Life has a funny way of making us feel like we're not up to much, doesn't it?" The author describes a painfully shy boy who froze in front of his class and later learned that he did not have to stay that way.
It gives you one simple rule. "When God provides an opportunity, start with 'yes' until God gives you a compelling 'no.'"
It is full of real adventure. The book opens at a three-in-the-morning feast in a remote Papua New Guinea village, and it follows the author to Costa Rica and Kenya.

It is as much about the street as the jungle. His first day in prison, a stop at a gas station and a movie theatre show that mission work "isn't always about crossing oceans; sometimes, it's about crossing the street."
It includes lessons from people in Scripture. Moses, Mary, David and Paul appear as ordinary people who said yes despite their doubts.

sections.h2: For believers who feel their lives are too small to matter
paras: The author knows the feeling. "Trust me, you're not alone in this." He says the point of the book is "your life has significance. Your life has meaning."

sections.h2: For anyone who has said no to God out of fear
paras: The letter to the reader names the fears: "lack of time, lack of money, fear of failing, worrying about what others will think, feeling like you are not qualified." His answer is to give them to Jesus before they hold you back, and to start with yes.

sections.h2: For men and women balancing work, family and faith
paras: The author built a business career and shares his faith with the people around him. He writes that "Whether through family, business, or ministry, the ripple effect of these decisions creates a legacy that honors God and enriches the lives of many."

sections.h2: For small groups and mission teams
paras: The short chapters read well aloud, and each is built around a story of obedience. The author says that mission work "isn't always about crossing oceans; sometimes, it's about crossing the street."

stories.h2: A feast at three in the morning
paras: The introduction takes you to a remote village in Papua New Guinea, reached by four-wheeler and then a three or four hour walk through the jungle. The children had never seen a white man and ran away screaming. His friend's father announced a feast, and the guests bunked on bamboo mats over a dirt floor until it was ready. "So, at three in the morning, we all woke up excited for the feast." As the honored guest, he had to eat first. What struck him was the welcome: "He just wanted to give his best, no hesitation." He adds, "It was an adventure I wouldn't have had if I hadn't said 'yes' to God."

stories.h2: A shy boy and a verse
paras: Chapter 1 tells of the author as a child, around seven or eight, "painfully shy and unsure of myself," who had to give an oral book report in front of the whole class. When his turn came, he "froze, and couldn't say a single word." The sense of failure stuck, until a Sunday School teacher shared a verse, 2 Timothy 1:7: "For God did not give us a spirit of fear, but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind." That verse, he writes, "became my life anchor," and although he is still a fairly reserved person, "I am no longer shy at all."

stories.h2: Lord, send me to the gas station
paras: In Chapter 12, the author is stopping for a quick meal on his way home when he sees a van with a sign on the windshield asking for gas. He feels a nudge from the Holy Spirit to go and talk to the couple, even though he is in a hurry to beat the traffic. He listens, feels some skepticism, and buys them gas, telling them he does it in the name of Jesus. They answer: "we're believers too, and we just asked God to send someone." His lesson is "I was the answer to their prayer." It is about being open to saying yes "in those unplanned moments, which might seem small to us but are huge to someone else."

author.bio: Michael J. Gaetke grew up in a church-going family that prayed nightly for missionaries, and his grandfather was a pastor in Los Angeles. A painfully shy child, he committed his life to Jesus at a junior high camp at thirteen. He built a business career, sharing his faith with employees, subcontractors and clients. Over the decades he has served in missions from Papua New Guinea and Costa Rica to Kenya, where he has taught and spoken with Africa Servant Leader, and he has been involved in church planting and prison ministry.

publisher.name: Vector Reach Publishing
publisher.about: Say Yes to God is published under the Vector Reach Publishing imprint, and its ISBNs are held by the author. It was first published in 2024, in paperback, hardback and eBook editions.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The author's reason is in his letter to the reader. "My goal in writing this book is to lead you to a deep understanding: your life has significance." He says he wrote it "because of God's profound love for you and His desire for you to experience real life."
His invitation is the title: "buckle up, say 'yes' to adventure, and get ready for the ride of a lifetime."

faq.q: What is Say Yes to God about?
faq.a: Michael J. Gaetke's true story of answering God's calling: a Christian memoir of mission work from Costa Rica to Kenya and the birth of Africa Servant Leader, told in twenty-two short chapters.

faq.q: Is it a book about calling?
faq.a: Yes, in the sense that matters to most readers. It is about answering what God puts in your path, from the jungle to the gas station. The author does not write about a calling as a career test. He writes about saying yes to opportunities and keeping the yes "until God gives you a compelling 'no.'"

faq.q: Is Say Yes to God a Christian memoir?
faq.a: Yes. It is a warm, humble Christian memoir about how saying yes to God carried an ordinary businessman into a life of service in his own city and around the world.

faq.q: What adventures are in the book?
faq.a: The book opens in the jungle of Papua New Guinea at a three-in-the-morning feast, and includes mission work in Costa Rica and Kenya, his first day in prison, church planting, and ministry in a gas station and a movie theatre.

faq.q: What does the book say about missions?
faq.a: That missions can be far or near. The author writes that he has served in Latin America, Papua New Guinea and Kenya, and that "mission work isn't always about crossing oceans; sometimes, it's about crossing the street."

faq.q: What is Africa Servant Leader?
faq.a: The ministry whose birth the book tells in Chapter 9. After a first trip to Kenya, the author and others founded a nonprofit, Africa Servant Leadership Development Initiative, to support teaching servant leadership there, and he remains on its board. He has also spoken at a graduation dinner for people who completed the Africa Servant Leader course.

faq.q: What does "start with yes" mean?
faq.a: The author's principle: when God provides an opportunity, start with yes until God gives you a compelling no. He says it is not about being someone special: "I'm no one special, but I serve a special God!"

faq.q: Is it only for people who travel?
faq.a: No. Some of the best stories are close to home. "You can be on adventures in faraway and exotic places, but sometimes your great adventures are right where you live."

hero.audience_line: For children ages 4 to 7 who are about to start school or worried about making new friends, and for the parents and grandparents who read to them at bedtime.
hero.tagline: An Ice Age bedtime story: on the night before kindergarten, a nervous boy named Silas wakes in a prehistoric land and finds his way home with a little mouse and a gentle woolly mammoth. It ends with a page of real woolly mammoth facts.

audience.headline: On the night before kindergarten, a nervous boy falls asleep, wakes up in the Ice Age, and rides home on a woolly mammoth.
audience.body: For children ages 4 to 7 who are about to start school or worried about making new friends, and for the parents and grandparents who read to them at bedtime. Kenneth W. Pullin sends Silas from a dinner of pancakes in Niceville to a land of gray boulders, cave people, a little mouse named Whiskers and a gentle giant named Woolly, then back to a morning that is not quite what he expects. A note on subjects: this is a gentle bedtime adventure. Silas gets lost, cold and hungry, the sun starts to set, and a hill shakes and rises under him before he finds out it is a mammoth. A deep river has to be crossed. Everything ends warmly, with a hug, a dance and a surprise in a bookbag.

quote.text: “He wondered if it would be hard to make new friends.”
quote.cite: Silas and Woolly the Mammoth, the night before kindergarten

what_makes.title: What makes this book for children who are nervous about a first day
paras: Silas is excited about school, but he is also "a little nervous," and the book says why: he wonders if it will be hard to make new friends. Then the story gives that worry somewhere to go. By morning he is excited about kindergarten, and he has made a friend who is eleven feet tall.
Five things set it apart:
list: It starts with a real bedtime. Dinner is pancakes, then a bath, teeth, prayers with his mom, and a story. The adventure begins as his eyes close.
It names the worry out loud. A child hears that being excited and being nervous can happen on the same night.
The hero is a mammoth. Woolly is big, strong and kind. He carries Silas across a deep river and bounces him back up his head whenever he slides.
The mouse stays with him. Whiskers curls up beside Silas when he is scared, and the book finishes with a question about him.
It ends with real mammoth facts. After The End, a full page tells how tall they stood, how much they weighed, how long their tusks grew and how scientists know how old they were.

sections.h2: For children about to start kindergarten
paras: If your child is counting down to the first day, this gives the nerves a story. Silas is brave in the end, but he is scared on the way, and he is lost for most of the book. The ending says he was not nervous anymore, and that he was excited for his new adventure.

sections.h2: For parents and grandparents who read at bedtime
paras: The book is built for the end of the day. It begins with pancakes and a bath, moves into prayers and a story, and finishes with a morning. The sentences are short, the pages turn quickly and the sound words, such as aw-da-sudden, are fun to say out loud.

sections.h2: For kids who love woolly mammoths
paras: The mammoth is not a side character. He has a name, a voice and a sense of humor, and he knows the land. At the back of the book, the facts page tells a young reader how tall mammoths stood, what the tusks were used for, and where scientists have found them frozen in ice and mud.

sections.h2: For families who want a gentle story about making friends
paras: Silas worries about friends at the start and finds two before breakfast. The book does not lecture. It shows a boy who follows a mouse, trusts a mammoth, and discovers that new friends can turn up in unexpected places.

paras: I'm happy that you're my new friend.

I'm happy that you're my new friend.

details.Subtitle: A Dream Adventure with a Gentle Giant
details.Author: Kenneth W. Pullin
details.Binding: Paperback (perfect bound), full-colour interior

paras: Silas wakes up alone. Whiskers is gone, and he feels alone and sad. Then the hill begins to shake. It rises so high he almost falls off, and he holds tight to some brush. When the hill starts to move forward with big back-and-forth motions, "like a boat on the ocean," he realizes the truth: he is on top of a real woolly mammoth. He screams so loud that Woolly stops moving, and Silas slides down his head to the ground.

Woolly knows where to go, but the river is deep, so Silas has to ride on his head. Whiskers squeaks and joins them. Woolly asks if Silas can swim, and Silas says he has a pool in his backyard where he practices all the time. The water is calm at first, then the current grows stronger. Woolly is so big that it does not bother him, and Whiskers stays right beside Silas the whole way.

Silas wakes up in his own bed, eats breakfast and hugs his mom and dad. As he heads out the door, something moves inside his bookbag. Out pops Whiskers. Then comes the last question of the book, left open for the child:
"Or was it really a dream?"

author.bio: Kenneth W. Pullin is a lifelong Virginian whose love of writing began in high school. For years he has written poems to mark the milestones in his children's lives, and those poems have grown into books. The Chess Nut and Little Bird brought his family's stories to young readers, and The Pitted Nail shared his own true story of God's grace on the Chesapeake Bay. Silas and Woolly the Mammoth grew out of funny things a child in his family once said.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The idea started with small things a child said. The dedication remembers a little girl running into a room to ask:
"Mama, how do you spell aw-da-sudden?"
That word became the sound of the story, and it turns up each time Silas is whisked somewhere new. The same dedication adds the line that explains the hero:
"And Silas is the inspiration for the main character."

faq.q: What is Silas and Woolly the Mammoth about?
faq.a: It is a woolly mammoth bedtime story by Kenneth W. Pullin. On the night before kindergarten, a nervous boy named Silas falls asleep, wakes in a prehistoric land and finds his way home with a little mouse named Whiskers and a gentle woolly mammoth named Woolly. It ends with real woolly mammoth facts.

faq.q: Does it have real woolly mammoth facts?
faq.a: Yes. After The End, a full page called The Woolly Mammoth says they stood up to eleven feet tall and weighed over 6 tons, had two layers of fur, and were more closely related to Asian elephants than to African elephants. It also says remains have been found frozen in ice and mud in Siberia. The phrase woolly mammoth book is our description, and it fits a story with a facts page at the back.

faq.q: Is it a good bedtime story for kids?
faq.a: It is framed as one: Silas eats dinner, takes a bath, says his prayers and falls asleep while his mom reads. The adventure is his dream, and he wakes to his mom's voice. The word bedtime is not printed in the book, and the bedtime routine is what makes the framing.

faq.q: Is it a good read aloud for kindergarten?
faq.a: It is a short read-aloud with a kindergarten morning at the center. The word kindergarten appears twice, on the night before the first day and in the closing pages, when Silas says he is excited for his new adventure. It has 42 pages, short sentences and a question at the end for a class to talk about.

faq.q: Is it one of the books for 4 year olds?
faq.a: It is written for ages 4 to 7. Younger listeners will follow it by the pictures and the funny sound of aw-da-sudden, and early readers can try the short lines on their own.

faq.q: Is the book about starting school?
faq.a: It is about the night before. The school day itself is only the last page. What the book gives a child is a way to talk about the worry, with a boy who thinks he may not make friends and ends up with two.

faq.q: Is there prayer in it?
faq.a: Yes, briefly. Silas says his prayers before bed, and he says them with his mom. The story is not a Bible story. It is a bedtime book that begins the way many family bedtimes do.

faq.q: Who wrote it?
faq.a: Kenneth W. Pullin, a lifelong Virginian who writes poems for the milestones in his children's lives. He also wrote The Pitted Nail, a true story of one summer day on the Chesapeake Bay.

audience.headline: A publisher's 120-page playbook for the author whose book is published but not selling, with fifteen short chapters from the first launch team to the first podcast interview.
audience.body: For independent and Christian authors who have put a book on the market and are waiting for readers to find it, and for authors who have not published yet and want to plan their marketing before they do. Kevin White, CEO of Spirit Media, draws on the lessons his team learned marketing his own books and those of Spirit Media authors. He treats marketing as part of the writing calling, and the book is full of steps you can act on. A note on the book: it is a practical guide with a Christian perspective, and Scripture appears throughout. It is also written by a publishing company, and its conclusion invites authors to partner with Spirit Media. Many of the statistics in the book come from third-party sources named in the text and listed in its reference pages.

quote.text: “It is never too late or too early to consider a book makeover.”

what_makes.title: What makes this book for authors who want their book to be found
paras: The book opens with a hard fact: it says most independent authors' books sell fewer than 250 copies, and it names a cause: they were put on the market but never marketed. Then it shows, chapter by chapter, what an author can do about it.
Five things set it apart:
list: It starts before you publish. Chapter 1 says to begin marketing while you are still writing, and it also tells authors with a published book that a makeover is still possible.
It is built from real makeovers. The opening chapter walks through how a book was retitled, redescribed and relaid out to become easier to find.

It covers the whole map. Fifteen chapters run from your brand and email list to launch teams, a web page, social media, the world's largest online bookstore, paid ads, reviews, awards, book clubs, podcasts and influencers.
It is generous. One chapter treats giving books away as a marketing strategy, with the author's own numbers.
It is short enough to use. At 120 pages in a large 8.5 x 11 inch format, with callouts and numbered steps, it is meant to be worked through with a pen.

sections.h2: For authors with a book that is not selling
paras: If your book has been out for months with few sales, the first chapter is for you. It says a book is not set in stone and explains the changes that made a difference for one author: a new title built around what readers search for, a new description and bio, a table of contents and a fresh layout.

sections.h2: For authors who have not published yet
paras: The book says the best time for an author to take responsibility for marketing is while writing. If you are still writing, use the early chapters to plan your brand, your email list and your launch team before the release date.

sections.h2: For Christian and independent authors
paras: The guide is written for authors who feel a message from God for the nations. It reminds you that Psalm 96:3 says to publish His glorious deeds among the nations, and it argues for publishing in every format everywhere. It is also useful if your message is not religious, because the tactics are practical.

sections.h2: For authors who dislike marketing
paras: The conclusion speaks to authors who hate marketing and says plainly that some authors refuse to do it. It offers a choice: follow the steps yourself, or let a publisher partner with you. You decide which fits your book.

stories.h2: A book retitled around its reader
paras: In Chapter 1, an author with four decades as a minister and marriage counselor, who had published with a well-known Christian publisher in 2019, asks the team to look at a book that was not selling. They found three reasons: it was put on the market but never marketed, it was not published with marketing in mind, and the cover did a poor job of showing what was inside. They retitled it Escaping Anxiety, wrote a new description and author bio around the words readers search for, added a table of contents and gave it a fresh layout. The team's summary of the lesson:
"You need to do whatever it takes for your book to be found."

Chapter 3 tells how the author decided to give away thousands of copies in order to sell millions. In June 2021 he arranged a bulk print of 2,000 paperbacks and cut the cost from over eight dollars a copy to under three. He reports that more than $150,000 was donated to a missions charity by people who had received one or both of his books as thank-you gifts, and he draws one conclusion:
"One of the best marketing strategies in the world is generosity."

stories.h2: The surfer who is not ready
paras: In the introduction, the book compares publishing to surfing. The best surfers know that anyone wanting the next big wave must be ready, and that without preparation it ends in a wipeout. The book carries the picture into Chapter 6, where it says that authors who sell more than 250 books have carefully implemented smart strategies and that the first step is a launch team of people who volunteer to help promote the book.

author.bio: Kevin White is the CEO of Spirit Media. He says Spirit Media was born in November 2021 when his second book, Get to the Point, was published in paperback, hardback, eBook and audiobook at the same time, everywhere, worldwide. He is the author of Audacious Generosity, Get to the Point and What's Your Word, and he served as Executive Director of Global Hope India, writing of two decades focused on missions in India. He invites readers to write to him if they have a tactic that is not in the book.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: Kevin White writes that the book represents years of research with his team at Spirit Media, who tested each tactic in the field. He says one reason he created Spirit Media was to have a team that could help authors work through the many tasks of publishing and selling, and that he wants more authors to take their message to the nations. The conclusion closes on a promise he takes from his own experience:
"Where God guides He provides."

faq.q: What is the Ultimate Book Marketing Guide about?
faq.a: It is a 120-page guide by Kevin White that teaches authors how to market a book, covering your brand, email list, launch team, web page, social media, the largest online bookstore, paid ads, reviews, awards, book clubs, podcasts and influencers.

faq.q: Is it for authors who are new to marketing?
faq.a: Yes, and for authors with a book already out. The chapters are short, each one is built around a single tactic, and the introduction explains why most books go unfound. It is a practical overview, not a technical manual for every platform.

faq.q: Is it for self-published authors?
faq.a: Yes. The book is written for independent authors and for authors who have used a publisher. It lists the many tasks of publishing and selling a book and says one reason Spirit Media was created was to have a team that could help authors through them.

faq.q: Does it cover the largest online bookstore?
faq.a: Yes. Chapter 9 says that bookstore is the number one seller of books in the world, and it names four strategies: a strong listing, fulfillment, protecting your work and paid ads. It also says the listing either sells or fails.

faq.q: Is it a Christian marketing book?
faq.a: It has a Christian perspective throughout, and Scripture supports its argument for taking a message to the nations. The tactics themselves, such as email, reviews, awards and podcasts, apply to any author.

faq.q: Can it help me get reviews, awards and podcast interviews?
faq.a: Chapters 11, 12 and 14 cover each of those. Chapter 11 explains why editorial and customer reviews matter and how a launch team can help, Chapter 12 offers a list of book award sites, and Chapter 14 shows how to prepare a portfolio, an offer and a vision to get booked as a podcast guest.

faq.q: When should an author start marketing?
faq.a: While writing. Chapter 1 is titled Start Marketing While Writing, and it tells authors who have not yet published that they can use it before they publish. For authors whose book is already out, it says the book is not set in stone and a makeover is still possible.

sections.h2: For people buried in paper
paras: Chapter 3 starts the clearing with a First Sort: make three piles, pick up one item at a time, and ask what it requires from you. The book says clients often find that “50% or more of their piles go straight to Toss, they just never stopped to decide.” A bill you have not paid is an Action, a child's report card is a Reference, and an expired flyer is a Toss.

sections.h2: For anyone whose inbox is overflowing
paras: Chapter 6 applies the same three choices to email, and it takes a firm line on one popular habit: “We no longer recommend the popular 2-minute rule,” because it can fill a session with minor tasks and leave your most important work untouched. The chapter's advice for old mail is gentle: “Today's Mail is tomorrow's pile.” You do not have to clean up the past, only start organizing for the future.

sections.h2: For people who have tried systems that did not last
paras: The authors list what helps a system last: “A system you trust,” “A simple rhythm” and “Support when you drift.” The last chapter says a sustainable system “doesn't prevent that” change in life and priorities. It “supports you through it.”

sections.h2: For retirees and caregivers managing family affairs
paras: The Introduction speaks to readers who are retired but managing their own affairs and, increasingly, the affairs of an aging parent. The File Index is described as useful for more than paper: it works for storage, memorabilia, binders and client papers too.

audience.headline: Find anything you file in seconds, on paper or on your computer.
audience.body: For professionals, business owners and retirees whose desks hold piles of paper, whose inboxes are overflowing and whose hard drives look like a digital junk drawer, and who have tried systems that did not last. Andrea Anderson, CEO of the Productive Environment Institute, writes with Barbara Hemphill, author of Taming the Paper Tiger, in ten short chapters built around a keyword-driven File Index that works like Google for your filing cabinet.

quote.text: Clutter is postponed decisions.
quote.cite: SOAR To Success, Barbara Hemphill in the Foreword

what_makes.title: What makes this book for people who want a filing system that lasts
paras: Most organizing advice tells you where to put things. This book is about finding them again. The authors put it plainly: “most people don't mind filing, they mind not being able to find what they filed.” The answer they teach is a numbered, keyword-indexed filing system that anyone, even a family member or team assistant, can use to retrieve a paper in moments.
Five things set it apart:
list: It was born from a real frustration. Andrea Anderson was organizing a boss's office, and each time the work looked neat but nothing could be found. She typed “filing system” into Google, and the first result was Barbara Hemphill.
It is keyword-driven. You label a folder with a number, then record keywords in one File Index, so a search for a word such as Honda or mechanic tells you which numbered folder holds the papers.

It covers paper and digital in one way of thinking. Paper gets numbers, because “the drawers don't have search bars.” Digital files get a simple alphabetical folder structure, because search is built in.
It runs on one decision tool. Every item is an Action, a Reference or a Toss, a method the book calls the ART of Organizing Information.
It is honest about time. The introduction says “Will this work overnight? No.” and promises change through intention and practice.

blocks.text: The Introduction opens with the author's first meeting with Barbara Hemphill:

paras: When I first met Barbara Hemphill in 2005, I had no idea how much that connection would shape the rest of my life.

blocks.text: It describes who the book is for, the reader as “bright, capable, and hardworking,” then names the problem: “your inbox is overflowing, and your hard drive looks like a digital junk drawer.”
And it states the plan in three levels:

items: Methodology: understanding the big picture so you choose tools and processes that fit your life
Mechanics: step-by-step strategies to create a repeatable SYSTEM, short for Saving You Space, Time, Energy, and Money
Maintenance: building habits and support structures that keep the system going

stories.h2: A boss who could not find anything
paras: In the Introduction, Andrea Anderson was working for a family preservation agency and spending days, even weeks, putting a busy boss's papers in order. Everything looked neat when she left. The boss would return from a trip and say “it looks great, but I can't find anything.” After one more failed attempt she sat at the desk in tears and prayed, “God, there has got to be a better way!” Moments later she typed “filing system” into Google. The first result was Barbara Hemphill, and Barbara's numerical finding system, supported by a simple index, gave “every piece of paper” a clear place to go and “a reliable way to find it again.”

Chapter 1 tells how the File Index began. In 1978 Barbara Hemphill was using alphabetical folders, and they worked “until it didn't.” One person labeled a file Car while the spouse looked under Honda or Vehicle. She began writing file names on a yellow legal pad so others could see what existed, and that became her first File Index. The book compares it this way: “A File Index is to filing what a Chart of Accounts is to accounting.”

A retired educator came to the authors with six drawers of paper from two homes and no clear system. Once her Reference files had numbers and keywords such as insurance, Blue Cross and auto policy, she said “I've had these files for 20 years and could never find what I needed. Now I can find it in seconds.” She printed her File Index for the front of the drawer and kept a digital copy that is searchable on her phone.

author.bio: Andrea Anderson is CEO of the Productive Environment Institute. She began her career as a teacher, and her experience in education and mental health gave her deep compassion for people who feel overwhelmed. While working for a family preservation agency in 2005 she discovered Barbara Hemphill's numerical filing system, and within a year she joined Barbara's team, left her job and launched her own organizing business. Barbara Hemphill is the author of Taming the Paper Tiger and the founder of the Productive Environment Institute, and she wrote the Foreword to this book.

publisher.about: Spirit Media Publishing is a Christian publishing and marketing company with a vision to reveal our Father's heart to all nations. It offers full-service book creation and publishing in paperback, hardback, digital and audiobook formats, along with children's titles, compact Express Books, website design and SEO, and podcast and video production. We are honored to publish this guide to finding what you file.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: Andrea Anderson says the book exists “to offer you a way forward. To honor Barbara's legacy.” She wants the reader to feel hopeful: “You can accomplish your work and enjoy your life.” The book is also an invitation into a community, because the authors believe “Together, We Are Better!”
Barbara Hemphill adds one thing she wants a reader to keep: “If you remember only one truth from this book, let it be this: Clutter is postponed decisions.”

faq.q: What is SOAR To Success about?
faq.a: It is a guide to the Productive Environment Finding SYSTEM, a keyword-driven filing system with a File Index for paper and digital files, written by Andrea Anderson with Barbara Hemphill in ten short chapters.

faq.q: How does the filing system work?
faq.a: Paper folders are labeled with numbers, such as Ref 1 and Ref 2, and each number is logged in a File Index with keywords. Searching the index for a word like Honda or mechanic shows which numbered folder holds the paper. For digital files the book recommends a simple alphabetical folder structure, because search is built in.

faq.q: Is there a way to deal with a flooded email inbox?
faq.a: Yes. Chapter 6 teaches the ART of Organizing Email, where every message is an Action, a Reference or a Toss. It suggests triaging email by priority, and it offers the line “Today's Mail is tomorrow's pile.” It does not promise inbox zero.

faq.q: What does clutter is postponed decisions mean?
faq.a: It is Barbara Hemphill's phrase, and the book repeats it in the Foreword and in Chapter 3: clutter is not caused by having too much information, it comes from decisions not yet made. The chapter on digital clutter applies it to unread mail and unsorted files too.

faq.q: Does it help with digital clutter?
faq.a: Yes. Chapter 6 says “Digital clutter creates decision fatigue, even if you don't see it.” It advises starting fresh today rather than refiling thousands of old files: rename what you download, move processed email to Action, Reference or Archive, and keep a simple alphabetical folder structure.

faq.q: What is the Magic 7?
faq.a: The seven tools the book says to have in place before you organize anything. They are, in order: In / Out / File Trays; Toss / Recycle / Shred; Calendar / Planner; Contact Relationship Manager (CRM); Action System; Reference System; and Integrated Task Manager, which the book names the SOAR Board.

faq.q: Is it a book about daily planning and time management?
faq.a: Part of it is. Chapter 7 teaches planning your day, week and month, and it says the breakthrough “comes from learning how to spend the time you already have.” Its core, though, is the filing and decision system.

faq.q: Does the book depend on buying something else?
faq.a: The method is taught in the book, and the authors say you can use paper, a computer or both. The book also names its own digital tool, a CRM and a workshop that readers can choose for extra support.

hero.audience_line: For readers of warm, faith-filled historical fiction, book clubs that like a story about mercy and forgiveness, and anyone who enjoys a small village, fresh bread and a long ride to the big city.
hero.tagline: In a small Austrian village a baker named Big Leo refuses to fight when his emperor orders a military draft, and takes his praying wife and a wild-haired boy to Vienna, in a warm story about mercy, family and grace.

audience.headline: A baker who will not fight, a praying wife and a wild-haired boy set out for Vienna.
audience.body: For readers of warm, faith-filled historical fiction, book clubs that like a story about mercy and forgiveness, and anyone who enjoys a small village, fresh bread and a long ride to the big city. In a short novel of twenty-four chapters, a barefoot baker called Big Leo refuses to take up arms for his emperor, and a boy who wants to know why grown-ups are always fighting gets an answer he does not expect. A note on subjects: this is a gentle story with a tender heart, but it does not look away from hard things. It includes drinking and a bar fight, a child who has been frightened by her father, a mother in despair, and a scene in which a public execution is carried out in front of a crowd. These are told without graphic detail, and the book answers them with kindness. If any of this is close to your own life, please talk to someone you trust. If you or someone you know is in danger or thinking about suicide, contact your local emergency services or a crisis line right away.

quote.text: The whole world could be at war, but that doesn't mean you have to be.
quote.cite: Spring Birds, Chapter 2: The Courtyard

what_makes.title: What makes this book for people who want a story of mercy
paras: Spring Birds begins in a small village in Austria, at a yellow inn called the Heuriger, where beer, sausage and bread fill the air. From there it follows one family of three, a baker, his wife and a village boy, to the capital and into the lives of the people they meet on its streets. The emperor in the story is named Gier, and in Chapter 17 a character confirms the year as 1910.
Five things set it apart:
list: It starts with a refusal. When officers arrive with a conscription order, Leo does not argue about politics. He simply says what he believes God wants of him, and he sits the officers down to eat.
It is told through a child's questions. Max asks the question the whole book answers: why do grown-ups fight?
It puts forgiveness in plain words. A wife and a baker teach a boy to love people who do wrong, and the book then tests that teaching on a stranger's street.
It is funny. A teacher who calls a boy a loof, a grandmother who feeds blue birds at her window, a dough starter with a name and an emperor with a long neck all keep the mood light.
It is short. Twenty-four brief chapters, about eighty pages, easy to read in a weekend.

sections.h2: For readers of faith-filled historical fiction
paras: This one has an emperor, a palace, an old city and an inn built in the 1600s, all seen through a boy's eyes. The faith in it is practical: people pray over a meal, bless a guest, ask a priest for help.

sections.h2: For book clubs
paras: What does Leo owe an emperor, and what does he owe God? Is Rosina right that anyone can be reached by love? Why does Max keep asking? A short book, but a club will find plenty to discuss in how it treats people who are poor, drunk, proud or afraid.

sections.h2: For readers who love small villages, bread and food
paras: Bread runs through every page. A baker lifts a fifty pound bag of flour and shows a boy how his starter stretches like a tongue. A basket of rolls with honey changes the mood of a standoff. A Vienna bakery changes hands in a day, and a soup the baker can never match is served in a cottage kitchen.

sections.h2: For anyone who finds it hard to forgive
paras: The book does not make forgiveness sound easy. On his last morning in the village, Leo prays for the officers who came to draft him, and Max wants to know why. Leo's answer is short:
"Being hateful is exhausting. Also, they are my brothers."
The rest of the story tests that answer, first in a roadside tavern fight and then on a man in Vienna whose own daughter is afraid of him.

blocks.text: The story opens at night, in the village:

paras: It was lively and happy in the small village in the heart of Austria. The yellow Heuriger hotel glowed with light in the summer night, and there were people all in and around it. There was much laughter, and everyone's breath smelled like beer. The bar and restaurant of the hotel rang loud with banging and shouting, and the cooking made the whole village aromatic with fried foods, sausage, and bread.

blocks.text: In Chapter 2 Max asks his questions in the courtyard, and Rosina answers him:

paras: The whole world could be at war, but that doesn't mean you have to be. We are taught to love everyone and to forgive everyone.

blocks.text: She goes on, when Max asks whether he should love people who are bad:

paras: Maybe they are bad because no one loved them. Maybe no one loves them because they are bad. We need love as we need water. If someone is mean to you or hits you, don't hit them back. Love them still and forgive them, so there can be no evil in your heart, and then maybe it will make the evil in their heart go away.

Maybe they are bad because no one loved them. Maybe no one loves them because they are bad. We need love as we need water. If someone is mean to you or hits you, don't hit them back. paras: Three men in uniform come to the hotel with a letter of military orders. Leo does not take it. He tells them plainly that "God doesn't want me to fight you or anyone else." One of the soldiers, an old friend, shrugs and apologizes. Another quietly empties the basket of rolls. Leo offers him more: "It's great with a drop of honey." Then he invites all three to the bar for coffee, because "I know you haven't had anything." The officer, careful not to look too pleased, asks how long Leo has been a baker, and the standoff turns into a new offer. Leo sums it up with a dry line: "A minute ago you wanted me to kill people, and now you want me to feed people."

One night soon after reaching Vienna, Leo lies awake listening to the city and hears a trumpet in the alley below. "It sounded honest and sad. There was a humble pain in it." The next morning he meets the man who played it, a street musician who has been told his music is too slow. Leo does not tell him to change. He says, "I heard you play at night, my friend. It was truly beautiful." Leo offers an idea that is also a blessing: "God's an artist, you're a musician, and I'm a baker."

A girl with a flower in her hair has never been heard to speak. When she meets Max, he takes the flower she offers and leads her out of the city to a green meadow. "It looked like two does were meeting each other." They lie on their backs and watch the clouds. When Max starts walking through the flowers, she speaks, and the book marks it plainly: "Don't step on the flowers." Max is not surprised. He thinks her voice is pretty.
