why.title: Why this book exists
paras: What the story itself says is plain. Its first question comes from a boy: "Do I have to fight when I grow up?" Its answer comes from a wife who prays: "The whole world could be at war, but that doesn't mean you have to be."
Leo's prayer in Chapter 4 says the same thing in his own words, on the morning he leaves home:
"Holy Father, Forgive my sins, Forgive the soldiers as I forgive them, Bless them, And bless my marriage"

faq.q: What is Spring Birds about?
faq.a: A baker named Big Leo in a small Austrian village refuses to fight when his emperor orders a military call-up. He, his praying wife Rosina and a wild-haired boy named Max travel to Vienna, and the story asks why grown-ups fight and answers with love and forgiveness.

faq.q: Is it historical fiction?
faq.a: Yes, it is classed as historical fiction and Christian fiction. It is set in an Austrian village and in Vienna, with a fictional emperor named Gier, and in Chapter 17 a character gives the year as 1910.

faq.q: Is it a story about a conscientious objector?
faq.a: In effect, yes. The opening premise is that Leo refuses military service because he believes God does not want him to fight anyone. The words conscientious objector do not appear in the book. Leo's reason is his faith, he states it calmly, and the book follows what happens next.

faq.q: What does the book say about loving your enemies?
faq.a: Rosina tells Max that we are taught to love everyone and forgive everyone, and Leo prays for the soldiers who came for him. He tells Max that "Being hateful is exhausting. Also, they are my brothers." The phrase love your enemies is not in the book, but the idea runs through it.

faq.q: Is it a heartwarming novel?
faq.a: Yes. It is a warm, faith-filled story about mercy, family and grace, and much of it is funny. It also contains hard moments, and the note on subjects near the top says what they are.

faq.q: What does the title Spring Birds mean?
faq.a: The phrase appears in Chapter 10, where Rosina walks down a Vienna street and everyone she smiles at is happy for a while after. "She was pleasant like spring birds, innocent like their songs." Blue birds also gather at the window of Max's grandmother's kitchen in Chapter 2.

faq.q: What does the book say about forgiveness?
faq.a: Rosina tells Max to love people who do wrong and forgive them so there is no evil in his heart. Later in the book, forgiveness is asked for and given by people who have good reason to withhold it.

faq.q: How long is it, and who is it for?
faq.a: It is about eighty pages in twenty-four short chapters, for adult and teen readers who like warm historical fiction. Parents of younger readers should read the note on subjects first.

sections.h2: For anyone who knew Beetle, and anyone who did not
paras: If you knew him, you will hear his voice: the movie quotes, the Rubik's cube in his hand, the “Saweet!” he said when something went his way. If you never met him, you will feel as if you did. Dana writes him as warm, humble and quick, with a smile that said “I'll do anything for you” without a word. Friends, family and coworkers add their own stories at the end, from a school bus left in a ditch to a hardware store where every total was “a Thoooousand dollars.”

sections.h2: For readers who love funny true stories about friendship and practical jokes
paras: Act I is all pranks. Two teenage friends move a youth leader's car to the wrong side of a church driveway while a conference is under way, then wait to hear what happens. Later chapters go treasure hunting with a metal detector, fish for metal with magnets and set out on a bigfoot hunt. The humor is gentle, the friendship is the point, and the faith is never bolted on.

sections.h2: For readers who want to finish well, and anyone losing a friend
paras: Dana's closing hope for you is to “finish well in the race in which you find yourself.” The last third follows Beetle through a hospital stay in Maine, a solved Rubik's cube, hard news from a physician, and a homecoming to his own house and his dog, Max. It does not hide the loss. It also does not let sorrow have the last word. This is one friend's story, not a grief manual, and you will find company in it.

sections.h2: For church drama teams, small groups and anyone who reads aloud
paras: The book is written so it can be staged. A guide at the front, How to Read This Book, explains the five forms it uses: memoir narration, dramatic scenes, stage directions, tableaux and monologues, and short Reader's Notes. A glossary of theatrical terms comes before Act I, so any reader can follow along. Dana's preface invites you to read it like a story that is still unfolding, and to take your seat as the curtain rises.

audience.headline: A best friend who made everyone laugh, and finished well.
audience.body: For anyone who knew Beetle, and anyone who did not. Dana Morrison tells the true story of his best friend, a plump, freckled, kind and gentle man from Danforth, Maine, known to nearly everyone as Beetle, who turned every hard job into a punchline and carried his faith into his final days. It is a memoir written to be read, remembered, performed or passed along. A note on subjects: the last acts follow a serious illness, a hospital stay and a death at home, told gently and with humor, not in medical detail.

quote.text: From birth to his final breath, Beetle is living joy.
quote.cite: The Beetle Experience, Act I, Created for Joy

what_makes.title: What makes this book for readers who want laughter and faith in the same story
paras: The Beetle Experience is a funny memoir that is not shy about the hard parts. Dana calls it “not a traditional memoir” and “not a conventional stage play either.” It is something in between, and it welcomes you into the front row.
Five things set it apart:
list: It is a memoir-play hybrid. Prose memories sit beside dramatic scenes, stage directions, tableaux, monologues, vignettes and short Reader's Notes that give the time and place, so the book can be read quietly or staged with friends.
It is told by the best friend. Dana was there for the pranks, the summers at camp and the hospital room, and he narrates as himself, turning to the audience to give you the backstory.
It keeps its promise to tell the truth. “The stories you will see are true,” Dana writes. “The names haven't been changed to protect the innocent as there were likely none that were innocent.”
It lets you laugh and grieve in the same breath. In Beetle's last days, a room full of visitors is telling funny stories when he says, “I'm dyin' over here… and you guys are tellin' jokes!”

It ends with an invitation and a chorus of voices. After the epilogue come simple next steps for anyone who wants to start following Jesus, then “Last Words” from family, camp friends, coworkers and neighbors who knew him.

paras: In the summer of 1988, Dana, his best friend and another friend arrive as volunteers at Living Waters Bible Camp. A loud, laughing staff member hands out nicknames to everyone standing in the dinner line. Dana is “Crash.” Their friend is “Pee Wee,” to his fury. His best friend becomes “Beetle,” a play on his last name. Then the camp's assistant director insists that he gave the name first. Dana settles it by asking the audience to vote and concludes, “I guess Beetle just… named himself.” The same scene gives us the day Beetle tells a camper he is 45, and keeps saying it for years.

stories.h2: Captain Kidd's treasure, or what is left of it
paras: Every summer Dana and Beetle plan the fun they will have when he is back in Maine. One year Beetle has heard a rumor that Captain Kidd buried treasure near Wiscasset, so they take an old metal detector to the water behind his parents' house. They find spent .22 casings, a shotgun shell and a bottle cap. Dana admits that historians doubt Kidd ever reached the Maine coast, but says that without the rumor “he and I might have had some great memories stolen from us.” The next summer they research a real abandoned gold prospect near Danforth.

In the hospital in June 2023, Beetle reaches for the Rubik's cube on his bedside table. His hands tremble, but he works it click by click until the colors line up, and Dana sees a verse come alive: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith.” (2 Timothy 4:7) A few scenes later, the room explodes into laughter at Beetle's line about dying, and the laughter dissolves into tears. Dana writes that in one line Beetle gave them permission to hold both, “the comedy and the tragedy — side by side.”

author.bio: Dana Morrison was the best friend of the man known to nearly everyone as Beetle. Their friendship ran from teenage pranks and campfire years through hardship, time apart, treasure hunting and Beetle's final days. Dana wrote The Beetle Experience, shaping these memories into a memoir-play hybrid meant to be read, remembered, performed or passed along. Dana and Beetle share a birthday. His hope is that every reader receives the blessing of laughter and is inspired to finish well.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: Dana says the book began as a collection of memories, “funny, raw, sacred, and real,” about a man God used to shape his life. Every time he tried to write it as a plain memoir, it felt “too small.” Beetle, he explains, “isn't a man who speaks in paragraphs. He speaks in stories. Scenes. Punchlines. Pranks.” So he started staging the memories, and the book became a hybrid.

“Some stories are too full of laughter to be told quietly. Some lives are too bright to be dimmed by paragraphs alone.” It is an honest tribute, built on Proverbs 17:22 and on the belief that Beetle's joy pointed past himself to Christ. The epilogue says it plainly: “He ran his race, and he finished with joy.”

faq.q: What is The Beetle Experience about?
faq.a: It is the true story of Beetle, told by his best friend, Dana Morrison, as a memoir-play hybrid in six acts. The book defines Beetle as a laughter-generating, treasure-hunting, car-rebuilding, churchgoing, movie-quoting bundle of laughter, and it follows him from teenage pranks to his final days.

faq.q: Is it a memoir or a stage play?
faq.a: Both and neither. It is a memoir-play hybrid, with prose memories, dramatic scenes, stage directions, tableaux, monologues and vignettes that can be read, remembered, performed or passed along.

faq.q: Is it a funny memoir?
faq.a: Yes. It tells of pranks, tall tales, treasure hunting and a man who made everyone laugh, and it is rooted in Proverbs 17:22, “A cheerful heart is good medicine.”

faq.q: Is it a spiritual memoir?
faq.a: It is a Christian memoir. Faith runs through the camp years and the final days, and the closing pages invite readers who want to follow Jesus, with simple next steps, such as reading the Gospel of John and finding a church family.

faq.q: Does it include practical jokes and pranks?
faq.a: Act I is built on them, from moving a car at a church conference to “Operation Indian House,” and Dana says the stories are true.

faq.q: Is it set in northern Maine, and what is the Bible camp?
faq.a: Much of it takes place in and around Danforth, Maine, and at Living Waters Bible Camp, where the friends volunteered the summer of 1988 and where Beetle got his nickname.

faq.q: Is it a story about a faithful friend?
faq.a: Yes. Dana tells it as the best friend who was there for the pranks, the camp summers, the years apart and the hospital room. Beetle is shown as a faithful friend to many: the book's Last Words come from family, camp friends, coworkers and neighbors who each remember what he did for them.

faq.q: Is there a Rubik's cube in the story?
faq.a: Yes. Beetle almost always has one in his hand. In Scene 25, in a hospital in Maine, his hands tremble as he works the cube click by click until the colors line up, and Dana sees 2 Timothy 4:7 come alive.

faq.q: Will it help if I am losing a friend?
faq.a: It follows a friendship through Beetle's final days and homecoming, and it holds laughter and loss together. It is one friend's testimony rather than a guide to grief.

faq.q: Who is it for?
faq.a: Anyone who knew Beetle and anyone who did not, readers who enjoy funny true stories with faith and friendship at the center, and readers who want to be inspired to finish well in the race they are running.

sections.h2: For believers who want to be ready for the Lord's return
paras: If you have been wondering how to prepare your heart for the days ahead, this book gives you a daily rhythm instead of speculation. The author calls it "a roadmap to help us be ready for His return." It does not set dates. It asks you, one day at a time, to surrender, to trust the Commander and to obey.

sections.h2: For readers who want a 40-day devotional on identity, surrender and fearless faith
paras: Forty days is long enough to build a habit and short enough to finish. The first week focuses on who you are in Christ, and the remaining days on how a person who belongs to Him thinks and lives. Each day gives you something to say aloud, something to think about and something to do, so the truth reaches your week and not only your reading.

sections.h2: For men and women who want Scripture, a prayer and journal pages every day
paras: You will find a Bible verse and a set of affirmations at the start of each day, a prayer at the end, and a journal page you can fill in. The reflection questions are practical, such as asking where you still struggle with fear, what you have not yet fully surrendered, and where you have been relying on your own strength. You can read alone or share it with a friend or small group.

sections.h2: For believers who are afraid of what is coming
paras: The book is honest that hard days may come, and it does not try to scare you. Day 5 calls fear the first weapon the enemy uses, and the action for the day is to speak truth, take a step of faith and reach out to someone anyway. Later days turn to the peace of God and to being hidden in Christ. The aim is faith over fear: to stand because of who your Commander is, not because you feel brave.

audience.headline: Forty days to stand fearless, surrendered and ready for the Lord's return.
audience.body: For believers who want a 40-day devotional on identity in Christ, surrender and faith over fear. Patricia A. Daniel, who grew up the child of military parents, gives you Scripture, affirmations, a reflection, ways to apply it, a prayer and a journal page for every day, so that you can begin each morning with daily Bible reading and a prayer for strength. A note on subjects: the book uses military imagery as a picture of spiritual life under Christ's command, and it speaks of a possible season of persecution and even martyrdom for believers. It gives no instructions for violence and sets no dates. It is a devotional, written to encourage readers toward courage and trust.

quote.text: May this devotional serve as our trumpet call, awakening us to new levels of faith, commitment, and obedience.

what_makes.title: What makes this book for believers who want to be ready for the Lord's return
paras: A devotional in four sections and forty days. It begins by asking who your Commander is, builds up your identity in Christ, speaks of the training God allows, and then spends thirty-three days on the mindset of a believer who is hidden in Christ and fixed on Jesus.
Five things set it apart:
list: It gives you a plan. Each day has the same shape: New King James Scripture and affirmations, a biblical truth, a reflection, ideas for how to apply it, a prayer, and a closing affirmation of faith, with a page for notes.

It was born from a poem. The author wrote Marching Orders about being prepared to serve faithfully in the end-times, and "God would eventually use this poem to be the inspiration behind the devotional."

It is rooted in identity. Section Two takes five days on the surrendered, equipped, authorized, fearless and victorious warrior, so that you start from who you are in Christ, not from what you must achieve.
It tackles fear head on. Day 5 begins, "Fear is the first weapon the enemy deploys against a warrior," and the day closes with a prayer to renounce fear and entrust your life to the Lord.

It pairs courage with humility. Day 29 says true humility is "an accurate assessment of ourselves before God," and the book repeatedly describes the warrior as one who serves without seeking recognition.

details.Title: The End-Times Warrior: A 40-Day Devotional
details.Author: Patricia A. Daniel
details.Binding: Paperback (perfect bound), black and white interior on cream paper

stories.h2: Day 1: We serve a man of war
paras: Day 1 begins with the verse "The LORD is a man of war; The LORD is His name" from Exodus 15:3. The author reminds readers that when Moses and the Israelites stood at the Red Sea, "they didn't sing praises to their own strength or strategy," but recognized the true source of their victory. Under His command, she says, "we are offensive, not merely defensive; unstoppable, not easily deterred; and victorious, not defeated." The reflection asks you to take inventory of your readiness, to name what you have not yet surrendered and to write a personal declaration of surrender.

Day 5 names fear as the first weapon of the enemy, "because he knows that a frightened soldier cannot fight effectively." The author reminds readers that they stand in a long line of believers: Stephen faced stoning with a face like an angel, and "Paul and Silas sang hymns in prison at midnight." The action for the day is small and practical. Speak truth when it would be easier to stay silent, take a step of faith when you would rather play it safe, and reach out to someone when rejection seems possible. The prayer renounces fear and embraces the spirit of power, love and a sound mind.

stories.h2: Day 9: He is hidden in Christ
paras: Day 9 turns to Colossians. The author writes that when we come to Christ, our old self dies and our new life is hidden in Him, and that "This sacred concealment offers both protection and a new identity." She says the hidden position does not make us ineffective, but gives access to resources beyond human understanding. The reflection asks you to rest in that security today, especially when criticism or attack comes, and to remember that your worth cannot be touched.

author.bio: Patricia A. Daniel grew up a child of military parents and saw firsthand the discipline, order and commitment of those who served. She has served in multiple ministries over several decades, but most enjoys the Missions ministry, and has served in India and Brazil. She uses her administrative gift, her English as a Second Language certification and her writing gifts to edify the body of Christ. She is the author of three other books: a poetry collection, In Heaven I Can Fly, a children's book, The Purple Swan, and A Block From Grace, a memorial tribute to her parents that she co-authored. Her ministry blog, Destination Jesus, is where she shares her poetry, short stories and Bible teaching. She believes in what she calls legacy living, intentionally living so that your impact outlives you.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: It began with a poem. The author writes, "It was not too long ago that I penned a poem called Marching Orders about being prepared to serve faithfully in the end-times." She never imagined it would become the inspiration for a devotional.

She also wrote it because she believes God is preparing believers now. "God is raising up His End-Times Warriors," she writes, "men and women who will dare to believe, trust, and obey Him at ANY COST." She is clear about the limits of the book: "This 40-day devotional by no means captures the full breadth of all God is doing in us and for us in these end-times, but it can serve as a roadmap to help us be ready for His return." Her closing hope is that readers will "rest in the fullness of His grace."

faq.q: What is The End-Times Warrior?
faq.a: A 40-day devotional by Patricia A. Daniel that helps believers prepare to serve Christ as surrendered, fearless warriors and be ready for His return.

faq.q: How is each day built?
faq.a: New King James Scripture and affirmations, a biblical truth, a reflection, ways to apply it, a prayer and journal pages.

faq.q: What are the four sections?
faq.a: The Lord, Our Commander; The Warrior's Identity in Christ; The Warrior's Special Training; and The Warrior's Mindset, which spans thirty-three days.

faq.q: Does it include prayers for strength?
faq.a: Each day ends with a written prayer. Day 5, for example, asks the Lord to "Strengthen me to stand fearlessly against every scheme of the enemy," and Day 11 prays that Christ's life will supply what the reader needs.

faq.q: Does it cover the armor of God?
faq.a: Yes, as one of the truths in the Warrior's Mindset section. Day 8 is titled He Wears The Armor of God, 24/7. It is one theme among forty days, not the whole book.

faq.q: Does it help with fear?
faq.a: Yes. Day 5 is devoted to the fearless warrior, and the book returns to fear throughout, pointing you to peace, to being hidden in Christ and to the truth that "We're not fighting for victory; we're fighting from victory."

faq.q: Is it a book about the second coming of Jesus?
faq.a: It is a devotional and a roadmap to be ready for the Lord's return, with daily Scripture and prayer. It does not predict dates.

faq.q: Does it speak to identity in Christ?
faq.a: Yes. Section Two is entirely about the warrior's identity in Christ, and later days speak of being crucified with Christ, hidden in Christ and one of many living stones.

hero.audience_line: For believers who want to be ready for the Lord's return, readers who want a 40-day devotional on identity in Christ, surrender and fearless faith, and men and women who want Scripture, a prayer and journal pages for each day.
hero.tagline: A 40-day devotional in four sections that equips believers to serve as surrendered, fearless warriors under the command of the Lord Jesus Christ as they prepare for His return.

hero.audience_line: For young readers who love fairies and fantasy, and for the families, homeschool groups and Sunday school teachers who read aloud together.
hero.tagline: A Christian fantasy chapter book: when elves capture their families, a timid fire fairy and his friends turn to prayer and the Bible stories of Jericho and the fiery furnace to find the courage to bring them home.

audience.headline: When small elves carry off every parent, a timid fire fairy and his friends turn to prayer and Bible stories to find the courage to bring their families home.
audience.body: For young readers who love fairies and fantasy, and for the families, homeschool groups and Sunday school teachers who read aloud together. Jenna Kris sends Ember, Rose Petal and Raindrop from the land of Whimsy through Shadow Valley and the Hills of Moonlight to the mushroom libraries of the Questing Woods, where a fairy named Dickens helps them read about Jericho, the fiery furnace and David. A note on subjects: this is a gentle fantasy with some real fear in it. A dark valley with growls in the cracks, an ambush with flying arrows, parents carried away, a fire that spreads in a market, and a king who clings to his throne. The families are reunited at the end. The book presents prayer and trust in God as what gives its characters courage.

quote.text: “Ember didn't think. He ran toward the fire, not away from it.”
quote.cite: The Fairies and the Elf King, Chapter 12, The Rescue

what_makes.title: What makes this book for children who feel afraid
paras: It begins with a family trip and ends with the story of why you can be brave when you are scared. In between, a fairy who freezes behind a tree becomes the one who runs toward the fire.
Five things set it apart:
list: The hero is the timid one. Ember hides when his family is taken. His hands go cold and spark-less. He is not told to be brave. He finds out what courage looks like.
Friends hold on. When the families are gone, Rose Petal takes one of Ember's hands and Raindrop takes the other, and the three of them "held on tight and didn't let go."
Prayer is part of the plot. Dickens feels anxious about his friends, prays, and is told to go to the Hills of Moonlight. Ember prays the night before the rescue.
Three Bible stories carry the plan. The fairies read about the Battle of Jericho, King Nebuchadnezzar with the fiery furnace, and King David, and they use what they learn.
It has a gentle structure for reading together. Fourteen short chapters, Discovery Questions grouped by chapter, and a glossary of fairy words at the back.

sections.h2: For young readers who love fairies and fantasy
paras: If your child likes tiny creatures with big feelings, this book is full of them. A fire fairy can make sparks with a snap of his fingers and hear fire crackle and breathe. A snail named Quickie speaks very slowly and gives very good advice. A tall, thin library grows out of the side of a pine tree. The Nymphs of Moonlight have hair the color of moonlight.

sections.h2: For families who read aloud together
paras: The chapters are short enough for a night at a time, and each one ends on a turn: a noise, an arrow, a prayer, a plan. The dialogue is simple and the story moves, so it is easy to read out loud. A family can read a chapter and then use the Discovery Questions for that chapter to talk about it.

sections.h2: For homeschool families and Sunday school teachers
paras: The Bible stories in the book are the ones children often hear in class: Jericho, the furnace and David. The fairies read them in a library and then act on them. The Discovery Questions point back to the Scripture, ask what children think, and end with a prompt such as when they were brave even though they were scared.

sections.h2: For children who get anxious
paras: When Dickens feels anxious, he has already tried reading, and it does not help. Quickie tells him to talk to God about it. The book does not promise that worry will vanish. It shows a child praying, listening and finding peace, and then doing the next thing.

paras: Far away in the Questing Woods, a young fairy named Dickens cannot shake an anxious feeling about his friends. He asks Quickie what to do. Quickie says to talk to God. Dickens flies to the roof of a mushroom and prays:
"Dear God, I feel anxious and scared, and I don't know why."

He sits and listens. Nothing comes except a peace he did not have before. That night God tells him to go to the Hills of Moonlight, so he packs a bag, tells Quickie goodbye and flies out into the night.

stories.h2: The libraries of the Questing Woods
paras: In Chapter 6, the four fairies reach the Questing Woods and Quickie sends them to the war and battle library, number three. It is a tall, thin mushroom sticking out of the side of a pine tree, with a flat blue roof and a door carved with shields, swords and horses. They look for the Battle of Jericho, King Nebuchadnezzar and King David, and the first thing Ember says about Jericho is:
"A wall? How do you battle a wall?"
The next chapters are the answers: Joshua and the people march and obey, three men trust God in a furnace, and a shepherd boy faces a giant.

In Chapter 12, Ember stands in the Elf Kingdom market, bigger than he has ever been. His job is to distract the crowd. He juggles fireballs, then one wobbles and sails into a vendor's booth. The canvas catches and the fire spreads. His first instinct is to run.
"Ember didn't think. He ran toward the fire, not away from it."

He calls the flames back into the center of the square, away from an elf mother and her children, and puts them out with a clap of his hands. The book says what he knows about fire fairies: "Fire never hurts a fire fairy."

author.bio: Jenna Kris is a Christian fantasy author from Central Virginia who writes wholesome adventure stories filled with faith, courage and wonder. She brings imaginative worlds to life through heartfelt characters and meaningful lessons, and she wants her books to encourage readers to trust God, use their gifts and walk boldly in faith. When she is not writing, she enjoys baking gluten-free treats, gardening, crocheting and singing in her church choir. The book's About the Author page names her as the author of The Fairies' Quest series, and several characters, including Rose Petal, Raindrop, Dickens, Quickie and Indigo the blue bird, also appear in The Fairies Quest.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The dedication says it first:
"This book is dedicated to the Lord. May this book bring Him honor and glory."
The ending says what the author hopes a young reader carries away, after Ember thinks back over the Bible stories he has read:
"four little fairies got their families back because they listened to God and followed where He led, even when they were scared."

faq.q: What is The Fairies and the Elf King about?
faq.a: It is a Christian fantasy chapter book and family read-aloud by Jenna Kris, in fourteen chapters. A fire fairy named Ember and his friends, Rose Petal and Raindrop, are left alone when small elves carry off every parent. With help from a praying fairy named Dickens, they turn to Bible stories to find the courage to bring their families home.

faq.q: Is it a good book for bedtime stories?
faq.a: It is written in fourteen short chapters, so a family can read one a night. The word bedtime does not appear in the book, and the description fits how many families read it. There is some fear in the first half, and the ending is peaceful, with the families going home.

faq.q: Are there fairy books for kids with a Christian message?
faq.a: This is one. The main characters are fairies, and the faith is part of the plot: prayer, listening to God, and Bible stories as guides. The book is a fantasy first, and it does not use Scripture as a sermon.

faq.q: Is this a Christian fantasy book?
faq.a: Yes. The book is set in a made-up world of fairies, elves and Nymphs, and its Bible content is told inside the story. The Discovery Questions at the back include references such as Joshua 6, Daniel 3 and 1 Samuel 16:7.

faq.q: Is it one of the chapter books for 7 year olds?
faq.a: It is a chapter book in fourteen short chapters, for young readers who are ready for chapters, and younger children will enjoy it read aloud. The book itself does not print a reading age.

faq.q: Is the fiery furnace in the book?
faq.a: Yes. In Chapter 7, Of Kings and Statues, the fairies read about King Nebuchadnezzar's gold statue and the three men who would not bow. Ember thinks of that story again the night before the rescue and again when the elf king's golden statue is left standing in the empty square.

faq.q: Is it connected to The Fairies Quest?
faq.a: Some characters appear in both books, and the author note calls her the author of The Fairies' Quest series. Each book tells its own story.

faq.q: Where does the story take place?
faq.a: In the world of Fantasy, in the land of Whimsy and beyond: Shadow Valley, the Hills of Moonlight, the Questing Woods, Moonlit Ridge and the Elf Kingdom.

hero.audience_line: For children ages 6 to 10 who love fairies, talking animals and adventure, and for the parents and teachers who want a read-aloud chapter book that points to the Creator.
hero.tagline: Two fairy best friends, Rose Petal and Raindrop, set out for The Questing Woods to answer what came first, the chicken or the egg, and discover the Creator who made it all.

audience.headline: Two fairy best friends ask what came first, the chicken or the egg, and set out to find the answer.
audience.body: For children ages 6 to 10 who love fairies, talking animals and a good adventure, and for the parents and teachers who read to them. Jenna Kris sends Rose Petal and Raindrop from the land of Whimsy through the Honey Forest, the Garden of the Gnomes and Flutter Butterfly Meadow to the mushroom libraries of the Questing Woods, where an answer waits that is bigger than the question. A note on subjects: this is a gentle fantasy for young readers. There is a loud argument at a festival, a long trip with a few scary moments, including a butterfly ride in which one fairy falls and is caught, and a worry about whether everyone will agree at the end. The book presents God as the Creator who made everything, and it does that through a scroll about the fifth day of creation.

quote.text: All we can do is share what we learned about God, and they have to decide for themselves.
quote.cite: The Fairies Quest, Rose Petal in Chapter 11: Doubts

what_makes.title: What makes this book for children who ask big questions
paras: It begins with a spring festival and a question that sounds silly. By the last chapter the whole land of Whimsy has stopped to listen. Rose Petal and Raindrop go looking for an answer to calm everyone down, and they come home with more than they asked for.
Five things set it apart:
list: It starts with a question every child has heard. At the animal booths, fairies argue about the chicken and the egg until the chickens squawk and the baby chicks hide. Nobody actually knows the answer, and that is why the two friends leave.

It is a quest with places you can picture. The path runs past the Honey Forest and its Queen Bee, the Garden of the Gnomes, Flutter Butterfly Meadow, Lake Mystery, the Questing Woods and Singing Bird Haven, and then home to Whimsy.

It is about friendship that holds when things get hard. Rose Petal charges ahead and Raindrop stops to take notes. When Raindrop slips from a butterfly's back, Rose Petal is the one who reaches for her hand.

The answer comes from the first chapter of Genesis. A scroll called Birds and Fowl says that on the fifth day God created "every winged bird according to its kind," and a hyper young fairy named Dickens explains what that means.

It leaves room for doubt and for choosing. Raindrop worries that not everyone will like the answer, and Rose Petal answers, "All we can do is share what we learned about God, and they have to decide for themselves."

sections.h2: For young readers who love fairies and talking animals
paras: If your child likes tiny creatures with big opinions, this is for them. A queen bee holds court over a forest of honey. A snail at a bark desk speaks in a whisper and a caterpillar named Bobbin goes to fetch his sister. A blue bird named Indigo carries the fairies home in a woven basket shaped like a nest.

sections.h2: For parents who read aloud
paras: The chapters are short and end where a bedtime can. The language is simple and the dialogue carries the story, so it reads well out loud. The questions come up the way a child would ask them: "Where did God come from?" is answered honestly with "Nobody knows," and the book says plainly that believing takes trust.

sections.h2: For teachers and families who want to talk afterward
paras: The back of the book has Discovery Questions for chapter groups. They ask a child how it feels not to get the color of flower you wanted, what you think came first and why, how to answer a question you do not know, what helps when you are scared, which verse in Genesis chapter 1 talks about the creation of birds, where you can learn about God, and whether everyone who hears about God will believe. They work as a read-aloud guide for a family, a classroom or a small group.

sections.h2: For children who wonder where everything came from
paras: The question of the chicken and the egg is really a question about beginnings. The book takes it seriously and answers it inside the story, with a Creator who made birds, trees, mushrooms and fairies. It is a children's story that gives one clear answer and invites a child to think it over.

stories.h2: The question at the animal booths
paras: Chapter 3 finds Raindrop and Rose Petal at the festival, hoping to see baby chicks. Instead they find animal fairies bickering. The argument turns into a scene: worms wiggle everywhere, chickens squawk and baby chicks hide, and the arguing fairies are too busy to notice. Raindrop shouts for them to stop, and nobody hears her. Mother Kit tells them the only place that could hold the answer is "more than a week away," a place called The Questing Woods, and the two friends decide to go.

In Chapter 4 the fairies walk into the Honey Forest without asking, and the worker bees drop their honey. Queen Bee comes out to ask who is there. Rose Petal tells the truth, that fairies back home are bickering. Then the queen asks what Rose Petal believes the answer is, and Rose Petal has to admit that she does not know. The queen lets them pass and asks them to come back and tell her what they find. They keep that promise on the way home, and Queen Bee says, "I have heard of this God before."

Chapters 9 and 10 take place in a tall orange mushroom library with stairs winding to the top. It takes most of a day to find the shelf for farm animals. Dickens unrolls the scroll and reads the first sentence aloud, and then explains it in his rapid way: God made birds, not a pile of eggs left to hatch on their own. Raindrop is not sure. She asks who God is and where He came from. Dickens says nobody knows, and that you have to trust that He is real. She leaves the chapter thinking it over.

author.bio: Jenna Kris has been writing since she was a child. She loves to garden and paint, and to spend time with her cat. Much of her inspiration comes from being outdoors and from time with her little niece. This book was inspired by the Lord and by a couple of little girls she used to babysit and their love of fairies.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The author's note in the book is short, and it says where the story came from: "This book was inspired by the Lord and a couple of little girls she used to babysit and their love of fairies."

The story itself says what she wants a child to carry away. When Raindrop worries that the fairies of Whimsy will not accept the answer, Rose Petal says, "What matters is that we believe." In the last chapter Raindrop says that even if the others do not, "we do, and I know that I will continue to believe in God and creation no matter what."

faq.q: What is The Fairies Quest about?
faq.a: Two fairy best friends, Rose Petal and Raindrop, leave the land of Whimsy to find out what came first, the chicken or the egg, after the question splits the spring festival into two sides. They travel through forests, a garden, a meadow and past a mysterious lake to the Questing Woods, and they come home with an answer about the Creator.

faq.q: Does the book answer the chicken or the egg?
faq.a: Inside the story, yes. The fairies read that God created birds on the fifth day, so for them the chicken came first. It is a children's faith adventure. It is not a science text, and it does not claim to be one. The exact phrase chicken or the egg appears about ten times in the book, and the question drives every chapter.

faq.q: Is it for kids who like talking animals?
faq.a: Yes. Queen Bee speaks in the Honey Forest, Quickie the snail greets visitors at the Questing Woods, Bobbin the caterpillar and his sister Windy talk to the fairies, and Indigo the blue bird gives them a ride home. The festival opens with animal booths, baby chicks, squirrels and toads.

faq.q: Is there a water fairy in it?
faq.a: Raindrop is called a water fairy once, in Chapter 5, when a bucket falls down the gnomes' well and she raises the water level to bring it back. The rest of the time she is the careful friend with a notebook, drawing water wheels and thinking about how to feed the picky sparkle spike fish.

faq.q: Are there gnomes as well as fairies?
faq.a: Yes. Chapter 5 takes place in the Garden of the Gnomes, where Greenie shows the fairies how water flows through the trenches and Daisy gives them a place to sleep.

faq.q: Where did animals come from, according to the book?
faq.a: The book answers with the scroll in the Questing Woods library, which says that God created "every winged bird according to its kind" on the fifth day, and Dickens explains that He made the birds first and not a pile of eggs. The question is about birds, and the book keeps to birds.

faq.q: Does it teach about God?
faq.a: Yes. The subtitle names discovering the Creator. The fairies learn about God in the library, they take a scroll of the creation story home, and the new idea spreads through Whimsy. The story is a conversation between friends who are still working it out.

faq.q: Is it a fairy tale adventure for ages 6 to 10?
faq.a: It is an early chapter book of 88 pages for read-aloud or for children who read on their own. It has thirteen chapters and a gentle pace.

hero.audience_line: For working Christians in any job, business owners and marketplace leaders, and small groups and working lunch groups who want to live their faith at work.
hero.tagline: A Christian guide to faith at work that reconnects your career with your calling and shows how a faith lived in small things can move you from a forgotten witness to a known witness of Jesus.

audience.headline: Most of us spend 2,080 hours a year at work. This book asks whether the person three feet away knows you follow Jesus.
audience.body: For working Christians in any job: at a desk, behind a counter, on a shop floor, in a classroom or running a small business. Justin Creasman writes as a working professional, not a pastor, with twelve chapters and an epilogue on endurance, surrender, rhythm, boldness, community, workmanship, prayer, Scripture, service, witness, solitude and a rule of life, each with Reflection questions and a Reach Practice. A note on subjects: the book is a Christian living guide for adults. One chapter gives a general overview of religious protections under United States employment law, and it says plainly that this is general information and encouragement, not legal advice. The author also names stories from his own work without naming people or companies.

quote.text: “A Known Witness is not a louder Christian. He is a consistent one.”
quote.cite: The Forgotten Witness, Epilogue: Your Mission Field Awaits

what_makes.title: What makes this book for people who want to live their faith at work
paras: It starts with a plain question, "Do you feel purposeful in your career?", and it keeps its feet on the ground. The author says up front that this is not a book about perfect Christians at work. It is about a faith that shows up in the small things.
Five things set it apart:
list: It is written by a working professional. Justin Creasman has spent his career in the marketplace, starting prayer groups, Bible studies and discipleship bands at work.
It gives each chapter two tools. At the end you find questions for Reflection and a Reach Practice, an action to try that week.

It talks about the law without pretending to be a lawyer. The chapter on laws and policies explains Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 in general terms, names its limits, and tells the reader to consult an attorney for their own situation.
It is honest that not everyone has the same freedom. The author's note acknowledges readers in places where speaking about faith costs far more.
It ends with a clear picture of the goal: moving from a Forgotten Witness, present and faithful but unknown, to a Known Witness of Jesus.

sections.h2: For working Christians in any job
paras: If you have felt that your faith lives on Sunday and your career lives the rest of the week, this book names that split and offers small steps to close it. The preface pictures a face across a coffee counter, a coworker at the next desk, a law enforcement officer and a small business partner as the congregation you already have.

sections.h2: For business owners and marketplace leaders
paras: The book is written by someone who has managed people. It asks what you do when the trash is overflowing and you are hungry, how you treat people with less authority, and whether your team can tell what you believe from how you work. Two readers with marketplace leadership roles contributed advance praise.

sections.h2: For small groups and working lunch groups
paras: Each chapter ends with questions for discussion and a practice to try before you meet again. The author has led prayer groups, Bible studies and discipleship bands at work, and the book is written with that kind of group in mind.

sections.h2: For readers who want to share their faith without being pushy
paras: The book keeps returning to consistency over volume. The epilogue says a Known Witness is not a louder Christian but a consistent one. Evangelism here means a prayer before a meeting, the truth told when a lie would be easier, and a trash bag changed when no one is watching.

stories.h2: A semester at a fast-food restaurant
paras: In Chapter 1, the author tells how he entered college in 2007 meaning to become a neurosurgeon. Two years in, he burned out. He took a semester away to work at a fast-food restaurant, and he now calls that one of the best decisions of his life. It is the book's first lesson about endurance, and it comes with a line that fits any season:
"Your failures and miscalculations are building blocks for your future successes."
In Chapter 6, a shift has run long, the leftover food in the break room is calling, and the trash in the manufacturing area is overflowing. As a manager he could delegate. Instead he serves.
"I replaced the trash with a new bag and discarded the old one."
The food tastes the same fifteen minutes later, and another manager who saw it takes the same road next time. The chapter ties it to Mark 10:45.

stories.h2: What am I actually allowed to do here?
paras: Chapter 4 turns to a practical question that sits under every workplace witness:
"what am I actually allowed to do here?"

The author describes Title VII in general terms, names its limits, and stops to say it protects him in ways it will not protect every reader. What carries across every border, he writes, is how you work and how you treat people.

author.bio: Justin Creasman is a marketplace leader who has spent his career building formational communities in the workplace. Born and raised in Winston-Salem, North Carolina, he holds a bachelor's degree in biology from North Carolina Central University and is pursuing graduate studies with Antioch School. At work he has started prayer groups, Bible studies and discipleship bands, and he helped plant City Movement Church in the Raleigh-Durham area. His website is justincreasman.com.

paras: The preface gives the author's hope in his own words:

faq.q: What is The Forgotten Witness about?
faq.a: It is a Christian living guide to faith at work. Justin Creasman, a working professional and not a pastor, invites readers to reconnect professional life with spiritual calling, to see the workplace as a mission field and to make room for the Holy Spirit to guide, convict and strengthen, across twelve chapters and an epilogue.

faq.q: What does the book say about the Holy Spirit?
faq.a: It treats the Holy Spirit as the guide of a believer's workday. The book asks readers to let the Holy Spirit examine their hearts, to listen for the Spirit's leading, and to speak up when the Spirit prompts. The term appears about thirty times across the book.

faq.q: Is it one of the good Christian living books for working people?
faq.a: It is written for people who spend most of their week at work. Its chapters are practices, such as prayer, Scripture, service and solitude, not theology lectures, and each ends with Reflection and a Reach Practice.

faq.q: Is it a Christian leadership book?
faq.a: It is a faith-at-work guide that includes leadership. The author writes as a manager who stopped to change a trash bag and as someone who started groups at work, and several stories come from his own time as a manager.

faq.q: What is marketplace ministry, and does the book teach it?
faq.a: Marketplace ministry is living out your calling inside a job, not only at church. The book calls it vocational ministry and says the workplace can be a mission field. Two readers who lead in the marketplace wrote the advance praise.

faq.q: Is it an evangelism book?
faq.a: It is about being a witness, not about giving a sales pitch. It says consistency, workmanship and compassion speak before you open your mouth. Evangelism appears a few times in the book, and the practices are quiet and daily.

faq.q: What does the book say about faith at work and the law?
faq.a: One chapter offers a general overview of Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the religious protections it provides in the United States. It is general information and not legal advice, and it tells readers to consult an attorney licensed where they work.

faq.q: Can a small group use it?
faq.a: Yes. Every chapter closes with Reflection questions and a Reach Practice, which makes the book suited to personal study, a working lunch group or a small band of believers.

hero.tagline: Cinquante ans de vie chrétienne en montagnes russes, et ce que la grâce voulait dire depuis le début : quinze chapitres sur la grâce, la nouvelle naissance et le Saint-Esprit.

audience.headline: Elle était si frustrée dans sa marche chrétienne qu'elle s'est demandé si tout ce qu'elle croyait n'était pas faux. Alors elle est revenue à la première question : la grâce.
audience.body: Pour les lecteurs francophones qui aiment Dieu, qui font de leur mieux et qui se sentent pourtant épuisés, fatigués de ne jamais arriver à destination. Suzan Cartagena raconte comment une définition courante de la grâce, "tu ne le mérites pas, mais Dieu est bon envers toi", l'a tenue captive pendant cinquante ans, et comment un retour aux racines de sa foi lui a fait découvrir que la grâce est bien plus que cela. Quinze chapitres, avec les passages de la Bible qui fondent chaque idée. Une note sur le contenu : le livre propose des lectures personnelles de certains textes bibliques, par exemple de l'arbre de la connaissance du bien et du mal, et s'adresse à des lecteurs prêts à les examiner la Bible ouverte.

what_makes.title: Ce qui distingue ce livre pour les lecteurs qui veulent comprendre la grâce
paras: Beaucoup de livres sur la grâce la définissent en une phrase. Celui-ci la suit à travers toute la vie chrétienne.
Cinq choses le distinguent :
list: Il part d'une vraie frustration. L'auteure écrit qu'elle a longtemps vécu sa vie chrétienne comme sur des montagnes russes : un moment en haut, le suivant en bas. Elle ne cache ni le doute ni la fatigue.

Il pose les questions que beaucoup n'osent pas poser. Que signifie naître de nouveau ? Comment la grâce est-elle liée au Saint-Esprit ? Que veut dire attrister l'Esprit, blasphémer contre lui, frustrer la grâce de Dieu ou être déchu de la grâce ?
Chaque chapitre s'appuie sur la Bible. Les passages sont cités en tête de chapitre et au fil du texte, avec la version indiquée.

Il explique ses choix de traduction. La page de copyright précise que la plupart des versets viennent de la King James Française, puis de la Louis Segond et de la Darby, et que les versions anglaises sans équivalent français sont traduites littéralement.
Il se termine sur la puissance. Le dernier chapitre, « Vous recevrez la puissance », conclut sur la suffisance de la grâce.

sections.h2: Pour les chrétiens épuisés par la performance
paras: Si vous vous reconnaissez dans cette vie chrétienne en montagnes russes, ce livre a été écrit pour vous. L'auteure décrit des années de frustration et le moment où elle a commencé à poser des questions.

sections.h2: Pour les nouveaux croyants et ceux qui reviennent à la foi
paras: Le chapitre deux traite de la nouvelle naissance et le chapitre trois de ce qui change quand on comprend que la relation avec le Père repose sur des principes spirituels.

sections.h2: Pour les groupes de maison et les leaders d'église
paras: Quinze chapitres, chacun avec ses versets en tête, se prêtent bien à une lecture à raison d'un chapitre par rencontre.

sections.h2: Pour les lecteurs francophones qui cherchent un livre écrit en français
paras: Le livre est écrit en français et cite des versions bibliques françaises. Les citations tirées de versions anglaises sans équivalent français sont traduites littéralement et signalées.

stories.h2: Les montagnes russes de la performance
paras: Dans l'introduction, l'auteure explique qu'elle mélangeait ses propres performances et ce que Dieu avait accompli, et qu'elle se retrouvait "sur un tapis roulant", frustrée de ne jamais arriver à destination. Elle écrit que cette distorsion affecte la façon dont nous entendons Dieu.

L'introduction raconte une vision : quelqu'un a volé un tableau célèbre et peint par-dessus une fausse image. Chaque révélation reçue retire un morceau de la fausse peinture, et l'image dessous devient la plus étonnante de l'Évangile et de Dieu.

Au chapitre douze, l'auteure raconte qu'après un voyage missionnaire en Colombie, Dieu l'a convaincue d'y retourner. Elle ne parlait pas espagnol. Elle a obtenu son diplôme en mai, acheté son billet pour août, et à son arrivée on lui a demandé d'animer une étude biblique. Chaque leçon s'est centrée sur l'identité en Christ. Un pasteur l'a invitée dans son église, puis quatre pasteurs sont venus à l'étude, puis huit. Elle a alors compris :
“je n’étais pas la seule à traverser une crise identitaire !”

author.bio: Suzan Cartagena est diplômée du Charis Bible College à Colorado Springs, aux États-Unis, depuis 2006. En 2007, elle a épousé un camarade de classe, et le couple a développé un programme intitulé Christians Seeking Identity (Chrétiens en quête d'identité), né de leurs propres parcours pour trouver leur valeur et leur acceptation auprès de Dieu. Leur vision est d'équiper ceux qui équipent les autres : ils voyagent à travers le monde pour présenter des séminaires sur l'identité en Christ à des pasteurs, des responsables d'église et des étudiants d'écoles bibliques.

publisher.about: Spirit Media Publishing est une maison d'édition et de marketing chrétienne dont la vision est de révéler le cœur de notre Père à toutes les nations. Elle propose la création et la publication de livres en format broché, relié, numérique et audio, des livres pour enfants, des Express Books compacts, la création de sites web et le référencement, ainsi que la production de podcasts et de vidéos. Nous sommes heureux de publier un livre en français sur la grâce.

why.title: Pourquoi ce livre existe
paras: L'introduction explique que le livre répond à des questions que l'auteure s'est posées quand elle est revenue aux racines de sa foi :
“Pourquoi est-ce que je crois ce que je crois—en commençant par la grâce ?”

Comment la grâce est-elle liée au Saint-Esprit, comment frustrer la grâce, que veut dire être déchu de la grâce : chaque chapitre reprend l'une de ces questions. Le dernier se termine sur la promesse de 2 Corinthiens 12:9 :
“Ma grâce est suffisante pour toi”

faq.q: De quoi parle La Connexion à Dieu ?
faq.a: C'est un livre de 178 pages et de quinze chapitres qui explique, avec la Bible, ce que l'auteure appelle la grâce, notre connexion à Dieu, et comment une compréhension déformée de la grâce l'a tenue captive pendant cinquante ans.

faq.q: « Cinquante ans de captivité » veut-il dire que l'auteure a été en prison ?
faq.a: Non. Dans le livre, la captivité est celle d'une définition courante de la grâce, "tu ne le mérites pas, mais Dieu est bon envers toi", dont la première moitié dominait toujours ses pensées, et d'une vie chrétienne fondée sur la performance.

faq.q: Le livre parle-t-il d'une crise de foi ?
faq.a: Oui. L'auteure écrit qu'elle était si frustrée dans sa marche chrétienne qu'elle en était venue à penser que le concept de Dieu était un mensonge, ou que quelque chose n'allait pas dans ce qu'elle croyait. Elle est alors revenue aux racines de ses croyances, en commençant par la grâce. Au chapitre douze, elle parle aussi d'une crise d'identité qu'elle a découverte chez beaucoup de pasteurs.

faq.q: Que dit le livre du Saint-Esprit ?
faq.a: Beaucoup. Trois chapitres lui sont consacrés. Ce sont, dans l'ordre : L'impulsion du Saint-Esprit ; Attrister le Saint-Esprit ; et Blasphémer contre le Saint-Esprit. L'auteure y explique comment la grâce est liée au Saint-Esprit et comment il nous révèle les réalités du royaume de Dieu.

faq.q: Que dit-il du péché impardonnable ?
faq.a: Le chapitre neuf part des appels de chrétiens tourmentés que l'auteure recevait à l'école biblique, persuadés d'avoir commis le "péché impardonnable". Elle lit Marc 3 et écrit qu'en aucun cas Dieu ne refuse de nous pardonner : le problème est que nous annulons ce qu'il fait pour nous en répétant des mensonges opposés à ce qu'il dit.

faq.q: Que signifie naître de nouveau, selon le livre ?
faq.a: C'est le sujet du chapitre deux, Vous devez naître de nouveau. L'auteure écrit qu'on ne peut pas discerner les choses spirituelles avec la seule pensée naturelle, et que la nouvelle naissance rétablit notre connexion avec Dieu.

faq.q: Le livre parle-t-il du cep et des sarments ?
faq.a: Oui. Le chapitre quatre, Le cep et ses sarments, lit Jean 15 : Jésus est le cep, nous sommes les sarments, et il est la source de tout ce dont nous avons besoin. L'auteure raconte qu'elle lisait autrefois ce texte comme une menace d'émondage douloureux.

faq.q: Parle-t-il de l'identité en Christ ?
faq.a: Oui. L'auteure écrit qu'une distorsion de la grâce déforme notre identité spirituelle, et ses leçons à Bogota étaient toutes centrées sur notre identité en Christ. Elle et son mari présentent aujourd'hui des séminaires sur ce thème.

content_note.title: Note sur le contenu
paras: Le livre propose des lectures personnelles de certains textes bibliques, par exemple de l'arbre de la connaissance du bien et du mal. L'auteure écrit : "Je ne crois pas qu’ils aient physiquement mangé un fruit défendu." Il s'adresse à des lecteurs prêts à examiner ces lectures avec leur Bible ouverte, et non à des lecteurs qui cherchent une introduction neutre à toutes les traditions.

hero.audience_line: For readers of short, true Christian testimonies, for anyone who fishes or boats, and for people worn down by life's storms who wonder whether they still matter.
hero.tagline: Fifteen miles out on the Chesapeake Bay in 1989, every new nail broke. Kenneth Pullin tells how an old, pitted nail he had kicked off a dock that morning brought two young men home, and what it taught him about grace.

audience.headline: A true story of one summer day on the Chesapeake Bay, a storm, and the rusted nail that held.
audience.body: For readers of short Christian testimonies, true survival stories and anyone who has been through a storm that changed them. In the summer of 1989 Kenneth Pullin was twenty-eight, a husband and a new father. He and a friend borrowed a fourteen-foot Boston Whaler for a day of fishing. Fifteen miles out, a storm came down, the shear pin snapped, and every nail they had broke, one by one. Then he remembered an old, pitted nail he had seen no use for that morning. A note on subjects: the storm is told in physical detail, including the fear of drowning and his thoughts of his baby girl at home, and the author says the friend who shared the storm has since died. It is written for a general adult audience.

quote.text: “grace isn’t fragile, and God’s hands don’t slip.”
quote.cite: The Pitted Nail, Back to Shore

what_makes.title: What makes this book for readers who want a short, true story of grace
paras: Most survival stories are long. This one is short, told in four parts, and keeps its eyes on God.
Five things set it apart:
list: It is a true account, in the author's own voice. The author says it is the story of what he lived through in 1989, and that he is now "the only one left to tell it like it was."

The small object carries the meaning. The rusted nail he kicked along a dock that morning turns out to be the thing that gets the boat home, and the book asks what that says about people who have been through storms and come out changed.
It opens each part with Scripture. Psalm 46:10, Proverbs 3:5, Psalm 107:29 and Mark 4:40 begin the four parts, each with a one-line thought.
It starts with a childhood. Before the storm, the author describes a Virginia boyhood, Christian parents, Sunday dinners and hours of fishing on a lake.
It is honest about fear and about prayer. He says he made deals with God, felt he had no right to pray, and prayed anyway.

sections.h2: For readers who enjoy short Christian testimonies
paras: At 53 pages, it can be read in an afternoon. It tells one event well and then asks what it means.

sections.h2: For people who fish, boat or spend time on the water
paras: The author knows boats and bays. He describes the fog, the docks, the shear pin, the gas can and the river that brought them home in terms an angler will recognize.

sections.h2: For anyone who feels worn down by life
paras: The dedication is written for people who, like the nail, have been "weatherbeaten" by the trials of life. The final pages say that they, too, can hold when everything else fails.

sections.h2: For men's groups and mentors
paras: The book is a clean starting point for a talk about warnings ignored, honest prayer and the quiet kind of faith the author saw in his parents. Each of the four parts opens with a verse and a one-line thought to discuss.

details.Title: The Pitted Nail
details.Subtitle: My Rescue, God's Grace
details.Author: Kenneth Pullin
details.Binding: Paperback (perfect bound)

paras: Walking down an old dock in the fog, the author notices an old galvanized nail shaped like an L. He kicks it toward the water. It bounces down the boards, skips off the dock and drops into the drain well at the back of the boat. His friend buys a handful of new nails at the marina as stand-ins for shear pins.

One nail after another gives way. After the last new nail breaks, the author thinks of his baby girl at home and of his parents, and he realizes there is no way they can survive if the waves overtake the boat. He prays between his thoughts, even though he feels he has no right to.
He bails water from the drain well and sees the old nail wedged in the hole, battered and rust-streaked:
“That nail, the one that shouldn’t have been on board, was now our lifeline.”

They set it in place and the motor catches. He yells for his friend not to touch the throttle. The boat crawls home through the rain toward the Rappahannock River, the gas can nearly empty. Back on the dock, after a long silence, his friend finally says the nail is going in a frame.

author.bio: Kenneth Pullin is a lifelong resident of Mechanicsville, Virginia, and an account manager. He is a husband, the father of six and the grandfather of twelve. Inspired by his walk with God, he writes to share the grace and goodness of the Lord through heartfelt stories, and he is also the author of two children's books. In The Pitted Nail he tells of growing up in Virginia with Christian parents, Sunday dinners and long hours fishing on a lake.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The dedication says the book is for everyone who, like the pitted nail, has been through storms that changed their appearance and reshaped who they once were. It explains why the old nail held when the new ones broke:
“the tougher it gets the stronger you become,”

He also writes that only he and his friend will ever know what it was like out on that water, and that he is now "the only one left to tell it like it was." The acknowledgements add that a donation will be made, in lieu of sales, to Tunnel to Towers and the Wounded Warriors project.

faq.q: What is The Pitted Nail about?
faq.a: It is Kenneth Pullin's true account of a 1989 storm on the Chesapeake Bay, when a borrowed fourteen-foot Boston Whaler kept losing its shear pin fifteen miles out, and an old pitted nail became the last hope.

faq.q: Is it a story of divine intervention?
faq.a: The author tells it as a story of God's grace. The subtitle is My Rescue, God's Grace, each part begins with Scripture, and he writes that the nail carried two young men fifteen miles through the storm by the grace of God. He compares it to the three nails that held Jesus to the cross.

faq.q: Is it a true story of survival at sea?
faq.a: Yes. The author lived it at twenty-eight, with a friend, a small boat and a single can of gas. They had no cell phones and no flare, and no other boats were in sight. They were never lost: his friend knew every creek on the way home.

faq.q: Does it speak to faith over fear?
faq.a: Yes. The last part opens with Mark 4:40, "Why are you so afraid? Do you still have no faith?", and the line that peace does not mean calm seas but trusting the One who calms them. The author is honest that in the storm he felt fear like he had never known.

faq.q: Is it an answered-prayer story?
faq.a: Yes. He prayed in the storm even though part of him felt he had no right to, and he made deals with God. When the nail held, he whispered, Lord, please let it last another mile. He says that when he reached the dock he knelt and thanked God they were home.

faq.q: Where does the story take place?
faq.a: On the Chesapeake Bay in Virginia, in a fourteen-foot Boston Whaler borrowed from his friend's father. The storm drifted north while they turned west toward the Rappahannock River and the creek where the day had begun.

faq.q: Is it a good book for someone who fishes?
faq.a: It is a fishing story at heart. It starts with a boyhood spent fishing on a lake and a Saturday fishing trip on the Bay, and the author describes the fog, the docks, the shear pin and the gas can in terms an angler will recognize.

faq.q: Is it encouraging for someone going through a hard time?
faq.a: That is its purpose. The closing pages speak to people who think life's storms have left them too damaged to matter, and answer that the pitted nail was bent and worn and, in God's hands, still did its job. Be that nail, the author writes.

content_note.title: Content note
paras: The storm is described in physical detail: the boat taking on water, the fear of drowning, and the author's thoughts of his young daughter at home. The author also says a friend who shared the storm has since died. The book is written for a general adult audience.

sections.h2: For sports fans who want the story behind the jersey
paras: If you love basketball memoir, this is the view from inside Coach Wooden's program. John was named captain of a UCLA team the press wrote off as "The Team Without," after key players left for the NBA. He writes about the Bruins' routines, Wooden's lessons, teammates such as Kareem, and the road from Orange Coast College to Westwood. It ends with his induction into the UCLA Hall of Fame.

sections.h2: For families walking through childhood cancer
paras: His daughter was nine when she was diagnosed and twelve when she died. John writes about the treatments, the hospital, the wig that floated off in a hotel pool, and her determination to go to a Father and Daughter Valentine's Dance. It is told as one father's testimony, not a manual. If you are in that hospital hallway now, you will find company in these pages, and you should also know it does not hide how much it hurts.

sections.h2: For survivors, and anyone fighting a battle they did not choose
paras: John fought Non-Hodgkin's Lymphoma twice, and the book carries you through the diagnosis, the transplant and the rematch. Along the way he fought a long lawsuit against a bank with only a small legal team beside him. Whatever your battle is, the question he keeps returning to is the same: what does it mean to have done your best?

sections.h2: For coaches, leaders and anyone who learned from a mentor
paras: In Chapter 4, Coach Wooden hands his new players a sheet with a giant triangle on it: the Pyramid of Success, fifteen blocks that work together. He tells them the foundation begins with Industriousness, and that there is no substitute for work. John hangs the hand-out in his locker and comes back to Coach's teaching for the rest of his life, through his daughter's illness, a lawsuit and his own cancer, all the way to his Hall of Fame speech. If you lead a team or teach young people, you will see how one teacher's lessons outlast the game.

audience.headline: A boy too small and too slow. A dream of UCLA. Then the fight of his life.
audience.body: For anyone who loves an underdog story, and for anyone facing a battle they did not choose. John Vallely was undersized, overlooked and told he was too slow, and he still played for Coach John Wooden at UCLA and in the NBA. Then he faced a daughter's cancer, a courtroom, and his own lymphoma, and he turned to what Coach Wooden taught him.

quote.text: Success is a peace of mind which is a direct result of self-satisfaction in knowing you did your best to become the best that you were capable of becoming.
quote.cite: The Pyramid Principle, Coach John Wooden's definition of success as printed in Chapter 4

what_makes.title: What makes this book for readers who need hope in a hard season
paras: A basketball memoir that does not stay on the court. The Pyramid Principle is the true story of John Vallely, a former UCLA basketball player, NBA first-round pick and Houston Rocket. It moves from a boy shooting in an alley to the hardest opponents of his life.
Five things set it apart:
list: It starts in a stem cell transplant room. The book opens at Houston's MD Anderson Cancer Center, where a pint of stem cells flown in from Germany drips into his bloodstream while his blood count stands at zero, then goes back to the beginning to show how he got there.

It is built on a teacher's wisdom. John calls Coach John Wooden the greatest teacher of his time, and the book returns to Wooden's Pyramid of Success, with a quotation from Wooden opening several chapters.

It tells the loss honestly. His daughter was diagnosed with cancer at nine and the family lost her at twelve. John writes that the earthly pain of loss is as great as ever, and he writes of the comfort of heaven in the same pages.
It refuses a shallow idea of winning. Success, he says in his Hall of Fame speech, is not wealth, power or position as the world defines it, but the peace of mind of knowing you did your best.
It is a family story. After the loss of his daughter, his son told him, "Dad, we are still a family," and the book is dedicated to that son.

stories.h2: The boy who was too slow
paras: At Corona del Mar High School John was 5 feet 3 inches and 104 pounds, undersized even for a guard. Years of shooting in the alley made him a great shooter, and he grew six inches in his sophomore year. By his senior year he was 6 feet 2 inches and leading his team in scoring. His own mom, he says, told him he was too slow. A letter of interest from UCLA, signed by Coach Wooden, then arrived, with a catch: he needed a 3.0 GPA, and his was 2.9. The young woman who would become his wife helped him study and told him, "You can do this, John."

stories.h2: Nine hundred people for one little girl
paras: After his daughter died, nine hundred people came to her memorial service at Saint Andrews Presbyterian Church in Newport Beach: nurses, doctors, teachers, friends and children from the community. John knew he had to speak and did not know if he could hold it together. He writes that as nine hundred of her friends and their families sang Amazing Grace together, "It was like heaven came down to that Newport Beach Church." Years later, the family joined the "Dribble for Victory Over Cancer" event, where his daughter was the honorary captain and every athlete pinned the name of someone they loved to their shirt.

stories.h2: A fight in a downtown tower
paras: John's legal case against a bank was, in his words, "going uphill and sideways." He found a one-man law office in Costa Mesa and a lawyer who greeted him with, "I was a big fan of your days at UCLA." The chapter is named for the question Coach Wooden asked: "Are you right?"

author.bio: John Vallely grew up on Balboa Island in Newport Beach, California. Undersized at Corona del Mar High School, he began his college career at Orange Coast College before playing basketball for Coach John Wooden at UCLA. He went on to the NBA as a first-round pick and a Houston Rocket, and is a UCLA Hall of Famer. He has battled Non-Hodgkin's Lymphoma twice. The book was written with Paul Weissenstein.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: John writes that while he lay in that transplant room, in despair, he needed a way to hold on to hope in the face of uncertainty. "As I wrestled to find God's strength for my weakness in this battle, my only recourse was to turn to the same source of guidance and wisdom I have used for every critical struggle in my own life: the words and teachings of John Wooden, my UCLA basketball coach and a man I consider the greatest teacher of his time."

So the book is a record of what he learned and where it led. In the final chapter he writes, "I know in my head and from my experience that heaven is real," and "I still struggle and question. I'm still learning and growing." It is honest about faith in the way the best testimonies are: no tidy answers, only a man still choosing joy each day.

faq.q: What is The Pyramid Principle about?
faq.a: The true story of John Vallely, a former UCLA basketball player and NBA first-round pick, and how he drew on Coach John Wooden's teaching to face his daughter's cancer, a courtroom battle and his own lymphoma.

faq.q: Is it a basketball memoir?
faq.a: It starts there. The book follows him from a small boy shooting in an alley to playing for Coach Wooden at UCLA and in the NBA, then moves past the court to loss and illness.

faq.q: Is it an underdog story?
faq.a: Yes. John was undersized, a junior college player who was overlooked and still picked to start for Coach Wooden, and later he took on a bank with a small legal team.

faq.q: Is it the same as Minto's The Pyramid Principle?
faq.a: No. That is a different book on business writing. This is a sports memoir named for Coach Wooden's Pyramid of Success.

faq.q: Does the book describe a stem cell transplant?
faq.a: Yes. It opens in the transplant room at MD Anderson Cancer Center and returns to the treatment later as John's lymphoma comes back.

faq.q: Does it talk about heaven?
faq.a: Yes. The final chapter, "Faith," is John's personal testimony about heaven, grief and joy.

faq.q: What leadership lessons does it take from Coach Wooden?
faq.a: The book is built on Coach Wooden's Pyramid of Success, fifteen blocks that he taught work together to add up to success. They are, in order from the foundation up: Industriousness; Friendship; Loyalty; Cooperation; Enthusiasm; Self-Control; Alertness; Initiative; Intentness; Condition; Skill; Team Spirit; Confidence; Poise; and Competitive Greatness. John shows how each one carried him off the court.

faq.q: Is it a good book for a Christian athlete?
faq.a: It is a faith memoir by a former college and NBA player. It shows a believer carrying Coach Wooden's teaching and his trust in God through loss and illness.

faq.q: Who is it for?
faq.a: Sports fans, families walking through childhood cancer, cancer survivors, and anyone who has leaned on a mentor's wisdom in a hard season.

sections.h2: For believers who want to understand prophetic gifts
paras: If you have wondered what the Bible means by a seer, Chapter 2 gives a plain definition and a list. The author writes that the gift cannot be earned by study. It is given by the Holy Spirit. The same chapter lists the marks of the gift and says the Holy Spirit helps a seer interpret and pass on what is received.

sections.h2: For readers drawn to true accounts of angels and demons
paras: The Angel of Death in his mother's room, a spirit who visits him after his cousin's death, small demons that hold him down, thousands of angels lining a road in Iraq: the accounts are direct, and the author does not decorate them. Chapter 10 states its position without hedging. He writes that demons are real and warns readers about the occult goods now sold as toys. You do not need to agree with every claim to see what he believes and why.

sections.h2: For parents who have prayed for a wandering child
paras: His mother appears on almost every page of the early chapters. She prays in the night, tells him Bible stories at bedtime, and keeps praying through his reckless years. He writes that her prayers were "the invisible architecture that preserved my life." A parent who is waiting for a child to come back will find company here.

sections.h2: For soldiers, veterans and families who have waited at home
paras: Chapters 5 and 6 follow the author through basic training and a deployment to a war zone where improvised explosive devices were buried in roads. He writes about fear, about praying for each member of his unit by name, and about asking God for protection. Not every reader will share his view of what protected his unit, and the book offers it as his own account.

audience.headline: The son of a prophetess tells what he saw of angels, demons and the living God.
audience.body: For believers who want to understand prophetic gifts and spiritual warfare, for readers drawn to first-person accounts of the unseen, and for parents who have prayed through the night for a wandering child. Frank Theurer II writes in twelve chapters, most dated by year and age, about a Chicago childhood, years in the U.S. Army, a deployment to Iraq, visions and dreams, and a prologue that ends before the throne of God. A note on subjects: this is one man's account of his own experiences, written from a Christian faith that believes God still speaks in dreams and visions. It describes spiritual warfare, demons, hell, war and violent deaths of people he knew, told without graphic detail. Chapter 7 states that it is a prophetic vision and not an account of events that physically occurred. It is a testimony and a teaching on the gift of a seer, not medical or mental health advice. If you are troubled by what you read, please speak with a pastor or a licensed professional.

what_makes.title: What makes this book for readers who want a first-person account of the unseen
paras: It does not argue from a distance. A man who says he has seen angels, demons and Christ tells what happened, when, and what it cost. Then he explains what a seer is and what the Bible says about the gift.
Five things set it apart:
list: It is a family inheritance story. The book begins with his mother, a prophetess, who wakes in Chicago in 1987 to a figure at the foot of her bed and cries out in the name of Jesus.

It teaches as well as tells. Chapter 2 explains the biblical role of the seer, names Samuel, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Elijah, Ezekiel and Daniel, and lists three marks of the gift: spiritual sensitivity, discernment of spirits, and visions and dreams.
It is dated. Most sections carry the year and his age, from 1990 at age five to 2014 at age twenty-nine, so a reader can follow how the gift grew.
It goes to war. Two chapters follow his enlistment and his deployment to Iraq, and a third tells of a prophetic vision of the soldiers around him.
It ends with a call. The last pages are a plain invitation to believe the Gospel and "come to Jesus while there is still time."
