paras: Chapter 1 begins before he can remember. His mother and her two-year-old son are asleep in the same bed. Cold hands tap her leg. A tall figure stands at the foot of the bed and raises one arm to beckon her. She cries out to God in the name of Jesus to save her life and her child's, and the figure is gone. In her heart she understands that she met the Angel of Death and was rescued by the One who "holds the keys to Death and Hell." From that night, the book says, her life was lived entirely for Christ.

Later in the same chapter, a small boy waiting for a Chicago bus asks his mother whether he can ask God for anything. She says yes, according to His will. He kneels on the sidewalk and prays, "I asked God to show me an eagle." An eagle appears over the skyline and circles overhead "as if responding to my prayer." His mother smiles. The chapter says his sight was beginning to awaken.

In Chapter 6, a young soldier deployed to Iraq prays for each member of his unit by name. One night he asks God to send angels, and he hears a question, how many? He answers with one word, legions, and asks that they guard the unit whenever it leaves the base. From then on, he writes, he saw angels standing along both sides of every road, "like an honor guard stretching into infinity." He also writes that no soldier in his unit was killed or seriously injured on missions outside the gates, and that bombs were found before they could go off.

author.bio: Frank Theurer II grew up in Chicago in a home where faith was both whispered and thundered. His mother was a prophetess who prayed through the night, raised him on the stories of Scripture and interceded for him through his rebellious youth, and his father read the Bible with tears in his eyes. He served in the U.S. Army, including a deployment to Iraq. He describes himself as a seer, shaped more by dreams, visions and encounters with God than by textbooks. He writes and speaks to glorify Christ through the testimony of transformation and to awaken others to the reality of the Kingdom.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The author answers in the last lines of the prologue. After describing an encounter before the throne, he writes: "This is why I write. This is why I speak. Not to entertain, not to impress, but to declare: God is real, His eyes are upon us, and His call is urgent."

He also gives a sentence of purpose at the start of the book: "I exist to glorify Christ through the testimony of transformation." And in the closing pages he leaves the reader with a charge: "Believe the Gospel. Trust in Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins."

faq.q: What is The Seer's Journey about?
faq.a: It is Frank Theurer II's first-person account of growing up the son of a prophetess, his encounters with angels and demons, his years as a soldier, visions and dreams, and a prologue encounter before the throne of God. It also teaches what the Bible says about the seer.

faq.q: Does the book describe angels and demons?
faq.a: Yes. Angels line the roads in Chapter 6, demons attack in Chapter 4, Chapter 9 describes visions of hell, and Chapter 10 is a direct teaching on the unseen world. Both run through the whole book.

faq.q: Is it a book that says demons are real?
faq.a: It does, plainly. Chapter 10 opens with these words: "Let me state this clearly and without equivocation: Demons are real." The chapter goes on to warn about the occult and says that "The Devil requires permission to take over a human life." The closing pages urge the reader to put on the full armor of God daily.

faq.q: What does the book say a seer is?
faq.a: A person given the gift of prophecy by God. Chapter 2 traces the role through Samuel, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Elijah, Ezekiel and Daniel and gives three marks: spiritual sensitivity, discernment, and visions and dreams. The author adds that the gift is not earned by study.

faq.q: Does it talk about prophetic dreams?
faq.a: Yes. Visions and dreams are one of the three marks of the gift. The book describes dreams and visions from his childhood on and presents them as ways God gives insight, warning and comfort.

faq.q: What does the book say about the gift of discernment?
faq.a: Discernment is the second mark of the seer. Chapter 6 says that in a combat zone he received the ability to perceive the hearts and intentions of the people around him, and calls it a gift that "proved invaluable." Chapter 7 is presented as a vision about the people around him.

faq.q: Is the book about a prophetic gift passed from mother to son?
faq.a: Yes. Chapter 3 says, "The gift I had inherited from my mother, the mantle of seeing that had been passed down through her night of deliverance from the Angel of Death, was now manifesting in my own life." The book presents the prophetic gift as something that passed from her to him.

faq.q: Is it a Christian book?
faq.a: Yes. Scripture runs through it, quoted from the New International Version. The last chapter ends in prayer, and the author's stated aim is to declare that God is real.

sections.h2: For anyone living with chronic illness
paras: If you have been told to expect less, you may recognize a voice here. The author spent thirty years trying to outrun a prognosis, and then could not. She does not claim to have found a cure. She writes about what it was like to lose her independence, and about small things that helped: a class, a letter, a brother who called every day.

sections.h2: For caregivers, family and friends
paras: The book shows what it looks like from the bed. Her husband runs the household, her mother-in-law drives her to appointments for over a year, and her brother calls almost every day. If you are caring for someone who is sick, you will see what their small improvements cost and what an ordinary compliment can mean.

sections.h2: For nurses, teachers and veterans
paras: Her working life runs through the book. She writes about the pediatric ward, and about taking a bottle to a baby who needed feeding and using those twenty minutes to cry quietly after losing a young patient. She writes about the classroom and the years of teaching German. She writes about basic training, the language school and a veterans' hospital program.

sections.h2: For believers who want to hold on to God when answers are slow
paras: The book is open about prayer and about what faith did and did not do. She asks God to let her live, and she says that once she accepted the outcome was no longer hers to decide, a burden lifted. She does not say God healed her on request. She writes that she almost feels He walked beside her her whole life, and she leaves the reader to weigh that.

audience.headline: A pediatric nurse, math teacher and Army linguist tells how she kept going through a lifetime of illness, and where God was in it.
audience.body: For anyone living with chronic illness, for the caregivers and family who walk beside them, and for believers who want to hold on to God when the answers come slowly. Susan Mahon writes in four short chapters about a frugal family of seven children, a nursing career that began at twenty, Army training as a German linguist during the Cold War, a diagnosis she put on a shelf, and the long stretch when illness left her bedridden. A note on subjects: this is a personal memoir about serious chronic illness. It describes childhood sickness, hospital work with very sick children and the death of a young patient, years of pain, a long period in bed, depression, and a time when the author believed she was dying. It is told honestly and without graphic detail, and it contains one use of strong language near the end. It is not medical advice. If you are living with illness, please talk with your physician or another qualified health professional, and if you are in crisis or thinking about harming yourself, contact your local emergency services or a crisis line right away.

what_makes.title: What makes this book for people living with chronic illness
paras: This is a testimony, not a treatment plan. The author is blunt about that in the pages before chapter one, and then she tells what happened. She was a tough, stubborn girl who kept going, and she was sicker than she knew.
Five things set it apart:
list: It says what faith is not. A statement at the front says healing does not follow a formula, that faith does not guarantee a result, and that "God's work in our lives is personal, sovereign, and often mysterious."
It starts small. A pharmacist tells a seventeen-year-old cashier, "When you get sick, you're down for the count!" and she wonders for the first time whether being sick all the time is normal.
It comes from real work. She was a pediatric registered nurse at twenty, a math teacher, an Army German linguist during the Cold War, and a high school teacher for twenty years.
It tells the hardest years. A year and a half in bed, a scooter for almost six years, classes through a veterans' health program, and small steps that finally added up.

It ends with tributes and plain explanations. Former students and colleagues write short pieces about her, and a closing list, 35 Terms and Conditions of My Body, explains the author's diagnoses in everyday words.

details.Title: Too Stubborn to Die
details.Subtitle: Living Fully with Chronic Illness, Unbreakable Resolve, and Unshakeable Faith
details.Author: Susan Mahon
details.Binding: Paperback (perfect bound, matte laminate), black and white interior

paras: In Chapter 2, a classmate at the Defense Language Institute asks what is wrong with her eyes. A tear test and lip biopsy follow, and months later a physician tells her she has Sjögren's syndrome and that she will be "in a wheelchair, disabled and dead by fifty." She is twenty-nine, fit, and in the best shape of her life. She writes, "I decided to put the diagnosis on a shelf, high up and out of sight." Another diagnosis, rheumatoid arthritis, goes onto the same shelf.

Chapter 4 opens with the hardest stretch. She spends a year and a half in bed, cannot read or drive for a year, and is told there is too much organ damage for more to be done. She writes that she resigned herself to dying, bought a dress for her casket and spoke with her family. Then she prayed and asked God, if He would allow her to live, to let her spend her life helping others become healthy. "I felt a burden lift. Hope returned. So did strength."

At a veterans' program she takes a class for people with chronic pain and depression. One assignment is to write a letter consoling a friend who is going through what she is going through. She writes, and tears run down her face. "The compassion I had for this imaginary friend was the compassion I realized I needed for myself." A year later an instructor says, "You must be feeling better now." She frowns. He says, "You're wearing makeup. And you fixed your hair."

author.bio: Susan Mahon grew up in Arizona, one of seven children in a close, frugal family whose motto was "The Mahons stick together." She graduated from nursing school in 1975 and began her career as a pediatric registered nurse at age twenty. She later taught math and religion and coached volleyball at a Catholic middle school, then joined the U.S. Army and trained as a German linguist during the Cold War. She went on to teach for twenty years at Springstead High School in Spring Hill, Florida.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The author says it plainly at the front of the book: "This book began as a personal testimony written for my loved ones, a record of God's faithfulness during my journey through various medical illnesses."

She did not plan to publish it. "Friends who walked alongside me encouraged me to share it more broadly, in the hope that others facing illness might find comfort, perspective, and faith along their own journey." In her closing she names what she hopes readers will carry away: "I would like anyone struggling with health issues, mobility issues, or negative changes in these areas to have hope that things can improve in many situations."

faq.q: What is Too Stubborn to Die about?
faq.a: It is Susan Mahon's personal testimony of God's faithfulness through years of illness, from a childhood of repeated sickness to a career as a pediatric nurse, math teacher and Army German linguist, and a long period when illness left her bedridden. It is told in four chapters with a closing, tributes and two reference sections.

faq.q: Is it a book about autoimmune disease?
faq.a: In part. The author lives with several autoimmune conditions, and by one count in the book had "twenty-six diagnosed autoimmune diseases." They appear in the story and in the closing list of 35 conditions. It is a faith memoir by someone who lives with them, not a medical guide, and it says so: "This book is not intended as medical advice."

faq.q: Does it talk about rheumatoid arthritis?
faq.a: Yes, briefly. In Chapter 2 she describes knee pain she first blamed on running in military boots, and then writes that she was developing rheumatoid arthritis, which means her immune system was attacking healthy tissue. It also appears as term 29 in the closing list. It is one condition among many, and the book is about the whole story and not this diagnosis.

faq.q: Does it talk about Sjögren's syndrome?
faq.a: Yes. Sjögren's was her first diagnosis, given at the Defense Language Institute when she was twenty-nine. The book explains that it is an autoimmune disease in which glands do not produce moisture, and that for her it affected much more than dry eyes and mouth. Most of the other conditions in her closing list are described as related to it.

faq.q: Is it a personal memoir or a how-to?
faq.a: It is a personal memoir. It includes a few pages on lifestyle ideas she drew from a veterans' program and from Blue Zone research, but the notice at the front says medical treatment decisions should never be made solely on personal stories or spiritual testimony. Readers are told to consult qualified professionals.

faq.q: Is it a book of hope and healing?
faq.a: It is a book of hope. The statement at the front says she does not believe healing follows a formula or that faith guarantees a specific outcome, and the Closing says things can improve in many situations. It does not offer a cure or a guarantee.

faq.q: Who is the book for?
faq.a: Anyone living with chronic illness, the caregivers and family who walk alongside them, and believers who want to hold on to God when the answers are slow in coming. Nurses, teachers and veterans may recognize their own work in it.

sections.h2: For readers who want to understand the human cost of caste
paras: This is a novel, not a textbook, but it opens a window. The founder of Son-Shine, who wrote the foreword, asks you not to read it "as you would read another book, but to read it as you would a life." If you want the weight of discrimination and poverty explained through one child's days rather than statistics, this is where the story begins.

sections.h2: For readers who love stories of faith, rescue and hope against all odds
paras: The book follows a refuge that grew from "the humblest of beginnings," a veranda against a mud house, to a school with caregivers, a cook and a permanent water supply. Along the way it shows opposition, shortage and fear. If you are drawn to true-to-life stories of compassion that keeps going when the odds say stop, this is one.

sections.h2: For readers of Christian and world fiction set in India
paras: If you enjoy novels that take you somewhere you have never been, here is rural Andhra Pradesh, a village's edge, a mud house and an orphanage. The book is classed with Christian and world fiction and is written for adults.

sections.h2: For readers who love a coming-of-age story
paras: Naggya is five when the book begins and a teenager when his mentor first shows him ballet on a screen. In between are hunger, fear, an aunt who does not know how to raise him, school and friendship. If you like to watch a child grow up on the page, from running for his life to wondering how dancers can be so strong, the novel gives you the whole arc, and the title tells you where it is heading.

audience.headline: At five years old, Naggya had already learned to run. This is the story of what he ran toward.
audience.body: A novel inspired by real events, set among the Dalits of India, the people at the bottom of the traditional caste hierarchy. Richard Convery follows a five-year-old orphan in rural Andhra Pradesh and a young man who builds a refuge and school for children no one else will take, in a story of cruelty and discrimination and of compassion that reaches one child at a time. A note on subjects: the novel is about poverty, discrimination and violence against children and their families, including the loss of a parent and a child left alone. These scenes are part of the story the author set out to tell and are written without being the whole of the book, which is also about rescue, school, friendship and hope. It is a work of fiction for adult readers and is not a history or a guide to caste.

what_makes.title: What makes this book for readers who want to see the human cost of caste
paras: A 478-page work of fiction that the author describes as "lifted directly from the life-and-death experiences" of the founder of Son-Shine, an orphanage and school in India that has rescued, housed and educated many thousands of Dalit children since 2006.
Five things set it apart:
list: It is told through a child. The story opens when Naggya is five, running with his mother toward the jungle, and follows him from fear and survival to school, friendship and a future he could not have imagined.
It is rooted in a real refuge. A foreword by the founder of Son-Shine calls the book "a window into the world of our Dalit children and people's lives."
It shows how a rescue begins. A young man who once preached revolutionary philosophies at university meets a homeless six-year-old and begins a refuge in his parents' mud house with one child.
It is faith-based. The refuge at the heart of the book is a Christian ministry, and the novel is shelved with Christian and world fiction, though it is a novel and not a devotional.
It has a surprising arc. The title says From Beatings To Broadway, and the book has ballet and New York theater scenes, which are left unspoiled here.

paras: Chapter One opens on a dawn chase. Naggya, who is five, urges his mother to run faster toward the jungle where his father, a drinker, will not find them. What follows costs him his mother, and the next pages follow a child alone: three days and three lonely nights of wandering, a search for water, and an effort to find his aunt, the only relative he has ever met. When he is most afraid, "he silently repeated his mother's words: 'Son, you must be strong!'"

In a chapter about the young man who will found the refuge, a university student who spent his days "spruiking the philosophies of Lenin or Marx or Mao" comes home for a visit and meets a homeless six-year-old. One thought changes him: "if my parents had died like so many others, this boy could so easily be me." The next lines say that "An indescribable glow filled Elijah," and that he returned home determined "to start a revolution, not to the masses, but merely to one." The refuge begins in his parents' two-room house.

Years later, Naggya is a teenager when his mentor shows him something on a screen: ballet. He watches the grace and strength of the dancers in amazement, and then asks, "But how, how do they do that? It looks so, they must be so strong!" It is a lighter scene, and it opens a door that leads to the other half of the book's title.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The author met the founder of Son-Shine in 2009. In the thirteen years since, he writes, he has "relied countless times" on him "for insight and understanding," as "a westerner from Australia" trying to shed light on the lives of Dalits. He is clear about what kind of book this is: "Although Untouchable is a work of fiction, much of the content of this novel has been lifted directly from the life-and-death experiences" of the founder's world.

The founder, in his own foreword, writes of why he welcomes it: "Through this book, may your eyes be open to see the other side of the world of the Untouchable Dalits." He adds, "May God speak to you through this book."

faq.q: What is Untouchable about?
faq.a: A novel inspired by real events: Naggya, a five-year-old Dalit orphan in rural India, flees a violent father and searches for survival while a young man builds a refuge and school for Dalit children.

faq.q: Is it a true story?
faq.a: It is a work of fiction inspired by real events, much of it drawn from the life-and-death experiences of the founder of Son-Shine, who wrote one of the book's forewords.

faq.q: Does it explain the caste system?
faq.a: It opens a window on India's Dalits, the people at the bottom of the traditional caste hierarchy, through a story, and the first pages define the traditional categories. It is a novel, not a history or a guide to caste.

faq.q: What does the title mean?
faq.a: The book's own definition says that those at the bottom of the traditional hierarchy are "considered 'untouchables' or Dalits." The title names the people the story is about.

faq.q: Is it a Christian book?
faq.a: It follows a faith-based refuge and is shelved with Christian and world fiction, but it is a novel and not labeled devotional.

faq.q: What does Broadway have to do with it?
faq.a: The subtitle From Beatings To Broadway reflects the boy's arc. The book includes ballet and New York theater scenes, and the path from one to the other is left unspoiled here.

faq.q: Does it deal with social injustice?
faq.a: Yes. Discrimination, poverty and unequal treatment of Dalit families run through the story, and so does the response of a young man who decides to take in one child at a time.

faq.q: Is it suitable for every reader?
faq.a: It is written for adults and includes violence against a child and a parent's death. If these themes are difficult for you, read the note on subjects above first.

audience.headline: God gives you a choice, and you answer with one word.
audience.body: For believers who want to hear God clearly and act on a single word from Him, pastors, church planters and ministry leaders who want God's direction for family, work and church, and readers who want to slow down and savor Scripture one word at a time. Kevin White starts in Deuteronomy 30, where God sets before His people a choice between life and death, prosperity and disaster, and builds ten chapters, from ONE to WORD, on the power of a single word. A note on subjects: the chapter on DISASTER speaks plainly about violence, including a news story of a fatal shooting and a suicide, and about suicide, gun violence and the toll of the pandemic. It is told without graphic detail. The book is a faith teaching from one pastor's experience, not counseling, medical advice or financial advice. If you or someone you know is thinking about suicide or self-harm, please contact local emergency services or a crisis line right away, and talk with a physician or licensed professional.

quote.text: Now listen! Today I am giving you a choice between life and death, between prosperity and disaster.
quote.cite: Deuteronomy 30:15, New Living Translation, quoted at the start of Chapter 1

what_makes.title: What makes this book for people who want to hear God's word for their life
paras: A book built on ten words, each chapter adding to the last, like colors on a paint-by-number canvas. The author is a pastor, church planter and missions leader who says one word from God rewrote his philosophy of ministry.
Five things set it apart:
list: It begins with a choice, and that choice is the frame for every chapter. "Choose life" is where Deuteronomy 30 leads, and the book comes back to it again and again.

It starts with the author's own word. On a flight home from India in 1998, after years of working sixty, eighty, even ninety hours a week, he committed to pursue God's presence every day. One word, PRESENCE, "rewrote my complete philosophy of ministry."
It teaches you to notice words in Scripture. "What's Your Word? will help you notice, appreciate, and activate single words."
It gives you ten words in order. ONE, DISASTER, PROSPERITY, COLLISION, VISION, VALUE, WHY, NOISE, EVERYONE and WORD, each chapter building on the one before.
It is for every setting. The author says you can use it "in your life, family, business, church, and nonprofit."

sections.h2: For believers who want to hear God clearly
paras: The author writes that God "has prepared a very specific word for your life." Using thousands of words and never hearing God speak one specific word over your life, he says, is a tragedy. He wants you to finish the book "comfortable asking God for His word for your life."

sections.h2: For pastors, church planters and ministry leaders
paras: The author had served as a pastor for ten years before his trip to India. He writes that "The expectation I put on myself to do great things for God nearly killed me," and he offers this book as what he learned afterward: take action on a single word from God, and let Him carry the momentum.

sections.h2: For readers who want to savor Scripture
paras: "I know from personal experience that it is possible to rush through God's word and miss the importance of single words." He asks you to slow down and taste, as he had to learn to do at the table: "Taste and see that the Lord is good."

sections.h2: For anyone choosing a path
paras: The book is also for people at a turning point in family, work, church or a nonprofit. The author says the book will show you "how to choose God's path of prosperity for your life," and that "You choose your path."

paras: Chapter 1 begins with a peppermint stick. When the author was in third grade, his teacher gave everyone one, and he asked for another. She took the one back, broke it in half and handed it to him. "Now you have two," she said. "I was disappointed because I knew I still had only ONE." The point, he says, is that in Deuteronomy 30 God gives His people one choice: "life or death." "You must pick ONE." And you answer with one word. "God isn't looking for a thick book back from you, a paragraph, or a sentence."

The introduction describes the author's first trip to India in 1998. He had been a pastor for ten years, a church planter who "knew all the church growth strategies," and his work week had grown to ninety hours. In India he saw churches in thatch roof huts "without bulletins, budgets, or Bibles" and "an undeniable sense of God's presence." On the plane home, "I committed to passionately pursue the presence of God every day for the rest of my life." God, he says, focused his attention on one word. "PRESENCE."

In the chapter on NOISE, the author tells how his first book came back with an unexpected invoice because the manuscript was 75,000 words and the package he had paid for allowed 50,000. Halfway through a book on clear messaging, he felt sick to his stomach. "In seven days, I trimmed the manuscript down from 75,000 words to 48,000 words." If it didn't help to clearly make his points, it had to go. "I eliminated the NOISE. The pit in my stomach was gone." His editor voided the invoice and agreed the book was so much better. He applies the lesson to listening to God: "Being bombarded with so many words that we can't hear even one single word from God for our lives is a contradiction."

author.bio: Kevin White has served in full-time Christian ministry as a pastor, entrepreneur and church planter and holds a degree in theology. He is the author of Audacious Generosity and Get to the Point, and in November 2021 he launched Spirit Media to reinvent Christian publishing.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The author's reason is in the introduction. "What's Your Word? will help you unleash the power of God in your life as you activate one single word at a time."

He wants you to leave able to ask for your own word. "When you finish reading the book, you'll understand the significance of asking the question, 'What's your word?' You'll be comfortable asking God for His word for your life."

faq.q: What is What's Your Word? about?
faq.a: A book by pastor and missions leader Kevin White on how one word from God can redirect a life. Ten one-word chapters, from ONE to WORD, begin at Deuteronomy 30 and teach readers to notice, ask for and act on their own word.

faq.q: What does choose life mean in this book?
faq.a: The book starts where God sets before His people a choice between life and death, prosperity and disaster, and asks them to choose life. The author writes that "We choose which path we take by which word we act on."

faq.q: What is the presence of God in this book?
faq.a: It is the author's own first word, from his 1998 trip to India. He writes that his word became PRESENCE and that he committed to pursue God's presence every day. The word is the book's opening story, and it connects to his earlier book, Get to the Point.

faq.q: Is it a book about prosperity?
faq.a: Two of the ten word chapters are DISASTER and PROSPERITY, framed by Deuteronomy 30. The author sets words that lead to disaster against words that lead to prosperity, and he says God pleads with us to choose life. It is not a study of prosperity in the Bible, and it does not promise wealth. He names what prosperity meant to him: "living on a budget, avoiding debt, having high quality relationships, saving and investing, or being outrageously generous."

faq.q: Is it about prayer for guidance?
faq.a: It teaches you to ask God for a word and to act on it, and the author writes that "God is responsible for the momentum" while "You are responsible to act on it." It is not a collection of prayers.

faq.q: Does it teach how to hear God's voice?
faq.a: In the sense that matters here: it teaches you to notice the single word God speaks over you and to take action on it. The book says "I encourage you to place the burden of identifying the word on God." It is not a technical manual on hearing God's voice.

faq.q: Is it about obeying God?
faq.a: Yes. The last chapter says you can choose your word and then "You choose whether to obey or not." Having knowledge of God's WORD without taking one single WORD from God, he writes, is "a contradiction to the very WORD of God."

faq.q: Who is it for?
faq.a: Every believer who wants to hear God clearly, whether or not they already ask God for a word each year, and readers in family, business, church and nonprofit life.

sections.h2: For Christians who sense God gave them a story
paras: If you freeze at the thought of writing a book, start with the questions the booklet asks: "What bridge has God prepared you to build? How can your story carry others closer to God and each other?" Those questions are meant to be answered before the first page is written. The author also asks "What experiences can you share?" and "What lessons have you learned?"

sections.h2: For pastors, ministry leaders and speakers
paras: You may already be good with words in sermons, devotionals and conference talks, and the author says so: "You may be an experienced wordsmith, but a book is a different thing." Blogs, opinion pieces, sermons and speeches "can become part of your book project," and she explains how a person who prepares talks tends to think in blocks that take twenty to forty minutes to read aloud, and how to turn those into chapters.

sections.h2: For first-time authors
paras: The advice is practical and gentle. "Write. Don't edit!" is tip number three, because writing and editing are two different ways of working on text. The author says that if you try to edit as you go, "you'll get caught up in polishing the first sentences for days on end," and she adds, "Trust me, this is the voice of experience speaking!"

sections.h2: For busy people who want a writing partner
paras: Some readers will never find the hours to write alone, and the booklet says so. It describes working with an Angel Writer at Spirit Media, who talks through your vision, helps structure your material and drafts or refines text with you, checking back so it still sounds like you. It says most authors meet just one hour a week, and it tells of a busy ministry founder whose book was written in three months and published the same year.

Carlene Hill Byron, a professional writer and editor for more than forty years, shows you why we write, where the words for a book come from and how to begin.

quote.text: We write to build bridges.
quote.cite: Carlene Hill Byron, Why write?

what_makes.title: What makes this book for people who think they are not writers
paras: A short, warm, illustrated guide in small pages, written for the person who is holding it because they are "at least beginning to know inside you what message God wants you to carry forward."
Five things set it apart:
list: It starts with why. The first question is not how to write, it is "Why write?" Her answer, drawn from the one-lane bridges of her home state of Maine, is that we write to build bridges between people and God and between one person and another.
It names where the words come from. Words you have already written, words you find and save, and words you create fresh: three sources, so you are never starting from nothing.
It gives you a way to collect. Bins or folders by subtopic, an online tool, journal books, 3x5 cards, even the little sticky tabs the author puts in books she reads.
It is honest about the blank page. Two secrets from a long-time professional writer come before four practical tips, one of them the "WEIRDEST TIP" you will ever hear about how to write.

It shows what a finished bridge can look like. The author tells the story of one volunteer who began with a few boxes in a breezeway and built a ministry that has reached more than a hundred nations, with a book to explain how.

paras: The fourth tip is the one she calls weird, and she is careful to say it is not about getting up at four in the morning. It is a trick for your brain. "The part of your brain that creates, the writing part, actually 'wakes up' earlier than the part of your brain that edits." Her own practice: "What has worked for me is to get up at least 30 minutes earlier than I'm used to and go straight to my desk. NO COFFEE. The editor loves coffee!" After a few weeks, she says, you will know what it feels like to write without an interrupting editor.

Where do the words for a book come from? "You can collect them from things that you and other people have already written, and you can create them fresh." The booklet draws three pictures: words you have already written (blogs, opinion pieces, sermons, speeches), words you find and save (books, streaming media, news), and words you create for this project. For the blank page, she offers a comparison: "Would you step onto a Broadway stage and start dancing without feeling intimidated?"

stories.h2: One volunteer, a few boxes and a breezeway
paras: To show what God can do with a story, the author tells about a woman who began about forty years ago by having her Sunday School class and friends fill a few boxes with things missionaries needed. She kept them in the breezeway of her home until she could ship them. Today she runs a 17,000-square-foot warehouse and has shipped to Christian organizations in more than a hundred nations. The author asks whether God is finished with her yet and answers, "I don't think so!" Her book explaining the ministry was written in three months.

author.bio: Carlene Hill Byron has worked more than 40 years as a professional writer and editor. Her career has spanned a daily newspaper, a tech startup, a large engineering company, two regional faith-based nonprofits, a company that supported SEO for an online global marketplace, and a regional disability nonprofit. Today she is one of the editors and Angel Writers at Spirit Media, where she has helped authors share stories of God's work in their lives. She lives in Maine.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The author comes at it as a writer and an editor who has heard many stories. "Fabulous stories from God's people that I've been privileged to help share" is how she describes her work with authors. She believes those stories matter because "The stories we have been given to tell encourage and uplift others who need to know the truths we've learned."

She invites you to listen to God about the message He wants you to share, and then to take the first small step. "You bring the inspiration," she writes. faq.q: What is Write Before Coffee about?
faq.a: A short guide for people who think they are not writers: why your story matters, where the words for a book come from and how to begin, with practical tips from a writer and editor of more than forty years.

faq.q: Can I write a book if I am not a writer?
faq.a: The author says yes, and starts with why. She argues that the purpose is to write, not to produce finished text on day one, and that a professional editor is there to help with the rest. "The purpose of writing is to write, not to produce the finished text today."

faq.q: How do I start a book?
faq.a: Choose a strategy, either "Establish an outline and write to it" or "Write until you discover the outline," then gather words from three sources and start writing without editing. The four pro tips are Write, Write whenever and wherever, Write and do not edit, and Write before you wake up.

faq.q: How do I start a memoir or a testimony?
faq.a: The booklet is about telling stories of how God has changed people's lives, and about how to find the shape of your story. One of its tools is the Hero's Journey, a story structure that "often applies to stories from Christian living."

faq.q: How do I plan or organize a book?
faq.a: Collect your material by subtopic in bins or folders, an online tool, journals or 3x5 cards. The author shows her own sticky-note system: green for chapter heads, pink for chapter subdivisions, yellow for key scriptures and blue for applications.

faq.q: Is this a book for beginners?
faq.a: Yes. It is written for people who are not used to writing, and it says plainly that you are not expected to be highly skilled. That is why an editor gets involved.

faq.q: How do I create a book from material I already have?
faq.a: Start with the words you have already written. The booklet names three sources: words you have already written, such as blogs, opinion pieces, sermons and speeches; words you find and save; and words you create fresh. It notes that a person who prepares sermons and speeches is used to thinking in blocks of words that take 20 to 40 minutes to read aloud, and those blocks can become chapters.

faq.q: What does it take to become an author, according to the book?
faq.a: A message God has given you, and a willingness to start. The booklet urges authors to listen to God to understand the message He wants to share through them. It says you are not expected to be highly skilled, that the purpose of writing is to write, and that editors and writers can help you plan, organize and complete the book. It is a guide to getting your story onto the page, not a step-by-step guide to publishing.

Evans looks at time from a biblical point of view in nine short chapters: God as the One who controls it, the tools we use to measure it, how to put God, family and others ahead of the to-do list, and how to invest the hours we are given. Each chapter ends with an honest question to write about. A note on this edition: the words inside are the same in every special edition of Your Time. paras: This is the Special Edition for First Responders of a book about time. The words inside are the same as in the Work Staff edition, and the book itself is general. What it offers is a short, plain look at limited time and at giving it away, a subject anyone whose work is serving others will recognize.
Five things set it apart:
list: It is short enough for a break room. At 60 pages in a 4 x 6 inch size, it fits a pocket, a locker or a bag, and each chapter is a few pages.
It starts with limits. The author says we cannot control time, only monitor it and trust God with the time we try to manage each day.
It deals with interruptions. The Time-Management chapter says unforeseen situations can bombard us on any given day, including a health issue or an emergency with a family member or friend.
It treats giving time as a gift. The book argues that we are meant to give some of our time to others as Jesus did, and that doing so is one of the greatest ways to please God.
It asks you to check your priorities. The author hopes that by the last page you can honestly say you need to check yours, and he closes with a prayer.

sections.h2: For first responders who give their time to others every day
paras: The book does not mention first responders by name. Its Gifts of Time chapter, though, is about the people who stop what they are doing for someone else, from Jesus pausing to bless the children to Cornelius sending for Peter at once. If your work is to show up when others need you, those pages speak to the way you already spend your hours.

sections.h2: For people who come home tired and want to give their families more
paras: The author says that God, family and others are the most important things, and that the rest of the schedule should be planned around them. One of his Take a Moment to Focus questions asks whether you are spending enough time with your family, friends and others.

sections.h2: For chaplains, peer supporters and departments choosing a gift
paras: A short book with a prayer in it is easy to hand to a colleague. It does not claim to be counseling, and it does not replace help for anyone who is struggling. It is a short Christian reflection on time.

paras: In the first chapter the author points to Isaiah 38, where God turned the shadow on the sundial of Ahaz backward ten degrees because Hezekiah asked. He notes that there are several theories about how it happened, and warns that attempting to explain it can lead some to doubt God. He puts it simply, that faith requires no explanation, and then asks the reader whether they have faith that God can help with their time, even in supernatural ways.

In Gifts of Time, the author looks at Jesus stopping on the way to Jerusalem to bless children, and at Cornelius, who did not check his schedule or put off sending for Peter. He says God speaks for one of two reasons, to make us a blessing to someone or to give us a blessing, and he wonders whether our schedules are so tight that we would miss it.
In Proper Investment of Time, he asks whether you are investing your time in the right people, and gives three steps. The first is to acknowledge that time is limited:
"Acknowledge that not only your money and energy, but also your time is a finite resource."

The second is to become aware of where it goes, since, as he puts it, your calendar will reveal the truth. The third is to change what needs to change, including activities that are unproductive or unhealthy.

author.bio: Daniel W. Evans is a Christian author who says that he has traveled through the states as an evangelist and listened to many pastors talk about church growth. In Your Time he writes from that experience and from his home church in Durham, North Carolina, where he counted how many members give their time as volunteers and found the figure to be 36 percent. He uses Scripture and personal observation to urge readers to put God first and to steward every hour well. The back of the book describes two other offerings from him: a one-day process in five steps, and A Commitment to Unleash Your Leader Potential, a program for the leader in each of us.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The author's stated hope is simple. He wants you to see that your time is precious, that no one can replace it, and that God belongs at the top of the list. He puts it as a prayer:
“My prayer is that this booklet will help you recognize and realize that you are a potential success.”
After the chapter on idioms, he says why he wrote it at all:
“My prayer is that we will not neglect what is so valuable and be better stewards of our precious time.”

faq.q: Is Your Time a book on time management skills?
faq.a: Partly. It is a short Christian book about time, not a manual of techniques or apps. It does give plain steps: put God, family and others first, check your calendar to see where your hours really go, and follow the ABC's of investing time. They are, in order: Acknowledge that time is a finite resource; Become aware of where you are investing it; and Change what is unproductive or unhealthy.

faq.q: Is it a book on biblical stewardship of time?
faq.a: Yes. Stewardship is its closing theme. The prayer at the end asks God for help to be a better steward of your time, and the last Take a Moment to Focus question asks what changes you can make to be one. The book draws on Isaiah 38, Daniel 6, Luke 18, Acts 10 and Psalm 39.

faq.q: Is the book written about firefighters, police officers or EMTs?
faq.a: No. The Special Edition for First Responders has its own cover, edition name and ISBN, but the words inside are the same as in the other Your Time editions, and no passage describes emergency work. The book speaks to anyone whose time is given to others.

faq.q: Does it include a prayer for first responders?
faq.a: It includes one prayer, in Setting Your Time Straight, written for every reader rather than for first responders in particular. It asks the Father to forgive wasted time and to help you invest as much of it as possible in Him and in others.

faq.q: Does it help with work-life balance?
faq.a: Some of it. The book does not use that phrase. It says we work hard at managing our time and then try to fit God, family and others into it, and it asks you to plan everything else around those three instead. One question asks whether you are spending enough time with family, friends and others.

faq.q: Does it encourage a daily quiet time with God?
faq.a: Yes. The author says the top priority in our time management must be to give God time each day, and adds that it is not that He needs time with us: we need time with Him.

faq.q: What does it say about volunteering at church?
faq.a: It says serving at church is good, but it is not the only place to give time. The author counted the volunteers in his home church and found that 36 percent give their time, and he urges readers to give time outside the church as well, through visits, calls and follow-up.

faq.q: Does it have questions for discussion?
faq.a: Yes. Each of the nine chapters ends with a Take a Moment to Focus question and space to write. One asks: Is God included in your daily routines of managing your schedules? The questions work for one reader or for a small group.
